Uniform Title: Prāṇatoṣiṇī, Karmakāṇḍa Author: Rāmatoṣaṇa Compiler:
Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya Description: Compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya; originally published in Calcutta in the Bengali script as part of the Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: December 11, 2007.
Publisher: Kalikātā.
Year of publication: Pre-1900.
Country of Publication: India | Title Page || Śrīḥ ||
The *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
having compiled it from the Tantric scriptures.
And it was published by the learned Kulapati, the bearer of the title *upādhi*, Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācāryya, in the city of Calcutta.
Printed at the Kālikātā Press (4) in the Kāmyakāṇḍa (p.
416): the formless one, consisting of eternal bliss, exceedingly skillful, newly and freshly composed for the sake of accomplishing the desires of devotees.
May the stainless Vāgīśvarī, whose nature is wisdom, who embodies both word and meaning, and whose radiance is as bright as a hundred moons, ever shine resplendent within my mind.
May the illustrious Prāṇakṛṣṇa— whose mind is deeply absorbed in the lotus feet of his guru, who is renowned as a donor, a wise knower,

a performer of virtuous deeds, and an establisher of Brahman; and who is rich in enjoyments and long-lived— be present, by whose grace this very tender creeper, the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*, has arisen and may it delight the assembly of the learned with its various sections (*adrikāṇḍa*).
Because of the extreme rapidity of the instruction, the multitudes of faults that arise herein must be corrected by the wise; this is our further entreaty.
First is the glossary (nirghaṇṭa) of the Kāmyakāṇḍa, and then consciousness itself;
immediately after that, the meaning of the mantras for all the vidyās;
and likewise the Kullukā, the Setu, and thereafter the Mahāsetu.

Nirvāṇa, purification of the mouth, and thereafter the yoga of breath (prāṇayoga); then the description of the sequence of the awakening (dīpanī), the removal of defects (sūtaka), and recitation (japa);
likewise the location of Kullukā and others, and thereafter the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).

The first section is said to consist of: the preliminary rites such as the *vāramāsa-puraścaryā-rahasya* and others; the *puraścaryā* performed during an eclipse; the restriction of the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) therein; and the chapter on rosaries (*mālā-prakaraṇa*). || 1 ||
The determination of the locations for practice and the description of the great seats (mahāpīṭha);
the great seats, the seats, and likewise the deities of the seats;
the time for worship, its specific details, and the ritual procedure for the worship of the deity.

Then, after the determination of what must be performed according to the sequence beginning with a single day's rite when there is sublation, follows the expiation; thus ends the second section, which is the completion [of the discussion]. || 2 ||

The means of accomplishment for the lizard, mouse, cat, jackal, and dog; the various means of accomplishing desired objects; the means of accomplishment for the three enclosures (trivāṭa) and so forth;
the ritual application of Kārtavīrya, and immediately after that, his armor.
The conclusion of the third chapter follows hereafter. || 3 ||
Then follows the application of the *kukkuṭa* [mantra], then the *ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī*,
then *dhūmāvatī*, then the *kṛtyā* consisting of *parimālā*,
and then *jayadurgā* and so forth; this indeed constitutes the conclusion of the fourth section.

The determination of the time for the festival of Durgā, beginning from the sixth lunar day; the description of the basis for worship and the proclamation of prohibitions and injunctions regarding earthen images;
and the determination concerning the pair of bilva fruits according to the distinctions of the castes, such as Brāhmaṇas and others.
The description of the fruits of the pair of *ālūrī* [plants] in the directions starting from the east; (p.
417) the fault regarding the pair of *bilva* fruits and the earthen [liṅga], as well as in the case of a cowrie-shell;
the statement of the expiation for that; and the determination of festivals and so forth.
Therein, first is the abandonment of other activities, followed by the rite of worship;
then, according to the difference in location, there is the difference in form, and after that, the pavilion;
then the performance of the sixth-day rite, the guardians of the directions, and the ritual procedure for the worship of the Tantra.
Then follows the offering of the *bali* and so forth, and thereafter the invitation to the *bilva* tree. Next is the rite of the seventh day (*saptamī*), the worship of Kārtika and the others,
the worship of the *patrikā*, the hymn of praise, and the rite of the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*).
The duties of the night, the duties of the ninth day, and the rites of the tenth day are proclaimed as the conclusion of the fifth chapter.
The Durgā-mantra, its seer (ṛṣi), the preparatory rite (puraścaryā), and the yantra;
then the meditation (dhyāna), the hymn of praise (stuti), and the glorification of the greatness of Durgā’s names;
followed by the hymn known as the *Durgā-śatanāma* and the *Gītāvalī*.
The section on fire-offerings (homa) and the measurement of those substances; this chapter on measurement concludes the sixth division.
Then follows the ritual for the month [of Mārgaśīrṣa], the rite of the Khañjarīṭa bird and its fruit;
the rite known as Kojāgara, the ritual for the month of Kārttika,
the rituals for the month of Agrahāyaṇa (Mārgaśīrṣa), and thereafter the ritual for the month of Pauṣa.
The rites of Māgha, followed by the rites of Phālguna;
then the annual rite which is the means for recovering a lost kingdom or attaining sovereignty;
and the sixteen processions of the Goddess, month by month as they began from the first.
In Vaiśākha, the Mañju-yātrā is proclaimed as the first;
in Jyeṣṭha, the Mahā-snāna-yātrā; in Āṣāḍha (Śuci), the Rathayātrā and others; in Śrāvaṇa, the Jalayātrā; and likewise, in Bhādrapada, the Dhūnana.

In Āśvina there is the Great Worship (mahāpūjā), in Kārtika the Festival of Lamps (dīpayātrikā); in Mārgaśīrṣa the Festival of New Grain (navānnayātrā), and in Pauṣa the Festival of Body-Ointments (aṅgarāgarūpiṇī);
in Māgha the Festival known as Raṭantī, and in Phālguna the Swing Festival (dolayātrikā).
The Dūtīyātrā, the Rāsayātrā, the Vāsantīyātrā, and the Nītyayātrikā—
these four are considered the processions of Caitra, while the Ṣoḍaśīyātrikā is also recognized.
This glossary has been composed by me in brief for the purpose of providing a general orientation.
Other [factors] as well should be understood by the wise according to their proper place.

O Śaṅkarī! O Kālī! May this "Kāmyakāṇḍa" (Section on Desired Aims)—which, like a tree, is always filled with knots, branches, sub-branches, excellent leaves, stars, beautiful blossoms, and fruits—swiftly fulfill the constant hopes of the people who worship the Buddha within the lotus of their hearts.
May she reign, O Goddess worthy of worship by the Lord of Gods!
Now, regarding Consciousness (*caitanya*),
[it is described] in the fifth chapter of the *Kubjikāyantra*.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Blessed One! Lord of all gods! Bringer of welfare to the worlds!
O God, reveal to me that consciousness which bestows the four aims of life.
Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the most wonderful consciousness, a supreme secret and merit that must be guarded by you once more.
O Goddess, it has been made resonant by the power of consciousness (cicchakti) through the process of transformation.
Having completely abandoned the state of material color, [one attains] that which is stainless and pure by nature;
likewise, having pierced the six chakras, consciousness is proclaimed to be the eternal form of sound,
conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*.
Or rather, O lotus-eyed one, listen to another method,
without which no recitation, worship, or other rite whatsoever can be accomplished:
within the center of the *anāhata* [cakra], the supreme syllable is strung together.
O Goddess! O Maheśānī! Consciousness, which is the very form of yoga for yogins, has emerged through the path of the *suṣumṇā* into the region of the throat;
and by the process of transformation, it takes the form of phonemes within the *sahasrāra*.

One should meditate thus upon the Goddess, situated in the center of the pericarp and endowed with *nāda* and *bindu*, and contemplate consciousness again and again. O Maheśvarī! The syllables of the mantra are strung together within the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
O Goddess! One should contemplate those [lotuses] upon the thousand-petaled lotus as being of the nature of consciousness-mantra, bestowing the bliss of consciousness,
possessing the power of the sound of consciousness, and having the form of the letters of consciousness.
In Maṇipūra, one should always contemplate that which is the life-force of mantras.
Or else, O lady of excellent complexion, listen to another method:
the seed-syllable of Kāma, the seed-syllable of Ramā, and the seed-syllable of Śakti, O Sovereign of the Gods!
Having first recited these [syllables] and immediately thereafter the Mātṛkā,
one should mutter the root mantra enclosed [by them] one hundred and eight times; one obtains a merit of ten million times ten millionfold— of this there is no doubt.
Or else, O Pārvatī, listen to consciousness in another way,
by the mere knowledge of which one certainly beholds the Supreme.
One should contemplate the root mantra situated in the center of the solar orb.
One should recite the root mantra, which is the very form of the primordial knowledge, one hundred and eight times.
Therein, one should meditate upon the Guru as the eternal form of Śiva,
and one should meditate upon the Śakti there as the eternal form of Brahman.
O beautiful goddess! For one who meditates thus or recites [the mantra], there is nothing unattainable in this world; O Goddess, liberation is held in the palm of their hand.
Thus it is stated in the first chapter.
"O Varārohā! He who does not know the meaning of the mantra, the consciousness of the mantra, and the *yonimudrā*, does not attain success even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Even by reciting [the mantra] ten billion times, his *vidyā* will not be perfected; such is the reading in the *Sarasvatī-tantra*."
O Maheśvarī! I shall explain the great mantra and the meaning of the mantra, by the mere knowledge of which one becomes a master of all siddhis;
and solely through the intellect of inner disposition, O beloved of my life, one attains the meaning of the mantra.
Through the yoga of pure knowledge alone, one will certainly become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
O Dear One! Kālī, Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, and the Vidyā Dhūmāvatī—[these are the Great Sciences].
She is celebrated as Bagalā, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā;
she is saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and others, as well as by the four Vedas. O Goddess, bestower of enjoyment and liberation, you are hidden within millions of cosmic eggs.
By the mere grasping of this, the practitioner indeed becomes liberated while living.
In the sixth chapter of the Varadā Tantra,
Śiva said:

O Supreme Goddess! Listen as I explain today the meaning of the mantra, without which, O Śivā, success cannot be attained even through millions of practices. First, O Pārvatī, listen to the meaning of the *prāsāda* seed-mantra.
The letter *ha* denotes Śiva, while the vowel *au* is Sadāśiva;
the void (*śūnya*) signifies the removal of suffering. Therefore, one should worship Śiva with that [syllable].
I.
O Goddess! [The letter] *da* signifies Durgā;
the letter *u* also signifies protection (*rakṣaṇa*). Viśvamātā is the form of *nāda*, and *ku* is the meaning of the *bindu*.
Therefore, O Śivā, one should worship Durgā with that very same seed-mantra.
Dūṃ.
The syllable *ka* is said by Brahmā to signify Kālī, and the syllable *ī* signifies Mahāmāyā. The *nāda* signifies Viśvamātā, and the *bindu* signifies the remover of suffering (*duḥkhahara*).
With that very [mantra], one should worship the goddess Kālikā for the pacification of suffering.
Kṛṃ.
The letter *ha* signifies Śiva; the letter *ra* is said to be Prakṛti.
The word *īśa* has the meaning of Mahāmāyā, and *nāda* is remembered as the devourer of the universe.
The *bindu* signifies the remover of suffering; with these, one should worship the worlds.
Hrīṃ.
The letter *śa* signifies Great Lakṣmī; the letter *ra*, which is half of *dha*, is said to signify wealth.
The letter *ī* signifies satisfaction, while the other, the *nāda* or *bindu*, signifies the remover of suffering.
This is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Goddess Lakṣmī; with it, one should worship the Goddess.
Śrīṃ.
The syllable *ai* signifies Sarasvatī, and the *bindu* signifies the remover of suffering;
this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Sarasvatī, and with it, one should worship Vāṇī.
Aiṃ.

The letter *ka* is designated as Kāmadeva, or else it is called Kṛṣṇa; the letter *la* is Indra, and the letter *ī* denotes satisfaction (*tuṣṭi*). The syllable *aṃ* bestows both happiness and suffering.
O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, the meaning of the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) has been told to you.
Klīṃ.
O Goddess! "Ha" is said to be Śiva; "U" is here called Bhairava.
The sound "Na" has the meaning of the Supreme (Parārtha), while "Biṇdu" signifies the remover of suffering (Duḥkhahara).
Indeed, these three seed-syllables of the armor (Varma) have been explained to you here with care.
Hūṃ.
The letter *ga* has been told to you as signifying Gaṇeśa; the nasal dot (*bindu*) signifies the remover of suffering.
O Maheśvarī! Out of affection for you, the meaning of the seed-syllable *gaṃ* has been explained to you.
*Gaṃ*.
The letter *la* is considered to signify the pervasive nature of Gaṇeśa and his splendor;
the nasal dot (*bindu*) signifies the remover of suffering; therefore, one should worship Gaṇeśa with this [mantra].
Glauṃ.

The syllable *kṣ* signifies Nṛsiṃha and Brahmā; the vowel *ṝ* signifies the upper teeth; and the *au* signifies the meaning of "remover of suffering. One should worship Nṛsiṃha with that [mantra] which includes the *bindu*: *Kṣrauṃ*.
O Śivā! The first letter of the name of all things is said by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) to be their "name" (nāman).
By means of that [letter], one should know the meaning; one should contemplate that which is obtained through the meaning.
One should contemplate the meaning of the mantra according to its respective case-ending.
Through the conjunction of those respective letters and so forth, this has been told to you in brief.
The letter *ta* signifies the one who delivers from the difficult passage (Durga), meaning the Savior (*tāraka*);
the letter *ra* is said here to signify liberation; and the letter *ī* signifies Mahāmāyā.
The sound (nāda) signifies the Mother of the Universe, and the point (bindu) signifies the remover of suffering.
O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, the purpose of the seed-syllable of the bride has been explained here.
A woman.

In a mantra where there are two *bindus*, O Goddess, one is for the purpose of removing suffering and the other is for bestowing happiness; having understood this, one should contemplate the meaning. Where there are two *bindus* in a mantra, the other is considered to have a complete meaning.
O Goddess! *Svāhā* is proclaimed to have the meaning of "for oneself" (*svārtha*), while *Vam* is celebrated as being for the sake of others (*parārtha*).
*Vaṣaṭ* is said to be the mother of Śakra, a speech intended for the beloved of Hari (Viṣṇu).
*Phaṭ* is for the sake of the gods; one should prescribe the seed-syllable *Vrim* for Hayagrīva.
The seed-syllable for Vāyu is *yaṃ*, and that for Indra is proclaimed to be *laṃ*.
In the case of multi-syllabic seed-mantras, one should use the respective seed-syllable corresponding to its own name.
Having understood this, O Maheśānī, one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra.
Where one should conceive of two single seeds as having distinct meanings,
or for the sake of repetition (vīpsā), O Maheśānī!— having understood the mantra thus, one should indeed recite it with the intellect.
Thus, O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, the meaning of the mantra has been told to you.
If one recites the root mantra encased by the seed-syllable *īṃ*,
that very mantra certainly becomes conscious.
In the first chapter of the Sarasvatītantra.
Īśvara said:
O Supreme Goddess! Listen attentively to the meaning of the mantra.
One should contemplate the root-vidyā, one's chosen deity, within the mūlādhāra;
one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess as resembling pure crystal.
One should maintain the series of syllables of the desired, eternal Vidyā.
Having contemplated this for half a muhūrta, one should thereafter become intent on meditation. O Maheśānī! After performing meditation for half a muhūrta, beyond that—
Then, O Maheśānī! O lotus-eyed one!

the individual soul (jīva), having gone from there to the Svādhiṣṭhāna by means of the mind, should meditate upon his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā)—who resembles the Bandhūka flower in its reddish-brown hue, and is like the color of Javā flowers or vermilion (sindūra).
Having meditated upon the supreme series of syllables situated within the center of the lotus,
O beautiful one, the soul, with a tranquil mind, then goes together with the bird to Maṇipūra and should meditate upon the chosen deity.

Having visualized the supreme series of syllables situated within the center of the lotus—resembling pure crystal and resting upon the lotus of the head—the individual soul (jīva), O Maheśānī! O Pārvatī! [then departs] together with the bird.
O lotus-eyed one! [The mantra] quickly went to the heart-lotus.
O Great Goddess! One should meditate upon the beloved Vidyā upon a lotus;
having visualized the series of syllables with the luster of a great emerald.
Then, O beloved of excellent limbs!
O dear one! the soul, having gone with the bird into the dense lotus of the heart, O Pārvatī!
O Great Goddess! should contemplate the desired knowledge within the portion of the Command (ājñā).
O Goddess of gods! O Khajjana-eyed one! O lady of pure smiles!

O Great Mistress! Having visualized the desired Vidyā, which is the manifest form of Brahman itself, as a row of imperishable syllables of green color, O lady of beautiful countenance! [one should meditate upon it] together with the bird.
O Maheśānī! One should perform meditation upon the six cakras at the Ājñācakra.
O Parameśānī! O lady of pure smiles, having performed meditation upon the six cakras, that form which has appeared through meditation, O Parameśānī! [is to be realized].
Know that very thing to be the meaning of the mantra, O Parvati, O Supreme Goddess!
Now, regarding the *kullukā* and so forth,
it is stated in the third chapter of the *Sarasvatītantra*:
O Goddess! Mahānīla-Sarasvatī is the *kullukā* of Tārā;
the five-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as the *kullukā* of Kālikā. O Maheśvarī! [The mantra] ending with *phaṭ*, preceded by *kālī*, *kūrca*, *badhū*, and *māyā*, [is the *kullukā*].
O Maheśānī! For Chinnā, however, the Kullukā consists of eight syllables.
And at the end of "Vajravairocanīye," one should worship Varma (the armor-mantra). For Sampatpradā Bhairavī, the Kullukā comes first.
The twelve-syllable *kullukā* of the illustrious Tripurasundarī consists of:
first, the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable; immediately after that, the *kāma* seed-syllable; then, the *lajjā* seed-syllable; and following that, the word "Tripurā. (p. 422)
After that, at the end, one should extract two *ṭha*s for the Bhagavatī;
alternatively, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma-bīja*) is proclaimed as the *kullukā*.
For Śambhu it is the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsāda-bīja*), and for Mañjughoṣa it is the six-syllabled mantra.
The single-syllable mantra for Bhuvaneśvarī consists of eight syllables for Viṣṇu:
"Namaḥ Nārāyaṇāya," preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), and the Kullukā. For Mātaṅgī, it is the first seed-syllable; for Dhūmāvatī, it is Māyā (Hrīṃ).
The seed-syllable of the bride for Bālā, the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī herself,
the Vāgbhava for Sarasvatī, and Anaṅgakā for Annadā;
thus the mere mantra of the other deities has been proclaimed.
O Goddess! This Kullukā has been described by me to you in brief.
O Beloved! that base person who recites this Kullukā without knowing it quickly meets his death, and the loss of spiritual accomplishment occurs.
Likewise, all [practices] such as recitation will be fruitless; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, with every effort, one should wear the Kullukā upon the head.
Likewise: "The Praṇava is the bridge for Brahmins, and the same for Kṣatriyas;
the syllable Phaṭ is for Vaiśyas, and Māyā is said to be for Śūdras."
O Lord of Gods! He who utters a mantra without first reciting it in his heart has indeed no authority over any mantras whatsoever.
O Goddess of Gods! The Mahāsetu is [the mantra] of Sundarī, and Bhuvaneśvarī is [the mantra] of Sundarī.
The seed-syllable of Kālikā is her own [seed-mantra], while that of Tārā is the *kūrca* syllable.
For the others, O fair-faced one, the seed-syllable is *badhū*.
Having first recited the *mahāsetu*, one should then recite the mantra with undistracted mind.

In wealth he is equal to the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), in speech he is comparable to the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), in battle he is like the God of Death (Yama), and among women he is like the God of Love (Madana). For him, every moment is a time for recitation; of this there is no doubt.
Now I shall speak of Nirvāṇa; listen attentively, O sinless one!
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should extract the beginning of the Mātṛkā;
then the Mūla-mantra, O Maheśānī, and then one should extract the Vāgbhava.
One should again extract the Praṇava from all the Mātṛkās. Thus, one should recite the root-mantra encased [by the Praṇava] during the Maṇipūraka practice.
O Great Goddess! that base person who does not know this Nirvāṇa [method] is truly a fool.
Even in a thousand million eons, his accomplishment will not arise.
Now, the purification of the mouth.
In the fifth chapter.
The Lord said:

I shall now declare another supreme purification of the mouth, O Great Goddess! By performing [recitation] therein, one's chanting and worship become in vain. O Goddess, he who chants with an impure tongue is a doer of evil.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the purification of the tongue;
O auspicious one, this is the purification of the mouth of Mahātripurasundarī!
The Śrī-bīja, the Praṇava, Lakṣmī, the Tāra, and likewise the Śrī-praṇava— [The above constitutes the complete verse provided in the source.]
One should recite this six-syllabled mantra of Sundarī ten times.
Listen, O Sundarī! [I shall explain] the supreme purification of the mouth for Śyāmā:
O Goddess, [one should utter] one's own three seed-syllables, followed again by the three *praṇavas*.
The three *kāmas* (KĀM), the fire (*RA*), and the bindu (*M*), joined individually with the *ati-candra* (the letter *I*);
this is the nine-syllable mantra that purifies the mouth.
Listen, O lady of beautiful limbs, to the unprecedented purification of the mouth belonging to Tārā.
O Dear One! [The syllables] *Jīvanaṃ*, *Madhyamaṃ*, and *Lajjāṃ* Bhuvaneśī—this three-syllabled Great Vidyā (Mahāvidyā) should be known as the showerer of nectar. O fair-limbed one!
Listen now to the excellent purification of the mouth of Durgā.
Having extracted the twelve vowels and likewise three [consonants] joined with the bindu,
I shall further proclaim another [mantra] for the purification of Bagalāmukha:
the Vāgbhava, the Bhuvaneśī, and the seed-syllable of Speech (Vāgbīja), O Goddess worshipped by the gods!

O Goddess! The purification of Mātaṅgī consists of the Aṅkuśa and the Vāgbhava; this three-syllabled seed-mantra is indeed to be known as such. O lotus-faced Goddess! The purification of Lakṣmī consists of the Śrī-bīja.
The purification of Durgā consists of the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) encapsulated by the Vāgbīja (Aiṃ).
[The mantra is: "Durge! Svāhā," followed again by Māyā, the Vāgbīja, and again the Vāgbīja.
Then, having extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should take the letter 'da' (the last letter of the alphabet) adorned with the left ear (the vowel 'u').
Again, having extracted the Praṇava, there is the purification of the mouth of Dhanadā;
O Maheśānī! in this way, it shall also become the mantra of Dhūmāvatī.

O Goddess! The Praṇava with the Bindu is the five-fold end-maker (Pañcāntaka) of Gaṇeśa. O Supreme Mistress! The two-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu consists of the beginning of the Vedas (Om), the sky (Ha), fire (Ra), the Manu-yuga (E), and the Moon (U)—that is, *Hreim*. This is the purifier of the mouth.
O Goddess! For others, such as children and so forth, the *praṇava* is proclaimed;
for women, it is indeed said that [the mantra] is equal to that of a Śūdra. By the mere purification of the mouth, the tongue becomes composed of nectar.
Otherwise, the tongue always becomes unfit for the mouth;
the tongue is defiled by [unwholesome] foods, defiled by false speech,
and defiled by quarrels— how then could it recite the mantra?
Without performing that purification, a common person should never recite [the mantra] anywhere;
indeed, this applies necessarily to all [practitioners] of the Śaiva, Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and other traditions.
Otherwise, O beautiful lady, if one should recite the mantra out of delusion, [the result will be contrary].
O Goddess! all of that is in vain for him; the perfection of the mantra does not arise.
In the end, he too shall become a dweller in hell, and it cannot be otherwise—even if a deity were to recite the mantra without performing the purification of the mouth.
O Goddess of gods! Even for him there is a fall; how much more so for those who dwell among mortals?
In the sixth chapter.
Īśvara said:

Now, O Goddess of gods, I shall speak; listen to me regarding the yoga of the vital breath (prāṇa). Just as a body is incapable of performing any action without the vital breath, so too is a mantra ineffective even with hundreds of preparatory rites (puraścaryā) without the vital breath.

O Goddess! A mantra that has been enveloped by Māyā becomes endowed with life for one who recites it seven times; this rule is prescribed for all cases. Likewise, O noble lady, I shall now describe the "illumination" (dīpana) for every mantra.
Just as nothing at all appears in a house shrouded in darkness when it is devoid of a lamp,
so too is a mantra described [to be ineffective].
One should then recite the mantra, encased within the Vedas and other [scriptures], seven times again.
O Supreme Goddess! O Queen of the Gods! This has been declared as the illuminating [mantra] everywhere;
having encased it within the Vedas and so forth with effort, one should recite the mantra ten times for liberation from the two types of birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Now, the most wonderful sequence for this recitation (japa) is described,
by performing which a person becomes the sovereign of the hosts of Siddhas.
First, one should offer salutation to the names of the Guru and others, and thereafter one should take refuge in the crest-mantra (mantra-śikhā).
From that, one should practice the consciousness of the mantra and the contemplation of the mantra's meaning; then,
meditating on the Guru in the lotus of the head and on the Desired Deity (iṣṭa) in the heart,
one should thereafter practice the Kullukā, the Setu, and immediately after that, the Mahāsetu.
And from that, O Goddess, comes Nirvāṇa; as well as the visualization of the Yonimudrā,
the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), breath control (prāṇāyāma), the purification of the tongue,
the yoga of the vital breath (prāṇayoga), the kindling [of the fire] (dīpanī), and likewise the destruction of impurity (aśaucabhaṅga).

Between the eyebrows or at the tip of the nose, one should perform the bridge of vision (*dṛṣṭisetu*), the recitation (*japa*), the bridge [of breath] (*setu*), the breaking of impurity (*aśaucabhaṅga*), and breath control (*prāṇāyāma*); these are the successive stages.
In the fourth chapter.
Having performed the japa of the *kullukā* on the head, one should contemplate the *setu* (bridge) in the heart;
one should then extract the *mahāsetu* in the region of the throat for the sake of purification,
and the *nirvāṇa* in the *maṇipūra*, while the *mahākuṇḍalinī* is below.

O Goddess! O Śivā! Having meditated according to the rules upon the seed-syllable of Kāma situated at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which rests upon the head of Rākiṇī, one should then, O Goddess, visualize it extending from the vicinity of the Mūlādhāra up to the Viśuddha, as slender as a thread of lotus fiber.
For the site of the altar (vedīsthāna) extends to the end of the individual soul (jīva), being repeatedly enveloped by the root mantra.
(p. 425) However, other [details] regarding the seed-syllable (bīja), the cintāmaṇi, and so forth, should be sought elsewhere; they are not written here for fear of making the text too voluminous.
The *puraścaraṇa* has been maintained by the author of the *Tantrasāra* himself.
The specific details of the *puraścaraṇa* are now written down,
according to the *Kaṅkālamālinītantra*.

Alternatively, another method for the *puraścaraṇa* rite is described: O Goddess worshipped by heroes! on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the ninth lunar day, beginning at sunrise and continuing until the next sunrise.
Having recited [the mantra] that many times, one becomes free from all afflictions and a master of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Alternatively, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is described in another manner:
on the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights.
Beginning from sunset until the sun has set,
by reciting [the mantra] during that time, one becomes free from affliction and a master of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhīśvara*).
Alternatively, staying in a secluded place or lying upon a bed of bones;

By reciting [the mantra] during the day from sunrise until sunset, one becomes the master of all siddhis. Or else, O Goddess, by beginning at sunset on that same seat and reciting until sunrise, one becomes the master of all siddhis.
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
beginning from sunrise, ten ghaṭikās in succession shall constitute the seasons,
starting with spring, day after day throughout the day and night.
Spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season— of these,
spring is said to be the forenoon, summer the midday,
the afternoon the early rains, and twilight is remembered as autumn.
Midnight is known as the Hemanta season, and the remainder is remembered as Śiśira.
Beginning from sunrise until the end of Vasanta, O Maheśānī, one should perform the recitation with a concentrated mind; thus indeed the *puraścaryā* is accomplished.
Then, having performed the worship and other rites, the practitioner, endowed with spiritual power,
should give a sacrificial fee to the Guru and become a master of all supernatural accomplishments.

Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described: O Great Goddess, O Lady of Excellent Limbs, by reciting [the mantra] separately during each of the six seasons beginning with summer, the preliminary rite indeed becomes perfected.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes! Everything should be performed according to the previously stated procedure. Having recited the mantra during the fertile period (ṛtu), one should worship Śivā at the end of that period according to one's capacity.
By performing the ritual in this manner, one shall indeed become a lord of riches.
Alternatively, the procedure for the daily recitation (vārapuraścaraṇa) is found in the Svatantra-tantra.
O Goddess! By constantly reciting the mantra one thousand times for each day of the week, beginning with Sunday, the practitioner shall attain perfection;
this indeed constitutes the *puraścaraṇa* rite, and no further deliberation is required here.
Having performed such a practice, one should then perform it ten times over;
having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, one shall obtain all desires.
Now, regarding the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) according to the lunar day (tithi), it is stated in that very same source:
O Dear One!
Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the new moon (kuhu), one should increase the recitation by a thousand [times] according to the sequence of the lunar days (tithi).
Having thus performed the recitation, the practitioner of mantra shall then attain all desires.

O fair-faced one! This indeed has been described as the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite). O beloved! Starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) until the full moon (*rākā*), one should recite the mantra according to the sequence of the number of days.
The practitioner born on earth becomes endowed with all states of being;
through this alone shall there be prosperity—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Now follows the ritual procedure fixed for one month.

Today, in the month of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, or Māgha, when the sun is situated in such-and-such a zodiac sign (*rāśi*), on such-and-such a lunar fortnight (*pakṣa*) and such-and-such a lunar day (*tithi*), beginning from this time, I, [Name], of such-and-such a lineage (*gotra*), [Name] Devaśarman, desiring the accomplishment of the mantra of such-and-such a deity, shall perform [this rite] beginning from such-and-such a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) until the sun reaches the signs of Aries, Libra, and Capricorn.
Every day, [I shall perform] the recitation of the mantra of such-and-such a deity one thousand times, followed immediately by its tenth-part homa,
its tenth-part tarpaṇa, its tenth-part consecration, and its tenth-part...

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consisting of feeding Brāhmaṇas," one should, for the duration of a month, subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) while observing the rules, and recite [the mantra] one thousand times every day. Then, on the first days of the solar months of Jyeṣṭha, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Phālguna, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

One should perform it as follows: "Today," and so forth, "on this [date], in such-and-such month, when the sun is in such-and-such zodiacal sign, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar day, I, Śrī-Amukadevaśarmā of such-and-such lineage, belonging to such-and-such zodiacal sign, shall perform the recitation of the mantra of such-and-such deity current at the time of the sun being in such-and-such zodiacal sign, for such-and-such number of times, along with its tenth part in fire-oblations (homa), and the tenth part of that [in libations]."

For the sake of completing the purificatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of libations (*tarpaṇa*), its tenth part in the form of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and its tenth part in the form of feeding Brahmins, I offer this gold, dedicated to the deity Agni, as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you, the preceptor (*guru*), belonging to the [name] lineage and named Śrī Amukadevaśarman. Then, one should perform the rite for sealing the ritual's flawlessness (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*).

Now, he states the ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) beginning with the days of the week: "On this day," and so forth—"in such-and-such month, when the sun is situated in such-and-such zodiac sign, in such-and-such fortnight, on such-and-such lunar date;

beginning from this time, I, [name] of such-and-such lineage, the venerable [name]-devaśarmā, desiring the accomplishment of the mantra of such-and-such deity, shall perform [the rite] on all days of the week, starting with Sunday."

"I shall perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of the recitation of [the mantra] of such-and-such a deity, or of such-and-such a mantra, [for] a thousand times multiplied by the number of days.
Thus one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Then, on the remaining day or the following day, beginning with "Today," etc., [one should continue]: "of this performed [rite] for such-and-such a deity, of such-and-such a mantra..."

I shall perform the rites consisting of a thousand recitations on as many days as there are days from Sunday onwards, followed by a fire-oblation (homa) equal to one-tenth of that number, an oblation of water (tarpaṇa) equal to one-tenth of that, an ablution (abhiṣeka) equal to one-tenth of that, and the feeding of Brahmins equal to one-tenth of that.
Then follows the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):

"Today," and so forth— [this refers to] the performance of this thousand-fold recitation based on the occasion of Sunday and the other days, along with its tenth-part oblation (*homa*), its tenth-part libation (*tarpaṇa*), and its tenth-part [offering].

For the sake of completing the ritual of *puraścaraṇa*, consisting of the feeding of Brahmins one-tenth the number of the recitations performed, this [offering] is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth.

In the *tithi-puraścaraṇa*, everything is exactly the same; everywhere, the word "tithi" (lunar day) is to be used in place of the word "vāra" (weekday). Now, the ritual resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the *ṛtu-puraścaraṇa* (seasonal *puraścaraṇa*): "Today, etc., I, of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Amukadevaśarmā, desiring the perfection of the mantra of such-and-such deity, [shall perform it] from sunrise until the end of spring for the sake of such-and-such deity..."
I shall perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consisting of the recitation (japa) of such-and-such a mantra.
"Except for the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of recitation (*japa*) pervading the summer season, I shall perform it; thus it is in all cases.

At the end of the recitation, having performed worship, one should offer a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as follows: "Today, etc., for the sake of the completion of the preparatory rite consisting of recitation pervading the spring season of the mantra of such-and-such a deity, this [fee], etc."

Thus it is in all cases. The procedure for the libation and consecration is as follows: having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya), purified the seat (āsanaśuddhi), performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), and executed the ritual assignments of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa) and the assignment of the limbs (karāṅganyāsa); having meditated and worshipped mentally, and having meditated once more upon [the deity] in the water.

Having invoked the deity, [one offers] "This water-constituted *pādya* to such-and-such deity, *namaḥ*; this water-constituted *arghya*"— having thus worshipped with these water-constituted offerings (*upacāra*), and having gratified the retinue according to the procedure prescribed for the *saṃdhyā*,
one should recite the root mantra and say, "I gratify such-and-such deity, *namaḥ*," and thus gratify them.
Having meditated upon oneself in the form of the deity and having uttered the root mantra ending with "namaḥ," one should say,
"I consecrate such-and-such a deity," and consecrate the head with the water-pot mudrā;
then, one should dismiss the deity with the withdrawal mudrā.
(p. 428) Now follows the secret preliminary ritual (purascaraṇa) of Śrī Durgā according to the Svatantra Tantra.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Mahādeva, tell me the supreme cause of success,
by which all mantras that grant success attain perfection;
and at which specific times the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) must certainly be performed.
Śiva said:
I shall speak in brief; listen, O Daughter of the Mountain!
One should recite the supreme mantra ten thousand times during the month of Meṣa (Aries);
for this, O Beloved of Hara, constitutes the *puraścaraṇa*.
When the wise practitioner recites the mantra ten thousand times during the zodiac sign of Taurus, through that he shall attain perfect accomplishment; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Likewise, the mantra-master [should recite] the supreme mantra ten thousand times during Gemini.
One who is self-restrained should recite [the mantra] daily; this is called *puraścaraṇa*.
When the practitioner of mantra recites it one thousand times every day during the month of Karkaṭaka, by that all goals shall be accomplished, and he becomes one who has performed the *puraścaraṇa*.
And under Leo, one should recite twenty thousand repetitions of all mantras;
one will certainly partake in the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. And when the practitioner of mantras, devoted to the mantra, is under Virgo...
One should recite it twelve thousand times with a restrained mind;
for this is the *puraścaraṇa* rite that accomplishes all desires and goals.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one shall go to the city of the Goddess at the end.
In the month of Tulā, the practitioner of the mantra should recite it one thousand times every day;
by this method, O Goddess, he becomes one who has performed the *puraścaraṇa*.
In the month of Vṛścika, the wise one should recite the mantra ten thousand times while on his bed.
By that, all goals shall be accomplished and one shall obtain the fruit of the preliminary practice (*puraścaryā*).
When one recites the mantra ten thousand times with devotion during the month of Dhanus,
one becomes like Kandarpa in this very life— wealthy, powerful, and happy.
When the best of practitioners recites the mantra during the Makara transit,
striving with a disciplined mind for four ten-thousands (40,000) repetitions every day,
constantly contemplating it for the sake of spiritual merit— this is called *puraścaraṇa*.
When one recites the mantra ten thousand times with devotion during the Kumbha [transit],
by that all goals shall be accomplished and one becomes a performer of the *puraścaraṇa* rite.
And when, O Goddess, one recites it twenty thousand times during the Mīna [transit]...
Those who are experts in all the Āgamas declare that this is *puraścaraṇa*.
Recitation (*japana*) should be performed everywhere—even at night, during sexual intercourse, on a bed, and especially when approaching another’s wife. (p. 429)
O Goddess! At that time, one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite [the mantra] with a restrained mind.
Having performed such recitation, one should then perform the ten-fold subsidiary rite (daśāṃśa).
By giving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, one certainly becomes a partaker of success (siddhi).

O Daughter of the Mountain! I shall describe in brief those constellations under which supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises; listen. Under the constellation Aśvinī, the practitioner should recite the mantra one thousand times.

By this means, the practitioner attains accomplishment in this world; of this there is no doubt. When the wise one recites the mantra two thousand times under the asterism Bharaṇī, he abandons the realm of Yama and becomes a lord of wealth through his riches.
During the asterism Kṛttikā, the practitioner should recite the mantra two thousand times;
and when the best of practitioners recites the mantra during Rohiṇī,
whether a thousand or even a hundred times, he shall attain all his desires.
When a wise person recites the mantra with self-restraint during the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa five thousand times, he becomes equal to Bṛhaspati.
During the asterism Ārdrā, the mantra should be recited by practitioners who are well-composed.

O Goddess! When the conjunction with Punarvasu occurs, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims, the practitioner who constantly recites this supreme mantra one thousand and six hundred times attains the status of a preeminent god.
On the Puṇya constellation, one should recite the mantra seven thousand times;
by that, all success shall be attained—this rite is superior even to the preliminary service (puraścaryā).
O Goddess! when the practitioner of mantra, being composed, recites the mantra on the Aśleṣā constellation...
One should recite six thousand times for the accomplishment of all aims;
and having recited ten thousand times under the Maghā asterism with a concentrated mind,
the practitioner, becoming equal to Indra, may wander upon the earth.
A wise practitioner should recite it eleven thousand times during the three Pūrva [nakṣatras];
such a sādhaka becomes as rich in wealth as Kubera on this earth.
Likewise, O Goddess, one should recite it twelve thousand times during the three Uttara [nakṣatras].
It is constantly recited by practitioners for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
O Goddess! One should recite it thirteen thousand times at the time of dawn;
having become equal to the sun itself, the practitioner may then move about upon the earth.
On the asterism Citrā, the practitioner should recite the mantra two thousand times;
he shall become like Purandara upon earth, endowed with various enjoyments.
Under Svāti, the accomplishment of all aims shall occur by reciting it two thousand times.
The practitioner becomes one whose movement is unimpeded; of this there is no doubt.
O Dear One! When the practitioner recites the four-thousand-verse mantra during the asterism of Viśākhā, he will always be as pleasing to behold as the moon.
O Goddess, when the practitioner of mantra recites the mantra constantly under the asterism Anurādhā,
he will certainly become a sky-walker (khecara), endowed with sons and grandsons.
And when the wise one recites the mantra two thousand times under Jyeṣṭhā—
One attains accomplishment from the *japana* [of this]; there is no need for deliberation here.
O Dear One! If one recites the mantra five thousand times upon the *mūlā*, the practitioner attains various accomplishments; of this there is no doubt.
O Dear One! When a wise person recites the mantra two thousand times under the asterism Śravaṇā, he shall attain the eight supernatural powers; of this there is no doubt.
Under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, one should recite the mantra two thousand times with a concentrated mind.
Becoming equal to Varuṇa, the practitioner is born upon the earth.
When the wise one recites the mantra two thousand times under the asterism Śatabhiṣā,
he shall be liberated from great sins and will certainly partake of the fruit.
O Goddess! By reciting and praising the great mantra of four thousand verses under the asterism Revatī, one shall always attain the world of Soma,
whether standing at night, during sexual union, or while reclining upon a bed.

The practitioner should recite [the mantra] daily and accomplish what is beneficial for himself. He should always recite the mantra, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and remaining pure during the day.
He should give a fee to the guru according to the extent of his wealth.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is described in another manner:

the *puraścaraṇa* is said to be performed by means of the *vava* and other *karaṇas*. Whoever recites [the mantra] according to the number of yogas during the *viṣkumbha* and other yogas [attains success].
The practitioner, intent upon all accomplishments, should constantly perform one thousand [recitations];

for this preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) has been prescribed in every tantra. O Pārvatī, it should also be performed during all the solar transits (saṃkrāntis), such as the equinoxes (viṣuva) and others.
One should increase the recitation by a thousand according to the solar transits (saṃkrānti).
O Dear One! one who desires wealth should always recite the mantra facing east;
for the constant destruction of enemies, one should recite while facing west.
O Dear One! When one desires to bring the worlds under control, or for the sake of liberation, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind while facing north;
for the constant destruction of enemies, one should recite while facing south.
Thus concludes the secret preliminary practice from the dialogue between Hara and Gaurī.
Now follows the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) for the lunar eclipse.

The "seizing" (grahaṇa) refers to the sighting of Rāhu. However, there is a popular saying that he is of the nature of a Caṇḍāla; thus, a doubt arises as to how his sight can be merit-producing. Regarding this, it is stated in the sixth chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra:
Caṇḍikā said:
O Supreme Lord! Rāhu is renowned everywhere as a Cāṇḍāla;
O God! how can there be merit in touching him during the time of the sun or likewise the moon, O Protector? Such is the doubt in my heart.
Speak, O Parānanda! Afterwards, reveal another.
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:

Listen, O you who are beautiful in every limb! This is the most excellent of all graspings (grahaṇa). O Goddess, the grasping is threefold, conjoined with the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. Fire always resides in the forehead and the eyes of Śakti.
In the left eye is the Moon, and in the right the Sun is established;
O Goddess of gods! if union is performed by Śambhunātha, at that very moment, O Goddess, Sadāśiva is conjoined with Śakti, and there is an eclipse.
When the left eye is kissed, there is then an eclipse of the moon;
when the right eye is kissed, likewise an eclipse of the sun;
and when the forehead is kissed, O Supreme Goddess, there is an eclipse of fire.
Since fire arises from the semen of Śiva, it is therefore visible, O Queen of the Gods!
Rāhu is declared to be Śiva, and his power (śakti) is said to consist of the three qualities (guṇas). From the union of Śiva and Śakti, O Supreme Goddess, the eclipse occurs.
O Dear One! The time of the union of Śiva and Śakti is composed of Brahman;
for this very reason, O Great Goddess! one should not consider the zodiac signs and so forth, nor the lunar days, asterisms, or yogas, O Supreme Sovereign! Whatever yoga [occurs] therein—
At that very moment, O Supreme Goddess! one should perform the calculation of the zodiac signs and so forth;
for through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the entire world is composed of Brahman.
O Supreme Goddess! the names of months, fortnights, and lunar days should not be uttered.
It should be recited merely by looking [at it]; then one will certainly attain success. O Goddess worshipped by heroes! That time should be known as the supreme time;
whatever is done there, all of it becomes manifold—what more need be said now?
O Sovereign of the Gods! This secret, which has been revealed to you out of affection, must never be spoken in the presence of an uninitiated person, even at the cost of one's life.
Since the fruit of this [practice] is proclaimed here to be infinite, even the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites as a tenth part of the recitation (japa) need not be performed.
This has been stated in the Gāyatrītantra, in the first section, the Brāhmaṇapariccheda.

By reciting [the mantra] during an eclipse of the moon or sun, O Supreme Goddess, one becomes identical with Brahman; for this mantra, O Auspicious One, one need not perform fire-offerings (homa) and the like. If fire-offerings and such are performed, O Blessed Lady, that recitation will become fruitless.
O Maheśānī! Just as the mantra of Ananta is [efficacious] through mere recitation, by whom can even a tenth part of Ananta’s [merit] be produced?
In the sixteenth chapter of the *Bījārṇava Tantra*, as cited in the twelfth chapter of the *Śāktānandatarangiṇī* (p. 432).

Once, O Supreme Goddess! O Great Mistress! having seen an eclipse at Kāmākhyā, listen to what ought to be done, O fair-faced one! Where is the bath, where is the twilight prayer, and where is the breath-control, O Beloved?

"O auspicious one! Whence is the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and whence is ritual worship (pūjā), O lovely-faced one? O Goddess, O passionate one! Having abandoned everything out of fear of the passage of time, and having formed a mental resolve (saṅkalpa), perform the recitation (japa), O lovely-faced one!"
Even if devoid of the five ancillaries, it becomes perfected, and not otherwise—whether it be the mantra, the vidyā, O Maheśānī! the armor (kavaca), or even the hymn;
or the meditation (dhyāna), O Parameśānī! or the ritual placement (nyāsa), O Kamalekṣaṇe!
O Girijā! By a single recitation, that becomes ten million;
O Goddess! at the time of an eclipse of the moon or sun, that recitation is incalculable. O Supreme Sovereign! how then can there be a count for such a recitation?
Therefore, O Great Goddess! O lady of pure smiles, there is no fire-oblation (homa);
nor, O Queen of Gods, is there consecration (abhiṣeka), nor likewise libation (tarpaṇa); and O Great Goddess! O lotus-faced one, there is no eating (bhojana) here.
O Goddess! O Beloved! During an eclipse of the moon or sun, there is no requirement for the five ancillaries (pañcāṅga).
Even if devoid of the five ancillaries, one attains success; it is not otherwise.
O Goddess! One should perform the mental resolve (saṅkalpa) according to the prescribed rule as it has arisen in the mind.
One should understand that [the merit of] that resolve is gained during the eclipses of the moon and the sun;
therefore, O lady of tremulous glances, one should never fail to form such a resolve.
O Goddess, this mental resolve bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
Therefore, O Goddess, the mental resolve (mānasa-saṅkalpa) is declared to be primary;
indeed, a gross resolve is said to be useless for the act of grasping [the object]. O Goddess, whatever a man does without a resolve is in vain.
For all that is indeed useless; therefore, O Goddess, that mental [meditation] is supreme when an eclipse of the moon occurs during the first watch.
Having eaten on that very day, one would quickly go to hell;
but when, O Goddess, the darkness swallows the moon at midnight,
having eaten and drunk on that very day, one becomes filled with bliss.
During a lunar eclipse, one should perform the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*) and other rites;
having eaten and drunk at night, one should likewise perform the sacrifice of recitation and other rites. This applies to all *Viṣṇu* mantras, as well as those of the Sun and Gaṇapati.

"O Maheśānī! The constant recitation of the Śakti-mantra is highly praised," thus it was proclaimed by Śiva in the Bījārṇava Tantra. This ritual procedure is taught for both the wise and the ignorant alike.
In the Gāndharva [marriage].
Alternatively, another method for the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is described:
during an eclipse of either the sun or the moon, being pure and having previously fasted,
one should stand in water reaching up to the navel in a river that flows to the ocean.
With a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra from the stage of grasping (grahaṇa) up to liberation (vimokṣa).
Having seen [an impurity] and bathed with a firm resolve, one should perform the recitation up to liberation.
One should perform the fire oblation (homa) according to the rules with a tenth part of the recitation (japa);
for the sake of the oblation, one should, with a concentrated mind, recite the mantra twice that amount.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of the oblation (homa).
Then, one should feed the Brahmins with a tenth part of the consecration (abhiṣeka).
At the conclusion of that, the best of practitioners should perform a great worship.
Having given the sacrificial fee to the preceptor, one should satisfy the Brahmins with devotion.
In the Kālītantra.
Alternatively, the *puraścaraṇa* is desired in another manner:
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, from the moment of the first contact until liberation,
one should perform the homa and other rites for as many times as the mantra has been recited.
In the Jāmalam.
Even having bathed in pure water, composed and with a one-pointed mind in a clean place, one should recite the mantra from the beginning of a morsel of food until its completion;
by reciting thus, one becomes a partaker of the fruit of the recitation without doubt.

The teachers maintain that for one unable to observe the fast on the day preceding the commencement of the *grahaṇa*, since consuming fruits, milk, and the like lacks authoritative sanction, it is better to perform the *hariṣyācaraṇa*; furthermore, because the scriptures do not determine specific occasions [for such substitutes], the *puraścaraṇa* may be performed even without the fast, as the substitute is not an essential constituent (*aṅga*) of the rite when the occasion is uncertain.
In this regard, the hearing of the censure—"one who does not perform the *śrāddha* here sinks like a cow in the mud"—refers to the subject matter that has been prescribed.
However, the venerable teachers maintain that the necessity of the prescribed recitation (*japa*) is like that of ritual violence (*vaidhahiṃsā*). [This is stated] in the *Sanatkumāra-saṃhitā*.
"If a person should abandon the recitation (jāpa) out of regard for ancestral rites (śrāddha) and the like,
he becomes an offender against the deity and leads seven generations of ancestors to ruin"— this refers to the context of an already commenced *puraścaraṇa*,
because of the use of the word "should abandon" (*tyajet*).
Now begins the section on garlands.
In the ninth chapter of the Nityātantra.
Īśvara said:
Having taken recourse to the rosary, which consists of the forms of the *mātṛkā* letters,
it is then made of pearls and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

It brings the king under one's control and bestows all perfections; of this there is no doubt. O Girijā, just as a rosary made of pearls, so too one fashioned from crystal or a garland of rudrākṣa beads grants liberation and prosperity.
A garland fashioned from coral bestows subjugation and accomplishes all rites;
a garland composed of rubies grants the fruit of universal sovereignty;
and a garland of *putrañjīvaka* flowers bestows knowledge and prosperity.
A rosary made of lotus seeds bestows great prosperity;
a rosary made of red sandalwood seeds grants the fruit of subjugation.
In the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra: "Liberation is attained through crystal beads; rudrākṣa beads grant many sons;
beads made of jīvaputra wood bestow wealth; and those made of stone grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
O Dear One! A rosary of pure crystal bestows great prosperity;
however, for the ritual of Dhūmāvatī, there is one specific rosary made from the ashes of a cremation ground.
Likewise:

A garland made of gems, jewels, and coral, or fashioned from gold and silver, should be prepared with knots of *kuśa* grass; it bestows the fruit of all enjoyments. Thus it is stated in the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*.
Listen now to the sequence of all the rosaries according to the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) and the others,
by reciting which one quickly obtains that fruit which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
First, there is the rosary consisting of the nature of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
Furthermore, a rosary made of pearls bestows the fruits of pleasure and liberation;
a rosary that grants all accomplishments brings all kings under one's control;
and a coral rosary serves for the purpose of subjugation and grants the fruits of all undertakings.
A rosary fashioned from rubies bestows the fruit of universal sovereignty;
a rosary of *putrañjīvaka* seeds grants fortune and the *vidyās*;
and a rosary fashioned from lotus seeds always bestows fame and prosperity.

A rosary fashioned from gold, one made of crystal, and one of red sandalwood grant all desires; it shall bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. A rosary fashioned from rudrākṣa beads grants the fruit of all desires.
Having worshipped the entire rosary and anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should constantly perform recitation while relying upon it; thus one shall obtain the fruit as described.
O fortunate lady, these rosaries are honored within the five Āmnāyas.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
The Goddess said:
The akṣamālā has been described with care, yet it has not been fully revealed. What is the name "akṣamālā," and what is its fruit? Tell me this.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of gods! The akṣamālā, however, is of many kinds according to the distinction of desired results;
listen to that, O wise one, as it is being described by me in detail.
O Supreme Goddess! By means of the garland of letters arranged in both forward and reverse order— following the sequence from the beginning to the end and from the end to the beginning—
one must never, under any circumstances, leap over the letter *kṣa*, which is the form of Meru.
The fault of leaping over Meru, however, is mentioned in that very same [text].
A garland that lacks the *meru* (central bead), or one where the *meru-jaṅghā* (the stem of the central bead) is missing,
is impure, unsightly, and fruitless.
It should be variegated, resembling a lotus fiber, and situated within the *brahmanāḍī*.
A garland strung together by her bestows the fruits of all desires.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the *ādi-klība* (the initial neuter vowels). That which consists of the pair *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* is indeed declared to be the *klība*.
Or else, according to the division of the eight classes (varga) based on their respective desires, the eight classes are proclaimed in sequence as: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and śa.
Regarding the specific fruits resulting from specific types of recitation with a rosary, it is stated in the Nityātantra:
O fair-eyed Pārvatī! Having worshipped the rosary with sandalwood paste, the wise man, taking hold of it, should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind;
then all women of the seven continents shall be brought under his control.
Then, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should recite the mantra a second hundred thousand times;

indeed, the daughters of the great Nāgas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla will become submissive. Then, O auspicious lady, the most excellent practitioner should recite it three hundred thousand times.
O Maheśvarī! The celestial damsels indeed become submissive to him;
O lotus-eyed one! he shall destroy ten million great sins.
Through self-confidence, he shall attain good fortune, happiness, and beauty.
Having recited it four hundred thousand times, one becomes a great lord of yogins;
by five hundred thousand recitations, O Goddess, one shall attain the status of Kubera;
and by merely reciting it six hundred thousand times, one becomes an expert in all branches of knowledge.

O Goddess! By reciting it seven hundred thousand times, one certainly becomes a Khechara. Furthermore, by reciting it eight hundred thousand times, a man becomes worthy of worship by the gods and becomes the master of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with Aṇimā; of this there is no doubt.
Kings and women, especially, come under his control.
O Great Goddess! that best of practitioners who recites nine hundred thousand [times] becomes Rudra himself in person—the creator and the destroyer; of this there is no doubt.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
Listen further as I describe the garland used in the Northern Traditions (Uttarāmnāya). Now, the garland composed of letters (varṇamayi) is considered the most excellent of all;
likewise, a garland made of great conch shells (mahāśaṅkha) bestows the fruits of one's desired objects.
Furthermore, it is considered to be made from a tiny udumbara fruit.
In the second chapter of the first section of the Yoginītantra.
The Lord said:
The auspicious garland of letters (varṇamālā) is said to be the illuminator of all mantras;
O Goddess, its substitute is an auspicious one made of a great conch-shell (mahāśaṅkha).
For him who holds the great conch in his hand, accomplishment (siddhi) is not far off.
In its presence, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, she is made of crystal and bestows all accomplishments.
The *Muṇḍamālā Tantra* states that there is a difference in the results according to the specific type of jewel:
With thirty [syllables] she bestows the fruit of sovereignty; with twenty-five, she grants liberation.
Consisting of fourteen [syllables], O Goddess, she is the giver of liberation and the increaser of enjoyment.
With fifteen syllables, O Goddess, she is established for the rites of killing and eradication.
For the rites of paralyzing, deluding, subjugating, awakening, and for the application of collyrium to the body,

as well as for the collection of accomplishments such as the magical sandals, a count of one hundred is proclaimed; or alternatively, one should perform one hundred and eight repetitions, which grants all desires.
In the Yoginītantra.
O Great Goddess! I shall tell you the number of beads for the rosary:
twenty-five for liberation, twenty-seven for nourishment, thirty for the attainment of wealth, and fifty for the perfection of mantras.
O Maheśvarī! With one hundred and eight [recitations], all siddhis are indeed attained.
This has been declared as the common rule; now tell me the specific method for those who possess desire.
The illustrious Śiva said:

O auspicious one! A rosary of teeth should be used for recitation and worn around the neck by men. O beloved! If the count is to be made with teeth, the rosary that bestows all accomplishments is made with the *rājadanta* (the upper front tooth) as the *meru*.
O Maheśānī! In other cases as well, one should designate [the hand] as Meru and so forth.

One should perform the constant (nitya) recitation with the hand, but not the optional (kāmya) recitation, because of its restriction. O Priyaṃvadā! One may perform even the optional recitation with the hand in the absence of a rosary.
In this matter, one should perform the recitation using the fingers; one should recite with the fingers including the thumb.
Any rite performed without the fingers shall be fruitless.
In the first chapter of the *Utpattitantra*.
The wise man should perform the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites with his hand.
O Great Goddess! The karāmālā (finger-counting rosary) is free from all defects;
even defects such as being broken or split never exist in the hand.
O Goddess! The hand is indeed inexhaustible, and the rosary is of such a nature;
its knot is the Kuṇḍalinī power, whose form consists of the fifty letters.
For this very reason, O Maheśānī, the rosary made of the hand yields great fruit.
In the Yoginītantra.
In that manner, the stringing of the garlands is performed there for the purpose of awakening [the mantra].
Having first offered worship with devotion, being pure and having previously fasted,
the practitioner, remaining silent in a secluded place, should himself string the garland.
Having performed his daily rites, being pure and proficient in the mantras regarding the dice,
he should diligently bring the dice at the proper time according to his desire—
dice that are uniform in appearance to one another, and neither too thick nor too thin.

Those [leaves] which are not defiled by insects and the like, being neither decayed nor fresh, should be washed individually with the five products of the cow. [The leaf] fashioned by the Earth, the Lord of Gods, and virtuous women, free from knots— (p. 437) [is used].
Having tripled a cord made of three strands, or even a silk thread— white, red, or yellow, according to the rites of pacification, subjugation, or attraction—
the wise man should apply the cord, having washed it as before.
Taking each individual garland, the wise one should join them to the thread;
joining mouth to mouth, one should likewise join tail to tail.
It should be made like a cow’s tail, or it may take the form of a serpent.
One should place a single bead of that same kind at the front as the Meru;
furthermore, one should fashion a Brahma-knot within each individual string of the rosary.
In the *Utpattitantra*, chapter sixty.

"The recitation performed with the fifty-letter garland by repeating it one hundred times in both direct and reverse order— that indeed should be known as the supreme [recitation], so it is proclaimed.
Thus ends the first chapter, consisting of the description of the knots, in the fourth section on optional rites (*kāmyakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Now follows the section on the means of proof.
In the second chapter of the Śāradā-tantra.
A field of merit, the bank of a river, the summit of a mountain cave,
sacred sites, the confluence of rivers, and great purifying places;
secluded gardens, the foot of a bilva tree, and the slope of a mountain.
A temple, the shore of the ocean, and one's own home—
these places are praised for the practices of practitioners (mantrins).
[The phrase] "the bank of a river" refers to the bank of a sacred river, because the bank of an ordinary river is prohibited.
Secluded and devoid of people.
As cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Facing west, in a place dedicated to Śiva that is free from bulls and the like,
in a grove of Aśvattha, Bilva, and Tulasī trees, or surrounded by various flowers.
It is recommended in a cow-pen, at the foot of an Aśvattha tree, or in sacred fields.

Since the word "goṣṭha" (cow-pen) alone already establishes the location as a place for cows, the specific mention of "of cows" (*gavām*) is intended to indicate a connection with the cows at that particular time; therefore, acts such as recitation (*japa*) are recommended when performed near cows, which is precisely why it is said "in the vicinity of cows."
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā,
it is said: "Just as [the shadow] of the sun, of the preceptor, of the moon, of a lamp, and of water..."
"Japa is recommended in the presence of Brahmins and cows;
or else, one should dwell wherever the mind finds serenity.
Thus it is stated in the third chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
On a riverbank, at the foot of a *bilva* tree, in a cremation ground, in an empty house,
on a mountain with a single linga, in a temple, at a crossroads,
upon a corpse, on a shaven head, or in water that reaches the neck— (p. 438).
Whether on the field of battle, in the womb, in a place, or in a solitary forest;
wherever the spot may be, whether delightful or wherever the mind finds its absorption.
In the second chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
One should propitiate the Goddess, the bestower of all desired objects, at a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, at a crossroads, or in a palace.
He now states the characteristics of the solitary linga:
"Where no other linga is seen within a distance of five krośas, that is declared to be an ekaliṅga; there, the highest accomplishment (siddhi) is attained.
Thus, the ekaliṅga should be understood according to what is held in the Śyāmārahasya.
Likewise: in a thicket, on a mountain, or in a desolate place, at a crossroads,
in a temple devoid of a deity, at the foot of a *bilva* tree, or on a riverbank.
"In one's own home, in a secluded place, in the forest, or likewise in the vicinity of an Aśvattha tree"—
thus it is stated in the *Śyāmārahasya* and in the first chapter of the *Nityātantra*.
In a solitary linga, or in a cremation ground, or in an empty house, or on a riverbank;
or even in a subterranean abode, or on a mountain, or on the shore of a long pond;
in a field of power (śakti-kṣetra), at a great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha), at the root of a bilva tree, or in a temple of Śiva.
At the foot of a dhātrī tree, at the root of an aśvattha, and likewise at the base of any tree.
In the subterranean realm of Pātāla, within the midst of the earth.
Also in the second chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
O Goddess of the gods! These are the places for recitation (japa) and those which are seats of the Siddhas (siddhapīṭhas):
specifically at a seat of the Siddhas, upon a bed, especially on a wooden-framed bed;
likewise at a crossroads, at a Siddha-liṅga, and in the temple of one’s Guru or deity.

O Goddess of the gods, O Daughter of the Mountain! The places for recitation (japa) have been described as being at the roots of the banyan, the holy fig, and the wood-apple tree; likewise in a grove of plantain trees, on a riverbank, in a temple of Śiva, in a cave, or on a mountain peak.
Listen, O Goddess! specifically for the sake of the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya):
having gone to a prostitute’s house or to a cremation ground, one should engage in sexual union.
Then, O Goddess, by performing recitation (japa) and other rites, one obtains the fruit.
Alternatively, one who is devoted may perform it well at night in his own home;
he obtains the entire fruit, freed from anxiety and other fears.
In the fourth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa-tantra*.
O fair-faced one! A cow-pen, a crossroads, a triple-path, a desolate place,
as well as a forest, an empty house,
likewise a mountain, a riverbank, and the shore of a long pond.
At the root of an aśvattha tree, as well as at the base of a vaṭa tree, O Goddess! likewise at the base of a dhātrī tree and of a vakula tree;
wherever there is a lotus grove, O auspicious one!—whether white or red, O lady of beautiful countenance! (p. 439)

O lady of beautiful limbs! If, by good fortune, one obtains the supreme time for recitation (japākāla), which resembles the rising sun, at a specific location according to the *Annadākalpa*, in its second chapter; [then one attains the highest goal].
In a cowshed, on a ground of merit, especially in the house of one's guru;
at the root of a *bilva* tree, on a riverbank, on a mountain, in the presence of Śiva;
likewise in one’s own home, in a sacred abode, or in the temple of a practitioner (*sādhaka*).
The rite of initiation is commended in places such as the vicinity of an image of Śrī Durgā or in the presence of young women.
The specific results, however, have been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
Recitation performed at home is said to be equal [to one unit]; in a cow-pen it is a hundredfold;
likewise in a grove or a forest it is said to be a thousandfold;
on a sacred mountain it is ten-thousandfold, and by a river it is a hundred-thousandfold.
They say that ten million [times] in a temple, and infinite [times] in the presence of Śiva.
Now, the Siddhapīṭha.
In the Kubjikātantra, in the seventh chapter.
Śiva said:
Listen with attention, O devoted wife, to the Siddhapīṭhas,
by the mere practice of which one becomes the master of all supernatural powers (siddhis):
Māyāvatī, Madhupurī, Kāśī, and Gorakṣakāriṇī.
Hiṅgulā is a great seat (mahāpīṭha), and likewise Jālandhara;
Jvālāmukhī is a great seat, as is the seat born of Nagara. Rāmagiri is a great seat, and likewise Godāvarī, O beloved.
O beloved! [One should visit] Nepal, Karṇasūtra, and likewise Mahākarṇa;
Ayodhyā, Kurukṣetra, and the delightful Siṃhanāda;
Maṇipūra, Hṛṣīkeśa, Prayāga, and Tapovana.
Vadarī and Mahāpīṭha, Ambikā and Arddhanālakam; Triveṇī and Mahāpīṭha, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean; Nārikela and Virajā, and Uḍḍīyāna, O Maheśvarī!
Kamalā, Vimalā, and likewise the city of Māhiṣmatī;
Vārāhī, Tripurā, and Vāgmatī flowing with blue waters; Govardhana, Vindhya Mountain, and Kāmarūpa—these [are the sacred sites] in the Kali age.
O Goddess of the Suras! Ghaṇṭākarṇa, Hayagrīva, and Mādhava—O fair-eyed one, one should know these as Kṣīragrāma and Vaidyanātha;
[and] Kāmarūpa is a great pīṭha that bestows the fruits of all desires.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, recitation at Kāmarūpa is said to yield swift results.
Regarding recitation elsewhere, the fruit is stated in that very same [text] through the application of the three garments known as Ali and Kāma.
Having taken the garment of Kāmākhyā, one should perform recitation and worship;
O Goddess, one shall obtain the fulfillment of all desires—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
In the *Tantracūḍāmaṇi*, the description of the great seats (*mahāpīṭha*) is as follows. The Lord said:
O Mother! O Goddess, supreme beyond the supreme! O Sovereign consisting of all knowledge!
Tell me of every sacred seat (pīṭha), its Śakti, and its presiding Bhairava deity.
The Goddess said:
Listen, my child! O compassionate one, you who are kind to your devotees!
I shall declare those [seats] without which the recitation, the spiritual practice, and its rites do not succeed.
There are fifty-one seats (pīṭhas), with Śakti as the Bhairava deity.
Through the falling of my limbs and members, and by the wound inflicted by Viṣṇu’s discus,
this body of mine is described to you for the benefit of the gods.
Indeed, the Brahma-aperture is at Hiṅgulā, where Bhairava of terrifying eyes resides.
Mahādeva is Koṭṭarīśa, and she who is the triple-guṇa is Digambarī. || 1 ||
In Karavīra is my three-eyed goddess Mahiṣamardinī; Krodhīśa Bhairava is there. And in Sugandhā is Nāsikā.
The deity there is named Tryambaka, and Sunandā is the goddess. || 3 ||
In Kaśmīra is the region of the throat and Trisandhyeśvara Bhairava;
there is the Blessed Lady Mahāmāyā, who transcends the qualities (guṇas) and bestows boons.
In Jvālāmukhī is Mahājihvā; O God, [there is] Unmattabhairava.
Ambikā is named Siddhidā. 5.
In Jālāndhara is my breast.
There, the goddess Tripuramālinī is terrifying and formidable.
The heart-pīṭha is at Vaidyanātha; the Bhairava there is Vaidyanātha, and the deity is known as Jayadurgā. || 7 ||
O Śiva, may I be born in Nepal!
May the illustrious Kapālī Bhairava and the goddess Mahāmāyā [be my protectors]. || 8 ||
O Goddess Dākṣāyaṇī, take my right hand at Mānava!
There, the immortal Bhairava is the bestower of all spiritual perfections (siddhis). || 9 ||
In Utkala, the region of the navel is called Virajā-kṣetra;
she is the great goddess Vimalā, and Bhairava is Jagannātha.
And at Gaṇḍapāta on the Gaṇḍakī, there is accomplishment without a doubt;
there, that Gaṇḍakī is Caṇḍī, while Cakrapāṇi is Bhairava.
In Vahulā is the left arm, and the deity there is named Bahulā; Bhīruka is Bhairava, the bestower of all accomplishments. || 12 ||
In Ujjayinī, there is Kūrpara, clad in auspicious saffron-colored garments;
Bhairava is the manifest bestower of success, and the Goddess is Maṅgalacaṇḍikā. (13)
On the battlement is my right arm, Bhairava Candraśekhara;
there the goddess Bhavānī resides in manifest form.
Especially in the Kali age, I dwell within Candraśekhara. (14)
In Tripurā, the goddess is Tripurasundarī;
Bhairava is Tripureśa, the bestower of all desired objects. (15)
In Trisrotā is Bhrāmara, the Lord of Bhairava, with his left foot [extended]. || 16 ||

The Yonipīṭha is on Mount Kāma; the deity there is Kāmākhyā, who dwells there transcending the three guṇas, in the form of a red stone. There resides Mādhava himself, as well as Umānanda and Bhairava.
The Goddess should always dwell there; of that liberation, there is no doubt.
There resides the goddess Śrī Bhairavī, and there is no other local deity (kṣetradevatā) there.
There is Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, Mātaṅgī, and she whose essence is Tripurā.
Bagalā, Kamalā, Bhuvaneśī, and Sadhūminī—
these are the nine sacred seats (pīṭhas) praised by the excellent Bhairavas.
O cluster of fingers of the hand, become Lalitā at Prayāga! || 18 ||
At Jayantī is Vāmajaṅghā and Jayantī Kramadīśvara;
I am everywhere rare, yet in Kāmarūpa I am in every house.
Having ascended Gaurīśikhara, there is no rebirth again. (19)
Bhūtadhātrī is Mahāmāyā; Bhairava is Kṣīrakaṇṭhaka.
She, Mahāmāyā, who is the beginning of the Yugas, is my right thumb and foot.
Nakulīśa is in the seat of Kālī and in the toes of the right foot. (20)
Beginning from the Karatoyā river up to the abode of Dikkaravāsinī,
