this triangular region extending for a hundred *yojanas* bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*). Even the gods desire death there, so what need be said of humans and others?
Thus ends the majesty of Kāparūpa.
Bhuvaneśī, whose form is success (siddhi), resides upon the crown;
from the crown emerges the deity named Vimalā, and likewise Saṃvarta Bhairava.
In Vārāṇasī, the goddess is Viśālākṣī and the deity is Kālabhairava;
there is the famous Maṇikarṇikā, and Kuṇḍala is according to my tradition.
And at Kālyāśrama, Nimiṣa and Bhairava are my back;
all the deities are there. || 23 ||
And at Kurukṣetra, from the ankles upward is Sāvitrī named Sthāṇu, while the Bhairava is Aśvanātha. || 24 ||
And at the wrist is Gāyatrī, while Bhairava is Sarvānanda. || 25 ||
And on Śrīśaila is my neck, with Mahālakṣmī as its presiding deity;
Bhairava Saṃvarānanda is established in every land.
In the region of Kāñcī, there is the Bhairava named Kaṅkāla, also known as Ruru;
the deity is named Devagarbhā. || 27 ||
Nitamba is in Kālamādhava;
Bhairava and Asitāṅga are there, and the goddess Kālī bestows excellent success. || 28 ||
Having seen [them] repeatedly and having paid homage, one shall attain the perfection of mantras.
Bhadrasena is at the place called Śoṇa, while Narmadā is at Nitambaka. (29)
Likewise, at Rāmagiri there is Nālā, and Caṇḍabhairava is at Śivāna. || 30 ||
In Vṛndāvana, there is a mass of hair belonging to the deity named Umā; Bhūteśa Bhairava is there, the bestower of all spiritual perfections.
The goddess Nārāyaṇī is in the upper tooth during the month of Śuci, in the period known as Saṃhāra.
Mahārudra is in the lower tooth, and Vārāhī is in the five oceans.
On the bank of the Karatoyā, to the left, is the bedchamber of Vāmanabhairava;
there the deity Aparṇā resides, who is of the nature of Brahman and born from the hand.
At Śrīparvata is the right ankle; there resides the supreme Śrīsundarī.
[The deity] Sarvasiddhīśvara is accompanied by Sunandā and Ānandabhairava. (35)
Kapālinī is of terrifying form; she speaks while touching the left ankle.
Bhairava is Mahādeva, the bestower of all bliss and auspiciousness. (36)
And my [manifestation] Udara is at Prabhāsa, as is the illustrious Candrabhāgā, along with Vakratuṇḍa and Bhairava. || 37 ||
On the Bhairava mountain is Ūrddhvoṣṭha;
and in Avantī is Mahādevī, while Lambakarṇa is the Bhairava. || 38 ||
In Citraka is the goddess Bhrāmarī; in the water and on the land is the one called Kikubha; there Bhairava is the bestower of all accomplishments, and therein lies unsurpassed success.
On the bank of the Godāvarī is Gaṇḍa; Viśveśa and Viśvamātṛkā are there, as well as Daṇḍapāṇi and Bhairava.
On the left cheek, however, is Rākiṇī. 40.
Bhairava is Vatsanābha; there is no doubt that accomplishment (siddhi) is attained therein. || 41 ||
In the Ratnāvalī, Śiva as Kumārībhairava is on the right shoulder. || 42 ||
In Mithilā is Mahādevī; on the left shoulder is Mahodara. (43) In Nalāhāṭī is Nalāpāta, as well as Yogīśa and Bhairava; there resides the goddess Kālikā, the bestower of all supernatural powers. (44)
At Kālīghāṭa is Muṇḍapāta, as well as Krodhīśa Bhairava;
the deity there is named Jayadurgā, who bestows various enjoyments. (45)
The mind falls upon Vakreśvara; Bhairava is indeed Vakranātha.
There, the river is Pāpaharā, and the goddess is Mahiṣamardinī.
The lotus-hand of Yaśohara and the goddess Yaśohareśvarī,
as well as Caṇḍa and Bhairava, are present there where one attains perfection.
In Aṭṭahāsa, there is the goddess Phullarā, who is remembered as being situated on the four lips;
Viśveśa Bhairava is there, the bestower of all desired objects. || 48 ||
At Nandipurī, Hārapāta is Bhairava Nandikeśvara;
Nandinī is that great goddess, and there success is attained without a doubt. (49)
In Laṅkā there is indeed the Nūpura [Tīrtha], and Bhairava, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
Indrākṣī is the deity there, who was worshipped by Indra in ancient times. (50)
In the middle of the Virāṭa country, there is the descent of the toe-nail;
Bhairava is known as Amṛta, and the Goddess there is remembered as Ambikā.
O son! Therein reside the presiding deities of the sacred seats (pīṭha) as they have been described.
One may worship another deity, excluding the Lord who is the master of the field (kṣetrādhīśa);
however, all practice—including recitation (japa), worship, and other means—is seized by the Bhairavas.
O Śaṅkara! O Lord of Life! Without knowing the Bhairava-pīṭha and the Pīṭha-śakti, one will not attain success even through ten million recitations and other such practices.
This should not be given to the disciples of others, nor to a slanderer or an evil-souled person.
Having given [the mantra] to one who is deceitful or of cruel deeds, the practitioner of mantra will meet with death;
however, he should give it to a peaceful disciple for the sake of attaining the goal of the mantra.
Thus it is stated in the fifth chapter of the Mahānīlatantra.
O Great Goddess! The worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) is where unsurpassed perfection is attained. Kāmarūpa is the supreme among sacred seats and yields great fruit.
O Maheśvarī! Whatever worship is performed there, even but once—
Leaving aside all other seats (pīṭhas), I dwell within his body;
therefore, the Kāmākhyā-yonimaṇḍala is said to be a hundred times superior to them. O Maheśānī! How could I possibly describe its fruit?
There dwells the primordial Tāriṇī together with those who possess millions of virtues;
that sacred seat (pīṭha), which brings all happiness, is guarded by Brahmā and is difficult to describe,
for it is there that the gods, the Vedas, and the sages born of pure being reside.
All these manifest themselves; therefore, always keep it secret.
O Maheśvarī, that seat (pīṭha) which is of two kinds must be protected:
that which is secret from the mouth [of the teacher], which is of great merit and difficult to attain for the lowest of practitioners.
"O Mistress of the Gods! O Kulasaundari! It is evident that [the divine presence] is found everywhere.
O Mistress of the Gods! In connection with the *pīṭhas*, listen, O Bhairavī!
Listen, O highly wise one, to those which are the most excellent places."
These bestow spiritual success upon the virtuous and have been frequented by the great:
Puṣkara, the sacred field of Gayā, the banyan tree known as Akṣaya,
Varāha-parvata, and the holy site of Amarakaṇṭaka.
O beloved! [There are] Narmadā, Yamunā, Piṅgī, and likewise Gaṅgādvāra;
the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, Kuśīvarta, and Bilvaka;
as well as the auspicious Nīla mountain, and Kalamba and Kubjaka.
Bhṛgutuṅga, Kedāra, Sarvapriya, Mahābala, Lalitā, Sugandhā, Śākambharī,
Purapriya, Karṇatīrtha, Mahāgaṅgā, and Taṇḍulikāśrama as well.
And Kumārākhya and Prabhāsa, as well as Dhanyā and Sarasvatī;
the beloved hermitage of Agastya, and beyond that the hermitage of Karṇa;
preceded by the Kauśikī, Sarayū, Śoṇa, Jyotiḥsarā, and Puraḥsara.
Kālodaka is dear, as is the glorious and most excellent Mānasa;
Pataṅgavāpī, Saptārcis, and the great Mahāviṣṇupada; the great holy ford Vaidyanātha, and the beloved mountain Kālañjara.
Know that Rāmoccheda, Gargoccheda, Haroccheda, Mahānana,
the great pilgrimage site of Bhadreśvara, and Lakṣmaṇaccheda are there,
O most beloved one, as well as the Kāverī and the Kapilodakā.
Someśvara, Śuklatīrtha, Kṛṣṇa, Velvāprabhedaka,
Pāṭhalā, Mahābodhi, Nagatīrtha near me, O Goddess!
the meritorious Rāmeśvara, and likewise Meghavana of Hari.
Ailāvana, Govardhana (which is dear to Aja),
Hariścandra, Puraścandra, the very dear Pṛthūdaka,
Indranīla, Mahānāda, and likewise Priyainaka;
Pañcāsara, Pañcavaṭī, Vaṭī, Parvaṭikā, as well as Gaṅgābilvaprasaṅga, Priyanādavaṭa,
Gaṅgārāmācala, and likewise Ṛṇamocana.
Gautameśvara Tīrtha and Vasiṣṭha Tīrtha as well, O Goddess! likewise Hārīta, and Brahmāvarta, which is dear to Śiva;
the most excellent Kuśāvarta, and similarly Haṃsa Tīrtha.
The forest known as Piṇḍāraka and likewise Haridvāra;
similarly Badarītīrtha and likewise Rāmatīrtha;
and Jayantī and Vijayanta, O beloved, which bestows all auspiciousness!
Vijayā, Śāradātīrtha, and likewise Bhadrakāleśvara;
the highly renowned Aśvatīrtha, which is dear to Devaśiva;
as well as the river Oghavatī and the Aśvaprada Tīrtha.
Chāgaliṅga, the assembly of Mothers (Mātṛgaṇa), and likewise Karavīrapura;
the Saptagodāvara Tīrtha, the Liṅga known as Sarvamohana;
the Kirīṭa Tīrtha in the north, and the most excellent Tīrtha in the south.
O beautiful one, know that Viśālatīrtha, the forest of Kālī, Vṛndāvana,
Jvālāmukhī, Hiṅgulā, and the great Tīrtha Gaṇeśvara are the causal sites among all sacred fords.

O beloved! All the gods, great seers, ancestors, and yogins who are devoted to spiritual perfection are eternally present here. For those possessed of faith and devotion, their rites quickly attain success.
Whoever recites this at a time of merit, that merit shall become inexhaustible.
Whoever recites it or offers oblations with devotion at the time of a Śrāddha ceremony,
that offering to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible, resulting in supreme happiness for the Pitṛs.
Whoever recites this in this place attains accomplishment at that very moment.
Now I shall speak, O Maheśānī! Listen to which deity resides where;
listen as I tell you their respective names. I am immersed in the ocean of the nectar of that narrative, which is supreme bliss.
At Puṣkara you are Kamalākṣī, and at Gayā you are Gayeśvarī;
you are Akṣayā at Akṣayavaṭa, and Amareśā at Amarakaṇṭaka;
and on Varāhaparvata you are Varāhī, the beloved of Dharaṇī.
Narmadā is at Narmadā, Kālindī in the waters of Yamunā;
Śivāmṛtā is in Gaṅgā, and Aśvā is at Dehalikāśrama;
Śāradā is on the bank of the Sarayū, and Kanakeśvarī is at Śoṇa.
When the Goddess, consisting of light, was unmanifest at the confluence of the ocean,
she was Śrī on Mount Śrī, Kālī in the waters of Kāloda,
Mahodarī at the great Tīrtha, and Nīlā in Uttaramānasa.
In Mātaṅginī and Mataṅga are Guptārci and Viṣṇupādukā;
Svargadā is in Svargamārga, and Gaveśvarī is in Godāvarī;
Vimukti is in Gomati, and Mahābalā is in Pipāsā.
Śatadrū and Śatarūpā are indeed there, as is Candrabhāgā; and in Airāvatī, she is named Īr, the bestower of success at Siddhitīraka;
and at Dakṣapañcanada, I am proclaimed as Dakṣiṇā.
At the confluence of holy fords, you are Saṅgamā;
at the Bāhudā, I am Anantā; at Kurukṣetra, I am Raṇekṣaṇā; and at the hermitage of Bhārata, I am the most meritorious Tapasvinī Bhāratī.
She is Sukathā in the Naimiṣa forest, Pāṇḍarānanā among the Pāṇḍavas,
Viśālākṣī in Viśālā, and Śivātmikā on Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha;
she is Śraddhā at the Kanakhala ford and Śuddhabuddhi, the sovereign of sages.
Suveśā is at Sumanas, Gaurī at Lake Mānasa,
Mahānandā in Nandāpura, Lalitā in Lalitāpura, and Brahmāṇī,
the destroyer of great sins, is on the head of Brahmā.
Pūrṇimā is always extremely dear to Indumatī in Kāñcī;
Svadhā at the confluence of the Jāhnavī grants satisfaction to the ancestors;
Bahumati at Puṇyāha is meritorious; and Pāpanāśinī is at the water-station (prapā).
Śaṅkhasaṃhāriṇī, Ghorarūpā, Mahodarī, Mahāvārī at Svargoccheda, Prabalā in the great forest,
Bhadrā, Bhadrakālī, and Bhadreśvarī, the beloved of Śiva.
At Bhadreśvara is Ramā, the beloved of Viṣṇu; likewise at Viṣṇupada is Dāruṇā; at the confluence of the Narmadā is Kapileśvarī;
at Kṛṣṇavettā is Bhedinī; and at the confluence [of the rivers] is Śubhavāsinī.
Śraddhā is at Śukratīrtha, and likewise Īśvarī is at Prabhāsa;
Mahābuddhi is at Mahābodhi, and Pāṭaleśvarī is in the district of Pāṭala; Subalā is at Nāgatīrtha, and she is Nāgeśī, saluted by the nāgas.
Madantī, Madantī, Pramadā, and Madantikā;
Meghasvanā, Meghavāmā, Vidyut, and Saudāminīcchadā;
Mahābuddhi at Rāmeśvara, and the virtuous Vīrā at Celāpura.
Priyā is on Mārgaka; Sureśā is at Surasundarī;
the great goddess Kātyāyanī is at Govardhana as the soul of all;
Śubheśvarī is at Hariścandra; and Pureśvarī is in the city of Puracandra.
In Pṛthūdaka she is Mahāvega; in Maināka she is Akhilavardhinī; in Indranīla she is Mahākāntā; in Ratnaveśa she is Suśobhanā;
in Mahānāda she is Māheśvarī; and in Mahābala she is Mahātejas.
At Patyapāsara she is Sāraṅgā; at Pañcakaṭyā she is Tapasvinī; at Vaṭīśa and Vaṭikā she is Surangiṇī, who assumes all colors;
at the confluence of the Vindhya and Gaṅgā, on the Vindhya mountain, she is Śrī-Vindhyavāsinī.
You are Mahānandā on the banks of the Nanda, and Śivā on Mount Gaṅgavāla; you are Mahāryā in Āryāvarta, and Vimukti at Ṛṇamocana;
you are Cāmuṇḍā at Aṭṭahāsa, and Śrīgautameśvarī in the Tantra.
The Veda-born Brahmavidyā resides in Vasiṣṭha; you, O Arundhatī, reside in Harita; Hariṇākṣī resides in Harita; Brajeśvarī resides in Brahmāvarta;
Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī reside there as well; and Kuśapriyā resides in Kuśāvarta.
Haṃseśvarī is at the great holy site (mahātīrtha), and Parahaṃseśvareśvarī is at Piṇḍāraka-vana; Dhanyā is there, as are Surasā and Sukhadāyinī. Nārāyaṇī and Vaiṣṇavī bestow liberation at Gaṅgādvāra.
At the sacred ford of Badarī you are Śrīvidyā; at Rāmatīrtha you are Mahādhṛti;
at Jayanta you are Jayantī; at Vijayanta you are Aparājitā;
at Mahāśuddhi you are Vijayā; and at Śāradā you are Śāradā.
Subhadrā is the bestower of auspiciousness at Bhavyā; likewise, Bhadrakāleśvarī is there.
Mahābhadrā is at Mahākālī, and Gavīśvarī is at Hayatīrtha.
Vedadā and Vedamātā are at Videśa and Vedamastaka respectively.
Mahāvidyā resides in Yuvati; Mahodayā in Mahānadī; Caṇḍā in Tripada; Balipriyā in Chāgaliṅga;
Jaganmātā in Mātardṛśa; and Satī in Karavīrapura.
Malinī, Raṅgiṇī, Rāmā, Paramā, Parameśvarī;
at the holy site of Saptagodāvara, she is Devarṣi and Akhileśvarī;
and in Ayodhyā, she is Bhavānī, Jayadā, and Jayamaṅgalā.
Mādhavī in Mathurā, Devakī, the sovereign of the Yādavas;
Vṛndā, the sovereign of the cowherds, Rādhā, I delight in the Rāsa-vṛndāvana;
Kātyāyanī, Mahāmāyā, Bhadrakālī, Kalāvatī.
Candramālā is the Great Yoginī, the sovereign of great yoginīs;
she is Vajreśvarī, Yaśodā, Vajraśrī, and Gokuleśvarī.
In Kāñcī she is Kanakakāñcī, and in Avantī she is Atipāvanī.
Vidyā is in Vidyāpura, and Vimalā is on Mount Nīla;
Rāmeśvarī is at Setubandha, and Vimalā is in Puruṣottama; Virajā is in Yāgapurī, and Bhadrakarṇikā is also in Bhadra.
In Tamolipta, she is Tamoghnī Svāhā; at the confluence of the ocean, she is Kulaśrī, Vaṃśavṛddhi, Mādhavī, and the beloved of Mādhava;
in Maṅgala Koṭa, she is Maṅgalā; and in Rāḍha, she is Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
Jvālāmukhī is at Śivāpīṭha; Bhuvaneśvarī is on Mandara; Guhyakālī is at Kālighaṭṭa; and Maheśvarī is at Kirīṭa. The Great Goddess Kirīṭeśvarī is at Liṅgākhyā as Liṅgavāhinī.
He is the witness everywhere for his devotees; for non-devotees, he is not a witness at all.
Now, O beautiful one, I shall further describe the seats of the Siddhas,
which destroy all sins and bestow all perfections upon men—
those seats of the Siddhas which have been fashioned here by Śiva.
Having heard [this], these things should be contemplated in the mind and revealed to those who are qualified.
In the great sacred seat (mahāpīṭha) of Amareśa, there is that which is known as Kuśatuṅgāra;
therein are the two named Durgās, namely Caṇḍikā and Maheśvarī.
At Prabhāsa is that Somanātha and the goddess Puṣkarekṣaṇā;
at Naimiṣa is Śambhu, the Lord of the gods of gods, and Maheśvara;
there also is the goddess Prajñā, who is Śivānī and the bearer of the Liṅga.
In Puṣkara is Rājagandhī, the great goddess invoked at the forefront;
on Śrīparvata is she named Śrī, and Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura, is there as well;
Māyāvī is the Śaṅkarī there, bestowing all desired objects upon her devotees.
In the great sacred site of Japyeśvara, there is Śaṅkarī and Triśūlinī;
there Śaṅkara, the wielder of the trident, is the liberator from all sins.
At Āmrātakeśvara, the Supreme Goddess is Sūkṣmā, known by the name Sūkṣmā.
In Gaṇakṣetra, the one named Maṅgala is the great-grandfather Śiva;
in Kurukṣetra, there is Śivasthāṇu, and Śivāsthāṇu is supreme in splendor.
In Iṣṭalābha, the self-manifested (Svayambhū) Lord exists, and the Goddess is considered to be Svāyambhuvā.
Ugra is proclaimed at Kanakhala; Śivogre is the beloved of Śiva;
Viśvaśambhu is at Vimaleśvara, and Viśvāviśvapriyā is ever there;
Mahānanda is at Aṭṭahāsa, and Maheśvarī is Mahānandā.
Mahāntaka and Mahendra, and Pārvatī, who is Mahāntakā;
Bhīmeśvara at the Bhīma-pīṭha, and likewise Śivā as Bhīmeśvarī;
at Vastrapāda, the one named Bhava, and Bhavānī as Bhuvaneśvarī.
On Adrikūṭa, the Great Yogin is Rudrāṇī, the Supreme Sovereign;
in Avimukta, Mahādeva is Viśālākṣī, the supreme Śivā;
and in Mahāmāya, Hara is Rudra, while Śivā is likewise the highly fortunate one.
And at Gokarṇa there is Mahābala and Caṇḍikā Śivabhadrā;
at Bhadrakarṇa there is Mahādeva and likewise Bhadrā Karṇikā;
at the place called Suparṇa and at Sahasrākhya there is the Supreme Goddess Utpalā.
In Sthāṇusaṃjña resides Śivā, who dwells in Śrīsvara and is the auspicious Śrīdharā.
In the great place Kanakālaya resides the Maheśvara named Kamala,
and O Maheśānī, there dwells Kamalākṣī, the bestower of all goals.
Chāgalā, Kapardī, Prasabhā, Maheśvarī, Ūrddharetā, Vareṇyā, the Supreme Goddess known as Sandhyā,
Sākoṭāsyā, Mahākoṭā, Śivā, and Muṇḍakeśvarī.
In Mātuleśvarapīṭha there is Karavīrā and Śekharā;
in the illustrious Vyāghrapura, the assembly president named Dhara is manifest.
There, Śiva, known as Sabhāpati, dances as the Lord of the Assembly.

Where the Goddess of Gods beholds the Lord of Gods dancing in the great ocean of supreme bliss, filled with the great sound of the bliss of the Self; where Mahādeva swiftly becomes the bestower of boons upon his devotees.
Where the world is liberated upon seeing the Lord of All dancing,
this place is the most excellent among all sacred sites; indeed,
whatever actions are performed there truly become inexhaustible.
In that most excellent place, there is a wonderful lake named Śivagaṅgā; on its southern bank, Īśvara dances. Dwelling by this lake and bathing therein, one beholds Sabhānātha.
Being purified and filled with joy, one should recite it one thousand and eight times.

Those deities, ancestors, siddhas, and gandharvas who have been mentioned here always abide in this place; they are the bestowers of all accomplishments (siddhis). Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited, or used for bathing here yields inexhaustible merit.
Having worshipped whichever Bhairava name has been proclaimed,
beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one obtains the highest desired object.
He who feeds Brahmins here enjoys inexhaustible fruit.
Having enjoyed various pleasures here, one shall go to the city of Hara-Gaurī;
this Lord, a treasure-house of compassion, has created sacred fields upon the earth for the sake of universal delight and to destroy sorrow and suffering.
At this time, for those who are pure in merit through manifold means of accumulating merit,
and for those who possess faith, there shall be a dwelling here directed toward spiritual practice.
Therefore, the most excellent among men should diligently perform their practice here.

Now listen, O lady of beautiful limbs! [Tell me of] the seat that is beautiful in every part—the seat consisting of a rosary of beads—O Supreme Goddess! Tell it to me, wherein all undertakings reach fulfillment and where the abode of Śaṅkara resides.
O Maheśvarī, for Viṣṇu of unfathomable wisdom, for his beloved,
and for the other gods who dwell at their feet,
your grace is indeed swift, and there is supreme affection for them.
Now follows the time for worship according to the *Samayācāra-tantra*, in the first chapter.
The specific time for each of the deities in matters such as worship is called *samaya*;
by knowing that time, one attains immortality.
Likewise: "The morning, midday, the third period of evening,
and the first watch of the night are proclaimed as the four [periods]."
The fifth is midnight; thus five times have been proclaimed.
The time at the beginning of the first day is declared the first period;
the time that occurs in the middle of the day is proclaimed the second.
The third *pradoṣa*, occurring at the beginning of the night following the setting of the sun,
extending from the *brāhma-muhūrta* until after midnight,
should be known as a sixfold period that is difficult to attain even for the gods.

The rites of pacification (śāntika), as well as subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (stambhana), inciting enmity (dveṣaṇa), delusion (mohana), expulsion (uccāṭana), and killing (māraṇa)— these various rites [should be performed] at their respective times: the first period for the purpose of pacification, and immediately thereafter, at midday.
Evening is the time of sunset; this is the sequence of the three periods of the day.
In the fifth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.
When no specific time is mentioned, it should be done everywhere at the beginning of the day or on an auspicious day;

when no portion is mentioned, one should divide it equally; when no weekday is mentioned, it should be on a Thursday; when no lunar day is mentioned, the eighth (Aṣṭamī) is to be taken; and when no asterism is mentioned, Rohiṇī is considered appropriate.
p. 450) When no specific conjunction (*yoga*) is mentioned, the fixed conjunction (*dhruva-yoga*) is traditionally prescribed for all cases;
as stated in the second chapter of the first section of the *Yoginītantra*.
When the first watch has passed, up until the third watch, that time is declared to be for the recitation of mantras at night; now hear the time for worship.
When half a watch of the night has passed and half a watch still remains, [that is the time].

The time for worship should always be the watch (yāma) that bestows the fourfold aims of life. Those two ghaṭikās which are joined to the middle watch of the night are designated as the "Great Night" (mahārātri); what is performed then yields inexhaustible fruit.
Whatever has been recited, whatever has been offered in sacrifice, and whatever means for liberation has been performed—
all that becomes inexhaustible and is rendered fit for infinity.
(From the sixth chapter of the *Guptasādhanatantra*).
O Supreme Goddess! When the sun has set and the night has arrived,
once one watch of the night has passed and two further ghaṭikās have elapsed,
that is declared to be the "Great Night" (mahāniśā), and beyond that is the "Exceedingly Great Night" (atimahāniśā).
In another tantra, the reading is "only two *ghaṭikās*. Having spoken thus regarding the end of the great night, it says:
"One who remains in the state of a *paśu* should never worship the Goddess there."
O Maheśānī! Whatever worship is performed within ten *daṇḍas* becomes inexhaustible; O beloved! within sixty *krośas*, all that becomes nectar;
O Goddess! within seventy *krośas*, everything becomes like milk.
The section beginning with "At eight krośas" and so forth is the same [as before]. O Goddess! when midnight has passed, everything is remembered as being like milk.
O Goddess! at eight krośas, it is equal to the substance itself; of this there is no doubt.
Beyond this, O Maheśānī! there is nothing equal to poison; of this there is no doubt. All of this, O Maheśānī! has been declared by me from the perspective of the *paśu* state.
O Goddess! in the divine and heroic (*divya-vīra*) view, one should worship within the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

Having brought together the five principles (pañcatattva), if one should be intent on worship, O Goddess! one should avoid there any consideration of proper or improper time. When midnight has passed, O Goddess! the worship of the Kula is proclaimed.
One should perform all offerings and so forth according to the respective tantras,
as stated in the *Vṛhanmuṇḍamālātantra*.
In the *Āgamaprakāśa* and the *Dhṛti*.
In the autumn season or in Caitra, when the sun and moon meet— that is, on the new moon day— at midnight, the Goddess, when worshipped, bestows enjoyments, heaven, and liberation.
"When the sun and moon meet" means on the new moon day.
"Black" (asitā) means dark-complexioned (śyāmā), that is to say, Kālikā.
In the *Āgamasāra*:

O Goddess of the Suras! Having reached the new moon (kuhu) during the zodiac signs of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries, one should worship the goddess Kālikā for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
In the Nandikeśvara Tantra.
At midnight on the new moon day of the month of Kārtika, one should worship Kālikā on that day associated with lamps;
for her, Kālikā is the bestower of all desired objects.
One should perform the great festival of Kālikā every year.
Especially on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) during the month of Kārttika, at the midpoint of the night,

one should worship the Goddess there, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Furthermore, when the new moon falls on a Tuesday during the solar transit of Libra (tulā), [one should worship her].
One should worship the bold Jagaddhātrī with songs and auspicious hymns,
according to the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
O Daughter of the Mountain! On the fifteenth day, at midnight during the period of Tulāditya, one should worship Kālikā there—she who is fierce and wears a garland of severed heads.
In the sixth chapter.
O Maheśvarī, worship should be performed during the day; worship should be performed at night;
and worship should be performed at the junction of day and night (sandhyā). Then one shall attain accomplishment.
[But] never at a time that is neither day nor part of the night, nor at the junction of day and night.
One should worship the Mother of the World; one should fully worship her at the time of the ploughing festival (Halāyām).
One should not worship the Goddess by day, nor indeed by night.
One should always worship the Goddess, but one should not worship her during the day or the night [at those specific times].
The resolution regarding these three statements is that they pertain to the domain of divine heroes; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.
And so it is stated in the first chapter of the *Niruttara Tantra*:
The hero should not worship by day, nor should he worship at night like a beast;
O Maheśānī! the reverse of this is ordained for malevolent rites (abhicāra).

If it is objected: "But surely, since the worship of animals (paśus) is heard of in the previously cited statement from the *Guptasādhanatantra* as taking place during the night consisting of sixteen *daṇḍas*, how can the prohibition of worship performed by animals at night be consistent?"—this is true;
[the answer is that it is consistent] through its being a single coherent statement with the citations from the *Nandikeśvara* and *Muṇḍamālā Tantras* as preserved in the *Āgamaprakāśa*.
The statement spoken in the *Guptasādhanatantra* concerns the worship of Śyāmā and others to be performed on specific occasions such as the appearance of a lamp;
however, the *Niruttaratantra* concerns daily worship (*nityapūjā*). Thus, everything is consistent.
Furthermore, the prohibition of "heroic worship" (*vīrapūjā*) during the day should be understood as referring to worship that is devoid of the five elements (*pañcatattva*).

Otherwise, the previously mentioned statement regarding "proper time" (*kāla*) and "improper time" (*akāla*) would be meaningless. Furthermore, the prohibition of worship during the dead of night is intended to indicate an inauspicious time;
otherwise, the glorification of the substance as being nectar and so forth would be rendered purposeless.
Regarding the passage beginning with "sārddhayāma" and so forth, it actually concerns the subject of the Family Worship (kulapūjā),
as stated in the fourteenth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
The Goddess said:

O Lord! If, for some unforeseen reason, there should be an obstruction to the worship of the deities, what should be done by the devotees in that situation? Tell me that in truth. By what defects would the images of the gods become unworthy of worship?
By what fault should they be abandoned? Please state the means for that as well.
The illustrious Sadāśiva said:
If worship is obstructed for one day, the worship of the deity must be performed twice as much;
if it lasts for two days, it becomes double that amount, and for three days, it is again doubled.
Beyond that, if worship cannot be performed for up to six months, [the penance is increased accordingly].

Then, having bathed the deity with eight jars, the wise one should worship him. After six months have passed, the leader of practitioners, having again properly consecrated the deity according to the previously prescribed rite of purification, should perform worship.
A wise person should not worship a deity that is broken, cracked, mutilated, touched by one afflicted with leprosy, or fallen upon impure ground and the like.
One should cast into the water a deity that has missing limbs, is cracked, or is shattered.
However, that which is defiled by defects such as contact with impurities should be consecrated and worshipped again.
One should always worship one’s own chosen deity there— in the great seat (mahāpīṭha), the beginningless liṅga, which is free from all defects— for the attainment of happiness.
Now follows the expiation.
In the Śyāmārahasya and the Dhṛtaliṅga Āgama.

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the unsurpassed rite of atonement (prāyaścitta), as well as its purification according to the rules, as eloquently taught by Bhairava. A disciple who abandons his guru will certainly be subject to this atonement.
By reciting the *śrīpādukā* mantra one hundred thousand times, one is purified from that sin.
A disciple who has abandoned the mantra should never associate with him;
he must recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and become pure through fire offerings (*homa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*).

This, however, should be understood as referring to the abandonment of a divine or heroic guru. As for the statement in the *Śyāmārahasya* that "a Kula disciple must indeed abandon a Paśu guru," that is not correct, because for the Kaulikas there is no such requirement for expiation.
This has been stated in the fifth section of the Kulārṇava:
A Kaula should avoid these five: performing penance, falling from a height, renunciation, observing vows, and embarking on pilgrimages to sacred sites.
Therefore, the expiation concerns the animal and the disciple;
there is no expiation for the abandonment of the animal-guru, because such abandonment is prescribed by the scriptures.
That statement, however, is found in the Rudrayāmala and the Kulārṇava.

Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so a disciple, greedy for knowledge, goes from one guru to another guru. (An alternative reading is: "from mantra to another mantra.")
According to that view, one should abandon a mantra of an enemy, a mantra of a target (sādhya), or one that is lifeless or doubtful, and instead take up another mantra;
likewise, having abandoned a mere *vidyā*, one should take up a *mahāvidyā*.
That has been stated in that very same place:

If the mantra is incomplete, devoid of life-force (*jīva*), doubtful, or as if asleep, those mantras do not succeed; furthermore, the Guru would become a slayer of Brahman. Therefore, having suddenly recognized such a state, one should abandon that mantra-deity and Guru.
O fair-faced one! Even a teacher who is very learned should be abandoned once his essence has been understood;
however, even a teacher with little knowledge is worthy of worship if he knows what is *kula* and *akula*. He who sleeps or sits in the same place as his teacher [is likewise to be avoided].
He goes to a terrible hell for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras,
having treated the word of his guru with contempt and planted his own word in its place;
he whose mind is intent on conquering his guru shall fall into the ocean of hell.

The Goddess becomes enraged with those Kaulikas who consume the food of the bound soul (paśu) in manifold ways; one should never associate with them. Through association with the bound soul, the Kaulika forcibly enjoys the power of the bound soul.

And one should not, even with effort, allow him to be seen in the midst of a social assembly. If a Vīra who is a Māheśvara drinks a substance from a single vessel [with him], that drink becomes the excrement of a dog; such a Kaulika must perform penance.
Then, one may pacify that sin by means of a thousand *gāyatrī* recitations;
by performing oblations with clarified butter as the sacrificial offering, one will certainly become free from sin.
One should recite the *lopāmudrā* mantra three hundred thousand times, or otherwise recite the *ajapā* mantra one hundred thousand times.
One whose mind has been thoroughly purified should give gold to the Guru;
however, O Goddess of the Gods, having fashioned a *cakra*, he may worship it without an offering of libations (*tarpaṇa*).
Four things perish for him: longevity, knowledge, fame, and strength.

He who performs the office of an Ācārya when initiation (abhiṣeka) is lacking shall pass through hundreds of millions of wombs and go to the Raurava hell. Having abandoned the Mother-form, he practices with the Śakti in her form as a woman.
He goes to a terrible hell for hundreds of millions of births;
however, by reciting the *mūla-mantra* three hundred thousand times, the *ajapā* mantra one hundred thousand times,
and the *kūrca-bīja* five hundred thousand times, he shall thereafter attain purification.
The Mother of Mantra, the Daughter, the Sister, and the Noble Lady of the Kula—the Kaulika should never take pleasure with these; he should worship them correctly.
Having taken hold of the Śrīpātra vessel, he should then raise up the Cakra.
For him, the drinking of animal milk becomes the resulting expiation.
Now, regarding sexual intercourse with a mantra-mother, the penance ending in death is prescribed.
This has been stated in another tantra:
Whether by force or even of one's own will, he who should dally with the Mother of Mantra must recite the mantra ten hundred thousand times and then perform the fire-rite using chaff.

Regarding sexual intercourse with the wife of a son, a woman of the same lineage, or a sister, purification occurs through one hundred thousand recitations of the root mantra; this has been stated in that very same [text].
Whether she be the daughter of a mantra-adept, one's own daughter, a sister, or a woman of noble family,
by means of a lover and a hundred thousand recitations, the Kaulika becomes pure.
In another tantra:
On a festival day (parvan), having failed to worship the Goddess of the Gods, the Guru, and the Fire according to one's capacity,
and having failed to offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) there, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
This applies even when offering leaves, flowers, fruits, roots, mantras, drinks, or medicinal herbs.
One should not eat what is fit for food without having first offered it;
a man who eats without offering it becomes liable to perform penance.
By reciting the mantra of the Goddess one hundred and eight times, a man becomes purified.
Having killed a multitude of boneless creatures, one should recite the ten-syllable mantra;
having killed all birds, one should recite the eleven-syllable mantra three times.
[This applies to killing] a snake, a cat, a mongoose, a dog, a camel, a donkey, or a horse.

Having killed all wild animals, such as elephants and the like, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times. A wise man, having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, should recite it eight thousand times.
Having killed an animal, a woman, or a child, he should recite the mantra five hundred times.
One should recite eight thousand [times] for the killing of a virtuous Śūdra;
one should recite thirteen thousand for the killing of a divine being or a hero;
and likewise for approaching a hero’s wife or for drinking intoxicants in vain.
And the Kaulika also [commits a fault] by approaching the wife of his guru, a mantra-son, or a daughter.

Thus, however, it should be understood that purification for an act committed through ignorance occurs by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, whereas for an act committed knowingly, purification occurs by reciting it one million times.
This has been stated in the Brahmajāmalatantra:
Having committed the murder of a hero, drunk liquor in vain, or violated the wife of a guru,
the daughter-in-law of a guru, the wife of a hero, or the daughter of one who knows the mantra, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] ten million times.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the recitation for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) should be performed in connection with the *latā* (the creeper).
This has been stated in the *Kālītantra*:
It should be recited with the *latāra* mantra for liberation from great sins,
according to the second chapter of the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Rudrajāmala*.
First, listen to the procedure regarding the violation of vows by animals and so forth:
when there is a breach of a vow, a constant breach, or in the case of daily worship and other rites,
the practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra one thousand times for the pacification of the defect of the vow.
In the fifth Brāhmaṇa-paṭala of the Gāyatrī-tantra:
"He who performs the ordeal in the presence of a Śālagrāma stone or the like,
and he who performs the ordeal after having touched the Śālagrāma and so forth."
Likewise, O Great Goddess, the waters of the Gaṅgā and so forth, copper, cow dung, Tulasī, gold, the dust of cows,
the Vedas and other meritorious substances, as well as whatever other materials there may be—

By touching the names of sacred fords, seats, and so forth, one even performs a divine ordeal (*divya*). For the one who performs the ordeal and the one who causes it to be performed, there is no atonement from hell.
O Maheśānī! For the purification of that aforementioned sin, if he shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa;
Therefore, one is purified from that sin at that time, and not otherwise even in ten million eons.
Furthermore, I shall speak again; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Indeed, bathing in the Gaṅgā during the Nanda period and other such times destroys all sins.

O daughter of the mountain! That divine sin committed in the waters of the Gaṅgā—whether it be a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) or a secondary sin (upapātaka)—is destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā. A bath at Mauṣala on the Gaṅgā is the destroyer of great sins.
The formal resolve for bathing in the Gaṅgā as an act of expiation.

Today, etc., [this is] the performance of the divine rite preceded by contact with the Śālagrāma stone in its presence, the water of the Gaṅgā from the Śālagrāma, copper, cow-dung, cow-dust, Tulasī, gold, silver, holy sites (*tīrtha*), great seats (*mahāpīṭha*), the Vedas, and other scriptures; and the performance of the divine rite preceded by the utterance of the names of the gods and others.

"I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā at Nandā, desiring the destruction of the sin produced by such acts as the killing of a Brahmin committed through ignorance of the cause"— this is the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) for the destruction of accumulated sins.
"Today, desiring the destruction of sins produced by divine actions and divine causes, preceded by the touching of the waters of the Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
This is the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the destruction of sins, preceded by the touching of the waters of the Gaṅgā and the performance of divine rites.
Desiring the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin committed today— whether through knowledge or ignorance— I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Thus is the formal resolve for the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Branches," in the fourth section on Optional Rites (*kāmyakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Now, the specific means of accomplishment (*viśeṣasādhanāni*).
In the first chapter of the *Kṛkalāsadīpikā*.
The illustrious Nīlāvāṇī said:
Now, O Śaṅkara, tell us the means by which even the imperishable chameleon, though wearing the form of an animal, may be awakened through the speech of animals.
The Lord said:
"Excellent, O Goddess, is what you have asked regarding the empowerment of the speech of animals!
First I shall describe [the preliminary], and afterwards the supreme sādhana.
On the third lunar day of the month of Kārttika or Phālguna, at the dead of night—"

O woman of excellent complexion! Having gone alone and fearlessly to the funeral pyre, having attained a pure seat and meditated upon the goddess Carcikā—she whose throat is parched, who utters fierce cries, and whose eyes are most terrible like those of dogs—(p. 459).
I worship the youthful goddess who has two arms, shanks as long as palm trees, and loose, flowing hair.
Having meditated thus with diligence, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind:
*Tārā*, *Māyā*, likewise *Carci*, *Carcike*, and *Kṛkalāsaka*.
The mantra of the beloved of Fire (the letter *ra*) preceded by the two awakeners (*bo* and *dha*) is higher than the highest.
Thus, one should recite it a thousand times; thereafter, the unsurpassed accomplishment is attained.
Having recognized the cry of the chameleon, the practitioner becomes free from sorrow.
O Great Goddess! By His grace, success is achieved for him.
Whenever he recounts the entire account to the practitioner, he will swiftly bring the king under his control and likewise a woman; of this there is no doubt. || 1 ||
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess! having reached a cow-pen at midnight,
the best of practitioners should diligently worship Ugracaṇḍā with delightful incense and lamps out of devotion, using the Tāra-mantra and the Māyā-bīja.
Then, at that very moment, one should recite one's own mantra a thousand times;
thereafter it becomes perfected, O Goddess of Gods! No doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 2 ||

Alternatively, O beautiful one, one should apply a tilaka on the head with the nectar of the flowers of a passionate woman; thereafter, one should recite this mantra. At that very moment, one attains success—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Thus ends the accomplishment of the chameleon.
Now follows the accomplishment of the creeper (vallīsiddhi).
In that very place,
the wise man should accomplish [the rite] on a creeper by a riverbank at the dead of night,
having worshipped Ugrakeśī with special effort.
One should recite "Tāram" (Om), followed by "Hṛdu-grakeśīm" (O you whose hair is fierce upon the heart) in the dative case, ending with "Dviṭha" (Svāhā).
If one recites this a thousand times, one certainly attains success; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, O Supreme Goddess, one may do so while standing on a cremation ground with disheveled hair.
One should worship Bagalā with effort using the appropriate ritual offerings.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Bagalā! Māyā, svāhā"—this is the great mantra (mahāmanu) ending in *svāhā*.
With a one-pointed mind, one should recite it one thousand and eight times.
Then, O Goddess! having brought a house-born lizard (godhikā), one should worship it with diligence and perform the recitation (japa) once again.
From that time forward, O Mistress of the Gods! one becomes a knower of the term "vallikā."
He always speaks with ease concerning all matters, both past and future.
Alternatively, one should worship Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā at night with meat and other offerings;

one should recite the three *māyās* (the syllable *hrīm*) joined with the name [of the deity] and the suffix *ṅe*. One should recite this ten thousand times (*ayuta*), and then the mantra becomes perfected.
One obtains that very fruit; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
Having approached it at the time of dawn, one should recite this until the end of the day.
At the twilight (sandhyā), O Supreme Goddess, one becomes a knower of the term *jyaiṣṭhika*.
Now, the ritual procedure for the rat is described in that very same place.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the means for attaining the power of the mouse's cry.
Having fasted on the preceding day with a pure mind, being clean and wearing beautiful attire in the morning,
one should go to the bank of a river and diligently recite the mantra "Uṣī" (ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ"), together with the stars.
By the grace of the daughter of the illustrious King of Mountains, one shall become a knower of the sounds of mice until the attainment of perfection. || 1 ||
Or else, O Maheśānī! one may recite the mantra "ramāyugmam uṣīm" ending in the dative case (ṅe), up to the two ṭha-sounds, as previously described for the Avīti;
one should chant it a thousand or a hundred times at the end of the night, and then that very same result shall occur. || 2 ||

One should quickly approach the bed and recite the mantra with either one's own beloved or another's beloved: *vāṇīṃ ramāñca pradadāsi vidyāṃ lajjāñca tārañca punaśca lajjām | tāraṃ punarmūṣikaśabdapūrvaṃ vicarcike vahnivadhūsametam*. (Note: The mantra is: *Vāṇīṃ Ramāñca Pradadāsi Vidyāṃ Lajjāñca Tārañca Punar-cha Lajjām | Tāraṃ Punar-Mūṣika-Śabda-Pūrvaṃ Vicarcike Vahni-Vadhū-Sametam.*) *Vāṇī* (the goddess of speech), *Ramā* (Lakṣmī), *Vidyā* (Knowledge), *Lajjā* (Modesty), *Tāra* (the syllable Om), again *Lajjā*, again *Tāra*, then preceded by the word *Mūṣika* (mouse), followed by *Vicarcike* (O you who have itchy skin) joined with *Vahni-Vadhū* (the wife of fire, i.e., the letter Ra).)
Then, O Maheśānī! that assembly of kings speaks in secret regarding the multitude of sounds made by mice;
O Maheśānī! it quickly foretells for countries the good or bad fortune of famine or plenty, as well as bondage, and all other auspicious or inauspicious events.
Now, the sādhana of the cat is in that very same [text].
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme *mārjāra-śabda* (the "cat-sound" mantra).
In the month of Pauṣa or Śrāvaṇa, one who has conquered his senses and subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) should worship with incense,
lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), red sandalwood, and flowers.
Having worshipped with diligence Vikaṭākṣā, who is exceedingly fierce,
one should meditate upon her as she stands atop a cat, wearing armor.
One should utter the syllable *Tāra*, then *Māyā*, and then *Kaṅkaṭā* in the dative case (with the fourth case ending).
This vidyā is said to end with "svāhā"; one should recite it thirty thousand times.
Thus, for seven nights in the cremation ground, the best of practitioners should perform [the rite]. Once perfected, he then perceives the cry of a cat; it cannot be otherwise.
O Supreme Goddess! He speaks of news concerning the past and the future.
The sādhana of the jackal is also in that very same place.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme sound of jackals:
on the day of the new moon, a jackal that has struck with a single blow and its life has departed is placed upon the ground on a bed of *darbha* grass.
Having ascended that, O Maheśānī, the wise one should worship Phेरुक (Pheruka),
who has four arms, a broad face, is naked, possesses high breasts,
resembles molten gold, and holds a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a sword.
Having meditated with effort upon her who bears [the crescent moon], whose hair is loose, the supreme remover of all fears— with beautiful perfumes and flowers,
and with delightful food offerings consisting of meat and savory juices—
Having worshipped [the deity], O lady of excellent limbs! one should recite [the mantra] encapsulated by the *praṇava* (oṃ).
From Kālī, then Māyā, then Kālī again, up to Vahnikāntā (svāhā), O beloved!
a pure man should recite this at midnight for a measure of one hundred thousand times.
Then that jackal comes back to life, and from him a divine being is born.
"Choose a boon, O child! Whatever dwells in your heart," [said the god]. Then, O beautiful one, that best of practitioners addressed the God of gods.
"Having become self-controlled, protect me always for a thousand years.
Having thus prayed for this boon, O Goddess, one should worship her with great effort,
offering a meal of red vegetables and flour-cakes as is appropriate.
Then he remains there for as long as his lifespan lasts; of this there is no doubt.
That bed and that measuring rod he destroys merely by his glance.
Whatever the practitioner (mantrin) may request, he brings it all and bestows it.

O Maheśāni! O Pārvatī! He may give wealth by the hundreds or even thousands day after day; likewise, having brought a most beautiful woman from a distance of a hundred thousand krośas, he grants her as food according to his desire while performing the recitation.
O Maheśvarī! He speaks of future news even six months in advance, and he always speaks of past events from a hundred years ago;
he certainly makes himself aware of all the news concerning the Śivas.
One should recite that [mantra] every day with effort, offering it along with meat and food;
upon hearing the sound of jackals, one should perform a prostration.
Now, regarding the means of producing the sound of dogs, it is said in that very same [text]:
Having approached the root of a neem tree, one should worship the wicked during their meal with incense,
lamps, food offerings, and most excellent sacrificial gifts.
Having performed worship during the night, the wise one should recite the mantra eighteen thousand times:
"Sphiṃ sphiṃ Kāli! O beloved of Fire! This is the most supreme vidyā.
Then, O Maheśānī, having attained perfection, one understands everything spoken by dogs.
Then, O Goddess, one should understand everything and its meaning exactly as it is.
Thus ends the knowledge of the word "dog.
Regarding the means for that very [attainment]:
having reached the riverbank, one who has bathed and is clad in clean garments.

(459) Prajāpati, situated in the fire (Ra), conjoined with the Anusvāra—this triad is the mantra "Bheṃ Bheṃ" as it truly is. O Goddess! one should recite this mantra a thousand times every day for seven days.
Then, O Goddess, the foremost among men shall become a knower of the meaning of all principles;
he speaks even of past and future events exactly as they are.
Now follows the ritual for accomplishing [the goal] by means of a monitor lizard (godhā). Whether with a slain monitor lizard, or at the root of a *bilva* tree,
one should [visualize] the auspicious goddess Śāntimukhī, who is a female monitor lizard with a sword in her hand and fangs.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times for the sake of attaining the power of the lizard (*godhikā*), [visualizing her] with deep red eyes and red-colored hair.
O Pārvatī, when the lizard is mastered, what is there that cannot be accomplished?

She bestows forms according to one's desire, she gives food, and she grants abundant wealth. O beloved! She likewise provides news of the past, the future, and the present, in such a way that love and power may always remain as he asks.
Now, regarding the knowledge of the word "cow": O Goddess of the Gods! the wise one should cook barley-gruel with cow urine.

Therefore, for three days, a man wearing clean garments should recite the two earth-seeds (dhara-bīja) a million times, O Goddess! He should worship this virtuous goddess, who is blue-colored and beautiful.

Having meditated with effort upon her as having two arms, adorned with all ornaments, and marked by various auspicious signs, one shall behold her without doubt. O Goddess, in the house of such a person, there will certainly always be an increase in cattle.

One will undoubtedly understand all matters concerning cattle; prosperity shall remain stable in his house—of this there is no doubt. Now, regarding the knowledge of the sounds of deer, it is as follows:

O Goddess! Having approached the root of a bilva tree, one should worship the goddess Kamalā with auspicious perfumes and other offerings— she who is clothed in blue garments and adorned with blue unguents,
the supreme sovereign who possesses two arms and holds a pair of lotuses.
Having meditated thus with diligence, a person seated in a pure posture should,
O Goddess, recite eight thousand times each the syllables *kamala*, *māyā*, and *vahnibadhū* for the sake of attaining mastery over Kamalā.
When Kamalā is accomplished, one clearly understands the language of deer;
O Goddess, abundant wealth will certainly arise in his house,
no enemy shall arise for him, and all prosperities shall manifest.
A woman comes under one's control even if she were equal to Rambhā herself.
p. 460) Now, regarding the knowledge of the word "ram" (*meṣa*), it is in that very same place:
"O Goddess! Upon its fresh hide, which is the *mahāgaṇḍāraka*, having sat down, one should recite the *koṅkālā* vidyā, which has the luster of gold."
Having meditated with a disciplined mind upon the beautiful goddess, who is clothed in red garments, adorned with various ornaments, and possesses two arms— [one should recite], O Goddess,
the two seed-syllables of Earth (Dhara-bīja) as well as the two seed-syllables of Desire (Kāma-bīja).
This Vidyā is said to end with "svāhā"; the wise one should recite it eighty thousand times.
Thereafter, O Goddess of Devas! O Supreme Sovereign of Koṅkaṇa! it becomes perfected;
by its grace, O Goddess of Devas! he perceives the sound of sheep.
Now, regarding the knowledge of the word "chāgala":
one should cook excellent rice (*paramānna*) using only goat's milk. O Goddess, one should eat that very food and recite this mantra with undistracted mind.
One should recite the Koṅkaṇā-vidyā seventy thousand times without weariness;
by her grace, O Maheśānī, one becomes a knower of the sounds of goats. Now follows the knowledge of the sounds of wild cats.
The practitioner, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), should indeed recite this [mantra] during the latter part of the night for six days,
to the extent of six thousand repetitions; thereafter,
he will certainly perceive the sound of rabbits, and not otherwise.
By this very procedure, touching the Ṛtumūla creeper,
one should recite the mantra ten thousand times at twilight;
then, by her grace, one will become an expert in the cries of monkeys.
If one recites according to this very procedure for the duration of a day,
then one perceives the sound of wild cats and not otherwise.
Now, the knowledge of the sound of bears:
O lady of excellent vows! This Great Vidyā consists of Tāra, Māyā, a pair of Ramās, and Viśālā joined with the syllable *ṅe*; it ends with the Astra-mantra or with Svāhā.
[One should meditate upon] Viśālā, who has a terrible face, disheveled hair, and is naked.

Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess—who possesses lotus-like eyes, a smiling face, and breasts emerging in her youth; and who holds a sword, a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and a lotus while seated upon them—one should recite the mantra. One is liberated from [bondage]; there is no doubt in this matter.
During the night, having conquered the senses and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya),
one should recite the mantra while diligently worshipping with red sandalwood and flowers;
O fair-faced one, one should then offer oblations into the fire ten times the number of recitations using neem wood.
Then, O Goddess of gods, success is attained; one becomes an expert in the language of the stars (Ṛkṣas).
In debate, in crisis, and in battle, one becomes victorious—there is no other way.
By mere remembrance, the Ṛkṣa comes before that person.
In battle or even in dispute, one shall slay ten thousand enemies;
it shall bestow vast strength—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
If one applies a tilaka with the fluid produced from the rut of a lordly elephant, [the same result follows].
By the power of that command, one may slay an army of ten thousand enemies;
it will bestow vast strength—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
If the practitioner performs this very rite in a cremation ground, [the result follows].
By reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one becomes a knower of the cries of tigers;
by merely remembering wild beasts, one becomes intent on the conduct of the observance (samaya).
Following this very procedure, the wise one should recite it eighty thousand times.
One should perform oblations with a tenth part of that [number], and the accomplishment of the "elephant" (hastisiddhi) will occur.

Regarding the expression "with eight, ten thousand" (*aṣṭabhiḥ sahāyutam*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*); furthermore, because it is sometimes understood through its expressive power (*gamakatvāt*), a compound is also formed. Thus, it results in the meaning "ten thousand plus eight."
And he utters the word "elephant" (*kari*) in the assembly, O Supreme Goddess!
By the grace of the elephant, he shall be victorious and become all-knowing.
The meaning is that, intending the sound produced by an elephant, he utters it in the assembly.
O Maheśvarī! Whatever is spoken by him at that time at Hastikarṇa,
the elephant performs exactly that— namely, the breaking of trees and other such things—
if [this rite] is performed in the house of a woman in her menses according to this very procedure.
During the night, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times and worship with auspicious offerings in the house of a woman in her menses,
upon the circle of the womb;
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer ten thousand oblations of red lotuses.
Oṃ, salutations to the God of gods, the five-faced Great Soul!
By your grace, O Mahādeva, my perfection shall be attained.
Having praised him thus, O Maheśānī, one becomes a knower of the lion’s roar.
By the grace of the Lord of Beasts, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished for him;
whether in battle or in dispute, that man shall be victorious.
By the mere remembrance of the Lord of Beasts, the lion goes before him.
By the power of his command, he will certainly and eternally accomplish all tasks.
Thus, I have told you everything that is difficult to find in the three worlds;
in his home, the goddess Lakṣmī remains stable, abiding there as long as his sons and grandsons exist.
O Maheśānī! O Goddess! if one who subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite this mantra on a mountain peak, it will always grant success everywhere.
Now, the cognition of the word "pig."
Having reached the ground of mud, the wise one should recite this mantra—*tāraṃ ghurughurudvayaṃ ghūt ghūt svāhā*—seven times ten thousand times (*saptāyuta*).
Then, with effort, one should fill [the vessel] with a chisel; thus it is accomplished, and not otherwise.
(p. 462) Now follows the accomplishment of the skeleton (kaṅkālasiddhi).
Having reached the riverbank and performed his ablutions, being pure during the day,
he should diligently worship the Kaulikī with various delightful flowers,
with wines, meats, and red substances, and himself with dance, song, and other such offerings.

Having drunk the *kularasa* with effort and having gone to the *kula* with diligence, one should recite this mantra twenty thousand times, O Maheśānī! [The mantra is: *Kālī*, *Māyābālikā*, *Kaṅkālī*, and *Vahnivallabhā*.
Then, O Great Goddess! Kaṅkālī arrives there with effort;
having granted a boon to the practitioner, O fair-faced one, she either departs as his vehicle or always carries him as a mount.
It slays thousands of enemies and, in that very instant, causes one to traverse the earth;
it bestows immense strength—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. [The mantra consists of:
Tāra (Oṃ), Māyā (Hrīṃ), the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrīṃ), the name of the animal [victim], and the beloved of Agni (Svāhā).
O Supreme Goddess! He who performs the worship of Kālikā and recites the mantra a thousand times under the name of the sacrificial animal (paśu), his [inner] sound becomes awakened.
Now, the knowledge of the sound of a crow.
In the second chapter.

O Maheśānī! Having carefully placed the "crow's tail" (kākapuccha) upon one’s head, and likewise the seed-syllable of Kālī (the letter *ka*), this is the supreme mantra of Kālī known as "Kāka. One should perform six thousand recitations in a cremation ground, even without the accompaniment of fire-oblations (*homa*) or worship.
O Goddess of gods! By reciting [this] at midnight, a man shall then become a perfected one (siddha).
From that time forward, O Goddess of gods, omniscience arises within him;
through the awakening by the cry of a crow, he speaks everything exactly as it is.
A mortal shall become long-lived; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 1 ||
Now follows the accomplishment of the wagtail.
O Maheśvarī! O Parameśānī! One should worship the syllable *Tāram* (Om) for the destruction of darkness, and the seed-syllable *Māyā* (Hrīm) for her who destroys the darkness of the world;
then the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the *Khañjana* will occur—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, he shall always have the sight of wagtails;
even when that bird is carried upon his head by fate, he is not seen [by others].
One should recognize the sound of the wagtail, and one shall become beloved by all.
Now follows the accomplishment of moving through water and becoming a bird.
O Great Goddess! If one should recite this mantra in a cremation ground, or otherwise, to the extent of six thousand repetitions, one should worship the Goddess who dwells in the waters.
At that time, one becomes an expert in the cries of aquatic creatures and birds;
this is the mantra spoken for the practice of the *khañjana* bird.
O Goddess of gods! By mere remembrance, hundreds of birds in an instant [arrive];
all those birds previously present become subject to his command. (2)
Now follows the accomplishment of the peacock.
Having reached the foot of a banyan tree at midnight, one should worship Śivā— the supreme Caṇḍī— who is accompanied by her laughter, possesses a pair of full breasts, has disheveled hair, is naked,
is filled with various ornaments, bears the crescent of the moon, and is both terrifying and beautiful.

I worship her who is chanting the ocean of mountains, who by the weight of her excellent hips causes the entire circle of the earth to sink down on all sides, and who devours the hosts of the enemies of the earth.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, one should then [worship her] with pleasing perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped according to the ritual with liquors, meats, and great enjoyments,
one should again utter the seed-syllable of Kālī, O fair-faced one!
Then follows this mantra of the peacock's cry, which bestows many accomplishments.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra eighty thousand times, and then [the syllable] *hūm* one thousand times.
Then the Goddess, adorned by a multitude of peacocks, arrives with fuel-sticks of neem wood smeared with turmeric and beautiful bilva leaves.
Having granted a boon to the practitioner, the Supreme Goddess departs;
having become one who understands the cries of the peacock, he certainly attains omniscience.
Just as he desires, so he is capable of digesting poison within his body.
O Goddess! I tell you the truth: by offering a sacrifice of one's own flesh according to this very procedure, one attains victory over enemies;
with a mere word, he becomes equal to me—of this there is no doubt.
One should worship the goddess Kālikā with intoxicating drinks and charming meats;
then, O Mistress of the Gods, the *kula-siddhi* is accomplished and shall be eternally present.
Having become a knower of the terminology of the *kulas*, one certainly attains omniscience. (3)
Now follows the accomplishment of the specific power of the Vidyādhara-birds:
MĀYĀ, TĀRA, GAUṂ, and GAUṂ—one should cause these to fall immediately thereafter.
O Maheśānī! the wise one should recite this mantra at midnight.
And one should recite it ten thousand times, O Goddess! Then success will surely be attained;
having become a knower of the speech of the Gandharvas, one shall become powerful and possessed of sons. || 4 ||
Now, the knowledge of the crane's cry: Having recited seven thousand times the supreme *kāma* mantra for the sake of the couple’s play, one awakens the sound of the crane.
Having become an expert in the science of skeletons, one certainly becomes omniscient. || 5 ||
O Varārohā! Kolakāla [is the first], and after that Vahnikāntā.
O Maheśānī! One should recite [the mantra] at the root of a Bilva tree ten thousand times;
then one should worship the goddess Kālikā, and thereafter success will certainly be attained.
Having become a knower of the sounds of cranes, a man becomes omniscient. || 6 ||
Now, the cognition of the word "sparrow."
"O Maheśānī! Recite 'cāṭu cāṭu' seven times ten thousand times with effort, O Parameśvarī! First, recite 'spheṃ', and one should also worship Kālikā.
Then, O Deveśī, one perceives the supreme sound of a sparrow. (7)
Now, the cognition of the word "parrot."

One should recite ten thousand times the mantra beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by the pair of parrots (Śu-ka), then the two words "awakening" (bodhaya), and ending with "O beloved of Fire" (vahnikānte).
Thereafter, a person becomes a knower of the sounds of parrots; it is not otherwise.

By the grace of Śuka as well, one shall become possessed of great prosperity. O Maheśānī! Having renounced food at midnight, one should recite this mantra eight thousand times while offering the feet of Śārikā.
Having become an expert in the sounds of the śārikā bird, a man is born as omniscient. || 8 ||
Now follows the accomplishment of the crane.

Having extracted the seed-syllable *dharā* (Dhīḥ), one should extract the seed-syllable *bhaiṃ*. O Maheśānī! One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (*haviṣyāśī*) should, without sloth, recite this mantra seventy thousand times within a lotus.
Thereupon, O Goddess of gods, one attains success; there is no need for deliberation here.
By understanding the cry of cranes, a man becomes omniscient. || 9 ||
Now follows the accomplishment of the pigeon.
Having first extracted the sound *spheṅkāra*, one should extract two *huṃ* syllables.
This Vidyā is said to end with *svāhā*;
one should recite it ten thousand times (*ayuta*) after reaching the root of a *śālmalī* tree and worshipping Siddhikālikā.
Thereupon, O Queen of the Gods, she is accomplished; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Goddess! He understands the cry of the pigeon; of this there is no doubt. || 10 ||
Having uttered the word *kaurabera*, one should extract the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of *kūrca*.
Then, having worshipped Siddhikālī, one should recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times.
Thereafter, O Goddess of Gods, it becomes perfected; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Goddess! He understands the cry of the pigeon; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
If a wise person applies a tilaka on his head made from the droppings of a pigeon, he speaks of everything—past, future, and present—exactly as it is. (12)
Now, the knowledge of the cock's cry: Having uttered "kaṃ kaṅkāraṃ," one should then extract the seed-syllable of Kūrca. O Goddess! One should recite it eighty thousand times and worship Kālikā.
Through liquors and meats in a bower of creepers, one becomes accomplished; it is not otherwise.
When the mantra is mastered, the practitioner of mantra likewise becomes a lord of the earth and cities.
He truly perceives their sounds and certainly becomes omniscient.
O fair-faced one, as long as that excrement remains upon his head, it produces poetic genius for him;
he will certainly defeat any disputant. (13)
Now follows the accomplishment of Śarālu.
Having uttered *haṃ* and the syllable *haṃ*, one should then utter *spheṃ* and the syllable *spheṃ*.
Thereafter, O fair-faced one, one should say *haṃsa haṃsa* and recite it a hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).
Then, O fair-faced one, having worshipped Guhyakālī with wine and meat.
Then, O Goddess of gods! O lady of excellent vows! the word *haṃsa* indeed becomes perfected;
having applied the tilaka made from its excrement, one attains great omniscience. || 14 ||
Now follows the accomplishment of Kṣemaṅkarī.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable of Earth (L̥m).
After that, the word "Kṣemaṅkarī" (O Bringer of Peace) and at its end, the beloved of Fire (Svāhā).
Having gone to the root of a banyan tree or to a riverbank, a person should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
One should worship the goddess Kālikā with delightful wine and meat,
with red flowers, red garlands, and various ornaments.
Then, O Goddess of gods! he attains success; at midnight, O Beloved!
he becomes a knower of the sounds of the Kṣemaṅkarīs—of this there is no doubt.
Devoted to another's wife, O Goddess! he shall obtain his heart's desire. (15)

Now, the *ṭiṭṭibha-siddhi*: Having first recited the name of the *ṭiṭṭibha*, then one's own seed-mantra (*bīja*), and thereafter the consort of Fire (Ra), one should worship Kālī with effort; thus one becomes a knower of the word *ṭiṭṭibha*. (16)
Now, the accomplishment of the *koka* (the ruddy sheldrake):
A wise man should recite the mantra of the pair of *kokas* and the consort of Fire seventy thousand times;
he should worship Kālikā with diligence, and he will become a knower of the cries of the *kokas*. 17.
Now, the knowledge of the Cakora sound: A wise man should recite the seed-syllable of Kālī, "Cakorāya," eight thousand times;
then, having approached the root of a banyan tree, he should worship Kālikā.
Having become an expert in the sounds of the cakora bird, a man becomes omniscient. || 18 ||

O Goddess! A person should recite "Tāraṃ Kālī Cakorāya" eight thousand times. Then, O Maheśvarī! one should recite this mantra—consisting of Mahākālī, then the Weapon (astra), and then Vahnibadhū—one hundred thousand times, O Great Goddess!
One should worship Mahākālī with liquors, meats, and red flowers. Having performed this according to the prescribed rite, one should place its tail upon one's head;
then one becomes a knower of the cries of that bird—of this there is no doubt.
Now, the knowledge of the word *koṭa*.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the *kīṭa*.
Having approached the root of a banyan tree, bathed, wearing white garments, and being pure—
Having approached with tiger skins, fresh and charming meats,
incenses, lamps, food offerings, and most excellent oblations,
and having become entwined with creepers, one should offer the insect.
With high breasts, a pair of victorious arms, eyes like those of the cakora bird, and a smiling face;
drinking a stream of blood, with disheveled hair and naked;
bearing a sword and a severed head, she then appeared truly formidable.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra with effort and undivided attention. There, the dark Kīṭakālī, whose seed-syllable is *kāli*, dwells.
O Great Goddess! One should recite this mantra with a one-pointed mind.
One should offer a thousand lotus petals into the consecrated fire;
then Kīṭakālī arrives, of this there is no doubt.
Having granted a boon to the practitioner, Kālikā departs at dawn.

From that time forward, O Goddess of Gods, the practitioner becomes a master of the sounds of insects; by effortlessly mastering everything, he attains omniscience and becomes capable of understanding the cries of ants and other such insects.

Whether it be in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld (pātāla), whatever story exists—past, future, or present—it is always proclaimed for the sake of the sovereign practitioner; even insects proclaim it, O Goddess of Gods! There is no need for deliberation in this matter.
By the grace of Kīṭakālī, prosperity shall remain stable in one's home;
having become wealthy and possessed of sons, one shall attain heaven and liberation. || 20 ||
Now follows the actual proof from the fourth chapter of the *Muṇḍamālātantra*.
On the fourteenth or the new moon night, O beloved of Hara!
he who recites [the mantra] ten thousand times becomes perfected in all rites;
he is a lord of yogis, a knower of the true state of beings, and steadfast in all actions. || 1 ||
Likewise: At dawn, having gone to the foot of an Aśvattha tree, the most learned one should worship with supreme devotion, even using meat and blood.

O fair-faced daughter of the mountain! Beginning on the fourteenth day, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times using bilva fruits, bilva leaves, or bilva flowers. On the fifth day, one should worship the Goddess at the root of a bilva tree day and night.
Then one attains perfection of speech; clearly, one becomes a Vācaspati. || 2 ||
Likewise: Having seated a woman on his left side, he should worship the consort of Bhava with incense, fragrant perfumes, the chewing of betel, and other such offerings.
O Śaṅkarī! One attains pure perfection at that very moment through Bhavānī, the Tārīṇī Vidyā, the enchanting Brahmavidyā.
O Mother of the Universe, O Support of Victory, O Sovereign of the Universe, salutations be unto you!
O Karālavadanā! O Terrible One! O Beloved of the Moon-crested Lord!
Save me, O Illustrious One; grant me the unsurpassed Siddhi.
O You who are the form of the wish-fulfilling vine of desire! O Kāmeśvarī! O You of artistic intellect!
O Kāmarūpā! O Vijayā! O Nistārā! O Śavavāhinī! || 3 ||

Having seized the outcaste by his chest, forehead, face, and head; having repeatedly grasped and grasped his nose, both ears, the heart-lotus, the navel, the genitals, and likewise the anus, arms, back, and belly.

At the beginning, one should employ Māyā, then Māyā again, and Māyā once more; likewise, one should place the seed-syllable of the bride (badhū) and Lajjā into every limb of the mantra. Having recited it one hundred and eight times and having performed the binding of the corpse (śavabandhana), [one should proceed].
Furthermore, O Goddess, daughter of the mountain! by means of his own mantra-seed, with the blue fluid of the eye,
and through the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
having cleansed [the self] with the seed-syllable of Hara, he shall attain the state of a Siddheśvara.
O Daughter of the Mountain! O Queen of the Gods! the immobilization of wind, the immobilization of water, and the immobilization of fire occur at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī! In an empty house, one should face the northeast;
a rosary made of conch shells, or one of crystal, or silver, or a rosary made of gold, or likewise fashioned from coral, should be taken up.
Having recited the Kullukā mantra one hundred times at the location of the crown of the head, the practitioner of mantra should then recite the mantra; he becomes Maheśa, of this there is no doubt.
He is Śākta, a devotee of Śiva, Bhairava, and Sadāśiva. || 5 ||
Likewise: "At the foot of an Ashvattha tree, at the root of a Bilva tree, or in the house of his own wife,
he should meditate upon the Goddess, whether as the Divine Mother or as a beloved woman, as the Supreme Deity."

One should prostrate with hymns of praise before Caṇḍī— the primordial, luminous knowledge, the auspicious one who grants boons and fearlessness, and the destroyer of all defects. Whether situated in a cremation ground or even standing over a corpse, one should recite this supreme armor (*kavaca*).

Likewise, O Goddess of gods! O lady of excellent complexion! success shall be attained in a cremation ground or upon a corpse; then the Bhairavas will not be adversaries. Unmatta, Krodhana, and Bhairava in the form of Vaṭuka [are the obstacles].
Saṃhāra, Bhīṣaṇa, Kālabhairava,
and Mahākālabhairava— these eight Bhairavas,
O Queen of the Gods, beheld the cremation ground and the practice of the corpse-sādhana.
All the Bhairavas dance and roar with blood-red eyes;
today, whether it be one like me or even a madman,
I do not know how at all amidst the corpses and the cremation grounds.
"Do not fear; all these terrifying beings will speak for the sake of protection.
Lions, tigers, boars, and others of such forms are roaring on all sides.
Do not fear, do not fear, do not fear, O practitioner!"
He who shall speak before you is the Guru, the knower of reality.
In the fifth chapter.
On the eighth or ninth day of the dark fortnight, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times at night, preceded by meditation on the mantra; then one attains success.
Likewise: one goes to the Mahāpīṭha hermitage for the sight of the Mahāpīṭha;
endowed with supreme devotion, one should worship the Goddess in the Mahāpīṭha.
One should worship with red flowers and with red perfumes and ointments;
one should sacrifice to the Goddess with buffaloes, with rams,
and even with blood from the limbs of goats and Brahmins.
Then, having become a Siddheśvara, he shall attain the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.

Likewise, O beautiful consort of Śiva, through the recitation of hymns, firm knowledge, and worship, the Great Vidyā will become well-pleased; through her recitation, perfection shall come to pass. (8)
In the sixth chapter.

O Maheśānī! On a Friday, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand or ten thousand times. On a Saturday, on the fourteenth lunar day, on the new moon, or on a Tuesday, the wise practitioner, intent upon the attainment of mantra-siddhi, should sit upon a seat of kusha grass.
O fair-faced one, by reciting it ten thousand times with a spirit of devotion and one thousand times more,
and then having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), one shall become a master of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
O beloved! At the root of an Aśvattha or a Vaṭa tree, or else at the root of a Bilva tree, one should worship with supreme intelligence; thus a person shall obtain the perfection of mantra.
Likewise!
One should meditate upon the Goddess residing within the Suṣumnā, dwelling in the filaments of the lotus; through the purification of the channels, there is unsurpassed accomplishment of the mantra.
Likewise:
"One should recite the mantra of Kālikā or Tārā in a cremation ground, at the foot of an Aśvattha tree, near a corpse, or in an empty temple; then the Great Vidyā becomes propitious."
O Goddess! Through recitation, austerity, hymns, captivating internal sacrifices, worship, and armor-mantras, Mahāvidyā becomes propitious. (11)
O Goddess of the gods! [One should worship] her adorned with various ornaments in the wine on the left;
and in the Kula-cakra, O Goddess of the gods, one should recite the mantra, becoming equal to Śiva.
At night, in the Karālāsya-cakra, one should remain with disheveled hair and naked.
One should recite [the mantra] a thousand or even ten thousand times in the temple of Madana,
using white or red flowers accompanied by the fifth [note]. According to such a procedure, one should offer these to Mahākālī.
O Maheśvarī! Worship should be performed during the day, worship at night, and worship during the twilight;
by performing worship thus, one shall attain perfection.
Likewise:
Holding a *bilva* fruit in his right hand and a rosary,
the practitioner should recite the mantra of Pārvatī for the sake of accomplishing all purposes.
Having bowed with devotion, O Goddess of gods, one should mutter the Cintāmaṇi mantra.
By the grace of Cintāmaṇi, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
Having grasped the supreme Śivā, who is both Cintāmaṇi and Kalpalatā—
"O Caṇḍī! By reciting the Great Mantra, one becomes the Lord of the Gods of gods. — Thus it is stated in the fifth chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa of the Yoginītantra.
The Goddess said:
