O Blessed One! Knower of all dharmas! Bringer of grace to the world! O Compassionate One, tell me the sādhana of all mantras, which fulfills all hopes, and the sādhana of the perfected mantra.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the most wonderful practice (*sādhana*).

When half a watch (*yāma*) of the night has passed, the best of practitioners, having become naked (*digambara*), should properly perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules.
Having sprinkled [the bed] with the root mantra, one should lie down there upon the bed;
having worshipped the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru,
as well as the Parameṣṭhiguru, and Gaṇeśvara on the left.

And in the south, one should say: "Oṃ, obeisance to the one called Dhruva, the dweller of the cremation ground (Śmaśānavāsinī). Then, O Śivā! one should utter: "Māyā (Hrīṃ), obeisance to the seat. O Goddess! on the surface of the bed, at the end of the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should say: "Dhruva, Phaṭ."
Having written [the mantra] and sipped water with care according to the procedure prescribed in the *Svatantrottaratantra*,
one should recite: *praṇavaṃ maṇidharī caiva vajriṇī ca mahāpadam | pratisare rakṣa rakṣa māṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
O Goddess! having bound the topknot according to this mantra and the prescribed rite,
and having performed the placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement of the *mātṛkā*,
the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and so forth, one should then [worship] the supreme Śivā.

Having meditated with devotion and worshipped with mental offerings, O Maheśānī! O Varānanā! the best of practitioners [should place] the mantra upon the surface of the bed. Then, O Goddess, [he should utter] the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by "Salutation to the Vaṭukas."

With this mantra, one should mentally worship Vaṭuka with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. Then, having visualized a wall of fire all around by means of the seed-syllable of fire (vahnibīja) and having formed the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) with devotion, [one should proceed].

O Supreme Goddess! Having performed the recitation (japa) and offered it according to the rite, O Queen of Devas! he should again make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and then perform, O Śivā!, the fire-oblation (homa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and thereafter the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka) in due order.
And for the meal of the Brahmin, in his absence one should perform double the recitation (*japa*).

Having given gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should perform the rite of sealing the ritual's integrity (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*). O Goddess! having bid farewell to Vaṭuka with the words "Forgive me," one should dismiss him.
Thus it has been spoken, O Great Goddess! This supreme practice for preparing the bed quickly brings about the perfection of mantra and bestows union with us.
The means for preparing the special bed, however, will be explained in the section on the qualities-less (nirguṇa).
In that very same [text].
Now hear from me the method for the three-courtyard and four-courtyard [mandalas].
Having gone to a place where three roads meet or where four roads meet, O fair-faced one,
one should worship the Goddess as before with the mantra "Maṇidharī."
Having tied a knot at the end of his garment, the most excellent practitioner, free from fear, should pray:
"May all those gods, goddesses, and Bhairavas who dwell in the cremation ground show compassion; may they all become bestowers of accomplishment upon me."
One should bow down with devotion using this mantra beginning with the *praṇava*.
Then, O Maheśvarī, having sat down facing either the east or the north, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), one should cause the benediction (*svasti*) to be pronounced.
Having thoroughly swept that spot, the wise practitioner should write the seed-syllable of the *preta* right there.
O Great Goddess! Upon that seed-syllable, he should spread out the prepared seat.
Having sat upon it, O Queen of the Gods, he should remember his chosen deity within his heart.
Having worshipped them according to one's desire with the mind, one should offer oblations (bali) in the eight directions,
having especially worshipped Kālī and the others,
O Maheśvarī! [They are] Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī.

Vipracittā, Nīlā, Balākā, Ghanādviṣā, and Praṇavā— the first of these ending with the suffix -ī (in the dative case) are prescribed for worship with offerings, excluding [the specific] *bali* rite. Having formed the mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and perform the rite of sealing the ritual as faultless (*acchidrāvadhāraṇa*).
Having prepared the site and adorned it, one should go home while recollecting the Goddess.
Hereafter, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the practice (*sādhana*) of the root of the *bilva* tree:
the *bilva* root, O Great Goddess, measures sixteen cubits on all sides.
Therefore, O Goddess, that means of accomplishment brings pleasure to all.
Having gone there to the foot of a *bilva* tree, O Goddess, one should diligently worship the four gurus as before, and having fully honored the *kṣetrapāla*, [one should proceed].
"O Kṣetrapāla! O highly fortunate one! O Lord of the cremation ground! O observer of noble vows! Grant me success; O Creator of the world, grant me a place; salutations be unto you!
With this mantra beginning with the *praṇava* (Om), one should bow down to him.
Then, O fair-faced one, having worshipped that place, the best of practitioners should write there the Vāgbhava syllable,
the seed-syllable of the Preta, and again the Vāgbhava syllable;
at the end of those, he should write the root mantra.

O Supreme Goddess! Having worshipped Kālī and the others as before, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and ensure the rite is rendered flawless. Then, having purified the place and remembering the Guru, one should return home.
Thus has this been told to you—the essence of essences, higher than the highest.
It must always be kept secret, O auspicious lady! especially among the multitude of the uninitiated (paśus).
Now follows the ritual application of Kārtavīryārjuna.
In the Mantramahodadhi.
Just as: *Phrauṃ vrīṃ kloṃ hraṃ hrīṃ kroṃ strīṃ huṃ phaṭ*, obeisance to Kārtavīryārjuna.
The first [syllable] is joined with fire (ra) and the star (ta); Lakṣmī (hrīṃ) is joined with fire (ra), moon (i), and power (śakti).
It is enriched with Brahmā (ha), earth (la), moon (i), and peace (śānti). Then follows sleep-lord (sa), fire (ra), and moon (i).
Next are Māyā (hrīṃ), the goad (aṅkuśa), the bride (vadhū), armor (varma), and the weapon (astra); then the word "Kārtavī."
The letter *ra*, *vāyu* (ya), and *anala* (ra)—these two born of fire (*ra-ra*)—are situated in the right ear (*ya*).
*Megha* (sa) with a long vowel, *pavana* (ya), and *manuvaktra* (va) ending with the heart (*ha*).
This mantra consists of nineteen syllables; beginning with *Tārā* (Oṃ), it bestows the sacrifice of the gods.
Thus is the means of valid cognition.
Oṃ, homage to Kārtavīryārjuna.
Now follows its ritual placement (nyāsa).

For example: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One! O, O Kārtavīryārjuna! Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ! Tear asunder what is wicked in my heart! Strike, strike away misfortune! Grind, grind away evil! Bestow health, bestow it! Hāṃ Hāṃ Huṃ! [Destroy] enemies!
Oṃ phrauṃ vroṃ huṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ strīṃ huṃ phaṭ kārtavīryārjunāya namaḥ. This [mantra] consists of twenty syllables.
The second nyāsa.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One! O, O Kārtavīryārjuna! Oṃ phrauṃ oṃ! Tear asunder what is evil in my belly! Strike away misfortune, strike it down! Grind away sin, grind it to dust! Bestow health, bestow it! Hāṃ hāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ upon the enemies! 2.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Kārtavīryārjuna! Oṃ vrīṃ oṃ! In my navel, rend the wicked! Strike away misfortune! Destroy, destroy sin! Grind, grind! Grant health, grant health! Hāṃ hāṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ [against] enemies! 3.
p. 472) Oṃ and so forth (15). Oṃ klīṃ, "Tear apart the evil within my belly," and so forth. || 4 ||
Oṃ, etc. (15) Oṃ druṃ! Within my secret maṇḍala, the wicked ones... and so forth. (5)
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ Āṃ Oṃ, [I destroy] evil and so forth in my two thighs, knees, and feet. 6.
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ, [the mantra] beginning with "on my head, the evil," etc. || 7 ||
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ krauṃ. Oṃ, in my pair of eyebrows, [the word] "evil," and so forth. 8.
Oṃ, etc. (15) Oṃ śrīṃ oṃ. [I cast out] evil from my ears, eyes, nose, tongue, and mouth, and so forth. (9)
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ hūṃ oṃ; [protect] my throat and pair of arms from evil, etc. 10.
Oṃ, etc. (15 times). Oṃ kāṃ oṃ, [drive away] evil from all my limbs, and so forth. Oṃ, etc. (15 times). Oṃ phaṭ oṃ, [drive away] evil from all my limbs, and so forth. || 11 ||
Oṃ and so forth. 15. Oṃ oṃ oṃ, tear apart the evil within all my limbs, and so forth. 12.
Oṃ, etc. (15) Oṃ vīṃ oṃ; [drive away] whatever is evil in all my limbs, etc. (13)
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ rryāṃ oṃ; [the mantra continues: "Oṃ, in all my limbs, [remove] evil," and so forth. 14.
Oṃ, etc. 15. Straight [line]: Oṃ, "In all my limbs, evil," etc. 15.
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ nāṃ oṃ; [recite] "In all my limbs, the evil... and so forth. 16.
Oṃ, etc. 15 Oṃ yaṃ oṃ; [recite] "In all my limbs, the evil," and so forth. 17.
Oṃ, etc. (15) Oṃ naṃ oṃ; [recite] "In all my limbs, evil... and so forth. (18)
Oṃ, etc. 15. Oṃ ma oṃ; [recite] "In all my limbs there is evil," and so forth. 19.
Now, the Gāyatrī.

Oṃ, let us know Kārtavīrya; let us meditate upon the one of great heroism; may that Arjuna inspire us. This is declared to be the Gāyatrī; one should recite it at the beginning of any ritual application.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure as stated in the *Mantramahodadhi*.
Now follows its armor.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods! Omniscient One! Delighted in the welfare of all the world!
By what means may there be protection for men who are terrified in various calamities—such as afflictions from kings and thieves, or by the falling of weapons, fire, and poison?
In afflictions caused by Mārī, bad dreams, and torments; in fear of planetary influences and diseases; in the torments of fever and epilepsy; in the attacks of lions and tigers;
and in the assaults of Rākṣasas, Asuras, Vetālas, Piśācas, and Pretas.

O Maheśvara! In the face of great fear, great destruction, being cast into a vast prison, or into the ocean; in the terrible fear of great death, or falling into a great quarrel—by what means may there be peace for practitioners?
The non-loss of wealth, the recovery of what was lost,
the agitation of all enemies, and likewise the subduing of all—
these desired things come to pass for living beings; tell me this alone, O Śiva!
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess! This most secret [teaching], which must be guarded with great effort—even though it is not to be spoken—I shall indeed declare to you for the welfare of the world:
the armor (kavaca) of Kārtavīrya, together with its limbs and enclosures, in their proper sequence.
Having first performed recitation and meditation upon the multitude of mantras of one's own form and power,
[one should worship] within that which resembles a thousand suns, blazing with various jewels,
enriched with radiant banners and flags, and adorned with horses, weapons, and ornaments.
Resounding with the terrifying roar of the great cataclysmic clouds,
its path through the sky overspread by uplifted great parasols,
and beautified by swaying fly-whisks and networks of emanated bells.
Upon that radiant, preeminent great chariot, resplendent with various weapons,
he sat firmly established, adorned with a thousand vast and noble arms;
holding a beautiful quiver and a bow upon his left thigh, and other arrows in his remaining hands.
Adorned with various ornaments—diadems, necklaces, crowns, armlets, bracelets, and shoulder-plates;
with rings, waistbands, richly scented garments, girdles, anklets, and the like;
and decorated with diverse, radiant, and exceedingly costly decorations.
The hero, clad in armor, with a most serene lotus-face,
makes the three worlds tremble with the lion-like roar of his bowstring;
he is the destroyer of all enemies and the eradicator of all diseases.
To the bestower of all prosperity, who is attended by the glory of victory;
the auspicious one who grants all good fortune and destroys the fears of his devotees;
richly adorned with divine garlands and unguents, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
The Lord, standing in the midst of a multitude of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry;
the bestower of boons upon universal emperors and the sole protector of the world of men;
equal in splendor to the rising thousandfold sun.
Having meditated correctly upon the Great Powerful One— who possesses the sovereignty of the power of great yoga, whose fame has pervaded the three worlds,
who is descended from a portion of the glorious Cakrahari, and who is endowed with great strength—
one should utter the protection through the complete differentiation of the self.
Dattātreya is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (chandaḥ),
and Kārtavīryārjuna Viṣṇu, the universal emperor (cakravartin), is the deity. Furthermore, the application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for protection on all sides.
For the destruction of all that is evil and for the accomplishment of all goals,
may her five limb-forms, radiant as crystal, protect me—
those beginning with the Heart [mantra] located in the corners of Agni, Īśa, Asura, and Vāyu.
On all sides, they held in their hands radiant forms, heroic shields, and swords;
they were embodiments of unimpeded strength, sovereignty, power, and capability,
joined with the Śakti Kṣemaṅkarī, and were the destroyers of the pride of thieves.
May he who has arrows, arrow-rests, and weapons, who is accompanied by the Śrīkarā-śakti, and who shatters the pride of Mārī, protect the eastern direction for me.
May the glorious one, bearing the bow and arrow, protect my southern direction.
Endowed with the power of great sovereignty, the crusher of the pride of enemies,
and bearing a bow, may he protect the southern quarter for me.
Accompanied by the power that generates progeny, and the destroyer of wicked ones through his bow and arrows;
May the great Lord, accompanied by Vidyākārī and the destroyer of the wicked, properly protect my south-eastern direction, Citrabhānu. May the Lord,
bearing bow and arrows, protect my south-western direction.
May he who is endowed with the power of wealth, the destroyer of great calamities,
the wielder of the bow and quiver, protect my northwestern direction. May the glorious one, endowed with the power of longevity and the destroyer of fear, [protect me].
May the Lord who bears the bow and quiver protect my intermediate direction of Śiva;
may the all-pervading Lord, endowed with the glory of victory and manifest as the Thousand-rayed One,
become my protection in the upward direction, destroying great fear.
May the Bearer of the Conch, endowed with a great spear,
who is a sun that shatters the darkness of suffering, protect my downward direction; may he, joined with great yoga, protect the entire circle of the quarters.
May the Great Lord of Yogins, the Holder of the Lotus, protect me from all sides.
These directional forms are red, adorned with red garlands and garments;
they possess the forms of the principal deities and are each stationed upon an excellent chariot.
The Śaktis have lotuses in their hands and resemble blue water-lilies;
they wear very white garlands and garments, and are radiant with well-applied tilakas.
These attendant deities possess their respective vehicles, weapons, and ornaments.
May the mighty Indra and the other deities stationed in their respective directions protect me.
These have been declared to be all the deities of his [the deity’s] enclosures;
may they, endowed with all powers, always protect me from every side.
In the heart, the belly, the navel, the stomach, and the secret circle;
in the pair of thighs, the knees, and the feet; in the head and the pair of eyebrows;
and in the ears, eyes, nose, tongue, throat, and the pair of arms.
May the ten seed-mantras (*bīja*), which bestow perfect prosperity, which consist of radiant energy, and which are like wish-fulfilling trees, remain present and protect [us]. Furthermore,
may the other ten great syllables, which are the form of mantra and are intensely brilliant, [protect us].
May [the Lord], as the all-pervading one, protect us from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. May Kārtavīrya protect my head; may the Lord of the Haihayas protect my forehead;
may Sumukha protect my face; and may He who pervades the three worlds protect my ears.
May Sukamāra protect my jaw; may Dhanurdhara protect the pair of my eyebrows; may Puṇḍarīkākṣa protect my eyes; may Guṇākara protect my nose;
and may Brahmageya, the sage among the twice-born, always protect my upper and lower lips.
The support of all scriptures and arts is my tongue; the imperishable one is my chin; he who is dear to Dattātreya is my throat; the lord of royal lineages is my shoulders;
the destroyer of the pride of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa is my arms; and the one of great strength is my heart.
May he who grants all aims protect my hands; may he who is beloved by the world protect the tips of my fingers.
May the wise one protect my belly; may the conqueror of enemy cities protect my chest.
May he who is satiated by the play of the waters of the Revā protect my stomach.
Vīraśūra is my navel; the destroyer of all evil ones is my two sides;
the wielder of a thousand arms is my back; the lord of the seven islands is my waist;
the lord of Māhiṣmatī is my thighs; and the all-pervading beloved one is my knees.
May Vīrādhipa protect the calves; may Manojava protect the feet.
May he who bears all weapons protect every limb and all the vital points (marmas).
May Sarvaduṣṭāntaka protect the body composed of the eight elements (dhātus).
May He, who grants the desires of all the learned, protect the ten lords of life, beginning with Prāṇa;
may He, who has brought the collection of senses under control, protect all my senses;
and whatever place remains unmentioned, whether within or without the body—may He protect that as well.
May the Lord of the lords of all world-protectors protect all of that for me;
this body of mine, armored by the Vajra which is more solid than the essence itself,
is entirely free from hundreds of afflictions and devoid of fear.
Having bound on this divine armor, which cannot be pierced by the lord of the Haihayas,
I wander day and night with a fearless inner self,
even upon the royal highway, the great fortress, and paths crowded with thieves and other dangers.
In a rugged and terrible forest, in a forest fire or a mountain cave;
in battle amidst a mass of weapons, or in a place frequented by lions and tigers;
in a thicket infested with serpents, at twilight, or in the palace of a king.
In a dispute, in a vast whirlpool, at the seashore,
in a region crowded with waylayers, surrounded by bands of robbers,
when the loss of all one's possessions has occurred, or when a life-threatening danger has arisen.

When the earth is overcome by various diseases and old age, when beings have fallen into despair, when it is afflicted by pestilence, suffering, and the torments of nightmares, when it is defiled by betrayers of trust,
and when there is great physical pain and a great fever of the mind— p. 476).
Whether there be fear of mental anguish or physical disease, or obstacles, or even the affliction of fever— may no fear whatsoever arise for me who am shielded by this armor.
May all those who come seeking to harm, the celestial thieves and plunderers, [be repelled].
May that great chariot-warrior,
the crest-jewel of kings, swiftly destroy our adversaries with his thousand arms— pierced by arrows drawn from his own hands and shattered by thousands of shafts.

The son of Kṛtavīrya, the king adorned with a thousand arms, who possessed a thousand-spoked discus, [slew] the multitudes of wicked beings such as thieves— those torn by a thousand swords and afflicted by a thousand maces.
May the incarnation of Hari himself protect everything for me;
there shall be a king named Kārtavīryārjuna, possessed of a thousand arms,
by whose mere remembrance what is done and what is lost shall be recovered.
I bow to that Arjuna of great heroism, born from a portion of Hari on earth for the sake of protecting the world; he who is Kṛtavīryaka,
possessed of a thousand arms, with arrows and bow, clad in red garments, and wearing a red crown and earrings.
I bow to that Kārtavīrya, who destroys the fear of thieves and other evils, who grants all desires, and who manifests with great power;
O Kārtavīrya! O you of great heroism! O destroyer of all the wicked!
Abide everywhere and at all times, destroy the evil-doers, and protect me.
May he who bears five hundred arrows in his right hand and five hundred bows in his left protect us, who are distressed by hundreds of venomous serpents!
Arise, O Subduer of the Wicked! Sole Protector of the Seven Islands!
You alone are my refuge; protect me, protect me from all sides!
Arise! Why do you sleep? Why do you remain for so long?
Always protect us from all fears, as if we were your own children.
Those who are thieves, plunderers of wealth, enemies, and those who are harmful; those who create obstacles, the wicked, those of sinful intent, and those of evil disposition;
those with malicious hearts, corrupt kings, and wicked persons who ought to be honored—[may they all be overcome].

Those who obstruct their duties, those who are wicked and stand as adversaries, those who seize all one's possessions, and others who are deceitful; those Mlecchas who cause great affliction, as well as robbers and the base; [may they all be subdued].
Those who are great plunderers, deceivers with weapons in hand;

those who are sinful, performers of evil deeds, givers of suffering, and possessed of wicked intent; those who are extortionists, addicted to evil paths, and those who inflict various kinds of fear—[may they be subdued].
May all those who are constantly intent on seeking our vulnerabilities and are prepared to harm us— those who have been struck by the great conch and the boar of Kārtavīrya—
be utterly deluded and go suddenly to their destruction from afar.
Those who are Dānavas and great Daityas, those who are Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,
those Piśācas of great power, those Bhūtas and Brahmarākṣasas,
those who are Apasmāra-grahas, and those grahas that devour flesh;
There are Vetālas and Guhyakas who consume great quantities of blood;
they possess the speed of mind, intellect, and the senses; they are Sphoṭakas and those afflicted by great fevers; they are great eaters, consumers of offerings, and devourers of great corpses.
The Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, and those born from the wombs of gods and others; the Dākinīs, Ghonasas, Pretas, Kṣetrapālas, and Vināyakas;
[and those] in the form of great tigers, great rams, and great horses.
They are great offerings, like great lions and resembling great buffaloes;
they have the forms of bears, boars, and dogs, and the bodies of owls;
they possess the uneven heads of great camels, donkeys, cats, and serpents.
Great beings of various forms, who bestow thousands of diverse afflictions; who cause various diseases—mean, yet possessing great heroism and great strength;
those characterized by wind, bile, the terrible phlegm, and the combination of all three.
The Māheśvaras, Vaiṣṇavas, Vairivaṃśyas, and Mahāgrahas;
the Skāndas, Vaināyakas, and those cruel ones born of the Pramathas;
the Mahāśatru-grahas, Raudras, Mahāmārīs, and Masūrikās.
Fever that lasts for one day, two days, or three days; quartan fevers, those occurring every fortnight, monthly, or every six months;
and those occurring annually—these most terrible fevers are difficult to ward off.
And those great portents occurring in dreams, and the malevolent planets that cause suffering;
the Kuṣmāṇḍas, Jṛmbhakas, Bhaumas, Ghonāsas, and Nidhivañcakas;
the Bhrāmakas, the life-takers, and those such as the Bālagrahas.
Those who roam by day, those who roam by night, and those who are fierce during the twilights— whether they be heedless or vigilant— whoever is intent on harming us,
all of them shall be afflicted by arrows released from the bow of the Lord of the Haihayas.
May those who have lost their courage, strength, and effort perish by the thousands—
those serpents, those great nāgas dwelling in mountain caves,
the black vipers with great fangs known as the great pythons.
And the Anantakulikā and others, who are greatly feared for the venom of their fangs;
by this [mantra], there are the hundred-headed ones, the fierce ones with mottled tails,
the great-venomed water-scorpions, and the scorpions with red tails.
Venomous snakes known as *kālakūṭa* and *mahāhālāhala*,
water-snakes, aquatic predators, crocodiles, *māsika* fish, those with poisonous tails, and whatever other creatures dwell in the water.
Those born in water and those born on land, arising from hundreds of various species;
those that are six-spotted, spiders, bees, and those with parrot-like tails;
whether stationary, mobile, or artificial—all these are of great venom.
The guptarūpa, guptaviṣa, mūṣika, and gṛhagodhika [poisons],
the terrible apasmāra-poisons known as mahograviṣa—
those which desire to afflict us and destroy our bodies and life-breaths.

May all those— whether humans, beasts, trees, or forest-dwelling monkeys— be destroyed from afar by the thousand fragments of Kārtavīrya’s sword, their sensory powers and their arrogance utterly ruined.
Lions, tigers, boars, and buffaloes— those great beasts;
elephants, horses, gayals, donkeys, śarabhas, wolves, dogs,
slanderers, śūdras, and cats born from holes.
Jackals, rabbits, hawks, Garuḍas, and birds;
Bheruṇḍas, crows, vultures, swans, and other species of winged creatures;
those born from sprouts, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and those born from the womb.
Born into various distinct lineages and possessing diverse and manifold dispositions,
those who seek to harm us at the junctions of day and night, or by day or by night— they shall swiftly be pulverized by the thousands of maces of Kārtavīrya.
May those whose progress and manliness have perished perish from afar—
those who hurl insults, those who harbor hatred, those who are revilers, those who devise cruel machines, and others who are deceitful and full of guile.
Those who perform killing, expulsion, uprooting, hatred, and delusion;
those wicked men who are betrayers of trust and traitors to their masters;
those who are murderous assailants, the wicked, the sinful, and those who strike at cows—[for these, one should employ the following].

These beings of various forms, as well as others of wicked species, who inflict the extreme sufferings of burning, injury, poison, and the stroke of weapons, and who bring about the fear of seizing fields and wealth, imprisonment, and so forth.
Those who constantly cause suffering and seek to find a weakness to inflict harm—
may they all be torn asunder by the thousand wheels of Kārtavīrya;
may they be destroyed from afar and go to their ruin in a thousand ways.
Those clouds, those great rains, those winds, and those lightnings;
those blazing great thunderbolts and dreadful portents such as earthquakes;
those terrible falls of meteors, and those such as the bow of Indra (the rainbow), and so forth—
The Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and the terrible Ketus; the lunar mansions and the zodiac signs;
the lunar days, the solar transits, the months, the years, and the leaders of the Yugas.
The lords of the Manvantaras, the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis who have attained perfection through yoga,
the Śrutis beginning with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the sacrificial fires,
the seasons, the world-protectors, the ancestors, and the assembly of gods.
And the sixty-four branches of knowledge arising within the three worlds—
all these indeed have been proclaimed, as well as others that have not been mentioned;
may they always be auspicious to us and bring happiness at all times.
By the command of Kārtavīrya, the lord of yogins of immeasurable luster,
Kārtavīryārjuna— the archer, the king of kings, the sovereign of the Haihayas,
the most beloved of Dattātreya, and adorned with a thousand arms— [acted].
He was a wielder of the bow, the sword, the chariot, the arrow, the quiver, and the shield, possessed of great strength;
he was fortunate, fair-faced, peaceful, a universal monarch, and a mine of virtues;
he was the destroyer of the pride of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, content in his divine play, and exceedingly difficult to conquer.
The destroyer of the wicked, the subduer of thieves, the sovereign lord of kings, the master;

the omniscient, the giver of all, the illustrious one, the bestower of desires upon all the learned, the accomplished one; the crest-jewel of kings, the yogi, the supreme leader of the seven continents.
Victorious over all kings, possessed of great intelligence and free from greed, beloved by gods and Brahmins, learned, eternal, worthy of praise by the knowers of Brahman,
lord of Māhiṣmatī, a warrior of great fame and mighty arms.
The delicate great hero, the slayer of Māra, with intoxicating eyes.
Śatrughna, the eternal, the hero, the bearer of the conch, the beloved of the cowherds;
the great devotee of the Lord, the wise one, the destroyer of great fear;
he whose form is unassailable, whose nature is divine, who pervades the three worlds.
The repository of all scriptures and arts, stainless, and honored by the world;
a hero, rich in pure essence, and possessed of great strength and prowess;
consisting of the glory of victory and none other, he is the conqueror of enemies and the leader of mantras.
The bearer of the discus, the granter of desires, the beloved, the destroyer of desire, the lotus-eyed one;
he who is fond of auspicious speech, the physician, the wise, the giver of boons, the self-controlled;
he who has conquered his senses, who has vanquished his enemies, the Great One of infinite prowess.
The wielder of the wheel, the destroyer of enemy armies, honored by the rules of combat;
possessed of great wealth, lord of treasures, a great yogi, and dear to his preceptor; rich in yoga, the destroyer of all diseases, and the one who has illuminated the entire surface of the earth.
The wielder of divine weapons, the one of immeasurable soul, the protector of all, the greatly radiant;
the bearer of all arms, the bestower of desired boons, the conqueror of enemy cities;
the perfected in yoga, the one of massive form, the lord of hundreds of great hosts.

The treasury of all knowledge, ever striving to bestow all accomplishments—may these forms arising from the eight hundred names of the Lord of the Ten Directions, having completely pervaded the ten directions, protect me always. (p. 480)
Mental happiness, unimpeded well-being, freedom from disease, invincibility,
the destruction of suffering, the slaying of enemies, the increase of progeny, the dawning of prosperity, the attainment of desires— such is auspiciousness: impartiality and health.
Freedom from laziness, fulfillment of desires, the destruction of death, the increase of strength, the removal of fear, fame, beauty, great eminence in knowledge and intellect,
the non-loss of wealth, and the recovery of what has been lost.
May I possess long life, the attainment of my heart's desires, cherished delicacy, invincibility, freedom from disease, and great power,
by the mere recitation of Kārtavīrya, the lord of the Haihayas.
This armor of Kārtavīrya increases merit,
pacifies all sins, destroys all calamities,
brings about all peace, is secret, and eliminates every fear.
It bestows victory and wealth upon men, grants all prosperity, and is auspicious.
Whether one hears it, recites it, or even worships the book,
or whoever constantly wears it upon their head, they shall attain all desires.
One is liberated from all sufferings and shall be victorious everywhere;
one is never afflicted by plagues, thieves, and the like.
For one who recites this upon rising in the morning, bad dreams and other such evils perish.
He who recites this armor-mantra while lying upon his bed at night obtains his desired objects and is honored even by the gods;
for him, there is no fear caused by thieves, enemies, evil dreams, or the like.
When one sees that one’s own wealth, such as cattle and so forth, has been stolen by thieves,
then by reciting [the mantra] seven times at night while facing the western direction,
one obtains the lost property within seven nights; of this there is no doubt.

If one facing the eastern direction recites [this] twenty-seven times, then one shall ward off an enemy army resembling the hosts of gods and asuras. In debate, in strife, or in terrible conflict, he who recites this five times [shall prevail].
Victory comes to him; never shall there be defeat.
One should recite this properly twelve times at night for liberation from bondage.
Within three days, one seized by shackles is released; of this there is no doubt.
By this very procedure, in all rites of accomplishment,
the best of mantra-knowers may achieve even the unachievable within seven days.
That man who recites this at the time of departure and travels on the road, [shall succeed].
He shall have no fear of thieves, tigers, or other adversaries;
by reciting this constantly while remaining at home, he is filled with auspicious blessings.
No fear shall ever arise for him from wicked beings or the like.
In times of affliction by all diseases, one should recite [the mantra] three or five times.
He will not be harmed by disease, death, vetālas, bhūtas, or pretas.
One should perform a sprinkling upon the world, pouring water from cupped hands over one's own body.
And he is not afflicted by diseases such as those caused by poison or by boils;
whoever, having conquered his senses, recites this at the three junctions of the day for six months,
shall overcome even death when its time has arrived— of this there is no doubt.
If one recites this armor-mantra (*kavaca*), poison does not affect the body;
there shall be no dullness, blindness, or muteness, nor any fear of calamities anywhere.
Having meditated upon the deity as being of that very nature according to the prescribed method twenty times, [one attains this].
The practitioner should again recite the king of mantras obtained through the grace of the guru;
protected once more by the armor-mantra (kavaca), he should perform meditation on the mantra.
At the outset, he should perform an invocation preceded by meditation upon its name.
One should utter the four mantra-syllables preceded by the seed-syllable;
likewise, at the end of the mantras, one should utter them preceded by the seed-syllable.
Indeed, he who, being composed, performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body in this manner—
He shall immediately obtain the fruit as described and become one whose body is like adamant. One must not reveal this armor to anyone whatsoever;
it should be guarded with great effort, just like the word of Śiva.
One should bestow this upon a devoted and excellent disciple who offers all his possessions,
for the benefit of practitioners— this which was spoken by the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
and which, as the armor of Kārtavīrya, has indeed been told by me to you.
O Goddess! That which has been gazed upon by him does not decay even with the passage of time. Therefore, a wise person should wear this armor with every effort.
Kārtavīrya, the son of Kṛtavīrya, was indeed powerful and a hater of the wicked.
Sahasrabāhu, Śatrughna, Raktavāsas, Dhanurdhara,
Raktagandha, Raktamālya— the King who grants the desires of those who remember him.
Whoever recites these twelve names of Kārtavīrya, [attains his goal].
"Successes arise for him, and people are always under his control.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Armor of Kārtavīryārjuna," in the *Śrī Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra*, within the *Kārtavīryārjunakalpa* from the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Branches," in the fourth section on Desired Rites (*kāmyakāṇḍa*) of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*.
Now follows the ritual application of the cock (*kukkuṭaprayoga*).
In the second chapter of the *Phetkāriṇītantra*:
"Now I shall explain, in brief and according to the human tradition, the mantra of the cock (*kukkuṭa-mantra*),
just as it was formerly taught by the teachers of the Kṣapaṇakas who were intent on benefiting the worlds."
The mantra ending in *na*, followed by the sixth vowel (*ū*) with a *bindu* (*nūṃ*), known as "Cock" (*kukkuṭa*), repeated;
then again the previous word repeated;
and [the word] ending in *na*, followed by the fifth vowel (*u*)—this is said to be the *āyus* mantra.
This fifteen-syllable mantra, which bestows glory, power, happiness, good fortune, and prosperity, is said to have the cock as its presiding deity;
its form is augmented by the splendor and power of all the deities.

In the midst of the ocean of milk, upon a supreme island with ground composed of gold and jewels, there arose a vast and stainless tree— delightful, cooled by gentle groves of soft sand, pearls, and gems, and bearing a multitude of excellent jewel-like fruits.
One should again meditate upon him as standing upon a golden palm tree, which has excellent leaves variegated by the brilliance of many jewels; his entire body is radiant,
his face is adorned with a most beautiful crest, and his feet and claws are exceedingly sharp like those of a cock.
May He— who has six faces for His mouth, the Daughter of the Mountain for His belly, Kālahā for His back,
and two feet with the faces of a peacock and a dog,
one curved and the other straight; whose wings are the celestial trees, and whose jeweled chain is the bond that draws in all desires— protect us.
This is not a mere cock for us;
dwelling eternally upon the lotus-hand of Gaurī, with Kāma mounted upon his six faces, radiant with every ornament, with feet in constant motion, and expert in the flapping of its wings.

May the cock, who has the luster of gold, whose round neck is radiant with a crest-jewel made of gems, whose nature is his own form, who delights all people, and who bestows all perfections, protect us. || 1 ||
Alternatively:
Beloved by all, residing on a jewel-island in the midst of the ocean, a cock dwelling in a palm grove,
delighting in the sciences and enriched with every ornament— he quickly brings others under his control when well-served by men.
For the sake of prior service to that [deity],
having performed a great worship of the Lord in a temple of Śiva containing a single liṅga on a mountain peak by a riverbank— a temple of Śiva devoid of a bull— he sat facing the north.
At the western gate, one should perform the preliminary rites of mantra;
having bowed the head to the Guru, one should prepare a seat. Then, one should perform the purification of the hands, the purification of the body, and the triple clapping of the palms (tālatraya).
Thereafter, being intent upon it, one should perform the binding of the directions with the Vidyā-mantra;
then, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the Praṇava.
One should first project the Mātṛkā and thereafter perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should first designate the heart-mantra of the Bird-mantra;
having uttered the second word, one should join it with the head-mantra.
Having placed *vāṃ* in the crest, one should assign the third part of the Bird-mantra as the armor.
Having uttered the fourth word (*turīyapada*), one should apply it to the eyes.
Then, the six limbs (*aṅga-ṣaṭka*) joined with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) are prescribed for the two [eyes].
One should assign [the mantras] in sequence: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ*.
The wise practitioner should sequentially place the letters beginning with *pu* and ending with *vaṃ* on the forehead,
in the middle of the *bindu*, on the eyes, the ears,
the two nostrils, the mouth, the throat, and likewise on the heart.
One should place [the mantras] in the stomach, the region of the navel, the penis, and the secret parts.
Then, with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) starting from the head.
Having thus performed the placement upon the body, one should meditate on that which has the nature of both Fire and Śiva.
Having worshipped the deity mentally with the sixteen types of offerings,
having made a formal request and invoked the deity through sacrifice, and having diligently gratified Him,
one should meditate upon the cock-deity and recite the mantra a thousand times the number of suns (one million).
Having first performed one hundred recitations for the sake of propitiation,
the knower of mantras should perform the desired rites— such as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, paralyzing, and eradication— by means of this mantra.
Having inscribed on a palm leaf the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*),
interwoven with the mantra, and having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein, if one recites it one hundred and eight times and wears it, she seeks refuge [in the practitioner].
If betel is given for her to consume after being consecrated by reciting the mantra one thousand and eight times, [the same result follows].
By constant instruction, she will always remain submissive and grant the wealth and desired enjoyments one requests.
Furthermore, for him who mutters the mantra called *pañcakamala*, which consists of five parts and is joined with the five limbs,
and applies it to the rules for various kinds of food— whether solid or soft— that woman shall remain under his control until death.
Its root, along with radish, the bark of the tree called *citā*, its flower, the seed of *savarī*, *hastikusuma*, *svarṇāsikā*, *antarjala*,
and the leaf of *rohiṇa*— these five parts, when combined in a vessel and administered together to a man; or alternatively, [administered] individually.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over this ghee and *hayamāra* flowers,
if one casts it upon the head of someone for seven nights, that woman will come under his control by the power of love.
Hayamāra is Karavīra.

Having inscribed this mantra, interspersed with the name of the person to be subjugated, upon birch bark, and having placed it within the heart of a doll fashioned from the clay of a potter's workshop, one should establish the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein.

Then, having recited [the mantra] three times at each junction of the day for seven days, one should grind that [doll] with *bhāṇḍīra* flowers and smear [it]; [the target] will certainly be brought under control.
And it will also exist in other births;
*bhāṇḍī* and *bhārgī*.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, holding it with both hands joined at the heart and placing it upon the head along with its roots and stalks,
that excellent minister will certainly become beloved by all the world;
she who holds it with joined palms is modest.
Thus, by the recitation of the mantra, he should bear upon his head the flowers of the Lakṣmī-creeper of the hundred sacrifices, as well as the Samudrā, Bhadrakā, Viṣṇupriyā,
and Mūṣalī, along with Madhuka, Dūrvā, and Sahā, as they were held.
In that same way, even one [repetition] is capable of bringing about auspiciousness in the heavenly world;
what need is there to mention [the merit] in the worlds of men?
[The fruits are obtained] through ten, eight, six, three, two, and one [repetitions], respectively, in the sequence beginning with the *añjali* gesture.
Having combined the ten [ingredients] that bring everything under control,
and having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for each, and having again combined the ten and ground them into a pill, one should recite it eight thousand times; then,
by applying the rite of the *tilaka* mark with a pill ignited by the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), one achieves the enchantment of gods, women, and men, and so forth.

One should take a thousand wicks filled with various powders from which the soot has been removed, mix them with camphor, and consecrate them with a thousand recitations of the mantra. By applying this daily to the eyes, one will inevitably bring all people under one's control.
These are the applications for subjugation (*vaśya*).
Having meditated upon oneself as a cock by means of the power of one's own *gaṇa*,
and having bound the person to be acted upon by the neck with a chain, one should follow behind them while reciting the *kiṭi* mantra.

For three nights, remaining vigilant at midnight, one should recite a thousand times the name of the person to be accomplished along with one's own ritual action, joining it with the fourth crow-cry; this should be done in all rites such as subjugation and the like.
Beginning from that moment, as she recited this [mantra], Madālasā became crushed by intoxication; wearing only wet garments, her mind agitated by passion,
her secret parts and hips fully blossomed, and her clothes and ornaments loosened.
With her footsteps faltering, her bodice bristling with horripilation,
her sighs heated by the fire of passion, and her sprout-like lower lip radiant;
with her mass of hair disheveled, trembling, and her eyes rolling.
With palms joined in reverence, she comes of her own accord to his dwelling at night;

having inscribed this mantra— interwoven with the invocation of the *sādhya* and accompanied by the ritual action— upon the inner surface of a betel leaf using a stylus, and having performed the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Having recited this mantra eight hundred times over a lamp made from the milk of an *arka* plant,
within three nights, Urvaśī herself will become submissive and take refuge in him, as he is secretly enveloped by the flame of that lamp’s fire.
Having written this entire mantra on birch bark, encased within the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), [one should proceed].
Furthermore, having recited this one hundred and eight times until it has acquired its vital power,
and then reciting the mantra again for three nights while adding it separately to honey, milk, and ghee, one attracts the desired woman even from the realms of the Nāgas and other worlds before long.

Having written this mantra, together with her name and deed, upon a shallow dish using yellow pigment (*rocanā*) at night, and having performed one hundred and eight recitations while keeping the wind away,
one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood facing her navel; thus, she becomes helpless under the impulse of the bodiless god of love.
Or else,

having entered into the water up to the navel, one should recite the mantra— interwoven with the name of the person to be accomplished— for one thousand times over three days; thus, one will certainly attract the desired object.
Thus is the summoning.
One should grind together monkey hair, asafoetida, dārvī, and donkey skin.
That powder, consecrated with the mantra and interwoven with the name and the ritual action, [is to be used].
Furthermore, by that [rite],
even two who are exceedingly hostile will become affectionate toward one another, despite being previously estranged.
One should write the mantra, interwoven with the name and the ritual action (*karma*), upon a palm leaf.
Having performed the ritual installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and recited [the mantra] three thousand times over it,
one should split a poison-smeared object into two pieces and bury them on both banks of a river.
Through this, even between Umā and Īśāna, who are otherwise affectionate toward each other, there will swiftly arise mutual enmity.
On both banks of the Sindhu river,
on both sides of the stream, the best of mantra-knowers, having taken the wings of an owl and a crow,
should write the mantra— enclosed within the syllables of the person to be acted upon (sādhya)— into a shallow dish (śarāva) during the night.
One should bury [the mantra], over which the wind has been established and which has been recited a thousand times, at a crossroads;
this will certainly bring about paralysis for all beings, of this there is no doubt.
"Sthāpitapavana" means that the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) has been performed.

Or else, having quickly fashioned an effigy from charcoal from a cremation ground, hair, and cloth from a corpse— properly empowered by breath, with the name of the victim placed within the heart, marked on the forehead with mantras, empowered by breath through the wearing of the cloth,
consecrated by a thousand recitations, and established with life-force;
For the purpose of binding, one should perform an even more intense immobilization ritual using extremely sharp water;
having written the mantra upon a heap of ashes and fashioned a kila-stake, one should perform the rite together with the name and the wind-element.
Having performed three thousand recitations, one should then utter the sound on the path to bring about the halting of the vehicle.

On a Nimba tree planted by an enemy, one should bury at night this mantra—conjoined with the name of the foe and designated by that name—which has been empowered through nine thousand recitations and other rites; this shall obstruct the enemy's army on its path.
Thus ends the rite of immobilization.
Having recited [the mantra] over charcoal from a funeral pyre belonging to an enemy’s *nairṛta* asterism,

and having burnt it in a fire taken from that same funeral pyre, one should mix its ashes with a mere amount of the enemy’s name— accompanied by the ritual action (*manukarma*)— and write it upon one’s own head.
If this is recited eight thousand times on a Tuesday coinciding with the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*), O Śivā, that enemy is swiftly driven away.

One should bury a vessel called "Karma," into which the mantra has been recited one thousand times, at the gate of an enemy's house; thereby their eradication occurs swiftly. Having cast [the vessel] into a crow's nest, burnt it over a fire located in a cemetery, and mixed the resulting ashes with the mantra, [one should apply it] to the enemy.
Having written the name at the head of the mantra of the pair of vital points (*marmayuga*), one should perform the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) after reciting it eight thousand times.

On a Tuesday coinciding with the fourteenth lunar day, O Śivā, having performed the recitation three thousand times with the mantra enriched by the name of the action, and having placed it upon the head of the enemy, one should cast it down; thus he shall swiftly and immediately cause that enemy to be eradicated.

Or, having recited the mantra five thousand times over a garment born of a cremation ground while associating it with the name and actions of the enemy, one should throw it at the door; within seven days, it will cause the expulsion of such-and-such an enemy. Furthermore, the practitioner of mantra, performing the rite, should take a stake made of wood from a funeral pyre and empower it eight thousand times.

One should bury the mantra, recited over it, in the house of an enemy; this causes that person to be eradicated in an instant. Having prepared ink from the juice of the *unmatta* plant, one should write the mantra on a board made of *kāraskara* wood, encased between the name of the person and the action to be performed.
Having fixed one's vital breaths upon this [mantra], which is empowered by the eight poisons of the enemy,
one should recite it a thousand times at a cremation ground or a crossroads;
then, burying it in the enemy's house under the eighth lunar mansion of the foe, that enemy will quickly be driven to another land.
Because of this, he is always ill, and the other worlds are terrified of him.
Thus ends the rite of eradication.

Having written the mantra with the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) enclosed within it on a palm leaf, and having placed that [leaf] inside a doll and positioned it in a current of air, one should then recite it eight thousand times at night in a cemetery blazing with madness-inducing fire; then, having cut it repeatedly with sharp oil for three days until midnight, [the result follows].
One may cause delusion or death.
When empowered by reciting the mantra one thousand times over an image made from *madhyārka* wood, even a corpse in a cremation ground is pinned down.
By means of the mantra, one causes [the enemy] to split apart; whatever limb of the adversary is targeted by the empowered mantra, that very limb perishes.
Having fashioned a doll from clay mixed with earth from the footprints of an enemy and the soil from a cremation ground, one should write its name upon the heart, the head, or the feet;
and with charcoal from a cemetery, one should inscribe this mantra together with that person's name and their action.
Having quickly placed this wind-mantra (*pavana*) conjoined with the *cakrī* and *mṛdā* upon his heart,

and having fashioned an effigy (*puttalikā*), one should write its name upon the heart, the head, or the feet; then, using charcoal from a cremation ground, one should quickly place this mantra— conjoined with that person's name and deed— upon his heart.
One should recite the *pavana* mantra three thousand times; then,
having cut that effigy into a hundred pieces with an unbroken blade while facing the southern direction, one should [dispose of them] in the blazing fire of a cremation ground over ten days.

Having sprinkled extremely pungent oil and offered it as an oblation under the Naidhana constellation, the mantra-practitioner will surely cause the enemy to hasten to the city of the Lord of the Dead (Yama). "Under the Naidhana constellation" means under the star of the enemy's death.

On a Tuesday, at the rising of the Kulika, having drawn the image of an enemy established upon a leaf, and having performed the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), one should offer it as an oblation in the cremation ground after smearing it with poison; thus the enemy shall perish. Having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of cow dung, [one should place it] in its heart.
Having written the mantra interspersed with the name on a palm leaf,
and having placed it upon an image [of the person],
one should properly set down a silver or earthen jar filled with cow dung.
Therein, the wise one should place the mantra within a container known as "the written";
having established the life-force of the enemy therein in cow-dung water,
he should recite it at the three junctions of the day, and [the result] will come to pass in its shadow.
Having seen the shadow of the enemy in cow-dung water, one who is concentrated in mind should cut off whatever limb he desires with the Astra-mantra;
that very limb of the enemy perishes within seven days— of this there is no doubt.
If the heart, belly, or throat are pierced, death will occur;
if there is a wound from a weapon on the head, he will suffer from a disease of the head.
[The remedy is: dry ginger, asafoetida, *citraka*, black pepper, and *rohiṇī-pippalī*.
The wise have declared this poison to be like the smoke of a peacock from a fire of slow-burning wood.
[The plants are: Kāraskara, Āmalakī, Audumbara, Jambu, Khadira, and Kṛṣṇā;
Vaṃśa, Pippala, Nāga, Rohiṇa, Malina, Asana, and Bhrūmālikā.
The names of the barks are ariṣṭa, bilva, vikaṅkata, kadamba, and bakula;
and the roots shine like vañjula, panasa, arka, śamī, kadamba, and nimba.
Then, he who recites [the mantra] a thousand times with devotion using *kapīsī* flowers during the ritual of recitation shall become the abode of Ramā.
When the recitation is accomplished, one should daily recite this mantra one hundred and eight times over a cock;
one should meditate upon Maheśa, who has assumed the form of a cock with a neck [adorned] accordingly.
Honored five times [daily], his abode is filled within a year with various kinds of objects of desire and other such things.

Having meditated upon the Lord in the form of a cock, or else as Māyā herself through her own power, he who constantly at dawn, with a joyful mind, repeatedly scattered jewels all around from his own city with his foot— the supporter of the earth— [attains the goal].
If one recites the mantra with devotion to Upendra, Lakṣmī will look upon him as her own;
she will cover that earth—which has had its palm-leaf fans shattered by the truth—with fragments of jewels as fruits.
Having meditated on his own mantra, he who recites it with his eyes fixed [on the deity] attains a state like that of Indra, even if he was previously an enemy.
Shaking like the wing of his own side, having meditated upon the jewel of the supreme limit (parārdha)— which has rays as its golden-hued flowers—
and having recited the mantra with perfect concentration, he will surely attain abundant and mature prosperity filled with jewels.

For one who, while joyfully scattering streaks of golden dust and soil upon the ground, cooing with delight as he scatters heaps of grain with his beak and feet, meditates upon the radiant, ruddy cock with its neck slightly curved, and recites this [mantra]: [The mantra follows: *oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya mahābhairavāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalalocanāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalakeśāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalajaṭākalāpāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalavāsase kṛṣṇapiṅgaladaṃṣṭrākarālavadanāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalajihvālaṃbakāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalakarṇāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalanāsikāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalabhrūlatāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalalalāṭāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalottamāṅgāya kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāśaktidhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahātriśūladhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahākhadgadhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahācakradhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāhaladhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāgadādhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāmuśaladhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāparaśudhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāśūladhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāvajradhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahānetradhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāpātradhāriṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāśirābhakṣiṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāmarma-bhakṣiṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāsandhibhakṣiṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāparvabhakṣiṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāsaṃdhiparvabhakṣiṇe kṛṣṇapiṅgalamahāsaṃdhisaṃdhānabhakṣi
A granary is filled with grain and other riches.
The ash produced by burning the ten medicinal herbs, consecrated by this mantra and recited over it at night, should be worn on the body;
it removes the fear of evil, disease, poison, and malevolent spirits, and for those who resort to it, it is an exceedingly beautiful means of subjugation that bestows the Goddess of Fortune.
Fuel from dry land, leather, and ash, when consecrated three times according to the rules with a thousand recitations, provide protection for everything.
A birch-bark leaf upon which only the name is written, when held while accompanied by the recitation of the mantra— specifically the *taṇḍula-mantra*— swiftly protects a person.
He who knows that [mantra] likewise recited one thousand times over a cock will quickly conquer his own flocks of cocks in battle;
having remembered it and contemplated it a thousand times, he should recite the cock-mantra.
He who has arrived shall instantly conquer in battle his own warriors through those whose weapons are their feet.
What need is there for much here? Whatever is written by Manu is easily accomplished as soon as it is desired.
For him who recites this, the pure Kamalā (Lakṣmī) comes to dwell in his home without delay.

Thus, having observed the cock of those devoted to recitation, he—having cast down the faction of the enemies of Bhūta by means of the Kṣapaṇaka who carried away [the enemy]—was one who swiftly cast aside the wings of his own assembly; a protector of virtuous people who bowed before him while devouring all [others];
a *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) for all supplicants who desired anything; and one skilled in attracting and delighting the best of gods, men, and women.
Then [one should write] Ananta joined with Bindu, followed by the pair Puṅkolī;
then Vāṃ, which is Śakti, and then the pair Puṅkolī.
Then the syllable Vu mounted upon Varuṇa, Ananta, and Vāsa-Bindu.
One should extract the charming mantra from the crowing cock.
Thus ends the application of the cock.
Now follows the practice of the Ucchiṣṭā-Cāṇḍālī.
In that very same [text], in the sixth chapter:
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O Śambhu! Various types of mantras have been indicated by you to me previously;
now I wish to hear the mantra concerning the Goddess preceded by Ucchiṣṭa.
Śambhu said:
Listen, O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips! I shall tell you of that goddess, by the mere knowledge of whom a man becomes composed of wisdom.
The Goddess said:
O Lord! Please tell me with effort this secret that has been disclosed: what is the ritual procedure for this [vidyā], what is its fruit, and what is its nature as a vidyā within me?
Śambhu said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall declare the ritual procedure and the results, such as eradication (*uccāṭana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, O Goddess, even immobile poison (*sthāvaraviṣa*) is destroyed through the power of this knowledge.
Now, O Beloved, I shall further proclaim another most secret mantra of the Goddess.
The goddess Mātaṅgī, preceded by Ucchiṣṭa, who bestows all siddhis;
the goddess who removes all sins and is devoid of all defects—
by the knowledge of whom alone all calamities come to an end.

O Goddess of the Gods! This supreme knowledge, which destroys all sins, conquers poison—whether stationary, mobile, artificial, or even that which is mobile and resides within the body of a stationary being. This is the supreme lore, the destroyer of every evil.
Bestowing heaven and liberation, and granting the fruits of sovereignty and happiness,
this goddess was previously accomplished by me as free from poison;
this vidyā, when recited but once, is the purifier of even the slaughter of a Brahmin.

This [goddess] is the destroyer of all sins and the bestower of all good fortune. O Goddess! if one should ever remember the Goddess while having an impure mouth, then he becomes purified by sipping water (ācamana), even without the performance of the formal rite of ācamana.
The unfortunate shall surely become fortunate, and the sorrowful shall become happy;
even the barren woman shall obtain a son who lives for a hundred years.
The destitute shall acquire wealth, and the fool shall attain knowledge.
Whatever accomplishment one prays for, one shall obtain that very thing by means of Haṭha.
O charming Goddess! Listen, for I shall now describe the procedure here:
O Goddess, immediately after eating, even if the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) has not been performed;
Having first offered the bali-oblation with the root mantra, the practitioner should then meditate upon that Goddess and recite the mantra for the sake of attaining his desired success.
Listen to the mantra, O Great Goddess! I shall tell it to you exactly as it is.
Then one should utter "Namaḥ" preceded by "ucchiṣṭa," and likewise "cāṇḍālinī.
Thereafter, one should proclaim the goddess Sumukhī;
after that, Mahāpiśācinī; and beyond that, the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjā).

Furthermore, O Great Goddess, the two *ṭha* syllables joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*, and accompanied by the *visarga*, bestow all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). For this, no specific lunar day (*tithi*), nor asterism (*nakṣatra*), nor fasting (*upavāsa*) is prescribed.

For him in whom this mantra resides, there is no mention of the placement of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the placement of hands (*karanyāsa*), or the placement of syllables (*varṇanyāsa*); nor is there any restriction of place, nor obstacle, nor impurity, nor any restrictive rule. He is not overcome by obstacles.
O Sovereign of the World! I shall describe her meditation exactly as it is:
she is seated upon a corpse, clothed in red garments, adorned with red ornaments, and decorated with a necklace of *guñjā* seeds.
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon a sixteen-year-old maiden with full and elevated breasts,
holding a skull-cup in her hand, who is the embodiment of the supreme light,
by means of the yoga of the "young" (bāla) and "right" (dakṣiṇa).
Having offered the bali-oblation with the remnants [of food], one should recite the mantra with the mind fixed upon it.
One who desires success must perform the recitation of this [mantra] using only the remnants;
for all perfections arise for one who is engaged in the recitation of the remnants.
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen as I shall describe the fruit-yielding fire-oblation (homa) and libation (santarpaṇa) for her, which quickly brings about the accomplishment of one's purpose:
having composed oneself, one should draw a square mandala upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

O Goddess! the knower of mantras should worship the maṇḍala with the root mantra. Then, having established the Goddess as being present in the form of fire, and having meditated upon the Goddess, he should perform the homa sacrifice with curd, prepared rice, and grains.
By performing one thousand oblations according to the prescribed rite, a king becomes subject to his will.
Furthermore, he who performs a fire sacrifice for the Goddess with the flesh of a cat shall attain the supreme knowledge that transcends both weapons and scriptures.
One should perform a homa with goat meat combined with honey, one thousand times according to the prescribed rite; thereby, the attainments of wealth come to pass.
One desiring knowledge should perform the homa with sugar, honey, and milk-rice (pāyasa).

Furthermore, O Great Goddess, the fourteen accomplished vidyās indeed belong to him. Having performed a fire-oblation with the cloth of a menstruating woman, honey, and milk-rice, he shall bring the three worlds under his control.
One should perform the homa with nāgavallī, honey, and ghee ten thousand times according to the prescribed rite; then the *siddhividya* will certainly be attained.
Immediately, [the same result is achieved] with cat meat, ghee, and honey.

By means of [an offering] joined with the hair of a *cāṇḍāla*, the summoning [of the desired object] will certainly occur. By performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the flesh of a hare mixed with honey, one obtains knowledge, wealth, and excellent women.

By means of *dhustūra* and *arka*, the knower of mantras should perform a fire-oblation in the funeral pyre-fire with the feathers of a cuckoo and a crow; this will destroy his enemies. Furthermore, for the purpose of driving away enemies, the knower of mantras should perform a fire-oblation.
By means of the previously described rite, having performed an uninterrupted *homa* in the fire of the funeral pyre's wood with the wings of an owl and a crow,
one shall pierce the enemy so that they are mutually embroiled in strife and uprooted.
By means of an oblation of owl feathers, the fetus of an excellent woman may be caused to fall.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform this oblation according to the prescribed rite one thousand times,
using *bilva* leaves with clarified butter, continuously for one month.

Even a barren woman may obtain an excellent, long-lived son by offering Bandhūka flowers that are red and mixed with honey and sugar. O Goddess, for an unfortunate woman, this forcibly bestows the happiness of good fortune!
O Dear One! Whoever, having risen in the morning, should perform a fire-oblation day after day with one hundred and eight hibiscus flowers accompanied by clarified butter,
will certainly achieve the power of attraction through its practice for six months.
O twice-born ones, the daughters of gods, gandharvas, and mortals, as well as the wives of nāgas,
afflicted by desire, come to him of their own accord and forcibly embrace him.
An oblation for this vidyā is performed with offerings of sesame seeds mixed with milk-rice (pāyasa).
He attains the Great Vidyā, which is adorned with the words of a multitude of scriptures.
He should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) with honey and the flesh of the ruru deer.
Thus he becomes possessed of knowledge, wealth, and an intellect mastered by the sciences of weaponry and treatises.
O Great Goddess! This Goddess bestows the fruit of the Vāmācāra path;
she does not grant fruit through the practice of Dakṣiṇācāra. Having offered bali to her every day within the assembly hall, [one attains success].
O Dear One! One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times with the remnants [of the offering].
Whether in a forest thicket, a cremation ground, an empty house, or at a crossroads, the Goddess will certainly become manifest through the offering of the bali.
This goddess has been described by me for one who desires the form of Bhairava.
Thus has this goddess, the remover of all sins, been told.
O Goddess! By the recitation of the mantra, one is freed from all sins.
"Having abandoned the defilement of leavings, he shall certainly become pure.
Thus is the goddess Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, world-renowned.
O fair-faced one, listen now to a certain vidyā for various applications!
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess! to this Great Vidyā, which assumes the form of the sacred observance (samaya).
One need not consider the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the suitability of the practitioner and so forth.
She is renowned as the Mahādevī, who culminates in the initiation of Śiva.
O Goddess of gods! The sacred thread (yajñopavīta) is indeed worn by the practitioner;
he should worship the Goddess—who was accomplished by Mahādeva—with the remnants (ucchiṣṭa).
He should not remain occupied with anything else, however extensive the multitude of other texts may be.
O Goddess, what is the use of saying much? One could even accomplish the three worlds by this mantra; however, it should always be remembered by the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva).
A person should offer oblations with milk, jaggery, cooked rice, or meat.
One shall obtain longevity, wealth, sons, and knowledge as the eighteenth [fruit].
This must be protected with effort and must not be told to anyone.
Devotion to the Guru should be offered through both body and wealth.
O Goddess! Neither public scandal nor sin remains in the mortal world;
having enjoyed happiness in the mortal world, one shall go to the city of the Goddess in the hereafter.
O Goddess, listen to this lore which has liberation as its sole essence, the giver of wealth as its sole essence, and knowledge as its sole essence.
The wish-fulfilling cow upon the earth, who provides every assistance, whose essence is the ultimate truth, and who possesses great majesty.
Thus ends the ritual application of Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī.
In the fifty-eighth chapter of the Matsya-sūkta:
"I shall proclaim the village sacrifice (grāmamedha); when performed, one is not afflicted by diseases;
if unperformed, death occurs in the village. Therefore, one should perform it with great effort."
There, one should worship the Goddess, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, Bhadrakālī,
the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), and especially Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
Now follows the ritual application of Dhūmāvatī.
In the Phetpāriṇī Tantra.
Now this practice of Dhūmāvatī is being told by me:
the two seed-syllables [of the mantra] end with the letter *da*, the Lord of Wealth (*sārgheśa*), and the nasal bindu; here, *dhūmavatī* is followed by *dviṭha*.
This is declared to be the mantra of Dhūmāvatī, which effects the subjugation of enemies.
The knower of mantras should thus conceive of it as possessing six limbs and associated with its birth:
the sage is Pippalāda, the meter is Nīvṛt, and the deity is Vivarṇā—
unsteady, dark, tall, and clad in soiled garments.

With disheveled hair, coarse, a widow with rasping teeth, mounted upon a chariot with a crow-emblem banner, with pendulous breasts, a winnowing basket in hand, with extremely harsh eyes, holding a staff, and accompanied by a dog— Please note: The term *varānvitā* has been translated as "accompanied by a dog" (*vara*), following the common interpretation in this context of the *Varāha Purāṇa* and other sources where it refers to the dog (*śvāna*) that follows the messenger of Yama. If the intended meaning were "endowed with boons" (*vara*), the context would be significantly different. Given the preceding descriptions of a terrifying figure, the former interpretation is more consistent. If you prefer the latter, please let me know. I have provided the former here as it fits the standard iconographic description of the messengers of death.
With a greatly elongated and exceedingly crooked nose, possessing slanted eyes,
constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst, a source of fear and strife—
one should meditate upon such a [female deity] and then commence the ritual action.
The knower of mantras should form the limbs [of the mantra] using the fourth consonant joined with the sixth vowel and endowed with the six long vowels;
he should recite it on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight for the sake of accomplishing the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
Devoted to fasting, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] for one hundred thousand times, remaining silent day and night in an empty house,
a cremation ground, or a forest;
during the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, he should wear a turban and remain clothed in wet garments.
Having written the mantra over the object to be accomplished and having placed it upon that, one should go toward Śiva;
then, having seized Śiva by means of the name of the enemy, one should recite the mantra.
From more than a thousand [recitations], the enemy is seized by fever.
Peace for fever may be attained through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or even with milk alone.
Having written the first syllable of the mantra, one should then write the name of the enemy;
then, having written the second syllable of the mantra, one should write the name of the enemy once more.
If one recites [the mantra] ten thousand times in a forest, the death of the enemy will certainly occur.
Having inserted the name of the enemy into the mantra for the purpose of killing on a night-blooming lotus leaf, the destruction of the enemy arises from reciting it ten thousand times.
Having burned a crow in the cremation fire and taking its ashes, which have been consecrated with mantras,
one should immediately effect the eradication of an enemy in the eight directions of those who oppose him;
having fashioned a Śiva-liṅga with the ashes of the cremation ground, one should place it upon that [enemy].
One should recite [the mantra] during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), unobstructed by opposing names;
one should offer incense of buffalo milk, which causes calamity for the enemy.
Assuming the form of a buffalo, she shall strike down the enemy.
With this mantra, one should bury that ash in the enemy's dwelling;
it will swiftly drive away the foe—no doubt should be entertained here.
Having placed the description of the enemy upon the palm of the hand with funeral ashes, [one should proceed].

Placing his face downward toward the fire, the practitioner, filled with wrath, should recite the Dhūmāvatī mantra ten thousand times; thus he shall bring about the destruction of his enemies. As before, having placed [the mantra] upon the palm of the hand, he should place half of it upon the enemy.
Standing in water, the practitioner should recite the mantra; by the sound "huṃ," he shall destroy his enemies.
Taking charcoal from a cremation ground, he should worship it with flowers and other offerings. Mentally addressing the *bhaga* and the *liṅga*, he should contemplate the ritual action in his mind.
Having combined the leaves of the *nimba* and *kākacchada*, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
by offering incense while uttering the name of the target, one will immediately cause enmity among enemies.
By performing a fire-oblation of milk in a fire of funeral-pyre wood, peace is produced.
By the offering of dust and incense, Kālikā, assuming the form of a vulture, comes and slays the enemy; by means of the incense from the remains of a *śānti* offering, she kills him;
and by the incense of a boar’s tail, she, taking the form of a boar, destroys him.
(494) Peace is achieved through the incense of *aśvattha* leaves and not otherwise;
peace from all malevolent sorcery arises through the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*),
as well as with milk and the three sweets (*madhuratrika*), O Goddess of Gods!

Having pierced the name-syllables of the enemies into a *kīla* made from *kṣeḍatara* wood with the mantra, one should scratch them out; then, having recited the mantra over two written lines, one should bury it to effect the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of the foes.

Having given an oblation (*bali*) to the twice-born with clarified butter sprinkled with the dust from your two feet, and having recited that [mantra] over the ashes of a funeral pyre, one should scatter them at the house of the enemy.
It should be like that.
One should draw [the mantra] on a birch leaf in the northwest (Vāyavya) direction, having chanted it more than a thousand times.
Having chanted it, the deity of the wind (Vāyu-sura), even if one is emaciated by the beads of Śiva’s rosary, will not be an obstacle to that.
Powder consecrated with the thousand-syllable mantra, when placed upon its sprouts or upon the heads of enemies in their houses, causes the eradication of their lineage.
Having recited it in a grove, a cremation ground, on discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), or within the range of one's feet—
Having brought gravel to a place where donkeys dwell, to a site of spirits, to a crossroads, to saline soil,
to a place for urination, or to a house or cloud filled with flowers,
the practitioner, naked and facing south, should perform the rite.

Having cast it into a clod of earth from a cremation ground, one should likewise roast it in a fire there. One should recite the mantra over that powder one hundred thousand times and throw it into the enemy's house or into the midst of their army; within a fortnight, the eradication of all [the enemies] shall occur.
One who knows the mantra should offer the dust from the feet of ants found in a pit, along with food, into the fire for seven nights at night to the six-faced deity.
The enemy will wander over the entire earth like a crow until his death.
Having fashioned an effigy of the enemy under the birth-constellation, the knower of mantras,
having performed the consecration of its vital breath and pierced its vital spots with iron thorns,
should repeat the mantra on occasions such as a Saturday sunrise.
Having ground dhattūra juice with funeral pyre embers,
the mantra-practitioner should bind it to the back of the *nitya* [mantra] using his mass of hair; then,
having summoned the enemy to a cremation ground, he should recite the mantra while burying it in that person's house at night.
Enmity shall arise instantly, even between Gaurī and Śaṅkara.
One should write the name of the target, interspersed with the syllables of the mantra, upon the bark of an Aśvattha tree;
likewise, having recited it over the bark of another poisonous tree, one should plant it with the intent to perform that rite.
Having ground the aforementioned thorns, the wise one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times over each;
at that very moment, those two shall become mutually hostile even by name.
One should write those letters around the name of the enemy, enclosed on all sides by the syllables of the mantra in the corners.
In the center of the house of the wind (the northwest), one should separately place the target.
