Reciting the mantra, one should strike it with embers produced from gold using the [appropriate] words.
On Tuesdays and Sundays during battle, by means of cotton, one effects enmity against those on the earth.
Having assumed his former form and having drawn the enemy, one should purify [the image].
Having recited the mantra over a sharpened object in the sun, one should suspend it over fire.
Thus, for seven days, one should purify it by reciting over the substances and drawing [the figure].

Having thoroughly ground together *vyoma*, *agni*, *laśuna*, *unmatta*, *hiṅgu*, *siddhārtha*, and *śūraṇa*— along with balls made of salt combined with the juice of *unmatta*— the practitioner of mantras should write [the diagram] with that paste and recite the mantra.
One should dig a stake of appropriate form in the middle of the sacrificial offering (bali), and likewise upon it,
having kindled a fire, one should offer oblations of ghee mixed with cow-products while reciting the *hūṃ* syllable.
Having placed the image there, one should constantly recite the great mantra.
Then, one should go to the twenty-seventh pit, or else to an empty house;
it should be triangular with a trident-shaped blazing tip and provided with three girdles.
There too, one should bury a wooden stake and kindle the fire as before.
Then the practitioner should suspend an effigy over the fire,
having smeared it with the aforementioned substances, with its feet upward and its face downward;
having propitiated it with red substances, he should set it ablaze with fuel from poisonous trees.
One should utter "Hum" over the fuel and the image as they are set ablaze with sacrificial wood;
by means of the coverings and so forth, the immortal one enters dissolution—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the section on Dhūmāvatī.
Now follows the application of the *Kṛtyāparimala* [rite],
in the thirteenth chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra consisting of fragrance,
by the mere knowledge of which nothing remains unattainable in the three worlds.
One who is a great yogi, having bowed to the Consort of Rudra, should utter the word "Gaurī-pada."
One should recite the mantra ending with the word *bhuvanabhayaṅkarī* as the armor (*varma*). Alternatively, one may recite the word following the first [syllable], which is the word *brahmaṇaḥ*.
Then follows *parimala*, etc., up to *brahmādyakhaṇḍaparimalaḥ*.

The sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) is traditionally taught as follows: first, the heart [is placed] with the mantra consisting of half [the seed-syllable] joined with the six long vowels and conjoined with the weapon-mantra;
then, the head is placed with the other half [of the mantra], followed by the crest, armor, eyes, and weapon in due order.
The sage is Aṅgiras, the goddess is Gāyatrī, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī;
she is the lion-faced one who causes fear among living beings,
and her presiding deity is Mahākṛtyā— having spoken thus, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
She had the face of a lion and a black countenance, with pendulous breasts;
her mouth was formidable with fangs, she possessed three eyes, and she blazed forth on all sides.
She was clothed in a black bodice and possessed a radiance like a smokeless fire.

Having meditated upon the Kṛtyā according to the ritual procedure—her lotus-like hands holding a trident, a discus, a mace, and a skull-topped staff; licking with her great tongue; and terrifying with eyes like flashes of lightning—the best of mantra-knowers should worship her.
Having meditated, one worships Kṛtyā with red flowers for the purpose of subjugation;
likewise, she is black in rites of killing, using meat, blood, and fermented liquors.
One should also worship Madanā, Sarvakulyā, and Svacchandini.

Thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the Vidyās— Bhīṣaṇā, Śrīmatī, and Pratiṣṭhā— in succession upon the eight petals. On the eastern petal, however, is the one named Śāṅkarī, white in color and endowed with boons.
She has two arms, a gentle face, and holds a noose and a goad; she is auspicious.
On her right is the one named Bhīṣakā, who has a protruding tongue and a face like nectar.
She is black in complexion with a red face, adorned with red garlands and unguents.
Four-armed, delighting with the lion’s roar, and bearing a skull-cup;
holding a sword in her hand, adorned with a garland of heads and decorated with all ornaments;
in the west is the one named Vāruṇī, golden-hued and smiling-faced.
Having worshipped Surudramālikā— who possesses white fangs and always bestows fearlessness—
and [the goddess] named Bhīmikā in the north, who causes terror to the four castes,
one should daily recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Having obtained [the enemy], the minister should always employ him;
having discerned the proper time, he should have an image made of beeswax,
twelve finger-breadths in size, including the nails and hair of the enemy.
In the heart, there is the name; in the universal armor, the syllable *phaṭ*.

"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) of such-and-such is here; the life-force (*jīva*) of such-and-such is stationed here; all the sense-faculties of such-and-such, as well as the speech and mind of such-and-such, are here."
"May the beloved of Agni lead away the eyes, ears, nose, and life-breaths from here.
Having thus established the life-breath, one should then smear [the corpse] with black pepper.
Then, separately on the two feet, [one should apply] the hair of a deceased Brāhmaṇa and a Caṇḍāla.
Having tied an iron-faced [image] to a gateway made of *kāraskara* wood,
one should prepare a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) there, provided with a girdle, beneath it;
having established the fire of the deceased there, one should surround it with *śara* grass.
One who intends the killing of someone should fashion a sacrificial enclosure with *vibhītaka* wood;
he should offer oblations of the feathers of crows and owls smeared with neem oil, while uttering:
"Split him! Purify him! Kill him!"
Having worshipped Kṛtyā according to the rules at the conclusion of the fire-oblation with one hundred and eight recitations of the mantra, the wise man, in the presence of the fire, should say:
"Whether he be living in the same house as me, or very far away, or even nearby— "
Having uttered "Hum," one should offer his blood in the ritual act of drinking;
one should protect the fire according to the prescribed rite and perform it for nine nights. As long as one offers oblations, so long shall there be the death of this enemy.
Having ground black pepper and white mustard with the milk of the *arka* plant,
one should stir it in water while reciting the mantra. Visualizing the enemy with a fixed gaze,
one should step upon the edge of a black garment with the foot, [imagining] that enemy beneath it.
Having visualized a vajra as a trident, one should cast [the substance] upon it;
within nine nights the enemy dies—of this there is no doubt.
On a funeral pyre fire that has been established from afar, [one should offer] vibhītaka fruits smeared with oil.
The enemy dies while one is offering oblations; this is the truth spoken by Uśanas.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy upon a clean board made from the wood of the *sādhya* tree, one should grind black pepper with the milky sap of the *arka* plant and smear it upon that very image.
Having placed the syllable *phaṭ* at the heart and having fashioned Śiva with incense,
one should cast [the offering] on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight after reciting the mantra a thousand times; then,
having immediately performed an immersion, one should effect self-protection for whomever it may be.
Having recited the mantra according to the prescribed rite, one should cause [the enemy] to be split apart together with the mudrā;
within six months, the enemy shall die at both twilights.
Then, one should take a dry leaf of the *vaibhītaka* tree that has been blown up by the wind.
Having taken [the materials], the mantra-practitioner should write with the blood of a black cobra the name of the enemy, placing the seed-syllable of wind (YAM) at its end;
he should then bury it in that person's house within a crow-mouthed vessel, for this will certainly [bring about his ruin].

One should perform the rite of *uccāṭana* (the eradication) of an enemy by reciting "hum" while using dry leaves blown up by the wind, wood fallen by lightning, camel bones, and fresh embers; likewise,
with *dūrvā* grass, *guḍūcī*, fragrant substances, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and rice.
With *palāśa* wood for fuel, the wise man should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
He should likewise offer *bilva* fruits and leaves for prosperity (*lakṣmī*), and *nandyāvarta* flowers for fortune (*śrī*).
With *vajrapatra*, *apāmārga*, and auspicious *subhadraka* embers, he should likewise act.

One should perform the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakam*) with these ingredients combined with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*). It is stated even in the *Uttama-panasa-tantra* that after performing the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to the prescribed method, one should recite this *parimala* mantra.

One should constantly recite this auspicious mantra, which pacifies great diseases, one hundred and eight times with a one-pointed mind; it brings the world under one's control. One should mentally visualize her as mounted upon an elephant, stationed in the sky.
She shall quickly become submissive to him, as shall she when mounted upon a horse;
it removes the fear of thieves, tigers, wild beasts, water, and the like,
and by merely hearing it once, it destroys all sins.
Having drunk water consecrated seven times while remaining constantly composed,
one becomes intelligent and eloquent;
likewise, by performing the consecration through recitation seven times, even poison becomes nectar.
Whether for a month, a fortnight, two months, six months, or even a year—
any mortal who performs [this rite] in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
Now, I shall specifically describe the sequence of the ritual for the Great Peace (Mahāśānti).
It brings about all accomplishments, is meritorious, and destroys all sins;
it removes all demonic influences and destroys all portents of death;
it pacifies great diseases and eradicates epilepsy.
Yoginīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, kuṣmāṇḍas, and pannagas—especially the ḍākinīs and others—do not remain in that place.
O child! One should worship Kṛtyā there according to the prescribed ritual.
One should draw a sixteen-petalled lotus together with a pair of *yoni*s and a *bindu*.
In its center, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, one should place the letters beginning with *ya* in sequence.
In the middle of that, while recollecting the root mantra, one should draw a hexagon (*rasakoṇa*).
One should draw the lunar disc in the center and above it, one should draw an image.
In its center, one should place a jar adorned with garlands and wreaths in the forest;
in its center, one should place the Kṛtyā, endowed with all auspicious marks.
One should worship according to the prescribed rule and offer the *pāyasa* (rice-milk) oblation;
having satisfied [the deities], one should install the Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, into the jar:
Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodheśa, and Unmattabhairava.
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship the Kṣetrapālas outside of that,
worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and before the Goddess, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
One who is free from resentment should offer oblations of clarified butter, apāmārga, and unbroken grains;
likewise, one hundred and more [oblations] each of dūrvā grass tips, khadira, and aśvattha wood.
One should perform the rite of homa either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila).
On his right side, one should meditate upon Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite;
one should place the Goddess in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and remember Śrī on the right.
On the left side, one should remember the Goddess Hṛllekhā, the Supreme Sovereign.
On his very left side, one should worship the ten leaders;
one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times, which destroys death.
They know that for the sin of killing an embryo, one should recite it ten thousand times; this is called *parimala*.
Having first recited the mantra that pacifies great diseases,
a mortal who performs the consecration in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
He by whom the fragrance [of this mantra] is known, and which always resides in his mouth, [attains such a state].
"Indeed, one need not even report to him the fear of diseases"—
by such rules as these, the procedure known as *parimala* should be understood to be performed for the Moon.
It brings about great peace for men and destroys obstacles such as suffering.
Thus ends the *Kṛtyāparimala*.
Now, Jayadurgā, in the fourteenth chapter.
Having uttered the words "durge durge" and then the word "rakṣaṇī," [the mantra] ending with the wife of fire (svāhā) beginning with Tārā is the great mantra of Jayadurgā.
Having placed the mantra-word in the middle of the [seed] syllable, the wise one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
This protective rite has been taught for Jayadurgā, accompanied by her armor. Having meditated upon this Durgā— who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, four-armed,
and of fierce form, bearing a conch, a discus, an arrow, and a trident— one should [perform the rite].
In battle, legal disputes, and other such matters, a person shall be victorious by reciting this mantra.
One should daily worship Jayā, Śrī, Nityā, the conch, and likewise the dagger.
The mantra of Jayadurgā has been declared; now another mantra is being told.

Having uttered "Namo bhagavatyai," following that [comes] "Jvālāmālinyai. Then, surrounded by a host of vultures, the mantra beginning with Tārā and ending with Dviṭha is proclaimed: *Oṃ namo* is declared to be the heart, and likewise *bhagavati* is the head.

Then, one should place upon the body the *śikhā* [mantra] "Jvālāmālinī," surrounded by a flock of vultures; and the armor (*kavaca*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras, namely "Svāhā," joined with their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*).
The victor should worship this mantra of victory ten thousand or a hundred thousand times.
By joining *rudrāṅganā* and *agnijāyā*,
another mantra known as *Jvālāmukhī* is proclaimed, which is unsurpassed among the mantras of Jvālāmukhī.
Having anointed one's feet with lamp oil at midnight, beginning from a day sacred to the Guru...
One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times for twenty-three days;
she will undoubtedly give six pieces of silver every day.
Furthermore, the Nārāyaṇīya has been described by Agastya in nine ways.
Durgā is known by nine forms, specifically as the Nine Durgās;
a man desiring perfect success should recite them in secret.
O King, even today they remain entirely hidden from even the most righteous person.
One should perform the ritual of the Nine Durgās due to the gravity of the rite.
The king, having properly propitiated the mantra with various riches,
should, out of devotion and with constant care, keep it ever-present for the sake of protection;
it should be employed by himself in times of calamity, especially in rites such as killing.
Then the mantra-practitioner should diligently perform the rite of slaying. When the practitioner has been overcome by enemies, he should report everything to the king.
Having reported it according to the rules, he should afterwards consume [the enemy] with a shower of mantras.
Merely by recollecting [this], the practitioner of mantra shall destroy all enemies.
He should bestow upon him a thousand or even a hundred cows,
gold coins, or land abounding in grain.
One attains complete peace and becomes the embodiment of all protection.
Thus ends the application of Jvālamukhī, surrounded by the host of vultures of Jayadurgā, in the Phetkāriṇī Tantra.

Thus ends the description of the "Sprout" (pallava) consisting of the ritual applications of Kukkutocchiṣṭa, Cāṇḍālinī, Dhūmāvatī, Kṛtyāparimala, Jayadurgā, Gṛdhragaṇaparivṛta, and Jvālāmukhī, titled "The Narration of the Sprout," in the fourth section on Optional Rites (kāmyakāṇḍa) of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
The Fourth Chapter.
Now follows the festival of Durgā.
In the Matsyasūkta Mahāmantra, in the upper section, in the forty-first chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Then, having reached the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja,
and having propitiated Nandikā and Durgā, one who has conquered his senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should bathe in the water of a stream and worship her upon its bank.
Because of the feminine gender indication in the word "tasyāḥ," the meaning is that one should worship on the bank of a river.
The manner of worship is also described in that very same place.
On the first day, one should worship in a water-pot; on the second, in a book;
likewise on the third, in a sword; on the fourth, the purification of the hair;
on the fifth, in the solar disc; and on the sixth, at the root of a bilva tree.

On the seventh lunar day, the *patrikā* (the sacred leaf) is consecrated; on the eighth, it is placed upon the images. On the sixth lunar day, conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, the *bilva* fruit is consecrated with mantras.
When the first quarter of the Mūla asterism coincides with the seventh lunar day, the *patrikā* is formally introduced into the shrine.
On the eighth day conjoined with the asterism Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the Goddess should be worshipped with great festivities;
on the ninth day with the asterism Uttarā, one should worship Śivā with offerings;
and on the tenth day at the end of Śravaṇā, having prostrated, one should dismiss her.

By this, the explanation of the Smārta Bhaṭṭācāryas— that the statement from the Devīpurāṇa, "When the sun is situated in Virgo, beginning from the bright fortnight of Śakra [Śrāvaṇa], on the Nandikā," means that one should worship from the sixth day until the ninth— is refuted as being a mere assertion of a single continuous period.

It should be stated that what is said in the *Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī*—that the first lunar day (*pratipad*) is the *Nandikā*—is correct; for there is no evidence for the transgression of the sixth lunar day prescribed for the *Mahānavamī*. We consider it auspicious that the *Durgābhaktitaraṅgiṇī* has indeed stated that the *pratipad* is thus [the *Nandikā*].
"p. 501) *keśaśodhanam*": the nominative case is used here in the sense of the locative.
The meaning is that one should worship [the deity] upon a hair-comb for cleaning the hair.
He states in that very same place: "In the absence of the lunar mansions, there would be a failure of the ritual."

Even in the absence of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), one should perform the entire ritual procedure according to the sequence beginning with the sixth [tithi] and so forth; when the stars are obtained, there is the arising of fruit. "The arising of fruit" means the arising of distinguished fruit.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that in the absence of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), there would be an absence of results. This concludes the explanation of the ritual procedures beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad). Now, regarding the time for worship and so forth, it is stated in that very same [text]:
Whether it be Jyeṣṭhā or Ṣaṣṭhī, if they do not occur in the evening,
the consecration of the bilva branch should nevertheless take place in the evening.
One should avoid the previous Ṣaṣṭhī even if it is joined with its asterism and has arrived in the evening.
But when the worship of the leaf-offering (patrikā-pūjā) will not take place on the following day,
one should perform the formal selection (varaṇa) on that day which is the nearest preceding one, and on the next day, one should enter the branch.

But when, on the seventh [lunar day], the sixth has either elapsed or not elapsed, the seventh increases; however, this occurs only if [the increase] is by a mere *daṇḍa* (one-twelfth of a day) or more. The words "on the following day" (*pare 'hani*) are to be understood as the remainder of the sentence.

If the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) should extend beyond the ninth (navamī) by even a single moment (muhūrta), and the tenth (daśamī) likewise increases [in duration], then the rite should be performed as follows; listen. The meaning is that it applies not only when the ninth extends [into the tenth], but also when the tenth [extends].
On the seventh day, there is the selection of the *bilva* tree; on the eighth, the entry;
on the ninth, the eightfold worship (*pūjāṣṭaka*); and on the tenth, one should dismiss Śivā.
Here, some [teachers], fearing the sublation of the lunar days obtained through general injunctions, [place it] on the seventh.
Some explain this as "on the sixth day joined with a long-duration seventh.
In that case, it appears that the statement "the sixth has not emerged" would remain unconfused. [Furthermore:
"When the sixth extends into both the seventh and the eighth."
In the opinion of Svārtha, Iṇa, Pāṇini, and Vidyā, however, the *ṇic* suffix would increase;
that is to say, the locative case (*saptamī*) is the remainder [of the rule].
Furthermore, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) is for the sake of another, and on that very day occurs the "destruction of the day" (*dinakṣaya*).
Then, on the sixth day, on the preceding day, the worship of the *bilva* tree is prescribed;
on the seventh day conjoined with the sixth, the entry of the *patrikā* [the image] takes place;
and according to the *Atikalpa*, one should likewise enter the earthen image on the eighth day.
At the very dawn, at the break of day.

On the eighth lunar day conjoined with the seventh, one should perform the rites of the great worship festival; on the ninth, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali), and on the tenth, one should bid farewell to Śivā. Where the eighth occurs within the ninth and the ninth does not extend beyond it, [that is the proper time].
Or, if the ninth day is overlapped by the tenth on the following day,
then both the eighth and the ninth days— on which two occasions worship is indeed prescribed—
must be performed together with the offerings on that very same single day.
The worship on the ninth day (navamī) for the Aṣṭakā is that which extends through all three junctions of the day (trisandhyā); it is the latter [period].
On each such occasion, the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna) should be performed on the following day when it is joined with the ninth day.
However, if the eighth day (aṣṭamī) should extend through the three junctions of the previous day, [the rite is performed then].
One should perform the worship on the ninth day even if it is pierced by the tenth; of this there is no doubt.
The conjunction of the eighth and ninth days is superior, as is the conjunction during the night.
It is remembered that the merit is a hundredfold at midnight and twofold during the twilight.

If the conjunction with the lunar mansion (tārāyoga) does not occur during the forenoon on the seventh day or subsequent days, then one should begin in the forenoon and complete it within the portion of the lunar mansion. On the tenth day, when Śravaṇa extends throughout the day, one should likewise rise and perform the prescribed rites.
Having worshipped her according to the rules in the morning, preceded by dance and song,
and having awaited the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should dispatch Śivā once it has arrived;
provided that the triad beginning with the seventh lunar day (the three days of the festival) occurs while the moon is situated under a favorable constellation.
At that very time, some said there was a requirement for the Śravaṇā nakṣatra on the tenth day;
when the night had passed at the end of Śravaṇā, and at its conclusion on the ninth day,
they completed the rites appropriate for their respective positions, ending with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
If that [Navamī] is not attained on the tenth day, then on the tenth day conjoined with Dhaniṣṭhā, one should duly dispatch the Goddess Durgā with all the autumnal festivals. [For it is said:
"The Navamī joined with the tenth, and the Śravaṇā [nakṣatra] having passed into the night..."
Then, at the sight of the tenth day, one should dispatch the Goddess on the ninth;
however, if the ninth day occurs during the night following the end of the eighth-day period,
one should perform the great worship on that ninth day as well, even at the dead of night.

When the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) occurs at night following the rising of the moon, it is called Mahā-aṣṭamī; it is the supreme [day] that brings great delight to the Goddess. Subsequently, whichever ninth lunar day (navamī) follows, that is the lunar day known as Mahā-navamī.
Regarding that very point, he states the basis for worship:
In a painting, in a statue made of clay, and even in a bilva fruit; in the Great Yoni, in the lunar disc, in stone, and in the yoni-maṇḍala;
likewise in a book, in sandals, in a sword, and in the Great Image (mahābimba).
And at the holy site of the Gaṅgā, one should invoke the Goddess and worship her.
The injunctions and prohibitions regarding the means of valid cognition also apply to that very same [object].
A householder should not make [an image] out of clay, nor ever out of palm wood;
it should be three cubits in height, filled with grass, and one should worship it with a pair of bilva fruits.
A householder should not make an image out of mere clay, nor should a householder make one made of palm-wood measuring three and a half cubits;
he states the rule as "three cubits."
The phrase "an image three cubits [in height]" is stated for the purpose of excluding any greater measurement;
therefore, there is no fault in making an image smaller than that. He states an exception regarding an earthen image with the words "filled with straw."
Therefore, there is no fault in worshipping with an image made of clay containing grass.
The word "ca" (and) is placed out of its logical order [to indicate that one should worship] with a pair of *bilva* fruits containing grass.
He states the specific rule for the pair of *bilva* fruits according to the distinction of Brahmins and other castes:
For a Brāhmaṇa, it is praised when [the fire] is situated in the northeast (māhendra) or in the north (īśa).
O lady of beautiful countenance! For a Kṣatriya, it is situated in the north-east and the north;
for a Vaiśya, in the north-west; and for a Śūdra, O lady of beautiful countenance, in the east.
Or else, O beloved, it may be situated in the southeast or the northeast for all of them.
He states the fruit of the pair of bilva fruits beginning with the east.
When situated in the northeast, there is an increase in knowledge; when in the north, it grants all desires;
when in the northwest, there is the acquisition of wealth; and when situated in the north, there is sovereignty.
When situated in the south, there will be an increase in enemies; and if it occupies a corner, death shall occur.

Because the specific results for one situated in the north-east (vāyvīśāna) corner are stated [elsewhere], the word "corner" (koṇa) here— by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*)— refers to the south-east (agni) and south-west (nairṛta) corners.
In that same [text], he describes the auspicious characteristics and the unacceptability of a pair of *bilva* fruits.

That which is even, round, and even thick is recommended; however, that which is defiled by insects and the like, O Supreme Goddess, should never be accepted. That which extends upward through the center is not to be taken;
for that which goes upward belongs to the Kṣatriya and is thus unfit to be grasped.
"Equal" means equal for everyone.

Alternatively, the intended meaning is that even one situated above or in the middle— though not mentioned in the aforementioned locations— may be accepted, because no fruit of blame is heard [for such cases].
The fault of shedding [the fruit] from a pair of *bilva* fruits is also mentioned in that very same place.
O Maheśvarī, when the pair [of sandals] falls while being carried to the bathing place,
or wherever the fall of the earthen [image] occurs, death is certain.
To pacify that fault, one should perform ten thousand oblations with clarified butter.
One should give a cow as a sacrificial fee, along with a white horse and a white goat.
Thus concludes the expiation for the falling of a pair of *bilva* fruits from the image.
They know that the festival begins on the first day (*nandā*) and lasts until the tenth;
it is proclaimed as a "Great Festival" (*mahāmahotsava*) and is celebrated for three days.

O Maheśvarī! He who performs a sacrifice to another deity does not obtain its fruit; in the end, he shall fall into hell. Since everything is a hundredfold portion of the Goddess, one should worship no other.
p. 504) Having further stated [the rules] up to "on the eighth day" and "in the images," [it says]:
"At every watch one should perform a bath; at every watch an offering (bali);
at every watch a fire-oblation (homa), along with food and consecrated water."
And the offering of abundant oblations is praised on the ninth day;
worshipped on the ninth day, the Goddess bestows infinite fruit.
In that very same place, there is also a particular form of the deity in a specific region.
In the land of Oḍra, in Kaliṅga, and likewise in Madhyadeśa;
in Ayodhyā, in Surāṣṭra, in Cohāra, in Śrīhaṭṭa, in Kośala, and in Śavavallaka— the eight-armed Goddess is to be worshipped.
She should be depicted with eighteen arms on Mount Mahendra, Himālaya,
Kaurava, Mathurā, Kedāra, and Rāmaṭha;
one should worship her with twelve arms at Makarandra and Virātaka.
In Kaumāra, Gauḍa, Pāripātra, and Dakṣiṇa,
as well as in Marahaṭṭa and Gajāhvaya, the Goddess should be fashioned with ten arms;
likewise in Pūrṇa, Nepāla, Kacchaseśa, and Kaṅkaṇa.
The Goddess should have four arms [in the temple], but two arms near the ocean; however,
the location of the lamp and the position of the tortoise-disk (kūrmacakra) at the head are maintained by the author of the Tantrasāra himself.

By the statement, "One should never worship the Goddess in a place devoid of a lamp-stand or in a place constructed of bricks," it is indicated that there is no fault in using a house made of grass, wood, and so forth as a lamp-stand;
likewise, even in a brick house distinct from a lamp-stand, he provides an exception for that which is distinct from a lamp-stand.
In the northeast, or toward Mahendra, or to the north of the dwelling,
one should cause a divine residence to be built through the grace of wealth and sovereignty;
it should be thirty-one cubits in length, or even thirty-five.
It should be circular, measuring nine cubits or even four cubits;
having divided it into sections on both sides and made the center very beautiful,
one should have the Goddess fashioned right there according to the measurements for the four directions.
Now, the characteristics of the lion-throne and so forth:
one cubit in height, provided with hair,
[is] the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*), the great wheel (*mahācakra*), and the "auspicious in every respect" (*sarvatobhadra*).
One should draw a mandala with colored powder (rajas) and place a pedestal (pīṭha) there.
It should be made of milk produced from the *śrīpati* tree or even from the *sahakāra* tree;
it should measure one fist or one arm in length and one span (prādeśa) in height.
When it is obtained as eightfold, curved, quadrangular, and even, it is auspicious;
this is called the Bhadrāsana or the Kūrmāsana.
In marriage and in the worship of the Sun, one should avoid the Sahakāra (mango tree).

O Maheśānī! Wood from the *vāruṇa* tree, or *padmaka*, or *devadāru*—these are recommended for all sacrificial altars (*vedī*), as are those made of *śāla* wood. Then, with a reddish fragrance, such as saffron (*kuṅkuma*) or *gaja* [sandalwood], [one should perform the rite].
Having drawn the great *yoni* (womb) and surrounding it with two lotuses,
[one should do so] with elephant musk.
Therein, one should install the Goddess, the bestower of all desired objects. He states the ritual duties to be performed on the sixth day:
"Having daily performed [the rites] according to the rules, the householder should then, on the sixth day in the evening..."
Adorned, observing silence, and composed in mind, the practitioner should go to the root of a *bilva* tree; having fed the Brāhmaṇas and prostrated with the five limbs,
he should face the northern direction and prepare a seat.
Having paid homage to the five deities, the wise man should then form a formal resolve;
with the Tryambaka mantra alone, he should bathe the tree with water, with milk,
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and likewise with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having bathed, one should wrap [the linga] five times with a triple-stranded thread that has been sprinkled while reciting the verse beginning with "sūtramāṇeti"; then,
one should sow five grains in a clockwise direction.

Today, in the month of [name], in the fortnight of [name], at this meritorious spot of earth, I, [name] of the [name] lineage, for the sake of [specific desire], in order to worship [you] as the very form of Durgā, shall take a branch of the Bilva tree belonging to you— dear to Ambikā and Śiva, of the Śāṇḍilya lineage— which is joined with a pair of fruits still attached to their stalks.
Having worshipped with these at night, I choose [this boon]. Having placed my hand upon the foot of a tree, provided with fruits and garlands,
and having massaged and worshipped it thoroughly with those [materials], one should thereafter worship [the deity] upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should worship Gaṇeśa at the northern gate, Caṇḍa in the east, Pracaṇḍa in the south,
and Vetāla immediately thereafter in the west;
likewise, one should worship Ādhāraśakti and the others in the center, together with their limbs (aṅgas) and subsidiary limbs (upāṅgas).
Resembling great silver, with a face like the full moon,
she was strewn with various jewels and adorned with bracelets and armlets;
she shone brilliantly with her ten most enchanting arms.
Her lotus-face was blooming like an autumnal lotus;
she illuminated [the world] with her three excellent eyes, which were as dark as blue water-lilies, unevenly spaced, and possessed of unbridled streaks of brilliance.
One should visualize on the left side a trident, a sword, a discus, an arrow, and a spear;
as well as a shield, a full bow, a noose, a goad, and an axe, all adorned with garlands of flames.
One should contemplate [the deity] standing upon a buffalo with his left foot raised and his right foot on the ground;
beneath him, one should visualize the buffalo with its head severed,
and there, the great asura who has arisen, bearing a sword and a shield.
One should meditate upon her as residing in the *bilva* tree, the bestower of all desires and goals.
Having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, and having worshipped the seat,
one should perform the invocation with the root mantra and then offer the seat.
Then, having offered water for the feet and other offerings, and having performed the limb-worship (aṅgapūjā),
one should worship Jayantī and the others at the bases of the petals starting from the east;
likewise, one should worship Brahmā and the others on the tips of the petals, and the Bhairavas in the middle of the petals.
Having arrived there, one should worship at the foot of the tree and at the top of the tree Vetāla,
Maṇibhadra, and likewise Yakṣaka;
as well as the one known as Tripurāntaka, Kaṇa, and Hetuka.
One should worship Agnijihva and Rasa with fragrant flowers;
then, outside of that, one should worship the planets, the lords of the directions, and their weapons.

Regarding this, the specific procedure for the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons has been stated by the highly authoritative teacher Lakṣaṇācārya in the fourth chapter of the Śāradātilaka as follows:
First, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), accompanied by their primary retinues and joined with their weapons,
classes, and presiding deities, in the directions starting from the east in due order.
The meaning of the phrase "accompanied by their primary retinues" (*mūlapāriṣadānvitān*) is as follows:
when there is worship of Indra and the others within the enclosure of the Śaktis, then for each [deity] it is "together with the retinue of Śaktis";
likewise, in the worship of Gaṇapati, it is "together with the retinue of Gaṇeśas"; and likewise, in the worship of the Sun, for each [deity]...
"To Sūryapāriṣada.

Likewise, in the worship of Viṣṇu, [it is] "to Viṣṇupāriṣada. Regarding the term *heti*: in the case of a connection with each [deity], the lords of the classes (*jātyadhipas*) are uttered first, and subsequently the *hetis*; at the root [of this sequence] is the word *heti*.
Regarding the placement of words at the beginning [of a compound]:

it should also be understood that the various types of weapons, as well as the worlds of the gods, the radiant ones, the pretas, the rākṣasas, the javanas, the vātas, the kṣetras, the bhūtas, and the nāgas, along with their vehicles and their retinues, are to be included.
He speaks of the guardians of the directions in that very same place:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Pavana, Vidhu, Īśāna,
the Lord of Serpents (Pannagādhīśa), and below and above,
Pitāmaha; yellow, red, black, smoky, white, smoky, and both white.
These are proclaimed to be fair-complexioned and reddish in sequence according to their color. Their vehicles, as recorded by Rāghava Bhaṭṭa, are as follows:
The elephant, goat, buffalo, man, crocodile, deer, horse, bull, chariot, and swan—
these are their seed-syllables according to the *Kapila-pañcarātra*.
Those which are in direct order (anuloma) are the third; the second is from reverse order (viloma);
the fourth is by reverse order, and the eighth is by direct order;
the third is by direct order, not from reverse order as the third.
The fourth [vowel] and the seventh letter are arranged in direct order (anuloma);
the fourth [vowel] is in reverse order (viloma) with respect to *kha*, and the third [vowel] is in reverse order with respect to *ga*.
All of that is indeed pierced by *su* and *nāda* at the end of the *su* [syllables].
The seed-syllables for Brahmā, the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), Vāsava, and the others are extracted in successive order.
Those who know the tradition maintain that these seed-syllables are long.
Some, however, hold that Māyā belongs to both Ananta and Brahmā, and is the bond of the fettered (pāśavī).

"Those beginning with Earth (pṛthvī), Fire (agni), and Wind (pavana), and ending with Varuṇa, Anila, and Indu, joined with Ananta and Bindu, are to be worshipped with the Pāśa and Māyā. The application is as follows: *Pṛthvī*, *Agni*, *Pavana*, etc., ending with *Varuṇa*, *Anila*, and *Indu*, joined with *Ananta* and *Bindu*, [are worshipped] with *Pāśa* and *Māyā*. The ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: 1. *Pṛthvī*: *La* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *L̥m*) 2. *Agni*: *Ra* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *R̥m*) 3. *Pavana*: *Ya* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *Y̥m*) 4. *Varuṇa*: *Va* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *V̥m*) 5. *Anila*: *Sa* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *S̥m*) 6. *Indu*: *Ha* (with *Ananta* and *Bindu*: *H̥m*) [These are to be worshipped] with the *Pāśa* (*Pha*) and *Māyā* (*Hrīṃ*). Thus ends the application.
Oṃ lāṃ! Salutation to Indra, who is yellow in color, the lord of the gods, holding a thunderbolt in his hand, whose vehicle is Airāvata, together with his retinue and the attendants of Durgā.
Likewise, rāṃ! To Agni, who is tawny in color, the lord of fire, holding a spear in his hand, whose vehicle is a goat.
"Salutation to Durgā’s retinue together with their attendants," and so forth; this should be inferred accordingly. This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
The author of the work also states: "One of pure intellect should worship [the deities] in their respective directions, accompanied by their own classes, presiding deities, and retinues of weapons."
In the Nityātantra:
At the end, one should worship the world-protectors together with their vehicles and weapons;
thus, immediately after the worship of these [deities], one should worship the weapons.
In the Śāradā [Tantra]:
One should know their weapons in sequence as the vajra, the śakti, the staff (daṇḍa), the sword, the noose, the goad, the mace, the trident, the discus, and the lotus.
Also in the fourth chapter of the Merutantra:
Furthermore, the vajra, śakti, staff, sword, noose, goad, and mace, as well as the trident,
wheel, and lotus, are located from the east to the northeast;
thus the form of the weapons is described in the Śāradātilaka.
Yellow, white, black, sky-colored (blue), lightning-like, red, white, and black;
and having the luster of a *kuruvinda* ruby and pale-red (*pāṭala*)—these are proclaimed as the characteristics of the diamond (*vajra*) and the other [precious gems].
*Kuruvinda* means a ruby (*padmarāga*).
The formal application therein is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to Vajra, who holds a vajra in his hand, who is yellow in color, whose crown is marked with a vajra, together with his vehicle and retinue, and accompanied by the attendants of Durgā;
thus the rest should be inferred.

This has been stated in the *Matsyasūkta*, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "The deities are to be worshipped outside [the maṇḍala], joined with their own invisible crowns, their lotus-hands raised, each holding its own weapon and the gesture of granting fearlessness."

One should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite and perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) according to the rules. For the sake of pacification, one should present barley, milk, and śāli-rice; and to the yakṣas, one should offer either barley-gruel (yāvaka) or boiled rice with sesame (bhāṣabhakta).
Then, having joined his palms in reverence and knelt upon the ground, he should recite the awakening mantras for her who is worshipped by the gods:
"Aiṃ! For the sake of slaying Rāvaṇa and for the grace of Rāma."
In the past, Brahmā awakened the Goddess for you at an improper time;
therefore, I too awaken you during the month of Āśvina. On the sixth lunar day conjoined with the appropriate asterism, I awaken you in the evening.
For this reason, since the *tātparyārtha* (the intended meaning) is not equal to the literal sense (*asamatva-tattvāt*), it must be recited even when the *ārdrā* asterism is not obtained.
Born on the peak of Śrīśaila, you are the Śrīphala tree, the abode of Śrī;
you must be led by me—go, for you are to be worshipped in the form of Durgā.
For the sake of attaining all happiness without exception and for the cause of female prosperity,
you must be led to the home proclaimed by yourself; become the granter of all desires on the mountain peaks of Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, and Himavat.
O Bilva tree! You have been born as the beloved of Ambikā and Śaṅkara.
Salutations to you, the Bilva tree, the bestower of all desires.
When one's own constellation (nakṣatra) has risen, two fruits should be offered and worshipped with the hand.
"O Śrīvṛkṣa! You are dear to Mahādeva and the granter of all desires;
grant me one branch for the purpose of the Durgā sacrifice.
Then, he should cause it to be climbed from the northward-facing direction.
Having placed kuśa grass, flowers, fruit, and unbroken rice grains along with some lukewarm water in a conch shell, one should offer the *arghya* oblation;
then, having offered a tooth-stick made from the *bilva* tree, one should cleanse the mouth with *ariṣṭa*.
One should wrap the *siddhārtha* with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and a pair of garments.
Thus concludes the sixth-day rite, consisting of the invitation to the bilva tree.
Now follows the seventh-day rite, in that same [text]:
O beloved! When the sun has risen on the seventh lunar day joined with the Mūla constellation, one should go to the root of a Bilva tree and worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, taking up a very sharp knife held firmly in the fist.
A fist is known to be twelve finger-breadths in measure, and six finger-breaths for a closed hand.
One should utter "Chindhi chindhi" (cut, cut) twice, and likewise the pair of "Tāra" (Oṃs).
This is declared to be the Chinnamantra, ending with the heart-mantra followed by the weapon-mantra (astrāya).
The word *yugam* is in the nominative case used in the sense of the locative; thus, it means "in a pair," specifically referring to a particular branch provided with a pair of bilva fruits.
One should "give" or offer it—the ellipsis being "the aforementioned *kaṭṭāraka*.
Here, the root *dā* (to give) carries the meaning of "offering," as in the expression "he gives a garment to the washerman."
He states the mantra for the offering:
"Chindhi chindhi" (cut, cut), and not "Chindhi chindī," because by the latter [form], due to the word *yuga* (pair), there would result a fourfold repetition of "chindhī."
The mantra for cutting, however, begins with "tārayugmam" and so forth.
The meaning is that the mantra recited when the cutting has been performed is the "cutting mantra.
As for the mantra for moving [the deity]:
"O Cāmuṇḍā! Move the two feet and likewise move the two hands;
quickly enter the temple, the place of worship.
One should cause [the image] to move with this mantra, beginning with *Tārā* (OM) and ending with the wife of Vahni (Svāhā).
At the time of cutting, the sight of women and others is prohibited, as stated in that very same [text]:
"The sight of women and the sight of animals must not be present during the cutting;
one should act with effort in this manner and cause [the victim] to enter the palanquin."
One should direct [the mind] toward worship and other such acts; thus he says:
One should not employ one who is insane, fallen, impotent, dwarfed, or possessed of physical defects; nor should one initiate a poor person or one whose mantras are ineffective.
This applies especially during the acts of cutting, piercing, fixing, and installation.
If [the lamp] is extinguished, one should know it to be a sign of death; then one should perform the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
One should place a pair of lamps at the sides, supported by stalks of sugarcane.
And at the time of entering the house, one should set up a pair of water-pots (*ghaṭa*).

At every door, one should place an auspicious and beautiful vessel joined with a broom, tied with a red thread, provided with mango leaves, adorned with cut blades of *darbha* grass, and filled with garlands and flowers.

"One should place at the door a collection of garlands (sraktām), meaning a multitude of garlands—rooted, unbroken, and adorned with arches (toraṇa). The suffix *tā* is used here in the sense of a collective, as in the word *janatā*. This is the meaning.
When he reached the gateway at the entrance, the auspiciously endowed housewife,
preceded by virtuous young women who had performed the auspicious rites,
fanned him with a fan on both his left and right sides.

O Maheśvarī! Having placed the three pungents (kaṭutraya) with salt in his mouth, he should perform a kiss upon the Goddess; thereafter, he should place the leaf-offering (patrikā) in the courtyard of the house, the bathing-seat (snānapīṭha), and the garments and other items in the central area.
He describes the sequence for the *navapatrikā* (nine-leaved offering) according to specific regions:
"One should offer *māṇa* and so forth on Śrīśaila; *dhyānya* and so forth on Mount Malaya;
*kramuka* and so forth at the edge of the ocean; and *kacvī*, *ekāmra*, and so forth in [the region of] Kacchī."
O beautiful one! One who desires prosperity should worship Rambhā and the others at each sacred seat (*pīṭha*)— in Gauḍa, Vaṅga, Kaumāra, and Kālarūpaka— or alternatively,
[worship] Rambhā, Kacvī, Haridrā, Jayantī, Bilva, and Dāḍima.

Aśoka, māṇaka, and the nine-leaved plant beginning with *dhānya*—the leaves should be taken together with their roots, excluding *haridrā* and *dhānyaka*. The *rambhā* should likewise be with its roots; one should avoid the *rāmarambhā*.

The white Rambhā, the Rājya-rambhā, and likewise the Sugandhinī—one of these should be taken; one should avoid the seed-Rambhā. One should abandon a tree whose fruit is endowed with the sweetness of sugar.
One should avoid [wood] from trees that have three sons (three branches), one son (one branch), or whose offspring have died.
One should accept wood planted by the twice-born or that which originates from a mountain.
That which grows in the house of a Brāhmaṇa is superior to that produced at sacred fords (tīrthas).

A [linga] born in the abode of an outcaste, or one residing in a cremation ground, or one with hair-like branches, or one that is withered and causes distant vomiting, should be abandoned. In this very same manner, having brought it to a clay [liṅga], [one should purify it] with waters produced from auspicious sources.
One should bathe [the deity] with water from a conch shell and upon the mirror of the image;
then one should specifically offer a tooth-stick with the mantra,
O Goddess of Gods!— specifically with the ten-syllable mantra— and in between, with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thereafter, one should perform the placement individually with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*),

with the three cool substances (*triśīta*), with the three red substances (*trirakta*), and likewise with sacred water (*tīrthodaka*). Then, on the sacrificial altar (*vedī*), starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), the placement of the leaf-stalks (*patrikā*) is performed.
One should know that there is a cavity in the center, or else it has a single root;
one should fix it upon a plantain tree, having entwined it with three *viṣṇukrāntā* creepers. Upon the plantain tree, at a height of one cubit, there should be a pair.
One should wrap [the image] with a yellow thread and a crown,
using cloth dyed with safflower, or linen, or silk, or even silks from insects; O Goddess, one should especially avoid [cloth] first stained with lac.
Then, during the great festival, one should perform the rites preceded by the chanting of the Vedas;
likewise, one should cause the sound of virgins and virtuous women to be heard.
This applies to the ritual offering of oblations (balikarma), the procession, and the entry into a new house.
During a great festival or an auspicious occasion, the sound of women there is auspicious;
likewise, one should perform the *nirmañchana* rite with parched grain, rose-apple fruits, and other such items. One should offer a welcome, inquire after their welfare, and provide a seat.
Having prostrated upon the ground with both knees, one should recite the mantra with palms joined in reverence:
"Oṃ! O Great Goddess, Sovereign of the Universe, who have come here, please accept this autumnal worship. Welcome to you; salutations unto you!"

"I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, and our life has become fruitful, O Durgā, O Māheśvarī, since you have come to my hermitage! O dweller of Malaya, here is the water for honor (arghya), food, fruit, water for the feet, and a garland."
Accept it, O boon-granting Goddess! Bestow auspiciousness upon me. O Caṇḍikā, O you of fierce form, O bestower of all desires, O auspicious one! Accept this *arghya*, O Blessed One; come to my abode.
Having accepted this autumnal worship, you have come to the circle of mortals;
O Caṇḍikā, I bow to you today—please accept these flowers and the water offering.
O Caṇḍī, you possess a fierce form, O you of great strength and divine splendor!
"Enter and stay in my house while I perform the worship.
Then, having prepared the general *arghya* offering and accepted the seat,
one should scatter the *vikirāḥ* there and subsequently perform *prāṇāyāma*.
Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, and the guardians of the directions within the water-pot (kalaśa);
one should bathe [the deity] with their respective mantras and choose the vessel for the arghya offering.
Then, one should offer the arghya to the Sun and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
One should meditate on a red bubble by means of the ten-syllable mantra;
in its center, one should again pierce the golden cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
In the middle of that, one should contemplate the Goddess, the bestower of all desires.
She is endowed with a mass of matted hair, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel;
she is possessed of fresh youth, adorned with all ornaments,
three-eyed, with a full face, and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Likewise, he holds a trident, a discus, a sword, and an arrow;
similarly, on the right side there is a spear, and on the left a shield and a bow;
as well as a noose, a goad, a bell, and a magnificent necklace of serpents.
Likewise, one should depict below him a buffalo,
headless; and similarly, a Dānava arising from the severing of the head, holding a sword in his hand,
pierced in the heart by a trident, and adorned with entrails streaming forth.
One should meditate upon the Goddess’s right foot as being placed evenly atop the lion,
while her left foot is slightly raised with the big toe resting upon the buffalo;
having thus contemplated this in the mind and fashioned the image, one should install it.
One should worship the Self, the Inner Self, and the Supreme Self;
then, preceded by the placement of the *mātṛkās*, one should perform the placement of the *kalās*.
Having then performed the placement of the mantra, one should purify the *arghya* with the *tāra* (the syllable Om).

To the north of the *arghya* water, one should prepare the *pādya*, *ācamanīya*, and *madhuparka*; then, by the side, one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and mutter the mantra. The practitioner of mantras should recite the mantra eight times and thereafter protect [the area] with the *gāyatrī*.
"Oṃ, may we know Durgā; may we meditate upon Nārāyaṇī;
may she inspire our intellects"—thus one should recite.
With that water, O Goddess of Devas, one should sprinkle the sacrificial materials.
Then, in the northeast, one should worship Gaṇeśa, Gaṇapa, and the sandals of the Guru;
for after the Gurus comes the Supreme, and beyond the Parameṣṭhi Guru is the Guru himself,
as well as Knowledge, Detachment, and Sovereignty, in their proper order.
O Dear One! One should worship those who are red, dark-blue, green, and blue-hued;

as well as those with the appearance of smoke, gold, and lightning—representing Dharma and the other [qualities]. One should place Adharma and the others at the tips of the petals, starting from the southeast (Agni), according to the prescribed rule.
One should visualize unrighteousness (*adharma*), as well as ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*),
and lack of mastery (*anaiśvarya*) as being black, yellow, and red in color respectively;
one should likewise visualize virtue (*dharma*) and the others as having the colors of a goat, a sheep, and a swan.
At the side of the door is Mahākāla, tawny with black eyes; and Nandin, reddish-yellow, bearing a trident and a *khaṭvāṅga*,
resembling a white serpent, two-armed, and lotus-faced.

One should worship Caṇḍeśa, who has a terrifying face and tawny, upward-pointing eyes. Below him, one should worship Ādhāraśakti, who is mounted upon the tortoise and Śiva, whose face resembles the autumnal moon and who holds two lotuses.
One should worship Kūrma-āsana seated upon its head;
above it, Ananta, resembling a kunda flower, seated upon the Brahma-śilā;
and below, the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu), holding the Earth upon his head.
One should worship the Earth, whose limbs are dark as the *tamāla* tree, whose eyes are like blue lotuses, and who is girdled by the shimmering ocean; there,
one should contemplate a lotus with nine-fold filaments.
The minister should meditate upon the natural petals as having ten pericarp centers:
the element of earth, the element of the intermediate space (bhuvas), and likewise the element of heaven (sva);
and the triad of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas, which constitute the three spheres of the Sun and the other luminaries.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, for the one whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs,
the Great Lion, the armor-weapon Great Lion mantra is prescribed.
One should offer a seat with this [mantra] and fashion the form with the root mantra.
Having taken a red flower, one should form the *pāṇikacchapa* (tortoise-hand) gesture;
having prepared a full vessel along with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
one should place it upon the heart with devotion, meditating according to the previously mentioned method.
One should worship with offerings and other services, and then place [the deity] within the maṇḍala.
One should offer a seat, inquire about their welcome, and present the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
Then, having performed the worship of the limbs, one should offer the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should display the eight mudrās and then recite the invocation:
"Oṃ! You have been invoked, O Durgā, both in this earthen image and in the bilva fruit.
Becoming firm, remain as the mistress of the house and be the bestower of all desires within this home."
Come, O Durgā! O highly fortunate one! Let this leaf be accepted.
This auspicious place is yours; I bow to you for refuge.
O Goddess, Mother of the worlds, you who perform the creation and destruction [of the universe]!
O you who are present in all these leaf-manuscripts, establish your presence here!
Grant me long life, grant me wealth, grant me fame, and grant me sovereignty.
Being well-pleased, fulfill the heart’s desire in my home.
Then, one should worship Rudracaṇḍā and the others on the petals starting from the east:
Rudracaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍogrā,
Caṇḍanāyikā, Caṇḍā, Caṇḍavatī, Caṇḍarūpā, and Aticaṇḍikā.
Then, in the center, one should worship Ugracaṇḍā, who is fire-colored.
All [the goddesses] are young women with radiant limbs, bestowing boons and fearlessness,
auspicious, red in hue, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with various ornaments.
O Maheśvarī, one should worship [the goddesses] on the eight petals, especially at the tips of the leaves, with the three-syllabled mantra beginning with Vāk;
namely, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and likewise Caṇḍikā; and Brāhmī, possessing a golden luster and clad in a black antelope skin, holding a staff, a water-pot, a rosary, and the gesture of fearlessness. (1)
Carrying a trident, an axe, a razor, and a drum adorned with the moon,
the goddess Māheśvarī, who resembles snow, should always be meditated upon.
Holding a goad, a staff, a skull-topped club, and a noose in her hands, Kaumārī—resembling the bandhūka flower in hue and bestowing all desires—is to be meditated upon. (3)
Holding a discus, a bell, and a skull in her hands, Vaiṣṇavī—dark as a tamāla tree and radiant as lightning—is to be meditated upon. (4)
Vārāhī, possessing the luster of the fire of cosmic destruction, should be meditated upon as holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a plough with her four hands. || 5 ||
Holding a goad, a lance, a lore-weapon (vidyā), and a thunderbolt in her hands,
Indrāṇī, who resembles a sapphire, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity.
Holding a trident, a skull, and a human head in her hands, adorned with a garland of severed heads, Cāmuṇḍā, whose body is red, is to be meditated upon.
Bearing a rosary of seeds, a stream of blood, a skull, and a blue lotus,
she is golden-hued and radiant with a tiger skin.
Raktākṣī, Daṇḍikā, Nṛsiṃhī, Śivadūtī, Nārāyaṇī, she who is called Kālikā, Māyā, Bhrāmarī, Aravindā, Viśālākṣī, Bhīmā, and Sarasvatī.
Aparājitā, Somalatā, Anantā, Kapālinī, and Bhadrakālī— these sixteen heroines are in front;
they are youthful maidens with four arms, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a goad.
Blazing with all ornaments, seated upon lions, and crowned with the moon—
the deities beginning with Bālā, whose forms are red, are to be worshipped by means of the three-syllable mantra alone.
Thus it is stated in the twentieth chapter of the *Kālīvilāsa-tantra*.
First, the ten-armed goddess should be worshipped, preceded by the ritual installation of the water-pot (*ghaṭasthāpana*).
Having first worshipped the five deities, one should thereafter worship Mahiṣamardinī.
Following that, one should diligently perform the worship of Kārttikeya and the others.
And because of the statement, "Therefore, the worship of the *patrikā* is approved by the *Devīpurāṇa*," one should worship Kārttikeya and the others prior to the worship of the *patrikā*.
In that very same place, he states in what region [of] the Goddess [resides] and who is to be worshipped.
Jayā, the Vidyā, stands on the left, and Vijayā likewise on the right;
on the left is the god Kārttikeya, and on the right is Gaṇapati.
Now follows the meditation on Kārttikeya from the eighteenth chapter.
He who has the appearance of well-refined gold, who bears an excellent sword and scabbard,
whose head is adorned with a turban, and who has the noble peacock as his vehicle—
the hero within the cosmic egg, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other requisites, one should recite the mantra ten times.
Listen, O Kārtikeya, as I shall proclaim the appropriate mantra:
*hrīṃ guhāya kārtikeyāya senānye svāhā*.

The fourteen-syllable vidyā of Kārttikeya has been proclaimed. O beautiful-eyed one, having placed the thumb upon the heart-center of the image, one should recite the mantra ten times; thereafter, the placement of the vital breaths (prāṇanyāsa) shall take place.
Now follows the meditation on victory.
One should meditate upon her, who resembles molten gold, has two arms and tremulous eyes,
is endowed with side-glances as her arrows, is clothed only in the directions (naked),
is adorned with divine ornaments, and bestows spiritual accomplishments.
Having meditated, offered water for the feet and other offerings, and performed worship, one should recite the mantra.
The mantra is: *hrīṃ hrīṃ jayāyai hrīṃ hrīṃ*.
This seven-syllabled great vidyā is proclaimed as that of Jayā.

O Dear One! By the victory over the two illusions (māyādvaya), the seven-syllabled great vidyā, worshipped by the gods, is declared; it ends in "ṅe" and consists of the two illusions again. Placing the thumb upon the heart of Jayā, one should mutter the mantra ten times.
Then, O Goddess, the perfection of the vital breath (*prāṇasiddhi*) arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
Now I shall describe the supreme meditation on Vijayā:
she resembles crushed collyrium, has two arms, and eyes like those of a wagtail bird.

One should meditate upon that eternal Vijayā, who bestows all accomplishments, whose eyes are anointed with collyrium and curved with side-long glances like flaming arrows, who is clad in divine garments, and adorned with various jewels.
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should recite the mantra ten times.
The mantra is as follows:
the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], followed by the name of Śambhu’s consort (Śambhuvanitā) and then the vocative case ending.

O Dear One! If one places the thumb upon the heart of Vijayā and recites the seven-syllabled mantra consisting of *māyā* and *vāgbhava*, then, O Goddess, the perfection of vital breath (*prāṇasiddhi*) arises; of this there is no doubt.
Now, the meditation on the peacock.
O you whose limbs are adorned with various wonderful and diverse patterns! Your birth was from Garuḍa;
O you endowed with infinite power! Your meal is the serpent Kāla.
You are Garuḍa, O illustrious one! Therefore, I bow down to you.
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should recite the mantra once:
*Māyā-bhaga-nāda-bindu-ṅe-anta-nāma-sulocanā*.
If one mutters this seven-syllabled great mantra within the heart, [the desired result is attained].
Then, O Goddess, the perfection of the vital breath (prāṇasiddhi) will certainly belong to the peacock.
Now, the meditation on the mouse.
O bull-shaped one! O highly fortunate one! O you who possess the form of a bull! O you of great strength! O you whose form is action! You are indeed the bull that is the vehicle of Gaṇeśa.
I bow to you, O God; grant me the perfection of my worship.
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should cast three handfuls of flowers;
then, having uttered the two *māyās*, one should say "mūṣika," followed by the name of Śambhu’s consort ending in the dative case— this, O Dear One, is the mantra of Mūṣika.
The consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) is as before.
The Lion Meditation.
You are a lion, you are in the form of Hari; you are Viṣṇu himself, there is no doubt. Since you are indeed the vehicle of Pārvatī, I worship you.
The Lion Mantra.
Having uttered the two *māyās* (Hrīm) for Siṃha and Mahābala,
and again the two *māyās*, O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the mantra;
it is celebrated as the twelve-syllabled great lore (*mahāvidyā*) of the Lion.
Having meditated and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should recite the mantra once.
In the nineteenth chapter.
The meditation on the buffalo.
"O Great Hero! O Mahiṣa! O Śivarūpa! O Sadāśiva!
Therefore, I shall worship you; forgive me, O Mahiṣāsura!
Having meditated thus and offered water for the feet and other offerings, one should mutter the mantra once.
The two *māyās*, *nakula* adorned with *nāda* and *bindu*,
*mahiṣa* likewise ending in *ṅe*, the *kūrca*, and again the two *māyās*—
this eleven-syllable mantra has been proclaimed to you with devotion.
Now, the meditation on Gaṇeśa.
I worship the god who is the delight of Pārvatī, who embodies all the gods, who has a protruding belly, a massive body, an elephantine face, and three eyes.
Having meditated upon him and offered water for the feet and other honors, one should recite the mantra once.
Māyā (the letter *i*), the third letter of the *ka*-group (*ga*) joined with the nasal sound (*nāda*) and the bindu;
likewise Gaṇapati in the dative case (*ṅe*), and then again in reverse order for dissolution (*laya*).
The Meditation on Lakṣmī:
She resembles molten gold, has two arms, and tremulous eyes;
she is radiant with the arrows of her sidelong glances, and her eyes are adorned with collyrium.
One should meditate upon the beloved of Nārāyaṇa, who is clothed in white garments, radiant with the mark of sindūra on her forehead, and seated upon a white lotus throne;
having meditated thus and offered water for the feet and other honors, one should recite the mantra ten times.
The mantra, however, is as follows:
O Goddess of Devas! [The mantra] consists of Māyā, then Kāma ending in the dative case (ṅe), then Māyā again; this is the ten-syllabled mantra of the goddess Lakṣmī.
Now, regarding the meditation on Sarasvatī:
She resembles a conch shell, the moon, and a kunda flower; she has two arms and lotus-like eyes;
she is radiant with the arrows of her sidelong glances; and she is adorned with divine garments and ornaments.
I worship the supreme Goddess, who is Speech personified, enriched with divine ornaments and attire.
The mantra of Sarasvatī is as follows:
The *māyā* (h), the left ear (*v*), accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*,
followed again by two seed-syllables for Sarasvatī— this is considered the eight-syllable mantra.
Meditation on Brahman.
Resembling the rising sun, four-faced and four-armed,
with a countenance consisting of the four Vedas, bestowing dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa;
[this is] the Brahma-mantra.

The first letter of the *ka*-group, joined with the nasal sound (*nāda*) and the bindu, is *māyā*. "Salutation to Brahmā" is the first letter of the *ca*-group, joined with the nasal sound and the bindu.
The seven-syllable mantra of Māyā is proclaimed as that of Brahmā. O auspicious lady! Listen as I describe to you the worship of Sāvitrī.
The meditation on Sāvitrī.
She has the luster of the color of molten gold, possesses two arms, and has tremulous eyes;
she is enriched with divine ornaments and attire, and adorned with celestial garments and finery;
she is illuminated by a tilaka of vermilion, and her eyes are anointed with collyrium.
The Sāvitrī mantra, however, is as follows:
*Māyāṃ* (Hrīṃ), *Sāṃ*, then *Sāvitrī* (Śrīṃ), then again *Puraḥ* (Hūṃ), then *Māyāṃ* (Hrīṃ) once more;
O Goddess, this seven-syllabled mantra is proclaimed as that of Sāvitrī.
Now, the worship of the nine leaves (*navapatrikāpūjā*) is described in the *Matsyasūkta*.
O Śaṅkarī! One should worship Rambhā, who has two arms, is yellow in color, and holds a trident and a book, with this mantra using the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja):
"O Durgā, O Goddess, come hither; manifest your presence here."
O Goddess, in the form of Rambhā, grant me peace; salutations be unto you! || 1 ||
Holding a sword, a trident, and a goad, and bestowing fearlessness with your hands,
you appeared in the form of Kācvī during the battle with the demon Mahiṣāsura, O lady of noble vows!
For the sake of showing favor to Śakra, come to my abode.
She should be worshipped with the seed-syllable of Māyā; then one should contemplate Haridrā—
two-armed, clad in yellow garments, three-eyed, and holding a sword,
standing upon a buffalo, large-eyed, with a garment in her left hand.
O Haridrā! O boon-bestowing Goddess! O you of the form of Umā, O lady of excellent vows!
O Sovereign of the Gods, accept this worship for the destruction of my obstacles. || 3 ||
Jayantī, clad in red garments, and Caṇḍamālinī, who is yellow-hued,
both bearing tridents and discs and adorned with every ornament,
[were unable to overcome] Niśumbha even by the hosts of gods led by Indra.
O Jayantī, you have been worshipped; become the bestower of boons upon us. || 4 ||

One who always delights all the gods and acts for the pleasure of Mahādeva should worship her in the sky— she who destroys calamities, possesses two arms, rides upon a great bull, is white in color, and bestows fearlessness and boons.
Since you cause Umā joy, therefore I bow down to you. || 5 ||
She has pomegranate leaves, is red in color, and is adorned with red ornaments;
she wears red garments, is serene, and has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel.
She is four-armed, three-eyed, and seated upon a buffalo.

One should worship her who holds a sword and shield on her shoulder and a blue lotus and a book in her left hand, using the seed-syllable *maṃ* as the first of the [mantra] beginning with *bāla*. This mantra was previously perfected when it arose in the presence of Raktabīja.
Since you bring delight to Umā, therefore I bow down to you.
The Aśoka leaf is red, its form crimson as vermilion;
it holds an arrow and a bow, is gentle, stands upon a lotus, and has a serpent for its vehicle.
Indeed, the Aśoka tree brings joy to Hara and is the destroyer of sins.
For you are the one who brings joy to Umā; therefore, always make me free from sorrow.

One should worship her who has a dark body, who wears a necklace of jewels, who holds a blue lotus, who is mounted upon a buffalo, and who possesses three eyes, using the seed-mantra of the Virgin (Kanyā).
O Kaumārī! You dwell upon the leaf of the Māṇa tree, O beloved of Śacī!
And for the sake of favoring me, accept this worship as you please. || 8 ||

One should worship the auspicious, lotus-faced goddess— who is submerged in a grain-tree, has two arms, a white form, is seated upon a white lotus, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness— with the seed-syllable of Śrī accompanied by the *tāraka* mantra.
Created by Brahmā in ancient times for the welfare of the life-force of the world, this grain which brings pleasure to Umā—grant peace; salutations be unto you! (9)

Outside, on the pedestal, one should worship with ritual offerings the goddess named Jayantī and likewise the guardians of the directions along with their weapons— those who bestow joy and nourishment—
and further, the kumuda, utpala, padma, kunda, śephālikā, and javā flowers.
The eight flowers are said to be *vakula* and *tagara*.
One should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, during the interval between the offerings of the sacrificial food (*bali*), one should cook a portion of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Then, having joined his palms in reverence and touched the surface of the earth with his knees,
he should recite the hymn according to the rule, preceded and followed by the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja).
Now, the hymn: I perpetually bow to Ambikā, who is Durgā, Śivā, the bestower of peace, the consort of Brahmā, the beloved of Brahmā, and the leader of all the worlds.
I bow down to Caṇḍikā, the auspicious, beautiful, pure, partless, and supreme digit;
the sovereign of the universe, the mother of the universe. I bow to the Goddess, the mother of Īśāna, who removes the fear of all the worlds.
I perpetually bow to Umā, who is saluted by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu;
who dwells in the universe, whose abode is the universe, and who resides in the divine realm.
I prostrate before Caṇḍikā, the Yoginī and the Mother of Yoga.

I am forever prostrate before the Goddess Īśānī, the Mother of Īśāna, the Sovereign beloved of the Lord, Durgā, who carries one across the ocean of worldly existence. Whoever recites this hymn or listens to it with devotion—
Released from all sins, he rejoices together with Durgā.

Having bathed at the end of the day and completed the evening twilight prayers (*sāyaṃsandhyā*), [he should perform the rite] amidst the fivefold sounds of drums and the like, and the resonance of songs and musical instruments. (p. 519)
Facing the western direction and remaining silent, one should meditate upon the form of the Goddess in the east, adorned with perfumes and garlands, using the Haṃsa-mantra.
One should offer the arghya water and pay obeisance, and thereafter proceed to the temple of the Goddess.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess according to the rules with the five types of offerings;
then, having eaten sacrificial food, one should chew a tooth-stick.
Thus ends the ritual for the seventh day.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the eighth day.
Then, having risen at the break of dawn on the eighth day,
one should go to the bank of a river and perform a bath with a concentrated mind;
in the absence of such a stream, one should bathe in water where the sun is visible.
Then, having caused the benediction (*svasti*) to be recited and having paid homage to the five deities,
one should perform the ritual bath, the fire-oblation (*homa*), the offering of oblations (*bali*), and the hymn of praise; likewise,
the worship at each watch of the day, especially at midnight.
On the ninth day, one should likewise perform worship, and on the tenth day, the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*),
as well as the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the Brahmins, specifying their lineage and one's own name. Having thus made this resolve, the wise man should perform the bath of the Goddess.
Then, O beautiful one, listen to the words for water and milk ending in the dative case (ṅe), as well as the heart-mantra of Caṇḍikā;
listen also to the mantra for the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), which consists of the Māyā-bīja, the syllable *gaṃ*, and the heart-mantra of Gaurī.
*Tāra* (Om) and *Vāṇī* (Aiṃ) from the two eyes; *Sarvataḥ*, *Hṛdayāntaka*, *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Antanu*, *Vudā*, *Hṛdayārṇa* (Namaḥ), and *Śarkarā* (Svāhā).
O Girijā! *Tāra* and *Māyā* are declared to be the *Madhumantṛ*.
With water, one should again recite "māyāṃ śikhāyai namaḥ.
The mantra for curd is declared as "tāraṃ cakraṃ bhadrakālī kavacāya.
For oil, it begins with vāgbhava and ends with "māyāṃ gauryai namaḥ."
O Goddess of gods! likewise with warm water and with jaggery and ghee;
O Maheśānī! with the *vāṅmantra* and likewise with sugarcane juice;
and when [the specific mantra] is not mentioned, O Maheśvarī! it ends with *caṇḍikāyai śāntim* and *svāhā*.
O Maheśvarī! With the ten-syllable mantra and various scented waters— namely, water mixed with three red substances, three fragrances, and three cooling agents—
as well as with water from fruits, water from sacred fords (tīrtha), water from flowers, and water from *kuśa* grass.
Then, having performed the placement of the jar and completed the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā),
one should meditate upon [the deity] as before and then install [the deity] with the mantra.
One should ask the arriving [deity] "Welcome," and then offer water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings with devotion.
Having performed the limb-worship (*aṅgapūjā*), one should bathe the Goddess with the *gāyatrī* mantra.
Then one should offer the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) and again the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*).
On the petals starting from the east, the Mothers beginning with Jayantī should be worshipped.
Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā, Śivā, Kṣamā, Dhātrī, Svāhā, and thereafter Svadhā;
and likewise upon the tips of the petals there, Rudracaṇḍā and the others as well.
Rudracaṇḍā, who has the luster of yellow pigment (rocanā); Pracaṇḍā, with a reddish glow; Caṇḍogrā, who is black in color; Caṇḍanāyikā, who is dark green (śyāmā);
Caṇḍarūpā, who has a white radiance; and Caṇḍavatī, who is smoky-colored (dhūmra).

One should worship Ugracaṇḍā, who is fire-colored, in the center; she is exceedingly fierce, white in appearance, yet with a yellow complexion, using the mantra beginning with Vāk and ending with the Heart-mantra starting with Tārā.
One should worship the sixty-four [deities] in the eight seats (pīṭhas) starting from the east:
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī;
then, according to the rules, one should worship Jayantī and the others with the five types of offerings.
Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī,
Durgā, Śivā, Kṣamā, and Dhātrī should be worshipped with great effort. Furthermore, in the southern regions, one should worship Svāhā and then Svadhā.
Ambikā and Carcikā, as well as Kātyāyanī; then Raktadantikā and Sarvādimaṅgalā;
after that, Śākambharī, Bhrāmarī, and then Śivadūtī.
One should worship Mahākālī, Gaurī, Tarjanī, and likewise Bhāvinī; one should also worship Mahāmohā and Bhayaṅkarī. Then, at the western extremities, one should worship Bhīmā, Padmā, and Śacī.
Medhā, Mahāmāyā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, Bhrāmarī,
Mahāmāyā, Mahādevī, and likewise Mahāmedhā.
One should worship Kāmeśvarī in the north, as well as Kāmadā;
likewise Bhrāmarī, Kālarātri, and Mahārātri;
and then one should worship Cakreśvarī and Bhagamālinī.
One should worship Dhūmrā, Bhīmā, Śāntā, Vidārī, Mahāmbikā,
Lakṣmī, Suparṇā, and Mahogrā with due respect,
as well as the family deity (Kuladevī), using the three-syllabled mantra.
One should worship the *vaṭukas* at the door, arranging them in pairs according to their divisions:
the one named Siddha, Sandeha, the one named Kālaputra,
as well as Kriyākulanibha, Mantrāṅga, and Puttaka, O Goddess!
One should worship with the *maṇḍara* seed-syllable together with the *tārā*.
One should worship Bhairavas, beginning with Asitāṅga, and the Lords of the Field (*kṣetreśas*) in due order:
Hetuka, Tripurāṅga, and likewise Agnijihva.
One should worship Kālāsya, Karālāsya, the one-footed Bhīmaka,
Anugraha in the upper portion, and Nāsikeśvara below;
