ending with the heart [mantra] accompanied by the *tāra* (om) and the seed-syllable of Narasiṃha.
On the outer pedestal, the practitioner should indeed worship with that same seed-syllable:
Jambhaka, Maṇibhadra, and likewise Pūrṇabhadra,
as well as Virūpa, Virūpākṣa, and Citrakuṇḍala.
One should worship Citrākṣa, Citrarūpa, Kelimālin,
Varendra, Nandin, and Siṃha, as well as the planets and the world-protectors;
those who are the planets beginning with Āditya, and those planets of cruel deeds.
All the lunar days (tithis) and days of the week (vāsarās) are indeed present here in their vicinity;
may they come here for the sake of worship, for I shall worship them.
[In the phrase] "krūrakarmaṇaḥ," the short vowel occurs due to Vedic usage (chāndasatvāt).
Now follows the worship of the weapons (astras).

One should worship the goddesses and their weapons in the sequence beginning from the south, using their respective mantras and seed-syllables, along with perfumes, sandalwood, and flowers. [One should praise them thus:
"By whom this earth was upheld and the demon Mahiṣāsura was slain..."
Salutations to that pure-souled one who possesses a trident with three prongs.
O Dharmapāla! You are the sword, the slayer, the scimitar, the sharp-edged, and the unassailable; you are the womb of prosperity and victory—salutations be to you.
Thus, one should offer eight oblations with sharp-edged blades, and likewise a rod of iron with the mantra beginning "O Sovereign of the Wheel! (cakreśvarīti):
"O Sudarśana! O Great Wheel! O Terrifier of the King of Daityas!"
O glorious destroyer of Tripura! O sovereign of the discus! Homage be to you!
O you who are endowed with a multitude of beautiful limbs! Salutations again and again to the Discus!
This mantra of the Discus, together with its seed-syllable, is the destroyer of all obstacles.
Salutation be to the Five-Arrowed One, the stainless, the Great Soul;
salutation indeed to the Five-Arrowed One, whose very nature is the five principles (*pañcatattva*).
You are the power (*śakti*) of all beings, and the pervader of even those who pervade.
O best of Śaktis, salutations to you who seize both the opportune and the inopportune time!
The mantra is declared as the seed-syllable of Ramā (Śrī) together with the Tāra (Om) and Jaya.
Then, starting from the left of Vāmā and so forth, they are to be worshipped subsequently with mantras according to the prescribed rite.
O giver of dharma, you are the very weapon of all dharmas in battle. Since you must be protected by me, O sinless one, salutations to you!
You are held by Kṛṣṇa for the sake of protection and by Hara for the sake of destruction.
I bow to Sagara, the embodiment of the three Vedas, and to the bow and weapon;
to the bow that was exceedingly dear to Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, and to the beloved of Fire (Svāhā).
The mantra for the bow is declared to begin with "Vijaya" and end with "Śara."

O Nāgarāja! O Great Noose! For the sake of removing infinite obstructions, you were fashioned by Viṣṇu; therefore, protect us—homage to you, svadhā! You have been bestowed upon Caṇḍikā as one who possesses all powers and the brilliance of peacock feathers.
O Churikā! Protect me always, grant me peace; salutations be unto you.
[Recite] "to Churikā" and the two *ṭha*s.
O beautiful one, hear the mantra for the bell, ending with the word *koṇa*.
One should worship the mantras all around, as well as the gods and the sages;
immediately thereafter, one should worship the lords of the seats (pīṭheśas) and the lords of the living beings (jīveśas) with ritual offerings.
And in that very place, one should worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the Creator (Brahmā).

Then, with effort, one should perform [the rite] according to the divisions using mantras declared in the Vedas, the Āgamas, and likewise those in the Purāṇas, as well as those spoken in the Svatantra;
thereafter, with the pure Dadhi-sūkta and the Gāyatrī.

Having recited the mantra, one should perform a hymn of praise and offer oblations (homa) amounting to one-tenth [of the recitation]. Then one should perform an act of propitiation and recite this mantra:
"Whatever little has been offered by me with flowers, perfumes, and ointments..."
May you consume all of that; be gracious and become a granter of boons, [bestowing] nourishment, wisdom, fortitude, intelligence, health, and prosperity.
Now, the mantras for the sixteen types of ritual service (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Be gracious, O Mother of the worlds, O Savior from the ocean of saṃsāra!
Make fruitful this seat offered by me with devotion. (1)
The measurement of the seat is found in the fifth chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
A man should offer a silver pedestal four fingers wide,
along with appropriate ornaments;
for it is in the form of the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) that he brings forth all things, both moving and unmoving.
"I shall perform worship; welcome to you, O Maheśvarī! || 2 ||
O supreme mistress of the lords of speech, may this foul-smelling [substance] become a supreme fragrance;
this water for the feet is offered by me—be gracious, O Sovereign of the World! (3)
O Goddess worshipped by the three worlds, accept this *arghya* offered by me, mixed with *dūrvā* grass and rice, and filled with camphor and agallochum. || 4 ||
The waters are Nārāyaṇa himself; within the waters resides all that is moving and unmoving.
O Goddess! I offer you this water for rinsing the mouth. || 5 ||
"O fair-faced one! For the sake of attaining the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*vājimedha*), I have given this;
accept the *madhuparka*, O my Mother, Sovereign of the World! (523.6)
Alternatively, one may also offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) with the ācamanīya mantra. || 7 ||
O Goddess! May you accept this holy, fragrant, and most enchanting water for bathing, offered by me and contained within a conch shell. (8)
O Goddess! O Supreme Sovereign! O You whose nature is the Supreme Brahman!
O Auspicious One! Accept this garment and this sacred thread, O Goddess! (9)
You alone are the light of lights, without beginning or end;
adorn this ornament given by me. Homage be to you! 10.
"O fair-faced one, take a flower—fragrant, difficult to reach, and none other than one garlanded with white and blue lotuses—that bestows white, yellow, and reddish hues! (11)
O Supreme Goddess! Accept this incense, blended with guggulu and anointed with sandalwood and aguru, produced from the ten and eight ingredients. 12.
O eternal one! O Goddess of gods! May this lamp be accepted for my welfare—you who are the supreme light, the supreme Brahman, and the sole reality of the universe. (13)
O Supreme Goddess! Accept this most enchanting food offering (naivedya), consisting of fruits, roots, and other items, which has been given by me with great devotion. 14.
In the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
Having prepared various delightful food offerings (naivedya) accompanied by diverse fruits and mixed with sugar, one should also offer milk-rice (pāyasa);
thus it is stated in the Matsyasūkta.
O you who are the support of the entire world! O you who are worshipped by the three realms!
I pay homage to your lotus feet, which are honored among the wise; I circumambulate you. (15)
One should present a manifest arrangement of many fruits made from the powder of rice, mung beans, peas, lentils, and sesame seeds. || 16 ||
"Protect my life, protect my fame, and protect my sons, wife, and wealth;
for you, O Goddess, are the protector of all in the three worlds.
Just as in the case of the specific substances mentioned here in the formula written by the Smārta Bhaṭṭācārya regarding the offering of the *bali* oblation, [the same applies].
The expression [of the deity] according to specific desires has been stated in that very same [text].

"Listen, O fair-faced one, I shall speak briefly the words appropriate for the offering of substances: grant that which is complete according to the ritual manual (kalpa). Then, desiring victory as desired, one should give the fragrance, saying, 'I give this fragrance.'"
Desiring residence in heaven for ten million eons, one should offer a blended ointment, saying: "I give this anointment with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron.
Then, desiring to obtain the fruit of giving ten gold pieces, one should offer various kinds of appropriate flowers, saying: "I give these flowers."

One should offer flowers— whether specifically mentioned or not— including *jāti*, *yuktavimukta*, *campaka*, *bilvapatra*, *utpala*, *kumuda*, *mallikā*, *kāñcana*, *śephālikā*, *kahlāra*, *karavīra*, *jayantī*, *bandhūka*, and whatever water-born, forest-grown, or mountain-born flowers are available at the appropriate time.
(p. 524) Desiring to obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice today, one should offer two garlands of bilva leaves.
Then, desiring to obtain a threefold fruit greater than that of offering flowers, one should say, "I give this karavīra garland," and offer a bakula garland fashioned with various ritual elements.
Desiring today to obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows, one should offer two garlands of jasmine and a red lotus.
Then, one desiring to obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice should offer various kinds of incense, saying, "I give this incense.

One desiring to obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice should offer lamps with ghee, dedicating them by saying, "I give this ghee lamp," and should present individual lamps and torches within a row of lamps made of ghee.
Then, desiring to obtain the merit of a hundred Gomedha sacrifices,
one should offer these pure items— various fruits, leaves, flowers, diverse kinds of food, drink, betel, and so forth— which are pleasing to the heart.

Thereafter, one who desires to obtain the fruit of the gift of ten gold *tāraka* coins based on the *Puṣkara* rite should give— according to availability— pure and well-formed stalks of flowers and the like, the five types of grain, sprouted rice, lotus roots, lotuses, and lotus stalks.

Having said, "Desiring to dwell for as many thousands of years as there are threads in this garment in the abodes of Śiva and Durgā, I give these garments— linen, silk, or whatever else is available," one should offer garments that are fine and soft in texture.

Then, desiring to obtain the fruit of ten gifts of cows performed at the Gaṅgā, one should give [the gift] while designating it with the words, "I give this along with an upper garment and a sacred thread.
Then, desiring to obtain the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows, one should say, "I give gold," and give it.
Then, one desiring to attain a blazing desire whose locus is heaven should say, "I give this umbrella," and thus offer an umbrella.
One desiring to obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice should offer a fly-whisk, saying, "I give this fly-whisk.
Desiring today to obtain long life, health, victory, and uninterrupted, abundant enjoyments, [one should offer] that which is like a jewel born from the rays of the moon.
One who desires extreme good fortune,
or who desires to attain the world of Durgā as distinguished by thousands of forms, grains, and maidens,
should give a bed with its pillows, sandals, and so forth.
Having offered the bali-oblation, one should then perform [the sacrifice] with a black goat, which is the supreme among the supreme.
The specific details regarding the offering of the *bali* will be explained further on.
(p. 525) Having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should circumambulate [the deity] and always practice the recitation of praises (*stuti*). Now follows the praise:
Nārada said:
Oṃ! O Blessed One! O Destroyer of Fear! O Kātyāyanī! And O Kāmadā! O Kauśikī! O Great Sovereign! O Kālikā! I bow down to you. || 1 ||
O Pracaṇḍā! O Puttride! O Goddess! O Suprītā! O Leader of the Gods! O Illuminator of the Kula! O Ugrā! O Pārvatī! Be gracious to me! || 2 ||
O Durgottāriṇī! O Durgā! You who ward off all that is inauspicious!
O Goddess, bestower of all goals upon all! May you be the granter of boons to me. || 3 ||
O fierce and terrible one! O goddess, granter of boons! O Pracaṇḍā! O bestower of victory!
O goddess who fulfills dharma, artha, and kāma! O Kātyāyanī, homage be to you! || 4 ||
O Goddess! Destroy my sin, committed knowingly or unknowingly, throughout thousands of other births while I was in the wombs of animals. 5.
O Goddess who bestows peace and prosperity! O Mother, savior of the three worlds!
O Sustainer of the universe, you who manifest as the Bilva tree, I pay homage to you. (6)
Salutations to you, O Śivā! O Goddess, O all-pervading one, O daughter of Śaṅkara!
Grant me my desired duties, beginning with those pertaining to my own station, as well as prosperity. (7)
Since you alone are the sole protector of all, therefore I bow to you, O Queen of Gods! Be gracious and grant me boons. 8.
O Goddess! May this worship of Sarveśvarī which has been performed by me for you become entirely complete through your grace, O Maheśvarī! || 9 ||
May there never be a birth in that family— whether for one already born or for an embodied being still in the womb— in which the Goddess Caṇḍikā is not present.
Thus ends the ritual for the eighth day.
Now follows the ritual for the midnight hour.
Then, O Maheśānī, being composed in mind, one should perform [the rite] at midnight,
during the day, or at the twilight (saṃdhyā), first in the water of the Śaraṇā;
and on the eighth and ninth lunar days, it may be done according to one's desire upon a palanquin (śivikā).
One should undertake a night-journey at twilight, at the onset of the night;
thereafter, one should worship with devotion using offerings such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and other oblations,
accompanied by various dances, songs, and diverse musical instruments.
One should offer red flowers on the eighth lunar day,
O Goddess, or else with a thousand beautiful *vakula* blossoms;
and he who offers a white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), especially at midnight, [attains great merit].
One obtains all desires, as well as one hundred and eight [merits]. Now follows the ritual for the ninth day, in that very same place.
On the ninth day, one desiring prosperity should perform worship as before.
At twilight on the ninth day, one should offer to the Goddess meat-food with sugar;
if that is available, it should be accompanied by wine and meat.
Araṃ means sour gruel.

Having performed the rite of pacification (śānti), one should give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to the prescribed rules. One should present a pair of garments as a fee to the preceptor (ācārya).
Furthermore, for the sake of complete satisfaction, one should give gold to the knower of the ritual procedure.
One should give grain, silver, and copper to the Brahman priest;
likewise, grain and gold to the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
One should also honor the Brahmins, the maidens, and others as well.
One should worship the poor, the blind, and the wretched with devotion;
one should give them the food prescribed for the Sun, especially that which is fit for a day’s meal.
When he strikes his enemies with his arms for the sake of pacifying the obstacles to the offering of tribute,
he should worship the devotees of Śiva, especially those who are not devotees of Śiva;
for whoever they may be, O Pārvatī, both the devotees of Śiva and the devotees of Viṣṇu [are to be honored].
Having entered the house again with song and instrumental music,
one should worship the household with devotion and eat together with one's kinsmen.
Thus ends the ritual for the ninth day.
In that very same [text]:
"On the tenth day itself, having performed the daily rites with devotion at dawn,
one should go down to the ground on one's knees and then cause this to be heard:"
Oṃ! Kāli! Kāli! Mahākāli! Kālike! O destroyer of sins!
Kāli, you who have emerged from Karālī! O Kālike, homage be to you!
O rider of a lion! Cāmuṇḍā! Beloved of the wielder of the Pināka bow!

Having thus accepted this offering, be gracious, O Supreme Goddess! Om, arise, O Goddess Cāmuṇḍā! Having accepted this auspicious worship, go to the flowing water, and remain here when the tide has risen.
The Cāṇḍālī who wears the remains of offerings (nirmālya) is to be worshipped with perfumes and sandalwood.
Having offered [these] with the mantra, one should utter this mantra:
"Having immersed her in the water and worshipped her in the water honored by the surrounding time."
"You have been placed by me in the water for the sake of increasing the life and wealth of my son;
the sacrificer himself should likewise send Śivā Caṇḍikā [into the water].
One should not gaze upon the Great Goddess, nor should one send her into the water naked."
On the tenth day, when the moon has entered the asterism of Śravaṇā, the boy should be placed in the waters;
however, if that asterism is not attained, it may be done at any time except during the night.
One should present the materials for worship and offerings to the preceptor.
One who knows the ritual procedure should give half of that to the officiant and half of that to the Brahman;
he should likewise give the remainder to the *ṛtvij* priest for his satisfaction.
Furthermore, a householder should never look upon his own place of worship.
Having cast the Goddess into the waters, one should bestow her upon a Brāhmaṇa.
If a wise man causes a house to be built upon a site where the Goddess was previously situated,
his fortune, strength, and lifespan— all shall perish at that very moment.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the tenth day.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Ritual Duties Beginning with the First Day," in the section on the Durgā Festival within the fourth part, the Section on Optional Rites (Kāmyakāṇḍa), of the *Śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī*;
[this occurs] in the fifty-first chapter.
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall declare the mantra of Durgā according to all the tantras;
listen to its specific application in the autumnal rite as it is proclaimed:
the three syllables are Vāk, Śakti, and Kamalāsyā.
One should employ it for the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites, as well as for liberation (mokṣa).
Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), and Anuṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter (chandas). Śambhu is its deity (devatā); one should employ it for the four aims of life (caturvarga).
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (kāmalakṣa); the libation (tarpaṇa) should be one-tenth of that.
One should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the offering (bali), and the fire-oblation (homa), each being one-tenth of the preceding.
[The mandala consists of] the six cities, the eight-petaled lotus, the petal of the digits (kalā), and the city of the earth (dharāpura).
One should worship [the mandala] which has four gates, is endowed with seed-syllables (bīja), and is provided with seats (pīṭha).
Then, one should worship Brāhmī and the others on the petals, and Jayantī and the others in the six cities (ṣaṭpura).
Likewise, Śeṣa and Śeṣa are in the center, and Amṛtā and the other digits (kalā) are on the covering of the petals.
Meditative concentration.
She is endowed with a mass of matted hair, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
she is possessed of three eyes, her face resembling the full moon;
she has the luster of molten gold, is well-established, and has beautiful eyes.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with all ornaments,
possessing beautiful teeth and likewise full, elevated breasts,
she stands in the *tribhaṅga* posture as the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Understand that he holds a trident in his right hand, as well as a sword and a discus;
likewise, know that he also holds a sharp arrow and a spear in the right.
Furthermore, [he holds] a shield, a full bow, a noose, and a goad.
One should visualize either a bell or an axe in the left hand of the Goddess;
likewise, one should depict a buffalo below her with its head severed,
and similarly a Dānava with a sword in his hand, arisen from that decapitation.
With his heart pierced by a spear, adorned with protruding entrails,
his limbs stained deep red, and his eyes flashing with blood;
encircled by a serpent-noose, his face terrifying with a frown.
One should depict the lion drinking the blood of the Goddess;
the Goddess’s right foot is placed evenly upon the lion,
while her left foot is slightly raised with the big toe upon the buffalo.

Having meditated thus, one should mutter the mantra, offer the bali-oblation, and recite the hymn of praise. O Supreme Goddess! Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is declared to be Śambhu himself, while Caṇḍikā is the presiding goddess.

Oṃ! I bow to you, O Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman, who contain the Vedas within, and who pervade the entire universe; O Refuge-giver, I worship you! || 1 ||
I bow to you, O Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune— the sovereign lady known as Kāmākhyā, the granter of desires, dark-hued, capable of assuming any form at will, and enchanting to the mind.
I bow to you, Vijayā, the three-eyed Durgā who destroys all misfortune, adorned with every ornament and endowed with a smile. || 3 ||
I bow to you, Bhavānī, who are praised by Brahmā and the other gods, served by Siddhas and Gandharvas, the goddess Durgā who destroys all misfortune. || 4 ||
I bow to Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who possesses a divine form, who crushes Niśumbha and Śumbha, and who slays the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 5 ||
I bow to Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who possesses twenty-five arms, resembles pure gold, and has the form of Gaurī.
I bow to you, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who bears the trident, sword, discus, arrow, spear, and battle-axe.
I perpetually salute Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, who is identical with the universe, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), and the agent of creation and destruction.
This divine armor, a great mantra of great fruit—
whosoever, endowed with devotion to me, recites it daily,
to him I grant wealth and grain simply by its single repetition.
Thus ends the Durgā-stotra in the Matsya-sūkta. In that same work:
"O Durgā, [protect me from] the red chain."
The ten-syllable mantra is proclaimed as beginning with *nigama* and ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*). This knowledge is the Great Knowledge, celebrated as Jayadurgā.
Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and Gāyatrī is proclaimed as the meter (*chandas*).
The deity shall be Durgā; one should employ her for all purposes.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; this is declared to be the *tattvanyāsa*.
One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) consisting of a tenth part of that number, and libations (*tarpaṇa*) equal in number to the seasons (six).

One should offer the seat with the Mahiṣa-mantra; one should proclaim the seat and fashion the form with the root mantra. Listen to the visualization, O fair-faced one! It is on the shore of the ocean, adorned with rows of forests.
It was surrounded by *tāmāla*, *tāla*, *hintāla*, *pāṭala*, and *āmalaka* trees;
it was filled with the blossoms of *kunda*, *mandāra*, *dāḍīma*, and *kadamba*;
it abounded in *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *rambhā* trees, and was adorned with *candana* and *aguru*.
The forest near the lake was fragrant, its quarters perfumed by the scent of sweet-smelling flowers; it was crowded with herds of animals and flocks of birds,
and adorned with water-lilies, blue lotuses, white esculent lilies, and white lotuses.
In that place was a beautiful quartet of *pārijāta* trees that bestow nectar,
possessing fragrant sprouts and bearing clusters of blossoms;
there also was a jeweled pool, a pavilion, and a floor inlaid with gems.
Resembling the tip of a lightning bolt and possessing a radiance equal to the rising sun,
it was adorned with white umbrellas and shone with a celestial chariot;
it was beautified by hundreds of thousands of banners and white yak-tail fans.
There, one should visualize a beautiful lion-throne adorned with garlands of jewels; upon it, a radiant lion, born of the four Vedas as its feet, consisting of the twenty-four principles,
with a flickering tongue protruding outward, moving tawny eyes, possessing the luster of snow, and difficult for all to behold.

One should meditate upon a vast, radiant red lotus, possessing great majesty and power, endowed with six cities, and situated upon the king of beasts; within it, one should contemplate her who has the luster of molten gold and illuminates [the world] with divine, auspicious, three-eyed forms.
She wore two earrings of the moon and sun, and she joyfully bore the moon upon her crest.
Then Mahiṣāsura, his flood of strength and heroism severed,
emerged with a spear and a trident, facing her whose face was furrowed with a frown.

She looked again and again at the blood-drinking lion that had been assigned to her— a lion whose mane was seized by a future king of beasts who dragged away its mount, and who was even being devoured by most terrible tigers with red mouths.
The Great Goddess was being praised by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Rakshasas, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, and Uragas with the sounds of songs and musical instruments,
during the great festival, at the deep of night, whether she was rising or reclining.
In that great sacrifice, the great yoga,
one should apply meditation there upon her who is eternal, with the luster of a blue lotus, three-eyed, and crowned by the moon;
she holds in her four hands the conch, the discus, and a sword.
One should also meditate upon her with three crests and matted locks, seated upon a lion.
O Maheśānī! on the lion-throne, one should worship her together with the Śaktis:
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sūkṣmā, Viśuddhā, and likewise Nandinī.
Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā are the nine Śaktis.
In the Ṣaṭpura [mandala], one should likewise conclude with Bhairavī in the center of the remainder.
O Dear One! One should place Brahmā and the others at the front starting from the east; the rest is as before.
I shall now declare the mantra that bestows auspiciousness for the eighteen-armed [form],
which is proclaimed as being elevated to the state of *bhāva* when the principles (*tattvas*) are free from defects.
I shall also describe the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon the Goddess, which destroys all sins.
She stands in the center of a solar disc, with a radiance like a forest fire;
she is endowed with a mass of matted hair, possesses three eyes, and has the moon as her crest-jewel;
the goddess is eighteen years of age and adorned with red garments.

Listen now to the description of her who stands upon a lion-throne slaying a buffalo, and who holds in her right and left hands a spear, an irresistible trident, a thunderbolt, a sword, a goad, an arrow, a discus, and a lance.
Furthermore, [one should worship] Vaṭuka known as Siddha, and again Vaṭuka Sandeha;
likewise Samaya and the others, the limbs (aṅgas), the petals and so forth, and the ritual action (kriyā).
Among them, [one should place] the son Ananta and Vaṭuka to the left of the Śakti.
One should worship with the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) joined with the seed-syllable (*bhāva*) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Furthermore, [the goddesses are] Ajitā, Aparājitā, Jayā, and Vijayā;
likewise Kālī, Śyāmā, Maṅgalā, and Siddhi.

O Maheśvarī! I shall proclaim the mantra of Kātyāyanī, which accomplishes all aims. First, one should extract the seed-syllable of Jayadurgā, beginning with the letter *va* and rooted in the *tāra* (om);
then, one should extract the syllables beginning with *ka* for the twelve-armed goddess, starting with *kamala*.
One should perform the Māyā-nyāsa everywhere, and for the two-armed form, the Vāgbhava [bīja].
She resembles the brilliance of vermilion and the sun, possesses full and elevated breasts,
is three-eyed, the slayer of Mahiṣa, and is endowed with the rays of the crescent moon.
With his four right hands, he holds a sword, a trident, a discus, and a mace;
in his left hands, a shield, a goad, a bell, and five severed heads.
One should worship Yava and the others on the petals, and Śrīkaṇṭha and the rest outside of that.
Now, with a concentrated mind, I shall describe the meditation upon the eight-armed goddess:
she who resembles ten million suns, who has three eyes and the moon as her crest-jewel;
she who wears a deer-skin as an upper garment and dwells upon the shoulders of a lion.

O Dear One! With his eight arms, he holds in his right hands the sword, the discus, the thunderbolt, and the lightning-bolt; and in his left hands, in sequence, the skull-bowl, the shield, the bow, the arrow, the bell, and the axe—these indeed are his weapons.
The Mothers, Puṣṭi and the others, are on the petals, and Śrīkaṇṭha and the others are outside of them.
The meditation on the four-armed [form] featuring the Śrīvatsa mark is prescribed by the Vaiṣṇavas.
[One should meditate on her] as mounted upon a lion, extremely formidable, holding a trident, a discus, and likewise a bow.
One should meditate upon her as striking the conch, the lotus, and the buffalo.
Thus concludes the specific worship of Durgā.
Now follows the greatness of the names of Durgā, wherein her true nature is revealed in the Rudrajāmalatantra:
The third letter of the dental class (ta-varga) joined with the fifth vowel (u),
and the third letter of the palatal class (ka-varga) with the letter *ra* above it, O Dear One!
joined with the second vowel (i)— this is proclaimed to be its name.
Now, regarding the greatness of the Name:
in the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra, it is said:
"Indeed, there is no worship equal to that of Durgā; indeed, there is no recitation equal to that of Durgā."
Indeed, there is no knowledge equal to Durgā; indeed, there is no austerity equal to Durgā. Wherever the life-story of Durgā exists, there is the abode of Kailāsa.
(From the Third Chapter)
O Goddess! The fruit born of remembering Durgā—the fruit born of remembering Durgā!
What indeed cannot be accomplished on this earth by the mere remembrance of Durgā?
Whether one be a devotee of Śiva, a devotee of Viṣṇu, or a devotee of Śakti, O Daughter of the Mountain!
One should worship Durgā, remember Durgā, and sacrifice to Durgā, the beloved of Śiva;
at that very moment, O Goddess of the lords of gods, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. Likewise:

You have heard in various tantras the mantra of Durgā in the form of the syllable *Ā*. O Caṇḍī! that person who constantly worships the supreme mantra of Durgā, namely "Durge Durge," is liberated while living.

The grammatical connection is as follows: "O Durgā! O Durgā! In terrible distress, whoever should worship and recite the supreme mantra of Durgā—the hundred names beginning with 'Durge'—he shall become liberated even while living.
It states the further result in that very same place:
In times of great portents, great disease, and the peril of great calamity;
when great suffering, great grief, and great fear have arisen—
he who always remembers Durgā and who recites the supreme mantra.
O Goddess of the gods! that person in the world of the living shall attain the state of Nīlakaṇṭha (the Blue-throated One).

He who, during great portents and other calamities, should bring Durgā to the range of his memory, and he who, while reciting [her mantra], should bring her to the range of mental perception—he shall attain the state of Nīlakaṇṭha, just like [the god] who [drank] Kālakūṭa.
By being the one who brings about great portents and the like, one obtains [the state of Śiva];
furthermore, in what follows, everything is entirely consistent, including the state of Nīlakaṇṭha and the state of Śiva.
(p. 532) He clarifies that very point in the fourth chapter.
"Whether with faith or even without faith, whatever man remembers Durgā,
having crossed over a hundred difficulties, he goes to the supreme goal.
(From the Seventh Chapter)
O Goddess! Various systems of Tantra and various jewels have been revealed;
yet who on this earth is capable of knowing the true nature of Brahman?
Like animals with ruined intellects, they run about along various paths.
Leaving the lotus feet of Śrī Durgā, they go to the netherworld (rasātala).
I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial; I speak what is wholesome again and again:
there is neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation without the service of Durgā.
In the eighth chapter: One who with devotion remembers, recites, and meditates upon the Blessed Goddess Durgā, the destroyer of suffering and poverty, is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
He who is devoted to the Tantra is to be known as one liberated while living;
he who follows the feet of Durgā is a practitioner and a possessor of great knowledge.
O Daughter of the Mountain! For him, there is neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation, nor even a [particular] destination.
O Mother of the Universe! Without Durgā, life would be fruitless.
O Śaṅkarī! Those who, having devoted themselves to the path of Śakti, then run toward another path—no followers of Śakti will even look upon their faces.
O Mother of the Universe! Those who are deluded by the nets of words and treatises worship other deities, being whirled about in various scriptures, without [worshipping] Durgā.
(From the third chapter of the Pūrvakhaṇḍa in the Picchilātantra).
There is no name on the surface of the earth equal to the name of Durgā;
by the mere remembrance of it, the calamities of the earth flee away.
By the recollection of the name of Durgā, he states that all branches of knowledge are recollected.

Tāriṇī, Sundarī, Kālī, Durgā, Bhairavī, Bhuvaneśī, and Mahālakṣmī— among these, the name "Durgā" indeed belongs [to one of them]. By the use of the plural "tāsām" (of these), the entire group is understood.
He clarifies here the status of the previously mentioned name as a mantra:
"The great mantra of the name Durgā is the most excellent among all mantras;
the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is prescribed by reciting it exactly one hundred thousand times."
When one has encountered fear from kings and others, the name of Durgā is the supreme refuge. In great calamity, in great terror, and in the crisis of extreme poverty,
great misfortunes flee by the mere recitation of the mantra one hundred thousand times.
In the Jāmalam: Śiva said:
"The great arising of health, prosperity, and knowledge."

O beloved! This very name is the supreme cause of liberation for those attached to worldly existence, especially in the Kali age, even for those who have committed great sins. One should know that the recollection of the Name is the seed of deliverance.
Even one who is devoted to another's wife, or a thief of another's property,
or even one who has committed a heinous crime (atipātakī)— he too shall be liberated from sin.
[These include] the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife.
Therefore, even from that one may be liberated if the wise person should remember it; for,
O Supreme Goddess, the name of Durgā is declared by those who know the four Vedas to be superior to the thousand names of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, by the chanting of the name of Durgā, all sin perishes at that very moment;
this is well-established in the Vedas, Āgamas, Tantras, and Purāṇas.
For Vaiṣṇavas, it is remembered that there is nothing superior to the name of Hari.
In such a view, it should be known that the name "Durgā" is even more supreme than that;
O beautiful one, there is nothing difficult to attain for him, either in this world or in the next,
who constantly remembers Durgā— he indeed is Śrī Sadāśiva himself.
Even one devoid of purity and right conduct, if he should remember the Supreme Goddess,
he alone is said to attain the supreme state, O you who are praised by heroes!
Such is the destiny of the pure Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas.
O Queen of the Gods! By this act—namely, the remembrance of His name as well as that of the devotees of Śakti—Yama has no authority over me.
What more need I say to you regarding one who performs the recitation of Durgā’s names?
O beloved! Even for hundreds of millions of years, I am unable to describe [the merit of] those who take refuge in the name of Durgā;
they shall remain in heaven as long as the earth, wind, ether, water, fire, moon, and planets endure.
He who, being pure, recites [this] with devotion one hundred and eight times every day shall become wealthy, possessed of sons, happy, and long-lived on this earth. Furthermore,
the devoted man who recites it one thousand and eight times [shall attain the same].
O Supreme Goddess! Listen to the fruit of his merit for doing this daily:
one who desires wealth obtains wealth, and one who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge;
the afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and the bound is released from bondage.
One who is afraid shall be liberated from fear; one who is a sinner shall be freed from sin;
and one who desires a son shall obtain a son, O Goddess! This is the truth, there is no doubt.
O Supreme Goddess, he who recites this ten thousand times every day with devotion—
Capable of both restraint and favor, he would become a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*);
from his anger comes death, and through his grace comes perfection.
Thus one should know him to be competent in all ritual actions.
O fair-faced one, for him who performs a hundred thousand recitations month after month,
there shall be no affliction from the planets, nor separation from kinsmen;
his sovereignty shall not decline, nor shall he ever suffer injury from serpents.

O Goddess! There shall be no fear of fire or thieves, nor fear in the forest or in water; nor shall there be fear from lions, tigers, and the like when climbing mountains, nor shall there be fear of bhūtas, pretas, or piśācas anywhere at all.

O beloved, there shall be no fear of enemies, nor fear of robbers on the road; and no disease such as fever shall ever abide in the body. O you who are worshipped by heroes! It has been declared that one shall become a dweller in heaven in the next world.
O fair-faced one! Having become equal to the moon and the sun, one may dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas;
whatever fruit might be obtained from a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices, O fair-faced one, that same fruit is obtained daily by chanting the name of Durgā.
The practitioner who recites [the mantra] at the time of worship on the banks of the Gaṅgā obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
it is like the merit found in the Prājāpatya vow or likewise in the Cāndrāyaṇa.
O Goddess of the Suras! Whatever fruit is declared for fasting on Ekādaśī for ten million times,
or for going to the Gaṅgā during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
or for giving away all one’s possessions at Kurukṣetra— [that fruit is attained here].
Whatever fruit is obtained at holy sites such as Prayāga through the ritual bath in the month of Māgha,
and whatever is gained by worshipping Śambhu on the fourteenth day of Śivarātri,
that same fruit is attained by beholding Lord Vāmana mounted upon his chariot in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama.
Having worshipped Mahāmāyā in Kāmarūpa within the maṇḍala of the womb of Kāmākhyā, the fruit obtained is such that the name of Durgā is even superior to it;
[this is especially so] on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar day, at the dead of night.
And one should perform the recitation in a cremation ground upon the heart of a *cāṇḍāla*,
provided that one is naked, free from fear, and has disheveled hair;
he shall attain success that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
O Goddess! O beautiful one, if there should be a lunar eclipse on a Saturday or a Tuesday,
whoever recites ten thousand [mantras] at that time during the dead of night shall be free from all affliction and worthy of being saluted by the gods and the lords of sages.
O Great Goddess! If the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) should fall on a Tuesday,
one should worship Pārvatī there with a thousand bilva leaves,
offer an oblation according to the prescribed rite, and recite the Thousand Names.
Whatever is most desired in the world, that he certainly obtains;
on the night joined with the eighth day of the dark fortnight, he shall become a member of the Gaṇas. Having gone there to the cremation ground on a Saturday, O fair-faced one!
Having performed the slaughter of animals and having assumed the *yonimudrā*,
the practitioner, liberated from all sins, shall accomplish the goal of Śivā,
O Pārvatī, on the eighth, the fourteenth, and the ninth lunar days.
Whoever performs the recitation of the names of Durgā one hundred and eight times shall obtain every desire in this world and in the next,
especially when in the presence of the waters of the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, or Yamunā.
The practitioner who, with devotion, recites [this mantra] one thousand times on the new moon day,
shall cause to perish all the sin arising from the abduction of another's wife or the theft of another's property— sins that are the cause of rebirth in the Mahāraurava hell.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes! He who recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times at night at the great sacred site of Kāmarūpa, in the presence of the womb of Kāmākhyā,
shall become a master of speech and attain the state of Śiva in the hereafter.
Whoever performs the recitation (*japa*) in Vārāṇasī in the presence of Bhavānī,
even if poor, becomes wealthy and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the fruit of the name of Durgā.
Now, the hymn of the hundred names of Durgā,
from the second chapter of the Muṇḍamālā Tantra:
"O wife of Bhava, listen to the hundred names of Durgā!"
Durgā, Bhavānī, Deveśī, Viśvanāthapriyā, Śivā;
she with terrible fangs and a formidable mouth, adorned with a garland of skulls;
Rudrāṇī, Tāriṇī, Tārā, Māheśī, and the beloved of Bhava.
Nārāyaṇī, Jagaddhātrī, Mahādevapriyā, Jayā, Vijayā,
Jayārādhyā, Śarvāṇī, Haravallabhā, Asitā,
and likewise the goddesses Aṇimā, Laghimā, and Garimā.
She is the power of Maheśa, the sovereign of the universe, Gaurī, the daughter of the mountain;
she is eternal, stainless, desireless, and perpetually fresh;
she is red, with a red face, the goddess of speech, joined with the Vasus, and the bestower of wealth.
The beloved of Rāma, devoted to Rāma, the bestower of boons upon the Lord of the Raghus;
the sovereign of kingdoms, delighted in royal power, the dark-complexioned one, the bestower of boons upon Kṛṣṇa;
Yaśodā, Rādhikā, Caṇḍī, Draupadī, and likewise Rukmiṇī.
She who is dear to Guha, she who delights in Guha, she who sports in the lineage of Guha;
the mother and progenitress of Gaṇeśa, she whose form is the universe, and Jāhnavī;
Gaṅgā, Kālī, Kāśī, Bhairavī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
She is stainless and fragrant, the daughter of Devaka, worshipped by the gods;
born of Dakṣa, she is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), skillful, and the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice;
she is of excellent character, beautiful, gentle, Mātaṅgī, Kamalā, and Kalā.
The destroyer of Niśumbha, the destroyer of Śumbha, the destroyer of Caṇḍa;
the annihilator of Dhūmralocana and the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
Umā, Gaurī, Karālā, Kāminī, and Viśvamohinī.
Thus, O fair-faced one, these hundred names have been told;
by the mere remembrance of these names, a man becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He who, having risen at dawn, recites them while remembering the two feet of Durgā, [attains liberation].
One is liberated from the bonds of birth; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Whether at the time of twilight, during the day, at night, or at the onset of night, by reciting these hundred names, one will certainly attain the perfection of mantra.

If one should practice the ten sciences without knowing this King of Hymns, even then no accomplishment shall be attained; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī! Thus ends the hymn of the hundred names of Durgā in the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.
Now, the Durgāgītā;
likewise, in the seventh chapter:
"O Goddess! The doctrines of various tantras and various jewels have been revealed."
Who on this earth is capable of knowing the true nature of Brahman?
Like senseless cattle, they run along various paths;
abandoning the lotus feet of Śrī Durgā, they go to the netherworld.
"I speak the truth; I speak what is beneficial; I speak what is wholesome again and again.
Neither worldly enjoyment nor liberation is attained without the service of Durgā.
Pārvatī said:
In Goloka I am indeed Rādhā; in Vaikuṇṭha I am Kamalā;
in the world of Brahmā I am Sāvitrī; and in the form of speech, I am Bhāratī;
on Kailāsa I am the goddess Pārvatī; and in Mithilā I am Jānakī.
In Dvārakā I am Rukmiṇī, and in Nāgasāhvaya (Hastināpura) I am Draupadī;
I am Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas, and I am Sandhyā for the twice-born.
In the midst of Yoga I am Pūṣā, and in Puṣpa I am Kṛṣṇā Aparājitā.
The *mālūra* leaf is upon the vessel, and the pedestal is of the nature of the *yoni*.
This Vidyā, whose essence is Hari and Hara, is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. O Lord Śaṅkara, she is to be known specifically through her special grace.
O Lord Śaṅkara! O Mahādeva! Wherever Śakti resides, there alone am I; this is my firm and supreme conviction. Indeed, he who abandons the path of Śakti and runs toward another path [is lost].
Abandoning the jewel held in his own hand, he runs after the burden of ashes—
the burden of ash.
Thus ends the Durgāgītā.
(p. 537) Now, the bali offering.
In the Tantra of the Conduct of the Samaya.
Listen to me regarding the offering of oblations (bali) to all the deities,
by performing which the practitioner quickly attains the supreme fruit as described.
At the time of eating, the practitioner should [perform it] daily with the root mantra.
O Dear One! One should perform the offering of the *bali* before the meal;
thereafter, with a steady mind, one should eat.
O Goddess! After eating, one should remain in a state of purity.

One should collect the *bali* offering and place it in a secluded spot; having placed the *bali* there, O Goddess of Devas, one may then enjoy oneself as one pleases. She who is proclaimed as Mātaṅgī in the Northern Traditions (*uttarāmnāya*)— [End of excerpt]

O fortunate one! At the conclusion of the meal, even without performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should offer the bali-oblation day after day with the root mantra. Then, having performed a brief recitation (japa), one should proceed with the sipping of water and other rites.
Furthermore, having diligently offered the *bali* to all at night, one should perform it according to the prescribed rite and shall obtain the stated fruit.
And the *bali*, O Goddess, is of two kinds: *sāttvika* and likewise *rājasa*.
The *sāttvika* offering is said to be devoid of flesh, blood, and the like;
the *rājasa* offering, O beloved, is declared to be possessed of flesh, blood, and so forth.
(From the Gāyatrī-tantra, Chapter Five, Brāhmaṇa-paṭala).
Three kinds of offerings are proclaimed: superior, inferior, and middling.

The superior [practitioner] should give the superior [offering], and likewise the middling [practitioner] the middling. O Goddess! The inferior is said to be for the inferior; even in the case of the inferior, the result is inferior.
That [offering] in which there are ten numbers of oblations is called the middling;
it is the sattvic, supreme worship if one should offer a great oblation.
One should offer a great oblation at the junction of the eighth and ninth [tithis], where there is a great [spiritual] power.
Whether it be a hundred, a thousand, a lakh, ten thousand, or even millions upon millions, O best of kings, such an offering is praised when making worship with a *sāttvika* disposition.
By a single offering of this *bali*, one may attain the fourfold aims of human life.

Through many offerings of oblations, one becomes composed of the Supreme Brahman. O King, through many offerings of oblations and sacrifices of recitation (japa-yajña), a Sāttvika worship is performed; therefore, it is called Sāttvika.
The autumnal worship performed with ten animals, as well as with recitations and sacrifices,
is proclaimed by him to be *rājasa*;
the worship performed with the five offerings is proclaimed by him to be *tāmasa*.
In the Matsya-sūkta.

Practitioners are said to be of three kinds: the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and likewise the *tāmasa*, O Goddess! I shall describe their characteristics to you. The *sāttvika* practitioner, O beautiful one, is endowed with *sāttvika* characteristics.
One should diligently perform the *sāttvika* offerings of oblations (*balidāna*) and so forth regularly; O fair-faced one, the *rājasa* person, joined with *rājasa* qualities,
performs the *rājasa* offerings of oblations and so forth, O Mistress of the Gods, being endowed with *rājasa* traits.

O beloved! O beautiful one! A person of tamasic nature, joined with tamasic qualities and those of the rajasic type and so forth, has no faith in the offering of oblations, in worship and the like, nor in the recitation of hymns or fire-sacrifices; such a practitioner is a practitioner in name only.
In the seventh chapter of the Uttarakhanda of the Yoginītantra.
One should offer milk-oblations to the Brahmins, or else boiled rice (śālyanna) or milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should present sacrificial porridge (caru), fruit, and flowers soaked in ghee along with that [rice],
as well as cow’s milk, and offer mangoes and sour fruits.
Rice cooked with milk, or honey, or sugar-cane juice, or sugar-candied balls (modaka);
for kings, cattle are indeed prescribed as offerings, as are paddy for Vaiśyas;
for those of the Śūdra caste, honey, or else cattle for all.
One should offer a red-cheeked human, or a buffalo,
or a boar, or a goat, or likewise a yak,
or a ram, or a boar, and a monitor lizard.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
A Brahmin should not give a buffalo, nor a rhinoceros, a yak-tail, a boar, a tortoise, a porcupine, an iguana, or thereafter a human; likewise, he should not give liquor or a ruru deer.
It should not be discolored, nor human-like, nor even emaciated;
it should be a goat up to three years of age (trihāyaṇa) after one year has passed,
possessing two very beautiful horns resembling the tusks of a boar.
Endowed with the fragrance of musk and adorned with a line of hair,
such a black *tāraṇaka* brings satisfaction for twelve years.
Regarding the distinction between castes, he states the specific characteristics of the social classes (varṇa) in that very same [work]:
A white goat is especially recommended for a Brāhmaṇa;
a red one for a Kṣatriya, and a pale yellow one for a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra’s may indeed be of various colors, provided it has the luster of collyrium.
In the Yoginītantra.
And for domestic animals, the sacrificial offering (bali) may be made after six months have passed.
If it is a goat, it should be black or white, provided it is more than two years old.
Likewise, one may offer a horse, a deer, or a mountain goat.
Mūṣika, Karāla, and Kṣudramārjāra.
That which is to be avoided is also mentioned in that very same place.
The kākola, the kalaviṅga, the rājahaṃsa, and the śārika;
the parrot, the vulture, the kākola, the peacock, and likewise the citraka;
the horse, the veṇupṛṣṭha, and the black pigeon.
One should carefully avoid the vṛhatkapotaka, the khañjarīṭa, as well as the crane and the balāka.
He states another type of *bali* offering in that very same place:
One should offer an oblation (bali) consisting of plantain, jasmine, and citron, mixed with fragrant substances, especially on the eighth lunar day.
If one maintains these ritual applications, this is the oblation mantra for the practice.
O Goddess! One should daily offer a bali-oblation at midnight at a crossroads;
this wards off enemy armies, planetary afflictions, diseases, and magical spells (kṛtyā).
Having first uttered the Praṇava (Om), one should then utter "Ugratāre."
One should utter twice the mantra *vikaṭadaṃṣṭraṃ parapakṣaṃ mohaya*.
Having uttered the pair *khādayat*, one should again speak the pair of wings (*pakṣadvandva*).
Then: *ye māṃ hiṃsitumudyatā yoginīcakre tān dāraya huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
"Draw forth, draw forth all vidyās; cut, cut; strike, strike; seize, seize them in the skull-cup, svāhā!"
And with this very [mantra], O Goddess of gods! O Maheśvarī! one should offer the bali-oblation;
thus it is stated in the sixth chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
Then the king should offer the enemy-oblation prepared with milk;
he should sever the two [parts] with a wrathful gaze and with a blow-dealing [gesture], and with anger once, O Goddess! This is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī!
O Maheśvarī! Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of life-force) using the name of the enemy, O Maheśānī! the destruction of the enemy certainly occurs; there is no doubt.
Regarding the specific procedure for the enemy, it is found in the *Matsyasūkta*.
O Goddess of the gods! With this mantra, one should perform what was previously prepared:
O Kātyāyanī, O Ambikā! [The mantra consists of] Tāra (Om), two *hana*s, two *daha*s, two *paca*s, two *matha*s, and likewise two *prathama*s.
*Māyā*, the two [syllables] *vaśaṃ* and *caṇḍi caṇḍi*, and *tāraka*;
then the two *nārasiṃha*s, followed by *mandara* with *tāraka*;
*cāmuṇḍe*, *praṇava*, and "devour" (*bhakṣaya*), followed by the two *dahat*s.
One should place two *mathas*, two *pacas*, and two pairs of *chindhis*;
then [place] two *om*s, two *jayas*, and likewise two *sphoṭayas*.
At the end of the two *kartayas*, one should then utter *daha*.
Having rescued my enemy, one should then utter the seed-syllable;
"burn, burn" as a pair, then "cut, delude";
at the end of the two "cuts," then "separate."
Then, one should utter the mantra at the end of the word *śatrupada*:
first the *tāra* (OM), followed by the pair "hana," then the pair "bhakṣaya," then the pair "trāsaya," and after that, the pair "nāśaya. Following that, [one should utter] "āveśaya."
Then, at the end of the pair *ārohayasphoṭaya*, and at the end of the pair *uccāṭayayuga*,
and at the end of the pair *unmattayayuga*, one should utter this mantra;
taking a black flower, one should personally perform the ritual sprinkling (*nirmañchana*).
And for the wives as well, O Goddess of Gods! one should cause [the offering] to be given with this mantra:
"May all those creatures who harm me go to destruction;
may death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the heads of my enemies."
One should cast a hostile gaze and a wrathful look upon the head of the enemy.
Having recited the pair of armor-mantras (*kavaca*), one should utter the pair of *svāhā* mantras.
It is stated in the *Matsyasūkta Mahātantra* that among goats and other such animals, each subsequent species is more excellent than the preceding one.
Ten chowries are surpassed by a single goat;
O Lord, ten goats are excelled by a single tortoise;
and even a hundred tortoises are surpassed by a single hare.
O Maheśvarī! Even if a hundred rabbits were to shed blood from their own bodies until a lotus petal is filled,
a single porcupine quill is superior to those hundred cups of blood.
A boar is distinguished by a thousand quills;
two thousand of a boar’s [quills] are said to equal one of a buffalo. Two thousand of a buffalo [quills] are surpassed by a single rhinoceros.
With a thousand rhinoceroses, there is incomparable fruit for a human;
two thousand humans are praised as equal to one red-beaked [rhinoceros]; and two hundred red-beaked ones are praised as equal to one white-necked [rhinoceros].
Even for a hundred white-necked [deer], the iguana is considered superior;
even for a hundred iguanas, the young of a man [is superior].
Ten iguanas are equal to one black antelope, and ten spotted deer are equal to one black antelope.
Among ten spotted deer, one ram is distinguished;
among ten rams, a goat is distinguished;
and among ten goats, the black-colored one is distinguished.
Eight times eight [offerings] made with sesame, unbroken rice, and flowers are distinguished;
among goats, one of black color is distinguished by a single white [mark];
if there is a crown of ten white-colored [marks] upon its head.
One should recognize that as praiseworthy and examine it for any injuries;

from a hundred of those [other animals] comes one *lulāpa*, and from a hundred *lulāpas* comes one rhinoceros (*khaḍga*). Yet, among hundreds of rhinoceroses, a human being is distinguished as superior.
Among ten men, one boar is distinguished;
O Goddess, the fruit of a boar satisfies Śivā even more than that of a hundred buffaloes. Among a hundred buffaloes, the one called *godhā* (the monitor lizard) is distinguished.
And likewise, the blood from his own limbs [is offered] along with hundreds of lizards;
and similarly, Śoṇatuṇḍa and Śvetagrīva,
as well as Kuṣmāṇḍa of the mountains, O beloved, at midnight!
Regarding the gift of a buffalo, the fruit that is proclaimed for both cutting and giving it away is as follows:
A rhinoceros (khaḍga) ten years old and a buffalo after a year [of age] are recommended;
however, one should avoid a white-colored rhinoceros or a white buffalo.

O Maheśānī! [The great sage] should not eat anything at all until that man— who is like a white-and-black buffalo and as handsome as a dark-complexioned youth— reaches his full maturity beyond twelve years.
Birds, tortoises, and crocodiles— whether born on land or in water—
their desire is as follows:

Today, desiring to attain the world of Brahmā— characterized by the mounting of an excellent celestial vehicle adorned with rows of banners, preceded by the acquisition of long life, health, victory, and abundant enjoyments— one should offer ten goats to the Blessed Lady.
One should perform the consecration of the sword and cut with that very sword.
One should worship it with red flowers, with fragrance, and with sandalwood.
One should place the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), followed by the pair of *māyā* (hrīṃ hrīṃ), the pair of *kāli* (kili kili), and then *vikaṭa*.
O Daṃṣṭrākarālī, O Niṣpeṣaphetkāriṇī, devour!
O Nārasiṃhikā, emit [the sound] "aja," drink, drink quickly the blood!
Then follows the second pair, *kiri-kiri*, and thereafter the pair *kāli*.
The word *vrajeśvarī* ending in the dative case (*ṅe*) is remembered as being accompanied by a lotus, a sword, and a bow.
One should offer blood, sugar, and water with rock salt;
one should offer fragrant flowers and cast in a pair of *darbha* grasses.
The trident has three prongs.
Oṃ Kāli! Kāli! Mahākāli! Kālike! O destroyer of sins!
Accept this blood and the sacrificial offering (bali), O granter of boons, O lovely-eyed one!
[Then follow] Tāra, Tāra, then Māyā, Hrāṃ, Hraiṃ, Hrauṃ, and the two Ṭhas.
One should utter the *tāra* (oṃ), followed by the pair of *sthāṇu* (ha ha), and then extract the remaining limbs (*śeṣāṅga*).
Then [utter] "khaṭvāṅga," "nṛmuṇḍa," and "triśūladhāriṇī.
Following that, [utter] "vikaṭadaṃṣṭre," "karālāsye," "kapālamālini," and then "hāṃ hāṃ gṛhṇa."
At the end of the word *sāṭṭahāsinī*, there is the mantra and two *vikaṭas*.
Then follows *śivaṃ kāntaṃ tato vāntaṃ kaṃ kaṃ kālyai namaḥ* as the fixed formula.
This is the *mātsyabali*; having addressed it with "svāhā," one should cause it to be given.
*Tāraṃ* (the syllable *oṃ*), the pair flashing from *māyā* (*hrīḥ*), the pair *hana*, and the two *ṭha*s;

*indhanaṃ* (the word *indhana*), the pair of *aguru*, and "grasp, grasp" (*gṛhṇa gṛhṇa*) with the two *ṭha*s. Having performed the consecration of the earth, one should fashion the threefold aggregate (*trivarga*).
Pūtanā, Kauśikī, and Kālikā, in their proper order.
The specific procedure for the sword worship and other rites in the Yoginītantra is as follows:

Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, O beautiful one, [one should say] "Kālikālī," and thereafter the words "O Mistress of Vraja, for your iron staff, O man. Having thus worshipped, O Goddess of Gods, one should then worship Śakti.

"Huṃ huṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī and Brahmā; huṃ, and [obeisance] to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. O Goddess! O Caṇḍā! O Maheśvarī! one should utter these words and worship with "Obeisance to Umā and Maheśvara," and so forth.
After the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should then say "namaḥ kārtikeśvarābhyām.
By means of this very mantra, a person should employ the *śakti*.
Having thus worshipped the sword, he should worship it with special care.
"O Sword, destroyer of the wicked, intent upon the accomplishment of your purpose!
O Lord of the Sword, this sacrificial animal must be swiftly cut by you; salutations be unto you!
With this very mantra, one should prostrate before the excellent sword.
Taking a copper vessel filled with water and facing north,

one who desires joy should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) for the Great Goddess and for the animal. Having performed the sprinkling of the animal, one should release it with the thought that it is a deity.
According to the prescribed rite, let this be offered to you.
In the Matsyasūkta:
One should cut the supreme sacrificial offering with the Candrahāsa sword;
the Candrahāsa is four spans long and has the shape of a Karavīra petal.
The middle one.
The measurement for the blade is twenty-five finger-breadths, and the width of the blade is three and a half finger-breadths.
If a living being is killed with a sword having a single edge,
the killer does not obtain the fruit [of the merit] of that act, but rather goes to hell.
The withdrawal of the single stream, however, occurs in that very same place.
A single-edged blade shaped like the petal of a lotus leaf is praised;
a trident-handled sword is likewise commended for the rite of offering (balikarma).
By a single blow, the sacrificial victim (bali) shall face the north.
Having first positioned himself facing east, he should cut with vigilance.
Having placed the sacrificial offering (bali) facing east, he himself should face north;
the wise one should then cut it with a sharp sword in a single stroke.
In the Yoginītantra.
When that [line] is severed and fallen on the left side, it is censured;
when it falls in the middle, the wise man should contemplate it as a "severance of the Goddess" (devīccheda).
The expiation for that is also mentioned in that very same place.
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, one should offer oblations with fifteen [verses];
by that very means, one should cast away the defect and observe the offering (bali) endowed with its proper characteristics.
In the Matsyasūkta:
O Goddess of the Gods! Having severed the head and offered it as a sacrifice, one should likewise offer the blood of a goat, performing that which was previously prepared with this mantra.
Now, the vessel of blood.
In the Matsya-sūkta.

Silver, earthenware, bronze, brass, and likewise wooden vessels are recommended for the sight of blood; one should avoid those made of wood and iron. One should also strictly reject conch shells and stone vessels, as they are impure.
By offering water for the *arghya* with a *svastika* or a lotus-petal vessel, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a human being.
One should not offer the blood from the throat of a goat; indeed, that is specifically forbidden.
At the edge of the lotus petal and likewise at its center,
the measurement of the petals should be according to the sequence of the Mothers.
Now, the method for collecting blood is described in that same [text]:
One should offer a specific measure of flesh along with blood from the animal held upon the sword,
as well as the blood and head of the sacrificial animal in particular. One should cause the head of the animal and the head of the bird to be presented in their proper positions, without inversion.
O Maheśvarī! He who lights a lamp upon a tortoise, a yak-tail fan, or a peacock, shall fall into a miserable state before long.
Even by cutting a blade of *darbha* grass into two or five pieces with blood [as an offering], [one incurs such a fate].
One should offer [the oblation] starting from the eastern part and then in the middle;
having placed it on the palm of the left hand, one should consecrate it with this mantra:
"Kāli! Kāli! Mahākāli! Kālike! O destroyer of sins!"
"O Goddess of gods! Take this heated blood; salutations be unto you!
With the mantra "Kāli Kālī," one should offer it to Caṇḍikā.
[One should also offer to] Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the sinful Rākṣasī.
Having placed Kauśikī in front, one should cause red [offerings] to be given to the Goddess.
I shall now declare the mantra beginning with Kauśikī, which bestows the accomplishment of dharma, kāma, and artha:
*Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), *Kamalā* (Śrīṃ), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), *Kamalā*, *Kamalā*.

The Kāmakalā is declared to be *spheṃ spheṃ* followed by *khīraṃ* and ending with *dviṭha*. O Śaṅkarī, I shall now describe this mantra with every effort, using either the first syllable of each of those [syllables] joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*).
One who recites this mantra—*Tāraṃ vyoma tato māyāṃ yaśca padmam*—as follows: "O *Oṃ*, O Three-eyed One! O You with a terrifying countenance! O You adorned with a garland of weapons!
O You who bring an end to all asuras! You who wield the sword, the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and the trident!"

(544) O Goddess, you who hold the sword, the skull-topped staff, and the trident—I shall declare the Great Mantra: one should utter *Tāraṃ* (Oṃ), then *Krauṃ Krauṃ*. Then follow *Kauśikāya*, *Gṛhṇa Gṛhṇa*, and at the end of these, the two offerings (*balidvaya*).
Furthermore, there is *tāra*, *māyā*, and the pair *prasphurat*;
*daha*, the two *cala*s, *kuhu*, and indeed *kuhu* again, and the pair *gulū*;
and again the pair *māraya*—this is what has been proclaimed by the wise.
I shall now declare the mantra beginning with Viśākhā, by which auspiciousness arises:
first the *tāra* (Oṃ), then *vikaṭadaṃṣṭre* in the dative case (*ṅe*), followed by the two words *hana hana*, then *vai viśikhāya svāhā*. This is proclaimed as the mantra for the *bali* offering.
In the Yoginītantra.
Then, having taken blood, one should worship Vaṭuka and the others.
O Maheśānī! One should worship the fierce Vaṭuka-Bhairava in the southwest (Nairṛti), and in the northwest (Vāyavya) with "Huṃ Yāṃ, obeisance to the Yoginīs," and so forth.

And in the northeast, O Maheśānī! one should worship with perfumes and flowers, O Goddess, saying "Huṃ Kṣauṃ, obeisance to Kṣetrapāla," and so forth. In the southeast, one should worship saying "Huṃ Goṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa," and so forth.
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, one should present the bali offering.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
O Goddess of gods! As long as the attendants consume blood that has fallen upon the ground, for that long one should avoid applying the ointment.
Thus concludes the procedure for the offering of the bali-oblation.
Now follows the fire-oblation (homa).
In the fifth chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
Inspection is performed with the root mantra; sprinkling is considered to be done with the arrow-mantra (śara).
Striking with that same [mantra] using *darbha* grass is prescribed, while sprinkling is remembered as being done with the armor-mantra (*varma*).
Digging and lifting [the earth] are done with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), and filling it up is done with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*).
Sprinkling with the *samīkaraṇa* mantra and protection with the *varman* mantra are prescribed; pounding with the *heti* mantra and cleansing with the *marmamantra* follow,
after which comes the smearing and the fashioning of the artistic forms.
Thereafter, the tripling of the thread is performed; worship with the heart-mantra is prescribed.
One should perform the "vajrification" with the weapon-mantra and, using auspicious *kuśa* grass, effect the cutting of the threads at the crossroads with that same mantra.
One should consecrate the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the sacrifice with these aforementioned purificatory rites (saṃskāras).

According to the observation of the Sūtra, "one should sprinkle [them] with the hand turned upward while reciting the mantra 'phaṭ' with the syllable 'śara'," the sprinkling is performed with the fingertips using that very mantra, 'phaṭ'.

"Sprinkling and pouring with water using the hand in a clenched fist while reciting the *varman* mantra, namely *huṃ*—this applies to each of the four [mantras]: the *heti* mantra, the *astra* mantra, and the *varman* mantra.
This has been stated by Somaśambhu.

"Sweeping, smearing, the fashioning of the form of the *kalās*, the encircling with the triple-thread, and the worship of the armor with the heart-mantra. Regarding "the fashioning of the form of the *kalās*," this refers to the fashioning of the *kalās* of the moon, sun, and fire. "The making of the triple-thread" means by means of three threads.
The wrapping. "Vajrīkaraṇa" means making it firm like a vajra.
"With kuśa grasses" means with their tips pointing eastward and northward.
Having divided the central portion into the form of a crossroads, one should visualize the *āvasathya* fire and the others.
As it was stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The *āvasathya* is in the middle portion; Satya is in the east; and [Anvāhāryapacana] is in the west."
Then, one who knows the mantras should visualize the Āhavanīya fire, the Anvāhārya fire in the southern region, and the Gārhapatya fire according to the sequence from north to south.
By means of the mantra— the armor-mantra "Hum"— and the mantra for opening the door, the [door] is opened.

The syntactical connection is as follows: one should consecrate the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) with these aforementioned purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), such as the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) performed with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
He speaks next regarding those who are incapable [of performing all these].
Alternatively, one should consecrate those [materials] with the four [rites] beginning with inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*);
that is to say, with the four ending with sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*).
One should draw three lines each, directed toward the east and the north, while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
The deities for the lines pointing eastward are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Purandara;
those for the lines pointing northward are Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu.
By the distributive repetition "three by three," it is understood that there are three lines with their tips pointing eastward and three with their tips pointing northward.

Therefore, according to the traditional teachers, one first draws the lines with tips pointing eastward and subsequently draws those with tips pointing northward; moreover, all of them are to be measured at the length of a *prādeśa*.
This has been stated in the Sautrāmaṇītantra as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
One should draw [the lines] starting from the west, situated in the east and the north;
having thus drawn three lines each, one should sprinkle them with the Vāgbhava mantra.
Alternatively, one should draw a hexagon, a circle, and a triangle therein.
Having sprinkled all [the elements] with the *tāra* (om), one should then worship the *yogapīṭha*.

Here, however, having worshipped [the deities] beginning with *Ādhāraśakti* and ending with *Jñānātman*, one should worship the *yogapīṭha* with the mantra: "Obeisance to the *yogapīṭha* of Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśvarī."
One should worship Vāgīśvarī— who has bathed after her menses and resembles a blue lotus—
united with Vāgīśvara, using ritual offerings;
one should worship Vāgīśī with the Śakti-mantra or with the Sādhya-mantra.
This has been stated in the Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī:
One should [worship] Vāgīśī with the Śakti-mantra and Vāgīśa with the sādhya-mantra.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].

Having brought fire produced from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) or the like, or that which has arisen in the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) by means of a vessel.
By the word "and the like" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sun-crystal and the like," it is understood that fire produced from a fire-drill (*araṇi*) is also included.
This has been stated in the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"Born from the sun-gem, or from the fire-altar, or born in the house of a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), or even from the house of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
[The fire should be taken] with a vessel—a bell-metal vessel—or with another vessel covered over.
As it has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"One should perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in an auspicious vessel such as a copper bowl covered with another vessel, or even in a similar earthenware bowl (*śarāva*)."
As for that which is stated in the *Smṛtisāra*:

"One should not perform the bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*) in a shallow dish (*śarāva*), a broken vessel, a skull-cup (*kapāla*), or even one turned face-upward; for it brings disease, loss, and fear.
The intended meaning is that when a primary vessel with a [proper] opening is available, the shallow dish (*śarāva*) is not to be accepted.
It should be understood that one should discard the portion consisting of raw flesh with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
This has been stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa as follows:
Having established the fire with the Astra-mantra and having covered it with the Kavaca-mantra,
O Dear One, one should cast away the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda) toward the southwest using the Astra-mantra;
however, in other cases, the casting away of the flesh-eaters' portion is performed with the Vahni-bīja.
Thus it has been said: "The practitioner of mantra should discard the portion consisting of raw flesh with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ), and thereafter purify it with the weapon-mantra.
However, there is a specific distinction in the *Mantramuktāvalī*:
"Having brought [the portion] with the weapon-mantra to the southwest, one should abandon the portion consisting of raw flesh."
The wise preceptor should establish the portion of the deity with the root mantra before him; he should consecrate it according to the rules through the rites of inspection and so forth,
while meditating upon the single [nature] of Bhīma from the two fires— the digestive fire of the stomach and the lunar fire of the heart.
Then one should unite the consciousness with the seed-syllable of fire within the sacrificial fire.

The term *audarya* is well known as the *bindu*, which is the very nature of the Supreme Self; because it possesses the form of both fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*), it is called *vaindava* (the lunar) in relation to those two.
Others, however, maintain that *bindu* refers to the space between the eyebrows, and that which arises there is *vaindava*.

The syntactical connection is as follows: while recollecting each individual portion of the earth-dwelling, terrestrial fire known as Vasu, one should employ it in the sacrificial pits and so forth, and deposit it therein.
He now describes the manner of this deposition:

The preceptor, having consecrated [the water] with the *Tāra* mantra, rendered it nectar by means of the *Dhenu-mudrā*, protected it with the *Astra-mantra*, and subsequently veiled it with the *Kavaca-mantra*; then, having circumambulated it three times, he worshipped it above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Then, preceded by the recitation of the *tāra-mantra*, one should circumambulate [the fire] clockwise;
with knees touching the ground and facing the fire,
one should cast this [oblation] into the womb of the Goddess with the thought that it is the seed of Śiva.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) to this fire behind the deity and the goddess;
then the preceptor should kindle that fire with this mantra.
Having uttered the pair "cit-piṅgala-hana-daha-paca," this mantra previously mentioned ends with "sarvājñāṃ jñāpaya svāhā.
The specific detail regarding its kindling is as stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
Those who have offered oblations should perform the sacrifice with their hands, winnowing baskets, dipping-spoons, and other such implements.
One should not blow upon the fire with the mouth, nor should one fan it with a fan or similar object;
one must never blow on the fire with the mouth, for a defect of the mouth arises from doing so.
As for the statement "one should not [blow] on the fire with the mouth," that which people apply to the worldly fire—
The mantra for bowing to the fire is as follows:
"I revere the blazing fire, Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—
pure, golden-hued, kindled, and facing in all directions."
One should attend upon the fire according to the rule with this mantra of Manu.
One should place the tongues of the fire-eater within one's own body by means of mantras,
throughout the entire body— namely, in the genitals, the anus, the head, the mouth, the nose, and the eyes.

The teachers of the seven [tongues] have declared that the phoneme-mantras of the tongues consist of the letters from *sa* to *ya*, joined with *vahni* (the letter *ra*), *arghīśa* (the letter *ha*), and accompanied by the bindu (*m*).
Vahni is the letter *ra*; Ira is the letter *ya*;
Arghīśa is the letter *u*.

These letters, beginning with *sa* and ending with *ya*, from *sa* to *ya*, arranged in reverse order and accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*), are declared and taught by the teachers as the seven mantras of the tongues, each consisting of seven bindus.
He now describes the division of the seven tongues according to the distinction of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva*.
The tongues are said to be of three kinds according to the distinction of qualities in their functions:
Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, and Raktā; another is considered Suprabhā;
and Bahurūpā and Atiraktā are Sāttvika in yogic rites.
Parāgābhā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā; then after Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā—
these Rājasya flames, produced by the passion (rajas) of the fire, are prescribed for rites performed for specific desires.
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Manojavā,
Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī— these are declared to be the seven [flames] belonging to Tamas; these seven are employed by practitioners of mantra in cruel rites.
Thus ends the description of the divisions of the tongues.
He now speaks of the forms of the tongues and their presiding deities:
"The tongues of Kalyāṇaretas should have a luster equal to their respective names."
The immortals (amartyas), the ancestors (pitaras), the gandharvas, the yakṣas, the nāgas, the piśācas,
and the rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the seven tongues [of fire].
"Immortal" (amartya) refers to a god (deva).
The specific oblation of substances for each particular part of the tongue should be investigated in the works of Rāghavabhaṭṭa and others.
One should then project the limb-mantras of the Fire-god according to the path previously described:
Sahasrārcis, Svastipūrṇa, Uttiṣṭha, Puruṣa, and again [Svadhākāra].
"Dhūmavyāpin," "Saptajihva," and "Dhanurdhara"—
these are declared to be the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra), joined with their respective seed-syllables (jāti).
For the mantras beginning with "Sahasrārcis," the state of ending in the dative case is due to their being intended as recipients of offerings.
As for the ritual application (*prayoga*):
"Oṃ, obeisance to the thousand-rayed one, to the heart," and so forth, should be understood.
The preceptor should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the eight forms of Jātavedas upon his own body.

Furthermore, one should assign [the mantras] to the head, the sides, the waist, the buttocks, the sides of the waist, and the shoulders, following the direction of circumambulation; they are enumerated in order as follows:
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, and the one named Havyavāhana.
Another is named Aśvodaraja; furthermore, there are Vaiśvānara and others.
Kaumāratejas is one, and Viśvamukha is remembered as Devamukha.
