Tārāgni and the rest, beginning with Pada and ending with Nara, are the forms of Fire (Vahni).

*Tāra* is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). *Agnaye* is the actual form [of the word]. Thus, the analysis of the compound is: "those for which the word *oṃ agnaye*, ending with *agni*, stands at the beginning.
In practice, however, one should supply *oṃ agnaye jātavedase namaḥ* and so forth at the head [of each mantra].
Having prepared the seat, one should contemplate the form of that Fire:

resembling the color of the hibiscus, golden-hued, with three eyes, wearing a crown of matted locks, and holding in his long arms the desired Śakti, the Svastika, and the gesture of fearlessness. One should meditate upon Vahni as possessing the luster of a ruby.
Then, the most excellent of teachers should sprinkle water purified by *mūla-mantras* over the girdle (*mekhalā*).
He should spread *darbha* grass without their inner cores across the middle of the girdle.
The best of gurus should then place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) in the cardinal directions, excluding the east.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "the most excellent of teachers should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) in the directions, excluding the east.
Regarding the enclosing sticks, they have been described by Kātyāyana as follows:
"They place the enclosing sticks—moist, made from a single tree, arm-length in size, and consisting of Palāśa, Vaikaṅkata, or Bilva wood."
Having worshipped the forms beginning with Brahmā in those [positions] by circumambulating clockwise,
one should meditate upon the Fire and worship it in the center with perfumes and other offerings using this mantra:
"O Vaiśvānara, O Jātavedas, come here after [the word] 'pada'."

Accomplish all rites at the conclusion of the *lohitākṣa* mantra. This mantra, ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*), is declared to be the beloved of Agni. This worship is to be performed after the worship of the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) and the seven tongues of flame (*saptajihvā*).
As it is said in the tenth chapter of the *Matsyasūkta*:
"Now I shall describe the fire-sacrifice (*agniyajana*), which bestows prosperity in all sacrifices.
Having first performed the rite of the wind (*samīraṇa*), one should thereafter perform the worship."
Having worshipped the seat and taken a red flower,
one should meditate upon the god Agni as the flower situated within the vessel.
The meditation (dhyāna) is the same as that described by Śāradā.
One should worship on the petals starting from the east with:
"Haṃ, obeisance to Jātavedas; Haṃ, obeisance to Hutāśana."
Haṃ, obeisance to Suvarṇavarṇa; haṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇyākhyā; haṃ, obeisance to Susiddha;
haṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇya.
Haṃ, obeisance to the one whose face is turned in every direction. On the petals starting from the east:
the first tongue of Fire is golden-hued and of great splendor.
I bow to the one named Hiraṇyā, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, for the sake of perfect accomplishment:
*Oṃ yyāṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*. [I salute] Kanakā, who has two arms, is white in color, and holds bundles of *darbha* grass in her two hands.
Bearing a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), salutation to her who grants the success of the practitioner; Oṃ yyāṃ, salutation to Kanakā, Svāhā!
She resembles the rising moon in complexion, with four sprout-like arms.
I bow to her who holds a conch, a discus, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons; Oṃ, obeisance to Raktā, Svāhā!
Suprabhā is pale-white and has joined her two white hands in *añjali*.
May she who is seated in the lotus posture, whose tongue is the remainder, be gracious toward me.
Homage and svāhā to Suprabhā! Oṃ, homage and svāhā to Bahurūpā!
O Goddess, who resembles a blue lotus! O you of fire-like luster! O you worshipped by the gods!
O you who eternally assume the form of Javā! O you of immeasurable form! Be gracious to me!
Oṃ yyam yyam, homage to Abhirūpā, svāhā!
Or alternatively:
the two final consonant groups [kavarga and cavarga] without the letter *ra*, with the letter *ra* and the sixth vowel [ū] situated between them.
The seed-syllables of the tongues, joined with the drops (bindu) and crests (śikhā), are [placed] in sequence.
"Oṃ citpiṅgala hana-hana daha-daha paca-paca sarvājñājñāpaya svāhā.
With this mantra, the wise one should again worship the fire:
"O Śāpacāra, salutations to you; salutations to you, O Havyavāhana!"
O Destroyer of the Cow! O Best of Gods! Grant peace; salutations be unto you!
Thus, welcome! || 1 ||
Salutations to you, O Blessed Lord, O God! You who are the very essence of Nārāyaṇa and the waters!
For the sake of the welfare of all the worlds, please accept this water for washing the feet. Thus, the *pādya*. (2)
O Supreme Nārāyaṇa, O Eternal One whose form is light!
Accept this water offering given by me; O You of Universal Form, salutations be unto You!
Thus is the *arghya* offering. || 3 ||
Salutations to you, Jātavedas, whose nature is light, who always illumines the world in the form of the Sun.
Thus ends the water for sipping. || 4 ||
"O Dhanañjaya! Salutations to you, O destroyer of all sins!
I offer this madhuparka; accept it, O Supreme Lord!
Thus is the madhuparka. 5.
O you who are beyond the highest, whose form is threefold, and who are the support for the objects of the three gunas;
salutations to you, the consumer of oblations, the cause of the maintenance and dissolution of the three worlds!
Thus, again, the water for sipping. || 6 ||
Resembling the color of turmeric and vermilion, this bathing water, which destroys all sins,
is offered by me to you for the attainment of all desires and goals.
Thus ends the section on bathing materials. 7.
O Consumer of Oblations! O Great-Armed One! O Eternal God of Gods!
I offer myself unto you; grant me the supreme state.
Thus ends the section on clothing. 8.
O Acyuta, you who are the light of lights and devoid of beginning or end—adorn yourself with this ornament given by me; salutations unto you!
Thus ends the ornament [of style]. || 9 ||
The goddesses and gods find joy through its perfect union;
for the sake of pacifying all defects, may this fragrance be accepted.
Thus ends the section on fragrance. 10.
You are Viṣṇu, you are indeed Brahmā, and you are the Lord, the master of the luminaries.
O Lord of Gods! O Teacher of the World! Accept this flower which is worthy of You.
Thus ends the section on the flower. 11.
O Lord of the gods, O Śrī Dhanañjaya! May this incense, which is the singular and eternal happiness of the deities and the ancestors, be accepted.
Thus ends the incense offering. || 12 ||
They say that you alone, among all beings—both the stationary and the moving—are the Supreme; O you of supreme form, accept this lamp.
Thus ends the section on the lamp.
Salutations be to the Lord of Sacrifice, the Sovereign, Jātavedas;
for the sake of the welfare of all worlds, may this food offering be accepted.
Thus ends the food offering (naivedya). || 14 ||
O Consumer of Oblations! Salutations to you; salutations to you, O Consort of the Suras!
O Lord of the World! May there be salutations to you; salutations to you, O Jātavedas!
Thus ends the salutation. || 15 ||
Regarding the place for the worship of the tongues, the *Śāradā-tantra* states:
"In the center and in the corners of the Lord [the triangle], one should worship the tongues, radiant with flames.
One should worship the deities of the limbs according to the path described for the filaments."
Thereafter, taking up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with both hands and holding them face downwards,
the preceptor should heat them three times in the fire. Then, taking *darbha* grass,
he should purify their tips, bases, and middles in that respective order.
Having taken them with the left hand, he should sprinkle them upon his right side of the body.
Having heated them again, the mantra-practitioner should cast the *darbha* grasses into the fire and place those two [objects] within the *kuśa* grass on his own right side.
Then, having taken the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), one should sprinkle it with water from the cloth;
having poured the consecrated clarified butter into it— purified by the rites of inspection and so forth—
one should remove the embers to the northwest and place them back within it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
This is designated as *tāpana* (the heating) by the teachers who are knowers of the tantras.
Having ignited a pair of *darbha* blades and dipped them in clarified butter, one should cast them into the fire;
this, performed by the guru with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, is indeed the *pavitrīkaraṇa* (purification).

Having performed the *nīrājana* with a pair of blazing *darbha* blades over the clarified butter while reciting the *varman* mantra, he should cast the *darbha* into the fire; this is declared to be the "illumination" (*abhidyotana*).
Then, having displayed the blazing *darbha* blades within the clarified butter while reciting the *astra* mantra, the preceptor [proceeds].

One should place those [strainers] in the *jātavedas* fire; this is declared to be the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Having taken the clarified butter and pushed back the embers, one should touch water in the fire with the thumb and ring finger, holding two *darbha* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*) long.
Having performed the *upanayana* (bringing forward) with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the purification (*utpavana*) of this ghee.
Likewise, with two Kuśa blades and the Hṛdaya-mantra, one should perform the sprinkling (*saṃplavana*) toward oneself. These are declared to be the six purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).
Having inserted a pair of darbha blades with a knot, measuring a span (prādeśa) and placed within ghee,
one should divide them into two parts and contemplate them on the two sides:
on the left side, the iḍā channel, and on the right side, the piṅgalā.
Having meditated upon the Suṣumnā in the center, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding this specific location, there is a condemnation of performing the homa elsewhere in the fourteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta.
As follows:
If the oblation is offered on the ear, disease occurs; if on the eye, blindness is declared;
if on the nose, mental anguish; and if on the head, loss of wealth.
Among these, the primary oblations should be offered elsewhere; otherwise, the defect described by Śarada will occur.
For example:
having always taken clarified butter from the southern portion with the *sruva* ladle,
the preceptor should offer it into the right eye of the fire, saying, "Svāhā to Agni!"

Similarly, taking [the portion] from the left, one should offer it into the left eye of Fire with the heart-mantra, saying "Svāhā to Agni and Soma. Having taken clarified butter from the right portion with the *sruva* ladle using the heart-mantra, [one should offer it].

The Guru should perform the opening of the fire’s eyes and faces by offering oblations into its mouth with the mantra "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭikṛt," and thus complete the *heti* (the weapon) portion through the sequence of oblations of clarified butter and food.

p. 552) The most excellent of preceptors should again offer oblations of clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis* together with the stars; he should offer them three times with the *agni-mantra*. One should know that the form of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is the supreme body of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The head is declared to be in the east, the arms in the south and north;
the belly is said to be the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the yoni and feet in the west.
One should perform the rites for the fire, beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) and so forth, in their proper sequence.
With eight oblations of clarified butter, each accompanied by the syllable *praṇava*,

one should perform the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). Immediately thereafter, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) should likewise be performed.
Subsequently, there is the going forth [from the house], as well as the first feeding of solid food;

then the tonsure ceremony and the initiation (upanayana); furthermore, the Mahānāmnī verses, the Great Vow (mahāvrata), and the commencement of the Veda, which [also] consists of the Mahānāmnī verses.

Likewise, after the Upanayana, the Godāna, marriage, and death [are performed]. Among auspicious rites, those beginning with marriage are prescribed; among cruel rites, those ending with death are indicated by those who know the Agamas of the Fire-god.
Then, having fully worshipped his parents, he should unite them with his own self. He should offer five fuel-sticks— drenched at their roots and tips with clarified butter—
into the fire according to the prescribed rite, using the mantras of the tongues, limbs, and forms of the Fire-god in their proper sequence.

The preceptor, the most excellent among those who know the mantras, having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and covered it four times in the *sruk* spoon, should, while standing and with a restrained mind, offer one oblation for each [deity] into the fire with the *sruva*.
One should offer oblations with the fire-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* for the sake of prosperity;
one should offer ten oblations with the mantra of Vighneśvara.
This fire-sacrifice (*agnimakha*) is considered common to all tantras.

Then, having worshipped the pedestal, one should worship that deity who grants desired boons in the form of fire within the sacrificial fire. The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations into her mouth twenty-five times.
This is the unification of the faces with clarified butter using the root mantra. Visualizing the identity of the fire and the deity along with one's own self,
one should offer eleven oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.

This junction of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna) has been taught by those who know the traditional scriptures. The best of teachers should duly offer oblations of clarified butter, one for each, to the primary limbs and the surrounding enclosures in their proper sequence.
Then, the preceptor (ācārya) should move the consecrated fire into the other prepared pits according to the rules, starting from the east and so on with a concentrated mind; meanwhile,
the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should worship [the deity] together with the limbs and the surrounding enclosures using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Having worshipped these [deities] as prescribed in the Tantra twenty-five times, they should offer oblations with the root mantra using clarified butter and likewise with clarified butter mixed with *caru* rice;
the procedure for offering these oblations is found in the *Matsyasūkta*.
The most excellent preceptor, with his hands joined and the fingers closed together, should perform the oblation by pressing with the tip of the thumb using the upturned hand;
the offering of clarified butter and other substances, however, should be made with the *sruva* ladle held face down.
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds and other substances with the palm facing upward for the deities;
likewise, the offering of fuel-sticks (samidh) and the oblation of sesame, sweetmeats (modaka), and so forth,
are performed respectively with three or four fingers beginning with the thumb, as well as with bilva leaves.
Regarding the specific tongues [of fire] for oblations of specific substances, that is also explained in that very same place.
In the oblation of clarified butter she is named Hiraṇyā; from the oblation of grain she is Kanakā;
she is known as Raktā in the oblation of fuel-sticks (samidh), and likewise Kṛṣṇā in that [same] oblation;
she is Suprabhā in the rite of sweetmeats (modaka), and Bahurūpā and Atirūpakā [in other rites].
The seven tongues of fire are proclaimed according to the arrangement of flowers and leaves;
likewise, in the absence of the primary substance, a substitute is also prescribed therein.
It is said that [the wood] is not obtained there; one should perform the oblation with a substitute.
Udumbara is prescribed for the arka tree, and śamī for the khadira.
Palāśa should be used for the pippala, and pippala for the palāśa as well.
In both cases, it should be exactly thus: [use] Apāmārga or Palāśa;
in the absence of Kuśa grass, there should be Dūrvā, and in the absence of Dūrvā, there should be Kuśa;
in the absence of Ikṣu, however, there is Amṛtā, and in the absence of Amṛtā, Palāśa.
In the absence of lotuses, the enemy of horses (blue lotus) should be used, especially for water-born flowers.
Where ghee is not available, one should perform the oblation with pure milk.
For milk, curd is to be understood as the substitute, and for honey, jaggery should be used.
Sugar should be replaced by sandalwood paste or even by pieces of jaggery;
liquids should be replaced by juice, or all of them by sugarcane juice;
flour for the *modaka* should be known to be replaced by fruit, and fruits themselves by other fruits.
Just as wood is [joined] with wood and flower with flower,
so too is everything always [joined] with another among all substances.
In all rites for extraordinary purposes (*adbhuta*), however, one should face the north;
one should prepare the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*) and the covering, whereas in other cases the east is the direction.
The sacrificer himself should never, under any circumstances, offer the sacrificial fuel.
One may perform [the rite] with one's son, disciple, and so forth, but one should not employ one's own son [as the officiant].
Likewise.

A wise man desiring prosperity should never, at any time, perform the offering of blood in a domestic sacrifice (*gṛhayajña*); such is the opinion of those who know the Tantras. Where clarified butter (*ājya*) and other substances are used, and where sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are prescribed for the month of Śrāvaṇa, [that is the proper practice].

The wise mantra-practitioner should not apply the remainder elsewhere; likewise, he should never place even a single limb of the *lagna* in one vessel. The preceptor, facing east, should proceed according to the sequence beginning from the northeast (*aiśānī*).

One should perform the sweeping with mantras while circumambulating from left to right. For those who maintain the sacred fire (*sāgnika*), this is preceded by mantras; for those without the fire (*niragnika*), it is simply a matter of sight.
In a great sacrifice (*mahāyāga*) such as a marriage and the like, one should use three *kuśa* blades to form a triple-leafed tuft.
In the Vaiśvadeva rite, however, there is but a single vessel, and likewise in the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
In the great sacrifices (mahāyāgas), one always spreads [the sacrificial grass] around in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
in the mere offering to the directions, in the daily fire-oblation, and likewise in the Vaiśvadeva, it is the same.
If one performs occasional rites (naimittika) in vain without having first performed the obligatory rites (nitya),
then one should perform the occasional rites after first providing flowers, fruits, and other offerings.
Likewise.
Having offered daily oblations to Prajāpati, as well as to Indra, Agni, and likewise Soma,
and having immediately thereafter performed the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks (samidh),
one should subsequently offer with the Vyāhṛtis; O Maheśvarī, it is thus everywhere.
O Śaṅkarī! At the end, one should offer the *sviṣṭikṛt* oblation with the sacrificial substance using the fivefold mantra beginning with "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā" and ending with "tatra.
This applies to the various types of sacrifices, including those involving gifts, and specifically to the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) performed within a hundred [repetitions].

In the sevenfold division, these [offerings] are complete; furthermore, they are of three kinds in sequence. The officiating priest (mantrin), touching the shoulder of the priest (ṛtvij) or touching his right arm, the best of teachers (deśikottama), together with the sacrificer (yajamāna) and his wife, should perform the oblation.
One should offer the *pūrṇā* oblation while standing, never while seated.
When the tongue [of the fire] is golden or red during a sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*),
a single *pūrṇā* is prescribed at the conclusion of a hundred *graha-homas*.
At the end of a thousand [repetitions], one should perform two [offerings]; at the end of ten thousand, the fourth.
In an offering of food (anna-homa), one should give a pair; in a lotus-offering (padma-homa), the fourth.
And in an offering of ghee, parched grain, sesame seeds, and so forth, when reaching ten lakhs [of repetitions].
The second [type of oblation] is declared to be with jackfruit and mango fruits;
it is used for fifty or twenty-five oblations during the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*),
the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), and in expiatory offerings (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
In the case of an oblation of curd, as well as in obligatory rites, one should avoid the full oblation among these.
Now, regarding the measurement of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa), it is stated in the fourteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta:
In a ghee oblation, one karṣa is prescribed; for milk, two tolas are remembered.
Pañcagavya consists of five tolas of honey and milk;
curd should be the measure of a handful (prasṛti), and parched grains (lājā) should be equal to a fistful.
p. 555) By the measure of a large wooden ladle, or else by the previous filling;
one handful of roasted flour (śaktavaḥ), half a *tolaka* of sugar, and three *tolakas* of jaggery—this is remembered as the limit for the first two [substances] of the sugarcane group.
A *modaka* is the measure of a *dhātrī* fruit; a path is the measure of a jujube (*vadara*).
As for the measure of a *piṇḍaka*, it is the size of a coconut or similar joint. A *tāla* is two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and a *panasa* is by the number of its seeds.
For the rites of killing and expelling, the jackfruit is divided tenfold;
the coconut is divided eightfold; the citron is considered threefold;
the wood-apple fruit is divided threefold, or otherwise in ten parts.
A fuel-stick of one span (prādeśa) is prescribed, as is a triple leaf of dūrvā grass; and at the concluding oblation of the leaves, one should likewise prepare a measure of one span.
The specific types of sacrificial fuel are as described in the Rāghavabhaṭṭa.
Those that are shattered, split, short, crooked, thick, thin,
double-ended, bitten by insects, long, or skinless are to be rejected.
A shattered [reed] causes the destruction of life, while a split one gives rise to disease.
If it is short, one incurs disease; if crooked, it always causes obstacles.
If thick, it takes away fortune; if thin, there is the ruin of the sacrificer. If it is split in two, there will be eye diseases; if bitten by insects, it destroys wealth.
Long sticks that lack bark are known to cause defects and destroy life.
Fuel-sticks that are not withered, nor too large, nor too small, grant all desires.
[They should be] possessed of moist bark, have even surfaces, and be as thick as the ring finger.
A wise person should offer such oblations and thereby attains vast prosperity;
four types of sacrificial fuel (samidh) are proclaimed for use in both Śrauta and Smārta rites.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
Four finger-breadths of *guḍūcī*, one handful of *vrīhi* rice, and a *sarṣapa* according to the measure of a *sūkti*; a *sūkti* consists of five *tolakas*.
Having made twenty [units] for black pepper, they know ten to be used in the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
The lotus stalk should be ten parts, the radish seven parts,
and the *kaśeru* one part each;
the citron should be equal in size to a thumb of ginger, and this should be served as food accompanied by condiments.
The measurement shall be as before, and the rice shall be of equal quantity;
likewise with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Having ascertained the lineage of the *nakula* (mongoose), one should [use] other substances according to the lineage.
Just as a yogin is not [attracted] by scent, especially in the desire for sovereignty,
so too have these [substances] been taught by the tantrikas as being the size of a tamarind seed.
Also in the Yoginītantra:
One *karṣa* of clarified butter should be given, and milk is prescribed at the measure of a *sūkti*.
Curd should be a *prasṛti* in measure, and honey should be half of that.
O Pārvatī, listen as I duly describe the procedure for these.
A wise person should give ghee measured at eight *suvarṇas*;
milk should be half of that amount, and curd five *suvarṇas*.
Curd should likewise be half of that; thus do those who know the rules of measurement understand it.

Thus, when there is wealth, the wise man should understand that the measure of a hundred is its strength, while fifty is the measure therein; this applies everywhere. Now begins the chapter on measurement (mānādhyāya).
In the second part of the Yoginītantra.
A streak of sunlight visible through a window-lattice is called a *lekhikā*;
eight *lekhikās* make a speck of dust (*dhūli*); eight specks of dust make a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*);
and four mustard seeds are designated as one *rattikā*.
Twenty *rattikās* and one quarter are proclaimed [to be one *tolikā*].
A *tolikā* consists of four quarters; four *tolikās* make a *prasṛtikā*. Two *prasṛtis* make a *karṣa*, and two *karṣas* become a *pala*.
Half a *pala* shall constitute a *sūkti*, and two *sūktis* are considered a *guḍaka*; this is stated in the *Hastihṛdaya-prabandha* cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*.

That which is seen when the rays of the sun enter through a lattice is called "dust" (*rajas*); this is considered the first unit of measurement. Eight such atoms (*paramāṇu*) are held to constitute one *trasareṇu*.
An *aṣṭaka* is to be marked by eight *bhūs*, and likewise, a *yūkā* is marked by eight *likhyas*.
A *yava* consists of eight *yūkās*, and a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) consists of eight *yavas*.
Four of those [finger-breadths] make a fist (*muṣṭi*), and two fists make a bow-length (*dhanurgraha*).
Three *muṣṭis* make one *vitasti*; two *vitastis* make one *aratni*.
Two *aratnis* make one *kiṣku*, and two *kiṣkus* make one *dhanus*.
A thousand *dhanus* make one *krośa*, and twice that is a *gavyūti*.
Four *gavyūtis* are calculated as one *yojana*, and [a *yojana*] is divided into its constituent parts.
But in the sixteenth chapter of the Matsyasūkta:
Four mustard seeds are designated as one māṣa.
In this context, the word *māṣa* denotes a crop.
Twenty māṣas are designated as one *rattikā*. Twenty *rattikās* are proclaimed to be one *pāda*.
A *tolikā* consists of four *pādas*, and four *tolas* make one *prasṛtikā*.
Two *prasṛtis* and one *karṣa* [make] two *karṣas*, which constitute one *pala*. Two *palas* make one *sūkti*, and two *sūktis* are considered one *dagdhaka*.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Flower," within the section on the Durgā Festival— consisting of the Durgā-mantra, hymns, the greatness of the hundred names, the bali-offering, the fire-sacrifice (homa), and its substitutes and measurements— in the fourth part, the Section on Optional Rites (Kāmyakāṇḍa), of the Śrī Prāṇatoṣiṇī.
Having paid homage to the chosen goddess who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
I shall now describe the duties of the month for the satisfaction of the learned.
Now, regarding the rites performed monthly:

here, the month is indeed the lunar one, because it is the basis for the rites associated with the lunar days (tithi); however, the verbal designations and so forth are according to the solar month, based on the statement cited earlier from the *Dharmakāṇḍa*.
In the Matsyasūkta, in the fifty-second chapter.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, on the eighth lunar day at the arrival of night,
that virtuous woman who practices dharma should perform the Siddhagaurīvrata.

Thus, because the Siddha-Gaurī-vrata does not exist in a current form in this region, it has not been written here; however, he who has need of it should seek it elsewhere. O Supreme Goddess, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvina...
She is renowned everywhere as Vijayā, the abode of all the Vedas.
O fair-faced one, one should worship Revanta and the Goddess there;
having attained happiness in this world, they shall go to the abode of Śiva.
With the mantra "Tejo 'si," one should worship him who has two arms, is seated upon a horse, and holds a sword and shield,
using this mantra: "Salutations to you, the son of the Sun, for the welfare of horses."
Bring peace to the horses; salutations again and again to Revanta!
O Keśava! You are born from the lineage of the Gandharvas for the sake of the protector of the earth;
you are outside the essential nature of Brahmā, Soma, and Varuṇa.
By the splendor of the sun, by their own play, and likewise by the feet of Rudra, by the celibacy of Brahmā, and by the strength of the wind;
[therein are] coriander, cattle, seed, meditation, and white mustard seeds.
At the end of the night, one should tie a lotus petal with a double-folded thread upon a rosary and especially around the neck; likewise, O auspicious lady,
[one should consecrate] weapons, missiles, and the constituents of sovereignty.
One should worship with flowers and other offerings corresponding to each seed-syllable, without hesitation.
Now, regarding the sight of the wagtail in that very same context:
On the tenth day, O beloved, after having eaten in the afternoon,
one should behold a beautiful wagtail and offer salutations for the sake of prosperity,
saying: "O you who grant the fruits of all desires in the form of Vāsudeva!"
O Khañjarīṭa, you have descended upon the earth; salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, O Khañjana, the bestower of all desired objects.
Salutations to you, the blue-throated one, the auspicious one, who possesses an auspicious form.
O Auspicious One! Grant me auspiciousness; O Filler! Fulfill my hope!
You are Svastika; bestow well-being! O Khañjarīṭa! Salutations be unto you!
O you who are the very form of Nārāyaṇa, O bestower of happiness for the year!

O Blue-throated One! O Mahādeva! O Khañjarīṭa! Salutations be unto you! O you who possess the form of Viṣṇu! Your auspicious sight increases the prosperity of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, and humans; salutations be unto you!
Now, the auspicious and inauspicious results of the aspects.
When [the lunar disc] is seen upon the pinnacle of a water-palace, on a mountain, or near water, it brings auspiciousness; when in cow-pens, it increases wealth;
when in lotuses or in temples, one shall become a king.
If [the bird] is on the bank of a pond, there will be wealth; if in a cremation ground, death will occur.
A black neck indicates Janārdana; a blue throat, Pārvatī; and a white throat, the Goddess. When the wings are fluttering, one should observe [the omen].
O Goddess of the Gods! When it is stable, it brings about prosperity;

yet by eating cooked food [therein], one becomes diseased, and even Indra, upon seeing the splendor [of the vessel], becomes ill with pride merely from its being praised. Furthermore, there shall be a depletion of one's lifespan.
Therefore, one should recite the name "Khañjana" without hesitation.
In that very [text].
On the night of the Kaumudī festival, a devoted housewife who is faithful to her husband should worship Indra and Lakṣmī with fragrant flowers and other offerings,
and present an oblation of milk-rice mixed with various side dishes.
One should worship the gods and the ancestors with coconut fruits;
one should honor one's kinsmen at night and engage in buying and selling.
Mahālakṣmī does not depart after having cast a curse upon him who fails to do so; she shall return to her city.
At midnight, Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons, speaks aloud: "Who is awake?
Having drunk coconut water and kept vigil with dice during the night, I shall grant him my prosperity. Who is awake upon the surface of the earth?"
And one should worship the Soma [deity] in a water-pot, on a cloth, or upon pedestals.
Now, the meditation on Lakṣmī is described in that very same place:
Endowed with fresh youth, resembling molten gold,
three-eyed, two-armed, and beautiful, wearing divine earrings,
she holds a bilva fruit in her right hand and a lotus in her left.
Adorned with every ornament and proud of all her finery,
she is served by Kinnaras, gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas;
one should then perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the seed-syllable joined with a long vowel.
One should worship with ritual services and the like, with various food offerings and prostrations.
The mantra for worship is found in that very same place.
O you who are born from the ocean of milk! O you who reside upon the chest of Viṣṇu!
Accept this worship, O Goddess of gods! Homage to you on this Kaumudī festival!
This is the mantra for prostration.
(559) O Padmā! O Padmālayā! O Auspicious One!
O Mahālakṣmī! Salutations to you; grant me joy.
Salutations to you, the bestower of boons upon all the worlds, O beloved of Hari!
May that destination which belongs to those who have taken refuge in you be mine through my worship of you.
O Lakṣmī! O Goddess! Salutations to you; be forever unshakable. O Kamalā! O boon-granting Goddess! May you bring glory to my lineage.
O Goddess, source of all auspicious marks! Just as [the power] resides in Nārāyaṇa for the welfare of all beings, so do you protect me!
O Kamalā, giver of boons, auspicious one, this worship has been performed by me with devotion.
"Accept this worship, O Queen of the Gods! Salutations to you, whose abode is the lotus!
Having worshipped the nine Śaktis, beginning with Bhūti, on the petals starting from the east, one should there worship Vāsudeva and the others, as well as Vāmana and the rest."
In that very same vessel, one should meditate upon Indra and worship him;
one should contemplate through meditation Indra, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, seated upon Airāvata, accompanied by Śacī, and bestowing boons.
The mantra for worship is also as follows.
O Vajrahasta! O Mahāvāha! O Bahunetra! O Purandara!
May you accept this worship for the sake of protecting all beings. One should first worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), the planets (grahas), and the Brāhmaṇas.
One should worship Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, and Bhāvabhūteśvara.
Having worshipped them with this [mantra], one should display the bilva-mudrā;
then, having recited the mantra, one should display the padma-mudrā and the dhenu-mudrā and recite a hymn of praise.
Thus concludes the ritual duties of the month of Āśvina.
In the fifty-third chapter.
The Blessed One said:
When the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Libra, especially during the bright fortnight,
one should worship the Goddess whose abode is the lotus on the very first day (the Pratipad) at the tip of a cow's horn.
Having fasted and subsisted on a diet of barley-gruel, one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having worshipped with *kundapuṣpa* flowers, one shall become the destroyer of all sins.
In that very place, O my beloved, one should worship the Goddess with a buffalo;
one should worship the Lord of the Worlds with *dūrvā* grass, sprouts, and flowers.

Then, having eaten śāli rice and sipped water, one should go to the edge of the water and prepare two kinds of ghee, O Maheśvarī! By making a *pala* [of it], one gains victory for a year; if it breaks, one should declare that his [victory] has been broken.
One should worship Vibhīṣaṇa, Bali, Sīma, and Parameśvara with perfumes, flowers, and various offerings of food and salutations;
likewise, during the dark fortnight, one should perform the worship of the divine couple.
One should consume honey and meat and subsist on a single meal per day.
On the second day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Dharmarāja;
having prepared *caru* according to the prescribed rite, one should then feed one's siblings.
One obtains sovereignty, happiness, and shall attain many enjoyments;
likewise, one should worship Lakṣmī with *kunda* flowers during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). One should offer an oblation (*bali*) of black substances to her, and she bestows wealth upon him.
On the third day, one should worship Gaṇeśa with flour-cakes and other offerings;
by subsisting on a single meal, no sorrow arises on earth.
On the fourth day, for the sake of well-being, one should worship the Goddess with *modaka* sweets.
One should offer an oblation of curd and sugar-candy; one's desire is certainly attained.
On the first day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the goddess Māheśvarī;
worship with white pigeons certainly bestows prosperity.
On the fifth [lunar day], one who desires knowledge, O Sovereign of the Gods, should worship Hara and Gaurī with bilva leaves and offer an oblation of sweetmeats (modaka).
By the mere consumption of milk, one is purified from sin; of this there is no doubt.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight, having worshipped the god Nārāyaṇa Hara in the Mahāyoni, one shall deliver ten generations of one's lineage.
In the Great Womb, known as Kāmākhya.
On the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the god who is the Lord of Wealth;
that person who gives sixteen [presents] rejoices in the sphere of heaven.
On the seventh day of both fortnights in the month of Kārtika, one should remain self-restrained.
One should worship the god Matsya, as well as Kāma and Indradeva;
one should feed Brāhmaṇas and married couples early in the morning,
and offer auspicious sacrificial fees consisting of fruits, roots, and grain.
Neither disease nor hunger shall arise in his family,
O Goddess of gods! Especially on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
one should worship Durgā and Mattānilī upon a black rhinoceros hide.
One who worships with devotion three times a day shall become illustrious and radiant. During the dark fortnight, one should diligently worship Śiva, Durgā, Kamalā, and likewise Kālikā—
worshipping the Goddess in earthen form at midnight with great effort.
And there shall be no terrible fear of disease for as long as the year lasts.
In the sixth chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
O Maheśānī! On that auspicious ninth day (Navamī) of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, the beautiful Supreme Deity (Paradevatā) Sundarī should be worshipped;
O auspicious one, the complete method of her worship has been described in the Paṭala of Sundarī.
In the Matsyasūkta:
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should perform a fire sacrifice with sesame seeds,
dedicated to the deity, which yields increasingly superior fruits on each successive fifth day.
On the seventh day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the Goddess and honor the Sun.
Bestowing the fortune of wealth and grain, and increasing sons and grandsons—
one who is self-controlled and pure should worship Madhusūdana with oil, specifically refined oil, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
In the dark fortnight, however, it is especially distinguished by milk and honey;
one should eat fruit at night and shall rejoice in the abode of Viṣṇu. During the dark fortnight, one should worship Kṛṣṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Śatakratu.
A woman who gratifies [the deity] with excellent food and other offerings shall not go to hell.
O illustrious lady, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one should perform a bath with white sesame seeds and worship Hari with three white flowers.
On the morning of the twelfth day, having performed his daily duties with a concentrated mind,
he should make a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and worship Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, the guardians of the directions,
and the planets in individual water-pots, as well as Hari upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), scents, and water from sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should worship with fallen leaves and the like, as well as with white water-lilies (kumuda) and lotuses (paṅkaja),
using autumnal flowers according to the extent of one’s means.
One should worship with devotion three times a day, and then perform the fire-ritual at night.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform the awakening ceremony at midday;
for there would be loss if the bathing were done during the day or the awakening at night.
O Maheśvarī! At the beginning, one should utter the eight-syllable mantra for each individual mantra.
Then, having formed the añjali gesture, one should recite this mantra:
"You are being praised by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, and you are worthy of worship by the hosts of gods."
"This twelfth day known as Kaumudī has arrived; therefore, O Lord of the World, you yourself must remain awake!
Then, having touched [the water], the practitioner should recite the mantra slowly;
subsequently, with rainwater from clouds, pure moonlight-water, wild flowers, and fragrant blossoms, [he should perform the rite].
"I give," for the sake of the Dharma—be watchful, be watchful, O Lord of the World!
Having fallen upon the earth on your knees, recite the mantra together with the *tāraka*:
"Be gracious, Nārāyaṇa! Kṛṣṇa! Viṣṇu! Mukunda! Lord of Lakṣmī! Homage be to You!"
Behold, O Lord of the World! Having resorted to and taken refuge in the manifestation of your glorious power,
O Great Goddess, one should pass the night with various dances and songs, by listening to the Purāṇas, and preceded by the fivefold sounds.
At dawn, one should worship with devotion and give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should worship the Brahmins with devotion, as well as the blind and the wretched. And during the turning over on its side, there is the mantra within the eight-syllabled [formula].
Be at my side, O Lord of the World! Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta!
Be gracious, O Blessed Lord, O Protector; be the one who brings an end to this cycle of worldly existence!
O Govinda, Acyuta, turn us as well toward that [state], even as you have turned Pārśva.
O beloved, it should be performed during the day according to the previously mentioned procedure;
on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform the satiation of Brahmins,
and on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, [one should worship] Śaṅkara together with Pārvatī.
By worshipping with bilva leaves, no sorrow arises on earth. Then, O Śaṅkarī, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Kārttika,
a man, having performed his morning bath according to the rules in a flowing stream, [should proceed].
Having drawn Umā, Hara, Ravi, and Viṣṇu with sandalwood paste, O Maheśānī, one should worship them with lotus petals and bilva leaves.
One should satisfy the deities with vegetables and subsist on vegetables oneself. Likewise:
At midday, one should bathe the jar and place a garment therein; thereafter,
one should sprinkle oneself along with one's kinsmen three times over the head with an Apāmārga flower.

O Goddess of gods! With a counter-clockwise rotation, one who is composed should perform [the rite] with an Apāmārga leaf, either according to what is about to be described or with the Gāyatrī mantra:
"Whatever evil deed has been committed by me, even throughout hundreds of births..."

O Apāmārga! By your grace, first remove [these obstacles]. Having heard from the twice-born the enumeration known as the *Saṃhitā*, the meritorious narrative, and the account of the deceased, one should give gifts for the sake of prosperity.

Likewise, the fourteenth day (Caturdaśī) should be worshipped together with the preceding [thirteenth] when it is joined with the New Moon (Darśa) on the following night; this is the supreme rule to be followed. At the end of the lunar day, one should offer a lamp.
Even if the fourteenth day has passed for the gods, if the full moon coincides with the fourteenth,
then the former [the fourteenth] must always be observed, even if it occurs during the night, for the purpose of bathing,
hearing the stories of the deceased, and performing the libations to Yama.
Men should observe the Preta-Caturdaśī occurring at sunrise;
beginning from the eleventh day until the fifteenth,
one should subsist on a single meal per day, avoiding meat.
This Bhīṣma-vrata has been proclaimed; one should observe it with leisure.

On the full moon day when the sun is in Libra (Tulā), one should worship the Lord of Śrī (Viṣṇu) along with Lakṣmī with devotion using sandalwood paste; thus, there shall certainly be no extinction of one's lineage.
When the sun has entered Libra (tulā), Lakṣmī abandons her sleep;
by worshipping her there alone, Lakṣmī becomes unfailing.
One should worship Lakṣmī in a white pitcher and Kuvera in a red pitcher.
One should worship Viṣṇu with various offerings of food and salutations using a yellow pitcher.
In the Nāradapañcarātra, in the seventh chapter of the second rātra.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, the worship of Rādhā and the adoration of Viṣṇu—
wherever these may be performed without restriction, they are the cause of supreme liberation.
The Matsya-sūkta.
If, at some time during the month of Kārttika, two new-moon days (darśa) should occur,

the first of them shall be Sukharātri, while the other is the intercalary month (malimluca). In that intercalary month, when the sun has entered Scorpio (vṛścika), following the awakening of the Lord from his slumber (vuṣṇūtthāna)...
When the awakening of Lakṣmī occurs, that is to be known as a "pleasant sleep.
If the conjunction of one *daṇḍa* of night falls on the new moon day (*darśa*) of the following day,
then, having omitted the previous day, the *Sukharātrikā* (Happy Night) shall take place thereafter.
There, the śrāddha performed by anyone certainly becomes inexhaustible. The merit born from performing the hundred-fold rite at that sacred ford (tīrtha) yields great fruit;
it should be performed with diligence, dedicated to one’s chosen deity and to the ancestors.
If one, desiring long life, O Goddess of gods, should offer a lamp in a temple of Śiva for the sake of his own life, he should offer a lamp at a crossroads;
having set aside thirty-two, O beloved, he should offer twenty-five.
A wise person should offer a lamp in the sky using nine, five, or three pairs [of wicks]; he should cause to be offered a lamp with three wicks, five wicks, or even one.
Carrying living beings [to safety], he indeed attains the state of Arghya; of this there is no doubt.

One should cause lamps to be offered at a height of three cubits, or one and a half cubits, or even just one cubit; by doing so, one obtains the desired fruit. [These lamps should be placed] on the head, on the chest, on a limb, or at the wrist.
O Goddess! he who offers a lamp is honored in the heavenly world. One should worship Kamalā, Hlādinī, Dharaṇī, Vijayā, Jayā, Lakṣmī, Subhadrā, and Mahāmāyā upon the petals.
One should first worship Brahmā and the others, as well as Vāsudeva and the rest;
one should worship Śaṅkha, Padmanidhi, Kuvera, and likewise Varuṇa;
having fully worshipped Indrāṇī, one should sacrifice with this mantra.
"Salutations to you," and so forth; "Of the universal form," and so forth:
"O beloved of Hari, you are the refuge of all beings and the bestower of boons!
O Goddess who brings joy to all, O you who possess all branches [of knowledge], salutations be to you!"
O Lole! O Goddess! Salutations to you, the one who carries us across the ocean of hell! O you who emerged from the churning of the milk-ocean! Be gracious, O Supreme Sovereign!
Victory to you, O Goddess whose abode is the lotus! Victory, O Lakṣmī, beloved of Hari!
O Goddess who bestows all bliss! O you who possess all branches [of knowledge]! Salutations be unto you!
Victory to you, O daughter of the Milky Ocean; remain firmly established in my home!
This is the annual worship, including the excellent food offerings and other rites.
"O Lole! O Supreme Goddess! Having taken all of that, please accept it!
One should recite this mantra immediately after the offering of the lamp:
"To Dāmodara, in the sky under the sign of Libra, together with Lole."
I offer this lamp to you; salutations to the infinite Creator!
May those seven worlds that are above and those that always abide below move about in illumination, having been granted this lamp of space.
May those beings dwelling in existence who are in the hells and constantly oppressed by suffering,
as well as those situated in darkness and those abandoned by the world, be illuminated by this lamp of space that has been offered.
For the sake of illuminating them, this lamp is offered by me;
for those men of mine who dwell at the most terrible gateway of Yama,
this lamp is offered by me for their intended benefit.

"O Keśava! There is no fault on my part regarding the extinguishing of the lamp due to wind, rain, moths, or the exhaustion of the oil and the wick. Homage to the ancestors and to those who have passed away; homage to Dharma, who is Viṣṇu."
"Salutation to Dharma, to Rudra, and salutation to the Lord of the Wilderness!
One should offer [this] in the northeast corner, in a garlanded place, or even in a secluded spot.
Likewise, a firebrand (ulmuka) should be offered at night while facing the south."
O Śaṅkarī, one should first cast [the offering] there with this mantra:
"Whatever Ulkāmukhas roam here upon the surface of the earth,
may they attain the supreme goal, consumed by blazing light."
"May my calamities perish by the grace of Mukharātri;
may my men flourish through the very illumination of this torch,
O illustrious lady, beginning indeed from the new moon day of the month of Kārtika."
One should perform the Kālarātrīvrata; listen now to how it should be done. The procedure for the vow and other details are to be sought in the fifty-third chapter.
Thus concludes the observances of the month of Kārttika.
In that very [work], in the fifty-fourth chapter.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vṛścika,
by worshipping Maheśvara with sprouts of dūrvā grass, one becomes a lord of the Gaṇas.
On the second day, having diligently worshipped Jagaddhātrī in the water, one should then take a single meal; on the third day, [worship] Janārdana;
on the fourth, Śrīkānta; and on the eleventh day, Janārdana.
On the twelfth day one should worship Brahmā, on the thirteenth day Indra (Śatakratu),
and on the fourteenth day the Lord of Gaurī (Śiva) with white lotuses;
wearing white garments and having restrained his senses, he should perform this worship at the three periods of the day.
One should satisfy the gods with honey; such a person is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
On the full moon day of the month of Vṛścika, having risen at dawn and restrained one's speech, one should worship Kṣetravighneśa, and likewise Kamalā on the fifth lunar day.
Having worshipped Vasu on the sixth day and Divākara on the seventh,
and likewise Tripurā on the eighth and Surasundarī on the ninth,
one should subsist on a single meal dedicated to Durgā and Bālā.
On the tenth day, one should worship that Goddess as well as the guardians of the directions;
having bathed the Sun, one should offer the *bali* to the gods at night.
(From the sixth chapter of the *Vṛhannīlatantra*).
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the bright fortnight, on the seventh lunar day favored by the Sun,
one endowed with sons and grandsons should worship Annadā with devotion; thus,
Lakṣmī will certainly remain steadfast as long as the world of moving and non-moving beings endures.
For that long, O Goddess! O Gaṇeśvarī! Lakṣmī shall abandon arrogance in his house and remain steadfast; this is the truth, the absolute truth!
And her worship, O Maheśānī! has been described here in your presence.
O Daughter of the Mountain, understand this correctly from the *Annadākalpaka* in the *Matsyasūkta*.
The full moon day in the month of Vṛścika (Kārttika) should be known as Kṣetrapūrṇimā;
in the Dvāpara age it was in Pauṣa, and in the Tretā age it was in the month of Māgha.
Having honored the best of the twice-born with offerings of rice-balls and pieces of jaggery, [one attains merit].
The donor shall destroy misfortune and obtain supreme prosperity by means of barley-gruel,
sugar, and various kinds of sweetmeats,
O Supreme Goddess, for three nights beginning from the full moon of Kṣetra.
Having performed this at night, O Maheśānī, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
This is declared to be the Surayajña, which bestows great prosperity,
brings wealth, grain, and fortune, and grants splendor and good luck.
On the first day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Viṣṇu, the Lord of Pārvatī;
by performing the fire-ritual at the three times of day, one becomes endowed with prosperity in one's family.
On the second day, having consumed molasses, one should also worship Sundarī.
On the third day, having consumed sesame seeds at night, one should then eat barley-gruel on the fourth day; having consumed curd at night, one is honored in the world of Śiva.
On the fourth day, eating only barley-gruel, one should consume the *madana* fruit and curd at night; thereafter, by consuming [these] at night, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.

On the fifth [tithi], one should worship the Lord of Day (the Sun) and Viṣṇu together with Lolā in a large water-pot; having consumed milk, one shall obtain prosperity. One should also worship Govinda, and one will become a lord even of cows.
On the seventh, eighth, and ninth lunar days, one who has conquered the senses,
being self-restrained and pure, should worship the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhyakṣa) with a white pitcher at the three times of day;
he shall attain great prosperity, and Fortune (Lakṣmī) shall become his constant companion.

O Goddess of gods! on a riverbank during the dark fortnight, having worshipped the Teacher of the World upon a painted cloth and consumed milk at night, one attains perfection through the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess! On the tenth day one should worship Indra; on the eleventh, Keśava;
on the twelfth, [one should worship] Mūla; and on the thirteenth, O Pārvatī, one should worship Kāma with Aśoka flowers, and Viṣṇu on the fourteenth day.
Having performed ablutions three times a day, one should subsist on a single meal.
By doing this once, O Goddess, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. [Likewise, one should offer] a cow at the new moon, and [offerings] at the neck, in the mouth of a Brahmin, and at the neck.
O Śaṅkarī! Having prepared a sacrificial oblation (caru) with cow’s milk for the sake of the ancestors,
and having offered libations at the three times of day with honey, jaggery, sugar-candy, salt, and water, one attains the desired object of one's heart.
Having attained incomparable sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
Thus concludes the ritual duties of Āgrahāyaṇa.
In that very same [text].
Then, O fair-faced one, when the sun is situated in Sagittarius (Dhanus) during the bright fortnight,

O Great Goddess, on the first lunar day (pratipadā), one who has conquered the senses and bathes in the morning should worship the Sun three times a day; thus one shall be liberated from diseases, and not otherwise.
During the dark fortnight, one should worship the Lord of the World, the husband of Pārvatī;
having performed the fire-ritual extensively, one shall then be liberated from bondage.
Specifically, beginning from the second day of the bright fortnight, one should proceed.
Then, O Maheśvarī, one should worship Āditya and the Rudras with a spirit of devotion until the fifteenth day; by doing so,
O Goddess, one is liberated from saṃsāra— of this there is no doubt.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight, when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Sagittarius,
O Goddess of Devas, one should worship Rameśa with a single meal;
on the fifth day, one should worship Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śacī, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana.

On the sixth [lunar day], one should worship Skanda and Viśākhā while consuming a meal of milk at night. O Śaṅkari! On the seventh, eighth, and ninth days of both fortnights, one should worship Kātyāyanī while subsisting on a single meal.

On the tenth day, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī; on the eleventh, Viṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī, with flour-cakes (piṣṭaka). One should personally observe the practice of eating only at night (nakta) until the fourteenth day and the new moon (amāvāsyā) arrives.
Then, on the full moon day, according to the ritual procedure, one should offer libations to the ancestors with the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); by this method, one never comes to grief.
Thus concludes the ritual duties of the month of Pauṣa.
In that very [work], it is stated thus in the fiftieth chapter:
The Blessed One said:
O illustrious lady, when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the bright fortnight,
one should bathe in river water on the first lunar day (pratipad), worship Janārdana,
and subsist on a single meal preceded by the performance of fire-rites.

An offering of milk (arghya) should be prepared; one is thus liberated from the ocean of sorrow. Likewise, on the second lunar day, one intent on devotion should worship Śakra, having anointed him with sandalwood paste, upon a seat or an aguru-leaf.
One who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) at night is born handsome;
having separately worshipped Umākānta on the third lunar day, Śrīpati, and Kamalālayā, as well as the Lord of Night (the Moon) with various kinds of kunda flowers.

One should partake of mung beans as a ritual food, which destroys even the greatest sins. On the fourth day of the bright fortnight, O Śaṅkarī, one should especially worship Gaṇanāyaka in a copper vessel containing the five gems.

One should consume sesame seeds at night and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with sesame seeds; such a person becomes exceedingly prosperous and wealthy. On the fifth lunar day, one should worship Jagaddhātrī at dawn with water from a river.
Having bathed that lady of excellent fortune with emerald jars,
one should worship Vasanta and Kandarpa along with Rati on the day known as Vasantapañcamī, which liberates one from all sins, O beloved!
By hearing the Vasantarāga, one obtains the desired prosperity;
some sages indeed call it Śrīpañcamī. One should observe this vow with a single meal, and there shall be no falling away from prosperity.
On the sixth day, having performed his morning ablutions, he should worship the Sun;
he should then offer an oblation of milk, whereby he is released from the bondage of disease.
For the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is indeed equal to an eclipse of the sun.
At the time of sunrise, bathing in that [river] yields great fruit.
Having taken seven leaves of the *vadarī* and the *arkapatra*, as well as red rice grains and *dūrvā* grass from a field of *śāli* rice, one should place them upon the head and immerse oneself.
Oṃ! Whatever sin has been committed by me throughout seven births, may the Mākarī Saptamī destroy that, along with my disease and grief.
[One should worship] with seven red arka leaves, rice grains, perfumes, and sandalwood.
Having performed the preliminary rites, one should offer an *arghya* oblation with fruits, *dūrvā* grass, and *javā* flowers, [reciting]:
"O Goddess who dwells in the solar orb! You who bring delight to the seven-horsed Sun, you who illuminate the seven worlds, you who consist of the seven *vyāhṛtis*, salutations to you!"
O Mother of all beings, O Seventh [Tithi] of the seven-times-seven!

O Goddess of the seven *vyāhṛtis*, salutations to you in the solar orb! It is declared that charity, fire-offerings, recitation, and the worship of the gods performed on this day yield ten millionfold merit.
After feeding the Brahmins, one should then partake of sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) oneself;
bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha) yields tenfold merit, while at the Gaṅgā it yields ten millionfold. When a Sunday arrives, the merit becomes ten million times ten millionfold.
One should offer a thousand, or a hundred, or even half of that as the *arghya* offering;
by ten thousand one obtains servitude, and by a hundred thousand, indeed, union (*sāyujya*).
If one is unable, one should offer twelve or even twenty-five.
O Maheśānī! Because it is twofold, the *arghya* offering is declared as a limb of the vow.
One should observe it when the Sunday arrives and when the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) has begun;
one should undertake the Daśamī vow under a lunar mansion bearing a masculine name.
Hasta, Maitra (Anurādhā), Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, Bhṛgu (Śravaṇā), and Punarvasu—
these are the asterisms named with masculine designations, so say the wise.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, one who has fulfilled his duties and is composed [should perform the rite].
One should worship Pārvatīśa and Gaṇeśa together with their beloved consort. Having performed worship at the three times of day with sesame seeds, milk-pudding, and sweetmeats (modaka),
the practitioner of mantra should thereafter eat only at night, O Śaṅkarī, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
Whatever fruit is obtained by one person alone on the twelfth Aṣṭamī, that same fruit shall accrue from this; therefore, O noble lady, with every effort and even at the cost of all one's possessions,
whoever performs a Śrāddha for the ancestors with their own devotion—

Whatever fruit they desired in every act of faith, that was undoubtedly attained; through the libation for the ancestors, all the twice-born castes were satisfied. One should offer three handfuls of water with sesame seeds to Bhīṣma.
O Goddess! With the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītin), facing the southern direction, one who is pure and of restrained mind should offer [the water] with this mantra:
"Come, O Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one, the delighter of Śāntanu's lineage!"
"Accept this water given by us; be the granter of boons.
To him of the Vaiyāghrapadya gotra and the Sāṅkṛti pravara, to this sonless Bhīṣmavarman, I offer this water."
For the Śrāddha rite, the Bhīṣmāṣṭamī that pervades midday (madhyāhna) should always be accepted;
for bathing, libations (tarpaṇa), and giving gifts, that which follows sunrise should be accepted.
However, if two Makarī-saṅkrāntis should occur within a single month—
If it should be Bhīṣmāṣṭamī, then the subsequent lunar day (tithi) should be observed;
by worshipping Gaurī, the mother of the world, together with Lakṣmī under a Bilva tree on the ninth day, one shall attain great prosperity.

Then, on the tenth day, having observed a fast at night during the seventh *saptakumbhaka*, one should worship with leaves of the *maru* tree and with extensive displays of various riches. Having honored a Vaiṣṇava sage, one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas.
And by pleasing [the deity] with a mind of devotion, O beloved, one becomes equal to Him!
Then, on the morning of the eleventh day, the observer of the vow should make the formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
He should worship Viṣṇu three times a day, accompanied by the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
O Supreme Goddess! By performing even a single fast, one whose soul is purified of all sins shall attain union with Hari;
one should observe a vigil during the night through the recitation of the Saṃhitās and other such rites.
In this matter, there is no fault regarding the day of the week in the month of Māgha or in the Ghaṭa-kumbha constellation;
one should never transgress the day of Viṣṇu’s rising or his reclining.
One should always avoid a day that is a *dinakṣaya* (the junction of two tithis) or pierced by a *daśā* (astrological period).
A householder, especially one who has sons, must not eat at night; otherwise, his merit perishes, except in the case of what was previously resolved upon.
Even on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), he should perform his bath in river water during the hour of dawn.
One should perform a bath with *dhātrī* (myrobalan) fruits, which destroys even great sins;
the observer of the vow should worship Govinda with devotion and then give a cow as a gift.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual fire-offering (*agnikārya*) and engage the Brahmins in the distribution of gifts.
Listen, O Goddess! to the fivefold vrata of Śrī Viṣṇu, which is a great secret.
These five are proclaimed as the Vibhūti-dvādaśīs, occurring in the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, and Phālguna.

O beautiful lady! On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and likewise on the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa when the moon is in Leo, there is the twelfth day named Aśūnyā. Whoever observes a fast dedicated to Janārdana [on these occasions], [attains great merit].
O Śaṅkarī! one’s bed shall never be empty throughout birth after birth.
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, which is called Vibhūtī-trayodaśī, by placing Mādhava within a water-pot, one attains eternal prosperity.
In the month of Māgha, during the bright fortnight, there is the celebrated Rāmacaturdaśī.
Even if it is pierced by the day of Kāma (the fourteenth), it should be observed according to the procedure for Śivarātri.
At dawn on the full-moon day, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, one should give gifts for the sake of prosperity;
by giving a cow to the twice-born, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should provide fuel and cooked food, and subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
On the first day of the dark fortnight,
one should diligently offer gifts to the foremost of the twice-born after worshipping according to the prescribed rite, dedicated to Skanda;
on the second day, one should worship, dedicated to the Lord of the World (Jagannātha).
One should offer cooked rice as an oblation and subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
On the third lunar day, one should likewise worship Dharma and Citragupta;
eating flour-cakes at night, one shall fall from the world of Dharma.

On the fourth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Lakṣmī in a water-pot; by always subsisting on milk-rice (pāyasa), there shall be no falling away from Ramā. On the fifth day, one should worship the god Madana, Gopāla, and Rukmiṇī as well.
A man who offers a heap of unbroken grains on a variegated cloth shall not go to hell.
On the sixth lunar day, one should worship Dhanvantari, Śambhu, and Kumāra at night;
O Maheśānī! by placing them before a jar of milk, no sorrow arises on earth.
On the seventh day, one should worship the Lord of Kamalā (Viṣṇu) in a jar of ghee;
then, together with one's wife, one should indeed offer a stream of water as part of the vow.
On the eighth and ninth days of the dark fortnight, one should worship Śaṅkara with bilva leaves.
One should worship with devotion three times a day on a cow-dung pedestal together with Pārvatī;
having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with the funeral cakes (piṇḍas), one should subsist on a single meal.
On the tenth day of the dark fortnight, the observer of the vow should fully worship Gaṅgā.
On the eleventh day, one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should worship Mādhava;
likewise on the thirteenth day, and on the fourteenth day at dawn,
before the sun has risen, one should perform a bath in river water.
Sin committed over a hundred lifetimes perishes at that very moment;
she is renowned by the name Raṭantī, the auspicious one who removes all sins.
In the seventh chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, known as Raṭantī,
one should worship Tārā with extensive and magnificent offerings;
one will undoubtedly become a great emperor, a universal monarch.
In the Matsya-sūkta.
O Maheśvarī! Having performed his bath on the new moon day, one who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya) should perform a śrāddha with offerings of sesame and rice;
he is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
Thus concludes the religious observances for the month of Māgha.
In the Matsya-sūkta,
the Blessed Lord said:
O Maheśānī! When the sun is situated in Aquarius (Kumbha), the preceptor should begin the worship;
likewise, during the dark fortnight, starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) in due order, he should worship Brahmā, Gāyatrī, Satī, Gaurī, and Jayantikā.
One should worship Kamalā, Pārvatī, Mahāmahiṣamardinī,
Sarasvatī, Mahāmāyā, Mahālakṣmī, Rati, Kālarātri, and Umā with these ritual offerings.
Quickly filling the ear with [the sound of] the *ākarṇanī* [flute], which bestows the joy of love;
and in the forenoon, men adorned with vermilion should play.
And one should worship Gopāla, the beloved of the cowherd girls, O Maheśānī!
One should worship the God according to the prescribed rites with *mandāra*, *kiṃśuka*, and mango sprouts, and then place him upon a palanquin;
at the auspicious moment of *abhijit*, one should conduct the procession accompanied by the five musical instruments.
In the Nāradapañcarātra, in the seventh chapter of the second rātra.
O Brahmin! Having performed the worship of Śiva on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight dedicated to Śiva (Śivacaturdaśī), fasting on that day is the supreme cause of liberation;
thus it is stated in the Matsyasūkta.
Now I shall describe the Śiva-vrata, which destroys all sins.
O Goddess, by performing it on a moon-lotus day (Candrābja), one attains union with Rudra. If the fourteenth day should touch the day of the new moon (Amāvāsyā), [one should observe this vow].
When the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) falls on the night of the fourteenth (caturdaśī), one attains incomparable enjoyment through the Śiva-vrata;
therefore, the Śivarātri vow and the worship of the lunar day should be performed there.
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight that falls between the months of Māgha and Phālguna,
when conjoined with the Śiva-yoga, is declared to be Śivarātri. One should know that the vow may be performed during the day, or it is indeed complete when performed at night.
O Śaṅkarī, one should perform the vow of Śivayoga even with humble means! On that Māghī which follows the full moon of Māgha— the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha—
one is liberated from all sins simply by worshipping on that day.
One should perform the entry [into the vow] during the interval between the yoga and the lunar day;
one should never break the fast at night, nor at the time of the two twilights (saṃdhyā).
One should perform the ritual bath and the invocation at the junction of the fourteenth day.
For one who is ill, it should be known that the merit of cleansing is ten million times greater than that of bathing.
O Supreme Goddess! One should offer the food offering eleven times its usual measure;
and one should perform the threefold bali-offering—listen, O lady of excellent complexion!
On the eighth or the fifteenth day, or even on the fourteenth; specifically,
the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the sixth day of Skanda, the fourteenth day of Śivarātri,
the conjunction with the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism, and that which is the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight joined with a yoga of Śiva.

When it occurs during the conjunction with the night, that [time] is considered most meritorious. Merit arises from the mere touch of the yoga, but the fruit is greater when it occurs during the night.
During the entire night it is tenfold, and during the daytime touch it is a thousandfold.
Having bathed the Liṅga, one should establish it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) where one intends to worship;

there, indeed, one should likewise perform the bath with water in a mirror, in a Śālagrāma stone, or in the mantra. Alternatively, the first bath may be performed with water while reciting the "pañcanadya" verse.
One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhi krāvṇo akāriṣam," honey with "madhu vātā," and jaggery with the Gāyatrī;
likewise, one may offer water containing gems while reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
With this mantra and likewise with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should wipe [the vessel] with a bilva leaf and begin the installation of the jar.
At the conclusion of the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), one should recite the mantra with palms joined in reverence.
Today, on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight sacred to Śiva, I shall keep vigil throughout the night;
I shall perform worship, charity, recitation, and fire-offerings according to my ability.
O Śiva! O Śaṅkara! O Omniscient One! O Bestower of the fruits of vows!
O Lord! By Your grace, I shall observe the Śivarātri vow;
having remained without food on the fourteenth day, I shall eat on the following day for the sake of worldly enjoyment and liberation. O Īśvara! Be my refuge.
Facing north, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should worship Gaṇeśa, the guardians of the directions, the planets, and the hosts of Maruts;
then, in each pitcher, one should worship Brahmā and thereafter the seat of the deity.
A wise man should worship Nandin and Mahākāla at the eastern gate;
he should worship Bhūteśa and Caṇḍapāṇi at the southern gate;
and at the northern gate, he should then worship Vetāla and Vṛṣabha.
In the center, one should worship the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) and the others, along with their limbs and sub-limbs.
O fair-faced one, listen to the meditation upon the Lord Maheśāna:
one should meditate on the lotus situated upon the bull-throne, and thereupon seated upon a lotus-seat.
Resembling pure crystal and endowed with the powers of the *maṇi* and other [siddhis], he holds in his ten arms the trident, the spear, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness,
as well as the *khaṭvāṅga*, the serpent, the bell, and the goad.
Then, one should install [the deity] who holds a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a citron (bījapūra), and a choice blue lotus (nīlotpala);
who is endowed with the thirty-two marks, has five faces and three eyes,
and is accompanied by the powers of Will and the others, along with the seed-syllable (bīja).
Having performed the worship of the limbs (aṅgapūjā), one should then offer auspicious water for the feet (pādya) and other requisites.

Thereafter, one should worship Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, endowed with their respective powers, on the petals in the directions starting from the east; and outside of that, one should worship the eight forms (mūrtis).
Having worshipped thoroughly with the ritual services (upacāras) until the conclusion of the limb-worship (aṅgapūjā),
one should offer the arghya for the sake of prosperity using this rite-mantra:
[it should consist of] curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (akṣata), combined with fragrance and flowers.
Having gone to the ground on his knees, the practitioner [should offer] with this mantra:
"Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful one, the remover of all sins;
on this Śivarātri, I offer this arghya; be gracious along with Umā."

O Queen of the Gods! In the first watch, a sweetmeat (modaka) or milk-rice (pāyasānna) smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu) is especially recommended. And in the second watch, it should be accompanied by the Vāruṇa [liquor].
One should perform the bath with this mantra; listen to the mantra, O fair-faced one!
"O Lord of Gods, I perform this bath for the purification of all sins, for those blinded by the darkness of ignorance whose souls are filled with impurity."
Having bathed as before, one should perform worship as before;
with the Rudra-sūkta and with desire,
one should worship Hara, Maheśa, Vijaya, Yakṣeśa, Varada, and Śiva.
Devoted to worship, he should honor both Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), he should offer an arghya consisting of honey, milk, and clarified butter,
combined with kuśa grass and flowers, and accompanied by jaggery and sugar.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On this Śivarātri, I offer this arghya, which accomplishes all desired goals.
Furthermore, during the third watch of the night, one should perform a bath for the sake of purification.
Having sprinkled [the site] with water using *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra to be spoken next:
"O Virūpākṣa! O Mahādeva! O Lord of beings, be well-considered by me;
on this Śivarātri, grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation to one who has performed the ritual bath."
"O Śiva! O Śaṅkara! O Lord of Gods! O Master! O Paśupati! O Hara!
Accept this *arghya*, O God; O Consort of Umā, be gracious to me. Having offered the *arghya* according to the rule, O Goddess, one should worship Hara as Manmatha.
O beautiful one, during the fourth watch of the day, the wise man should perform his bath before Yogeśa, Mādhava, Dharma, and likewise Viṣṇuloka; thereafter,
he should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with this mantra.
O All-pervading Lord! O Protector! That fruit which is obtained from the worship of eighty million liṅgas is attained on Śivarātri by the act of bathing [the liṅga].
[One attains] Pāvaka, Bhuvana, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Śatakratu.
One should worship Janārdana and Mādhava on the central pedestal,
as well as Gaurī and Vīrabhadra, who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
For the sake of purification from all sins, may this arghya be accepted by me.

O Śaṅkara! For me, who am consumed by the afflictions of saṃsāra, accept this arghya offered by me through this vow on Śivarātri; be gracious to me. Then, at dawn, having performed his daily duties with a concentrated mind, he [should proceed].
One should bathe the Lord Tryambaka with the Tryambaka mantra and then worship him;
one should duly give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa).
Then, one should feed the Brahmins with the mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya."

In the seventh chapter of the Vṛhannīlatantra: "O beautiful one! O Maheśānī! In the month of Phālguna, at midnight, in the courtyard, there should be an excellent grove of plantain trees in the four directions."
O Goddess of the gods! In the rite for the removal of sin, have a pleasing pavilion constructed.
O Goddess! You should have the pavilion covered with mango, holy fig, and banyan trees.
One should surround the pavilion with young maidens; such a pavilion is enchanting to all.
O King of the Gods! O Maheśvara! O you who are praised by the gods! Create for me that form of Tārā or the form of Kālī which bestows all accomplishments;
or indeed, create this form of Annadā.
One should carefully cause an offering to be presented to the Great Goddess with silk garments;
one should offer a blanket as a seat and a welcome prepared with honey;
one should offer water for the feet with milk and the arghya offering with kusha grass.
One should offer the *madhuparka* with ghee alone, and the water for sipping (*ācamanīyaka*) with water; having performed the ritual bath in due order, a red garment is prescribed,
and one should give silver ornaments that are pleasing to all the gods.
O Lord! O Beloved! one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented even without rice;
one should offer delightful items to be chewed, sucked, licked, and drunk.
One should recite the mantra eight thousand times using the seed-syllable of red sandalwood.
One should begin on the first day of the bright fortnight and conclude on the ninth;
one should offer an oblation to Mahādevī with a goat or a buffalo,
consisting of food, fish, meat, and most excellent ghee.
