One should offer to the Goddess a most divine and pleasing cake made of flour; O Lord of the Gods of gods! one should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite and according to one's capacity.
One should also worship the maiden with effort, using various kinds of ritual materials.
However, all rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth, if performed without the worship of a *kumārī*, will not yield their full fruit; indeed, the worship would not be truly successful.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining all accomplishments (*siddhi*), one should worship a *kumārī*.
Likewise, by worshipping Tāriṇī, Kālikā, Annapūrṇā, Bhairavī,
and Parā according to the prescribed rites with devotion, all perfections (siddhis) shall be attained.
O Lord of Gods! You ought to listen to the ritual procedure for worship without any doubt.
In the Matsyasūkta, Chapter Fifty-seven (p.
575), the Blessed Lord said:
"Now, O Goddess, I shall explain in brief the ritual actions associated with the months."

Abiding by his vows, he should bestow gifts and perform sacrifices according to the prescribed rules, in due order, at the proper time, and to the best of his ability; however, he must avoid accepting gifts, indulgence, and the gazing upon women.
One should avoid eating from vessels of bell-metal or iron, as well as the chewing of betel; likewise, one should renounce alkaline substances, pungent foods, and radishes.
One should also abandon bilva fruit, barley-gruel, black gram, bitter food, and honey.
Vegetables are recommended for all vows; those that are cooked once are especially excellent when combined with roots, leaves, stalks, fruits, and the like.
Thus concludes the observances for the month of Phālguna.

In the fifth chapter of the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*: "On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Madhu, having worshipped the Lord, the Beloved of Jānakī, with royal offerings, one should invoke Rāma in the Kali age."
Those who behold Kṛṣṇa mounted upon the swing during the months of Madhu and Mādhava are liberated from thousands of offenses; of this there is no doubt.
Those who keep a vigil before the Lord while He is mounted upon the swing [attain the same].
The attainment of the fruit of perfect merit shall occur at every moment.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, this supreme vow must be performed.
Rāma alone is the Supreme Brahman; that day is the one that pleases Rāma.
The detailed exposition of this vow should be sought therein; however, it is not written here for fear of excessive length.
The necessity of fasting on that day is also mentioned in that very source:
"He who, being of deluded intellect, eats out of ignorance on Rāmanavamī..."
He is cooked in the terrible Kumbhīpāka hells; of this there is no doubt.
For one who is unable to fast, even eating a single meal is prescribed in that very same context:
"O Rāghava, on the ninth day, by means of a single meal which serves as an ancillary part [of the vow], [one honors] Rāghava."
The ornament of the Ikṣvāku lineage is pleased [only] thus, and not otherwise.
Likewise, one who observes the vow of eating only once a day should remain there together with his preceptor, having conquered his senses.
O Sage! One should spend the remainder of the day listening to the divine story of Rāma;
everything else should be investigated in works such as the *Tithitattva*.
Likewise:
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, the Damanaka festival,
as proclaimed by Baudhāyana and others, should be performed every year. On that occasion, the offering of the Damanaka plant should be made to one's own deities, beginning with Agni.
Agni, Viriñci, Girijā, Gaṇeśa, Phaṇī, Viśākha, Dinakṛt,
Maheśa, Durgā, Antaka, Vighnahari, and Smara— all these are to be worshipped here on this lunar day (tithi) at the sacred seat (pīṭha).
The festival procession of Damanaka should be investigated in that very [text], but it is not written here for fear of excessive length.
The fruit of that [act] is as follows:
having personally worn [the ashes], worshipped them, fed one's kinsmen and Brahmins, and completed the rite, one obtains the merit born of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
If even a single *ghaṭikā* of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) is not obtained at the time of breaking the fast (*pāraṇā*),
then the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) should be accepted as the pure time for the offering of *damanaka*.
If the planting of *damanaka* in the month of Mādhava was forgotten during the month of Madhu, [it should be performed then].
Or that offering should be performed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, Śrāvaṇa, or Bhādrapada.
Thus ends the ritual for the month of Caitra.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should joyfully worship the Lord of the Universe situated in the water, continuing until the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight.
Having placed [the image] in a water-vessel during the month known as Mādhava,
those who worship Mādhava are gods, not men on earth;
whether in a vessel of gold, silver, copper, or even one made of clay.

O highly fortunate one! He who worships the Lord manifested from a Śālagrāma stone, or even an image, gains infinite merit. Therefore, O King, one should always worship Hari residing in water during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
The man, freed from evil, shall remain until the dissolution of all beings;
this should be understood as a distinction of time, or rather, for the liberated one, there are only two states.
Having completed the daily worship by placing scented water in that vessel, [he should proceed].
Having saluted the deity day and night and led him to his own seat,
one should worship him with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra), and having reached the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should dismiss him.
One should purify oneself, one's home, wife, and others with that sacred water.
One should worship [the Lord] at night in the water until the end of the twelfth lunar day, according to the teachings of the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*.
On the twelfth day, staying in the water at night, one should worship Him who reclines upon the waters.
Thus concludes the ritual duties for the months of Vaiśākha and Jyeṣṭha.
In that very same [text].
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the festival of the Churning of the Milk Ocean should be performed;
otherwise, according to the words of the Purāṇas, there will be drought.
When the thousand-rayed sun is situated in Gemini, one should lay Madhusūdana to rest.
When the Sun has entered Libra, one should again awaken the Lord;
for he who does not put Hari to sleep while the thousand-rayed one is situated in Gemini,
there will then be drought, occurring otherwise [as a calamity] along with the Vaiṣṇavas.
On this lunar day, the wearing of branded marks by Vaiṣṇavas is prescribed;
specifically, the wearing of branded marks heated [with fire] according to the method taught by Śaunaka must be performed by all Vaiṣṇavas in accordance with their respective traditions. (p. 577)
In the Sāmaveda as well:
"O lords of the plow, on the northern shore of the ocean of birth, they place upon their arms the well-heated discus and conch of Viṣṇu at the base,
the *praṇava* marks upon their limbs, and the heated weapons around their periphery."
The fruit of that has been stated by the Atharvaṇa:
"Those in this world who are marked with the signs of the Wide-strider (Viṣṇu) become possessors of great fortune."
The bearing of the mark (*aṅka*) by a Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa is also stated in the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*,
as follows: "Just like the daily fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), so too is the study of the Veda."
In the same way, this wearing of the heated discus-mark belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;

although it is not explicitly stated that it is for a Vaiṣṇava but only for a Brāhmaṇa, nevertheless, by virtue of its syntactic unity with the previously cited statements, it is understood to apply to the Vaiṣṇava.
The sequence for the ritual observance (*dhāraṇa*) is as follows:

having worshipped the Blessed One with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), one should worship the discus and the conch within the supreme, imperishable ether (*parama-vyoman*) with these two [mantras]: *śanno mitraḥ* and *saṃ varuṇaḥ*, and then [recite] the twelve-syllabled [mantra].
One should place [the fire] into the fire with the two verses beginning, "Not indeed from that fire of old age," and "Churn out the wise one.
One should pray to the fires with the verse, "May we be of the Vaiśvadeva.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the Puruṣasūkta and having praised the Blessed Lord with the Puruṣasūkta, [one should recite] the verse beginning, "He who [slanders] a Brāhmaṇa..."
One should prostrate oneself before him like a staff.
Then:
"O Sudarśana! O Mahājvāla! You who possess a radiance equal to ten million suns!"
"Show me, who am eternally ignorant of the truth, the path of Viṣṇu."
Having thus taken hold [of it], the installation of the discus (*cakrādhāna*) is performed with the mantra: *oṃ sudarśanāya vidmahe mahājvālāya dhīmahi tannaścakraṃ pracodayāt*. Then:
O Pāñcajanya! O you of the great sound! O destroyer of the accumulation of sins!
Protect me, a sinner fallen into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
"Having taken [the mantra] beginning with 'We know Pāñcajanya, we meditate upon Pavamāna; may that Conch inspire us,' this is the installation of the conch."
The fruit of maintaining the mudrās is also described in that very same place.
The learned Brāhmaṇa, a Śrotriya who is pure, who performs this [rite] in such a manner,
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Alternatively, the wearing of the mudrā-mark should also be performed on the Utthāna-Dvādaśī day.
At Śayanī, at Bodhinī, and likewise at Cakratīrtha,
by means of the ritual of the conch and the discus, a man becomes purified by fire.
Thus, according to that statement from the *Hṛdaya*, this is the procedure for wearing the mudrās.
Powdered parts of living beings, leather, water-lily, citron, and *bījapūraka*;
food and other edibles not offered as sacrifice—that which has not been offered to Viṣṇu; burnt food, lentils (*masūra*), and black gram (*māṣa*)—these are the eight kinds of forbidden meat (*miṣa*).

One should avoid fruits, roots, and other such items that are pleasing to the taste but obtainable only in specific regions; likewise, one should not eat flat beans (*niṣpāva*), kidney beans (*rājamāṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), *sanmita*, eggplant (*vṛntāka*), or *kaliṅga* while the Lord is asleep.
In the Matsyasūkta, in the fifty-eighth chapter.
Likewise, for seven days on the earth during her menstrual period,
and at the Vaṭa and Somavaṭa trees— even if honey is not offered—
one should worship Kṣetrapāla and the very powerful Jayapāla.

O fair-faced one, one should not perform [the rite] in the middle of a village, nor in a corner, whether in a city, a village, a pīṭha, or elsewhere, even if it be in the north or near Agastya; rather,
it should be done when the sun has reached the northern solstice, under an auspicious constellation, and on a favorable day.
One should first plant the tree while uttering, "Be firm!

One should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and wrap it three times with a thread. O beautiful one, this should be done by a Brahmin who knows what has been performed and what remains to be done, and whose wife is present.
At the end of Taurus, there are three days; at the end of Gemini, likewise three days.
During the sun's transit through the middle [of these signs], it is proclaimed as "burning of the earth.
In the Kali age, three days are to be avoided, starting from the end of Taurus and the beginning of Gemini.
At the sun's transit (saṃkramaṇa), there is a "burning of the earth" for three days.

During this burning of the earth, one should abandon all [undertakings]; in such a burning, one obtains the fruit of burning. In legal affairs, there is loss of treasury; from the birth of a son, there is emaciation.
Know that misfortune regarding women occurs when one looks with attachment;
I shall declare its complete pacification, which results in gold.
To pacify the fault, one should give gold, or one should give a golden mark (tilaka).
One should not perform optional rites (kāmya), occasional rites (naimittika), journeys, mantras, or ritual actions while menstruating, except for those previously resolved upon;
nor, O Śaṅkarī, should one dig even as much as the point of a needle into the earth.
The sowing of seeds must be performed during the twenty-four watches of the day;

if one should sow them through negligence, one should allow cows to graze there. Furthermore, for eating [the seeds] or digging [them up], one should perform the Kṛcchra penance and offer sesame and gold.
All six mothers, beginning with Durgā, become subject to menstruation.
Jaimini, Sumantu, Vaiśampāyana,
Pulastya, and Pulaha— these five are indeed the five who speak the truth.
One who recites this or keeps it in one's home shall likewise have no fear of water or fire.
One should offer very cool water to the image,
the great liṅga, and likewise to the śālagrāma.
Or, at the root of the sacrificial tree, whoever should offer even for a moment [an offering] consisting of five [items] endowed with three blades of grass upon my head, that of Viṣṇu,
having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, rejoices together with Brahmā.
One obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice by [worshipping] a Śālagrāma stone;
by giving a sweetmeat to a Brahmin, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice;
and by [giving water] even to creatures afflicted by thirst, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
He who gives water flowing from the tip of a blade of kusha grass day after day at the roots of trees goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
so too does he who offers a stream of scented water, or even jaggery and milk.

Even a single drop of water sprinkled [on the ground], or even a single day’s stream of honey, if it is anointed with sandalwood, leads one to attain the Supreme Brahman. He who should offer [this] mixed with camphor and agallochum, combined with sugar—
He enjoys vast pleasures in heaven together with his ancestors.
Thus concludes the ritual duties of Āṣāḍha.
In the *Rāmārcanacandrikā*.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the festival of Pavitrāropaṇa was prescribed by Śaunaka and others;
one who performs it has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
Hari attains great delight in one who performs the Pavitraka rite according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures; however, for one who does not perform the Pavitraka rite,
the Rākṣasas seize all the fruits of his worship and other offerings.
Thus concludes the ritual duties of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In that very [text].
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Karṇikā festival should be observed by Vaiṣṇavas together with the Śayana festival of Hari;
this occurs when the eleventh day of the bright fortnight arrives in the month of Bhādrapada.

The gift of a mat to Viṣṇu destroys great sins. Having led the Lord to a body of water according to the procedure for the festival of the couch, one should worship Him after making the formal resolve (saṅkalpa): "I shall perform the festival of the gift of a mat."
O God of gods! Lord of the universe! You who are accessible through yoga! Janārdana!
Today, when the auspicious month of Bhādrapada has arrived, I perform the gift of a mat (kaṭadāna).
By means of this, one should fashion a clockwise circle on the right side of the body.
Then, having performed the great worship as before, one should return to one's own home.
Thus concludes the duties for the month of Bhādrapada.
(p. 580) Now follows the ritual duties for the year.
In the second chapter of the Varadā Tantra.
With reference to the syllable known as Ādyā.
A wise person should perform ritual action for the attainment of results when the moon and other celestial bodies are auspicious;
otherwise, O Goddess, it shall be fruitless, except in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*). The annual worship of Kālikā bestows sovereignty even without other activities.
And that [worship] must also be performed there; listen, O Supreme Goddess!
That worship bestows sovereignty, bestows wealth, and bestows victory even amidst a multitude of inauspicious things.
It destroys the undertakings of enemies, accomplishes one's own tasks,
grants subjection to kings, and wards off all planetary afflictions;
it is said by me to bestow results swiftly, yet to cause harm when revealed.
On the occasion of the great equinoxal transit (*mahāviṣuvatsaṃkrānti*), one should offer a jar together with a cloth,
as well as sandals and an umbrella, for the sake of pleasing Kālī. Likewise, on the third lunar day known as Akṣayā, one should offer a jar in the same manner.
O beloved! The gift of water in the month of Vaiśākha—whether in a vessel of gold, silver, bell-metal, or even clay—is equal to the gift of gold.
In Jyaiṣṭha, it is through the gift of cooked food, and in Āṣāḍha, through the gift of jackfruit.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with *paramānna* (milk-rice);
in Bhādra, the worship is performed with cakes; and in Āśvina, there is the autumnal festival (*śāradotsava*).
Having offered precious garments and other materials to the Blessed Lady, [one should proceed].
Afterwards, one should personally partake of that which is to be consumed: with cold clothing in Kārttika;
with new grain in Mārgaśīrṣa;
with new mudga beans in Pauṣa; and with milk and ghee in both Māgha and Phālguna.
In the month of Caitra, a great worship with curd destroys all suffering.
This annual worship of yours bestows universal sovereignty.
One should indeed offer whatever object is dear to oneself in the proper manner.

O Maheśānī! During the rainy season, one should accomplish all desired objects. Furthermore, the best of practitioners who performs this every year regarding the *dakṣiṇā-vidyā* shall become the foremost among rulers of the earth.
In five years there shall be a kingdom, and in ten years an empire.
O Maheśānī! At twenty years, she bestows a great empire;
at one hundred thousand [years], there shall be lordship over a lakh, and at ten lakhs, a kingdom becomes an empire.
O Great Goddess! By performing one hundred lakhs [of recitations], one shall attain a great empire;
even a servant, casting off servitude, suddenly becomes a great person.
That which was not remembered by the mind, nor that which was not uttered by speech—[all that is attained].
One who serves with skill and truth shall likewise obtain a kingdom.
In the fifth chapter: I shall tell you the means for attaining sovereignty over an empire. Beginning at an auspicious time, one should practice this for one year.
O Maheśvarī! One should choose a day favorable to the moon and the stars;
having bathed in the morning, donned clean garments, and become serene in mind, one should perform the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the sake of regaining the lost kingdom.
Having received the three-syllabled Kālikā-vidyā from the mouth of the Guru and having performed the sādhana according to the rules, one will certainly obtain a kingdom.
On the first day, one should worship the Goddess with hibiscus, saffron, and barbara flowers.

O Supreme Goddess! At the conclusion of the worship, one should mutter the mantra a thousand times. Having stayed in a house devoid of people and completed that excellent recitation, one should then offer oblations one hundred and eight times with *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, and white flowers.
O Queen of the Gods! with this mantra, or with black aloe-wood and clarified butter—[recite] "Kāli! Kāli! and then "O Sovereign of Kings! O Bestower of Kingdoms!
Having uttered the word "rājyaṃ dehi" (grant a kingdom), then the word "dayāmayi" (O Compassionate One!), and finally "ṭhaṭhaḥ."
O Śivā! This indeed is the supreme root-mantra for the attainment of sovereignty;
the preceptor should perform recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) with this mantra.
O Queen of the Gods! Here, movement according to one's own will is permitted, and there is no requirement for the purification of locations and the like.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra every day for one year;
one should never abandon the mantra of one hundred and eight repetitions. O Supreme Goddess! there is no requirement for a preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) regarding this mantra.
With one foot touching the ground, he should recite the mantra on the full moon day;
with liquid black aloe-wood, he should satisfy Śivā in her friendship.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, he should [worship] the bilva tree, and on the fourteenth day, the hibiscus tree.
On all new moon days, the observer of the vow, having touched the excellent *śephālī* tree at sunrise, should recite [the mantra] ten times each.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, he should worship with great care.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations and likewise recited [the mantra] one hundred times at night, and having performed this for twelve months, one shall obtain a kingdom.
O Goddess of the Gods! When this is performed, the ritual application does not require great effort.

One shall regain a kingdom seized by an enemy equal to Indra, provided that within a year the powerful enemy becomes the practitioner's subordinate. Desiring to destroy that enemy's power, one should perform here what I shall now tell you.

"Amukaṃ stambhaya svāhā" is the three-syllable enclosure of Kālikā. For a Brāhmaṇa, it should be performed on Thursday; for a Kṣatriya, on Friday; for a Vaiśya, on Tuesday; and for a Śūdra, on Saturday.
In the forenoon, one should recite the mantra a thousand times in a secluded place.
Having done this for five days, one should worship Ghoradakṣiṇā.
Furthermore, on the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) corresponding to the name-syllables of the enemy, the root-mantra of Unmatta is supreme.
O Supreme Goddess! Having plucked [the flowers], one should rub them with saffron, combined with camphor, sandalwood, nutmeg, cloves, and jasmine.
Having mixed together red sandalwood, hibiscus, and dūrvā grass, one should offer the bali.

O Goddess of gods! with this mantra known as the Rāmatattva-mudrā, having first uttered the *praṇava* (Om), [one says] "Kālike! Kālarātrike!", then utters the phrase "maddattaṃ padaṃ" (the place given by me), and finally the two words "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" (take, take).
"Destroy the two feet of such-and-such an enemy;
cut, cut! Crush, crush! Grant me my kingdom!
With this mantra ending in the two *ṭha* syllables, one should offer the bali oblation on the eighth lunar day.
O Queen of the Gods! By means of this offering of sacrifice, the enemy’s power shall be diminished;
he will instantly become incapable of protecting his own kingdom.
When this is performed, one shall certainly regain the kingdom within a year.
O lady of excellent limbs! When the kingdom has been obtained, one should worship Kālikā, who possesses a terrible roar, with offerings of many kinds and auspicious oblations;
one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with water and the poor with wealth and riches.
Only in that case shall the kingdom be stable; otherwise, it will be fruitless.
One should not revile a woman in speech, in action, or even in thought, nor should one ever revile Brahmins, O Goddess of Devas, for the sake of a stable kingdom.
Now follow the sixteen processions of the goddesses.
In the Vāmakeśvaratantra, in the fifty-fourth chapter.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the unsurpassed procedure for the pilgrimage.
O Maheśānī, your pilgrimage is celebrated as the sixteenth;
among the twelve months, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is highly praised.
Performing rites such as worship in that [place], one shall attain liberation.
One should worship and recite mantras at night on a Kulavāra and a Kulatithi.
O Maheśvarī, Kula-vāras are to be known as Tuesday and Saturday.

O Mahādevī! The fourteenth, the eighth, the new moon, the full moon, and the ninth—these lunar days (tithis) are known as *kula*. When a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) occurs on them, it is proclaimed as a "Great Yoga" (*mahāyoga*).
O Maheśānī! On this day, the worship of the Goddess bestows happiness;
in Vaiśākha, there is the Mañca-yātrā and the preparation of sandalwood and agallochum paste;
and in Jyeṣṭha, there is the Mahā-snāna-yātrā for three days beginning with the Ambuvācī day.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, there is the chariot procession (rathayātrā), which lasts for ten days;
in Śrāvaṇa, the water procession (jalayātrā) is held with garments, ornaments, and chowries;
and in Bhādrapada, the procession known as Dhūnanā for Caṇḍikā takes place for three days.
In Āśvina, there is the Great Worship (mahāpūjā), the festival procession (yātrā), and the sacrifice and offerings dear [to the deity];
in Kārtika, the lamp-procession (dīpayātrā); in Agrahāyaṇa, the first-fruits offering (navānna);
and in Pauṣa, the body-anointing procession (aṅgarāgayātrā) with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
O Great Goddess! In the month of Māgha, the Caturdaśī is celebrated with loud chanting;
in Phālguna, there is the swing-festival (dolākeli); and in Caitra, there are four festivals:
the Dūtī-yātrā, the Rāsa-yātrā, the Vāsantī, and the Nīla-yātrikā.
Thus has been described the sixteenth pilgrimage, which brings liberation from worldly existence.
The Goddess said:
"O Goddess! O Lord! The sixteen-fold pilgrimage has been briefly described.
By whom should this pilgrimage be performed? Tell me the procedure, O Lord!
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim words that are the essence of essences;

by performing which, O Beloved, the best of practitioners becomes transcendent of ritual action (kriyātīta). By the command of the Guru, having been consecrated and having conquered the senses, he becomes transcendent of ritual action.
Free from desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy,
and having resolutely taken refuge in the Goddess by following the path instructed by the Guru,
one should worship her according to the rules with devotion through the actions of speech, mind, and body.
One should worship the Goddess day and night as if she were one's own self.
In the morning, one should perform the cleansing of the mouth with tooth-sticks;
then, having dressed her in clean garments, one should cause her to be anointed with oil.
One should perform the bathing of the Goddess with fragrant water alone;
one should worship her with devotion according to the prescribed rites and in accordance with one's wealth.
O Queen of the Gods! At the conclusion of the worship, one should meditate upon her through [mantras] originating from sacred utterances.

The meaning is: with hymns composed of sentences. Having caused [the deity] to lie down upon a variegated bed for the sake of comfort, and then having raised [the deity] at the time of twilight, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) with lamps.
On the night of specific lunar days, you are worshipped by practitioners with food accompanied by side dishes, curd, milk with sugar,
as well as jackfruit, mango, pomegranate, and orange.
The best of practitioners should offer that which is most excellent in the world:
honey, meat, flour-cakes, milk-rice mixed with ghee,
fish, seasoned condiments, and the supreme *mudrā* resembling the orb of the moon.
Coconut, watermelon, dates, palm-sweets, jackfruit, mangoes, pomegranate, and oranges—
[these he may eat]; then, steadfast in meditation, absorbed in recitation, the wise man becomes one who has conquered his senses.
One should commence the annual pilgrimage; listen to that with careful attention.
Fifty-five.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a platform measuring two cubits in width and likewise long in extent is prescribed;
having installed the Goddess of Devas there amidst the auspicious sounds of songs, musical instruments, and the like.
One should perform the cleansing of the body with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, lac-dye, vermilion, musk,
and honey; and one should cause the Goddess to bathe with waters scented with camphor.
Then, having worshipped in the temple according to the prescribed rites,
having performed the fire-oblation (homa) and offered the sacrificial gift (bali), and having gratified [the deity] with food and other offerings,
one should worship a young maiden and also feed the Brahmins.
Thus, one who knows the rules and procedures shines after performing the pilgrimage.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, a great ablution should be performed with highly fragrant substances such as camphor;
thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with one hundred and eight full jars.
Having wiped the body with garments, one should fumigate it with guggulu resin mixed with ghee.
Having carried [the image] from the bed to the temple, one should offer the bali-oblation, perform worship, and conduct the fire sacrifice (homa).
Then, having applied the eightfold perfumes as anointment according to the prescribed rite, [one should proceed].
O Goddess! One should cause the worship of one's own Kumārīs and the twice-born to be performed according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, one should partake of the *prasāda* together with one's sons, wife, and kinsmen.
Having thus performed the procedure for the pilgrimage, one should roam about like Bhairava.

O Lord! On the first day of the month of Āṣāḍha, for three days, one should place the Goddess in the secret chamber, wrapped in cloths. At night, during the period of Mahāniśā, the Preceptor [should perform the rites] according to the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra).
Having performed worship, offered the sacrificial oblation (bali), and conducted the fire sacrifice (homa), he should cause [the deity] to proceed.
On the second day of the bright fortnight, having established Caṇḍikā upon a chariot,
the practitioner should move it with dancing and singing, acting according to his own will.

Therefore, having brought [the image] into the house of worship, one should honor it with offerings, oblations, and so forth. One should feed all women, young girls, and brahmins with various kinds of food.
A practitioner of steady mind should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, the ritual procession on the water (jalayātrā) should be performed; having prepared an auspicious boat with garments, chowries, and ornaments, the practitioner himself should row it.
Having installed the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, he should proceed with hymns of praise to the Bhaga and Liṅga.
Then, having led [the deity] into the hall of worship, one should perform the worship according to the prescribed rites.
Beginning on the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should perform the auspicious rite for three days;
or, on the new moon (kuhū) or the full moon (paurṇamāsī), one should likewise carry out the ritual of waving lamps (ārati).
Every day at night, one should perform worship accompanied by offerings (*bali*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and recitations;
having presented various kinds of substances and whatever the mind desires, one should satisfy all women, maidens, and Brahmins.
On the ninth day of the month of Āśvina, the wise practitioner should commence the Great Worship (mahāpūjā).
Every day, he should worship the Goddess with offerings, fire-oblations (homa), hymns of praise, and so forth.
Daily, he should feed Brahmins, young maidens, and married women.
During the day, she should be worshipped by the *paśu* and the *vīra*; at night, according to the *kaula* tradition.
In this way, the best of practitioners shall attain the liberation of *nirvāṇa*.
O Goddess of the Gods! if one is unable even for that, one should worship Śivā for three days.
O Goddess! On the new-moon day of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the Dīpa-yātrā (lamp procession).
At night, during the period of Mahāniśā (the dead of night), having adorned the temple of the Goddess with lamps and other offerings, one should worship her with rituals such as pūjā, bali, and homa.
In the absence of a ghee lamp, one should employ an oil lamp.
O Great Goddess! In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should offer new grain according to the prescribed rites, as well as fish, meat, milk-rice, milk, curd, ghee, and honey.

The best of practitioners should offer and worship everything that is fresh and fresh: soup, vegetables, flour-cakes, sweet rice-mess, rice mixed with sesame, sesame-laddus, coconut, and sugar mixed with jaggery.

Accompanied by his wife and sons, the wise man should consume the *prasāda* of the Goddess. In the month of Pauṣa, having performed the rite of applying unguents and offered new garments and various ornaments, he should perform the ritual of worship.
Without the fire-oblation (homa), the ritual offering (bali), and the propitiation of the Brāhmaṇas, there is truly no worship of the Great Goddess; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
O Sovereign of the Gods! on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha.
O Maheśānī! On that day, one should worship the person who cries out upon the earth for the sake of destroying sin, according to the extent of one's wealth;
and having given gifts to the Brāhmaṇas, one should offer them for the pleasure of Caṇḍikā.
To one afflicted by sorrow, to one afflicted by hunger, to the poor,
and to the self-restrained, food, clothing, and gold are supremely pleasing to the Goddess.
On the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, having constructed a three-sectioned couch, [one should offer these].
There, one should decorate the Goddess’s throne with cloth wrappings;
in the four directions, one should cause banners, plantain trees, and small bells to sway.
One should swing the Goddess during the month of Phālguna, distinguishing between day and night.
One should honor and feed the Brahmins, as well as one's kinsmen, relatives, sons, and others;
one should always please Kālikā with dances, songs, and musical instruments.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, one should perform the ritual of the Dūtī-yāga.
Having worshipped the Goddess at night, one should worship nine virgins; in their absence, a Brahmin girl who is well-attired and endowed with youth,
[honoring her] with various ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as with perfumes, incense, and unguents.
Having adorned [the deity] and fed [the guests], one should partake of the meal oneself.
O Goddess of Gods! One should perform the ritual of worship at night according to the Kaula practice.
One should carry out all the worship and other rites with the mantra prescribed for the Dūtī-yāga.
For three days during the spring season, one should perform sacrifices with offerings, oblations, and so forth.
On the full moon day, at midnight, one should conduct the Rāsa procession of the Goddess.
Having established the maṇḍapa as before, one should worship the Goddess and the Goddess’s throne.
Having fashioned the form of a dwelling in their presence, accompanied by Bhairavī and Bhairava,
and having worshipped them, one should cause it to be carried around like a water-jar on a wheel,
amidst a clamor of drums and other musical instruments, dances, and beautiful songs.

The practitioner, with a joyful heart and a steady mind, should perform this; he must not harbor greed or deceit regarding wealth. The pilgrimage to the Goddess bestows happiness. On the day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), the mantra-reciter should commence the blue pilgrimage (nīlayātrā) of the Great Lord.
O Goddess! One should fumigate with incense for the satisfaction of Mahākāla. Together with Mahākāla, one should worship the Goddess at night.
The food offering (naivedya) should be rich in ghee and provided with various kinds of articles.
Having given [the offerings], having offered praise, and having bowed down, the practitioner, together with his kinsmen, should perform singing;
with a heart overflowing with joy, the mantra-master should engage in dancing. At midnight, for the sake of pleasing Śiva, the Śivā-bali offering should be performed.

From the full moon of Vaiśākha up to this point, it is the same as in the Kaula Tantra. Having thus performed the annual pilgrimage (yātrā), O Goddess of Devas, the best of practitioners becomes equal to Śiva by the grace of the Guru; of this there is no doubt.
Thus end the sixteen processions of the goddesses.

May the venerable one named Prāṇakṛṣṇa— whose fame is renowned throughout the earth, who shines like the sun upon the lotus-hearts of the multitude of the virtuous, who is affectionate and resembles the full moon, and whose realization is as pure as that of the Teacher of the Gods— be victorious here; may he be a tree for the wise and a great lamp for those devoted to the Mother (Mātṛkā).
By whose grace the Brahmins gathered together in that body.
Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa, acting for the welfare of the worlds and abiding by the instructions of Śrī Prāṇakṛṣṇa,
has composed this fourth section on the highest desired rites after bowing to the beautiful lotus feet of his chosen deity.

The root, the trunk, the branches, the twigs, the clusters, the sprouts, the beautiful blossoms, and the excellent fruit—all this is contained within the *Kāmyakāṇḍa*, which is exceedingly fruitful and worthy of being beheld by the wise.
O scholars! Behold this, which removes the impurities of the eyes and bestows the grace of divine vision.
Destroyer of various doubts, gladdener of the heart, benefactor of all the world.
Thus ends the fourth section, titled "Kāmya," in the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, composed by the venerable Vidyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya, which was approved by Prāṇakṛṣṇa.
